units.tr: Iacobus Aubertus, physician. Greetings.

units.la: Philosophia vitæ ducem, virtutis & veritatis indagatricem veteres esse dixerunt: cuius ope atque ductu homines principio congregati fuerint, & in vitæ societatem convocati. Cùm autem Philosophia potissimum in naturæ contemplatione, & in formandis moribus versetur: ac propterea præstantissimum hoc elogium Philosophiæ hisce duabus ipsius partibus conveniat : non tamen dubitans affirmarim, eam philosophiæ partem, quæ naturam contemplatur, & quam Physicen appellant, nobis ceu omnium antiquissimam in primis commendatam esse opportere. Nam ut memoriæ proditum est, quum Thales Mile[?]-sius (e cuius fontibus fluxerunt præstantissimi quique Philosophi) de rerum natura primus in Græcia disputasset, ab eo tempore hoc unum Physices studiū Philosophos omnes detinuit, usque dum ad Socratem uentum est, qui primus Philosophiam e cœlo devocasse dicitur, & in urbibus, atque etiam in familiis collocasse, quum de uita & moribus disputationes suas instituisset. Ex quo intelligi potest moralem Philosophiam e Physice veluti progenitā olim apud Græcos in medium prodiisse, quum rerum naturalium totiusque mundi series, ordo, pulchritudo,ipsiusque hominis conformatio,homi-nes commoueret,ut ad id quod bonum est, animum aduerterent, & quasi exau-dita voce naturae de vita recte instituen-da cogitarent. Quinetiam eo spectasse Thalem[?] ipsum verisimile est, qui cum ex [illegible, ~3 letters]quaereretur, quidnam esset om-nium pulcherrimum, fertur respondisse, Mundum, quippe cuius pulchritudi-ne ad ipsius Naturae contemplationem raperetur. Ea autem Physice non iu-cunda tantum est, verum etiam utilis-sima, atque adeo ad vitam hanc tuen-dam necessaria. Ecquis enim ne-scit quantus sit usus artis medendi, & quam hominibus necessarius? Quis porro, nisi plane rudis & expers philosophiae, non facile videat praestantissi-mam medendi scientiam niti ipsius Phy-sices veris certisque fundamentis? Quodsi ille demum medicus haberi debet, qui in naturali Philosophia accurate versatus sit, & in ipsius Physices sinus intimosque recessus penetrauerit, laudemus Physicen necesse est, & eam hominum generi maximè necessariam esse iudicemus. Quæ cùm ego apud me reputarem, & identidem Aristotelis Philosophorum omnium facile principis scripta physica in manibus haberem, existimaui non alienum nec inutile fore, si meorum studiorum eos facerem participes, qui ad medendi scientiam animum appulerunt. Occurrebat quidem illud Macrobij, philosophos etiam tacendo philosophari: sed me simul mouit dictum illud, quo apud Athenæum perstringuntur illi, qui dum philosophi videri volunt, in hoc tantum pythagorizant, quòd semper taceant. Quamobrem vt & ego pro mea virili parte iuniorum studia adiuuare, mihi mihi proposui philosophiam ab Aristo-tele traditam, non eam quidem dissu-fam, sed in epitomen contractam, ut qui sunt huiusce philosophiae candidati, tan-quam in tabula sub uno aspectu proposi-ta videre possint ea omnia, quae Aristo-teles de rerū omniū creatarū natura ac-curate in suis libris, & copiose disseruit. Fit enim saepenumero ut pleriq; a legedis Aristotelis libris, propter eorum multi-tudinem deterreantur: & quemadmo-dum viatores itineribus, ita illi libris lon-gioribus ab ipsa librorum lectione reuo-centur. Quàm autem sit excelles rerum naturalium scientia non opus est multis verbis explicare: quandoquidem res i-psa per se loquitur: & quot sunt res crea-tae, tot sunt linguae, quibus huius praecla-rae scientiae dignitas & praestatia celebre-tur. Quare non immerito laudamus non vulgares tantum homines, sed etiam Reges potentissimos, qui summo studio re-rum naturā indagarunt. Qualem fuisse (ne mihi plerique alij commemorandi sint) Solomonem memoriæ proditum est, eumque naturam stirpium & arborum accuratissimè à cedro ad hyssopum pertractasse: cuius libri si extarent[?], non dubium est, quin naturali philoso-phiæ plurimum lucis accederet. Quod si nobis deessent tot virorum celeberrimo-rum exempla, quibus ad studium Physi-ces incendamur, hac una certè ratio nobis satis superq; esse debet, quod in rebus creatis, tanquam in speculo debeamus summi Creatoris imaginem, hoc est eius virtu-tem, potentiam, sapientiam & bonita-tem intueri. Quo detestabilior est quorū-dam hominum stupiditas, qui dum Physi-cen consectantur, ita rebus creatis adhæ-rescunt, ut nolint (quæ est eorum perver-sitas) his tanquam gradibus ad Dei Opt. Max. cognitionem ascedere, perpetuo in rebus inferioribus subsistetes. At nos ita versemur in Physicis, ut Deum naturæ summū authorem, & cōseruatorem verè agnoscamus, amplectamur, & ex animo adoremus: atque ita statuamus nunquā eos [illegible, ~5 letters]ram posse cognoscere, qui naturæ authorem ignorant. Mihi vero de edendis his nostris institutionibus Physicis, cogitanti occurristi, Nobilissimeꝰ & amplissimeꝰ vir, cui hos labores nostros, quantulicunqueꝰ illi sunt, offerrem dicaremque: quod pios omnes viros & honestos non solum colas & vehementer ames: sed etiam quod liberalium artium & disciplinarum bonarum studio maximè flagres. Quod profecto ijs satis perspicuum est, ad quos tui nominis splendor peruenit. Nec vero militiæ & armorum peritia, qua velut generosissimi maiores tui, præditus es, unquam à bonis literis & disciplinis te avocare potuit, prohibuitque quominus ingeniosissimè Minervam cum Marte nexu arctissimo coniungeres. Itaque te oro, Generosissime & amplissime vir, ut hæc scripta nostra tibi oblata accipere libenti animo, & benignè digneris, ac in his non tam nos, quàm ipsam naturæ philosophiam audire velis. Deus autem Opt. max. ipsius naturæ creator & dominus te tuámque splendidissimam familiam suis donis præstantissimis, et o-mnigenis ornamentis in dies magis ac magis augeat. Vale. Datum Lau-sannæ Calendis Mart. Anni 1584.
units.tr: The ancients said that philosophy is the guide of life and the investigator of virtue, and that by its help and leading men were first gathered together and called into the fellowship of life. Since philosophy is concerned chiefly with the contemplation of nature and with the shaping of morals, and since this most excellent praise of philosophy belongs to these two of its parts, I do not hesitate to affirm that the part of philosophy which contemplates nature, and which they call Physics, ought to be especially commended to us as the most ancient of all. For, as has been recorded, when Thales of Miletus, from whose springs all the most outstanding philosophers have flowed, first discussed the nature of things in Greece, from that time this single study of Physics held all the philosophers, until Socrates came. He is said to have been the first to call philosophy down from heaven and to settle it in cities and even in households, when he began his discussions about life and morals. From this it can be understood that moral philosophy, as if born long ago from Physics, came forth among the Greeks, since the sequence, order and beauty of natural things and of the whole world, and the very formation of man, moved men to turn their minds to what is good, and to think, as if they had heard the voice of nature, about ordering life rightly. Indeed, it is likely that Thales himself aimed at this, for when he was asked what was the most beautiful of all things, he is reported to have answered: the world, since by its beauty one is carried off to the contemplation of Nature itself. Now Physics is not only pleasant but also most useful, and indeed necessary for preserving this life. For who does not know how great is the use of the art of healing, and how necessary it is to men? Who, unless he is utterly rude and without philosophy, does not readily see that the most excellent science of medicine rests on the true and certain foundations of Physics itself? If he alone ought to be held a physician who has been thoroughly versed in natural philosophy and has penetrated into the bosom and innermost recesses of Physics, then we must necessarily praise Physics and judge it most necessary to the human race. When I was weighing these things, and kept having the physical writings of Aristotle, easily the prince of all philosophers, in my hands, I thought it would be neither out of place nor useless to make sharers of my studies those who have turned their minds to the science of healing. The saying of Macrobius came to mind, that philosophers philosophize even by keeping silent; but at the same time I was moved by that saying, reported in Athenaeus, which censures those who, wanting to seem philosophers, only Pythagorize in this, that they always keep silent. Therefore, that I too may help the studies of younger people as far as I can, I have set before myself the philosophy handed down by Aristotle, not indeed differing from it, but condensed into an epitome, so that those who are candidates for this philosophy may see, as if laid out on a tablet at a single glance, all those things which Aristotle discussed accurately and copiously in his books concerning the nature of all created things. For it often happens that most people are deterred from reading Aristotle's books by their multitude, and just as travellers are turned back from their journeys, so are they turned back from reading by the great length of the books. How excellent the science of natural things is need not be explained at length, since the thing speaks for itself; and there are as many tongues as there are created things, by which the dignity and excellence of this famous science is celebrated. Hence we rightly praise not only ordinary men but also most powerful kings who have investigated the nature of things with the greatest zeal. Solomon, to mention no others, is recorded to have been such a man, and to have handled the nature of plants and trees most carefully, from the cedar to the hyssop; and if his books were extant, there is no doubt that much light would be added to natural philosophy. But if we lacked so many examples of most celebrated men to kindle us to the study of Physics, this one reason alone ought to be enough and more than enough for us: that in created things, as in a mirror, we should behold the image of the highest Creator, that is, his virtue, power, wisdom and goodness. All the more detestable is the stupidity of certain men who, while they pursue Physics, cling so closely to created things that they refuse (and this is their perversity) to rise by these steps to the knowledge of God the Best and Greatest, remaining always among lower things. But we engage in Physics in such a way that we truly acknowledge God as the supreme author and preserver of nature, embrace him, and adore him from our hearts; and so we judge that those who are ignorant of the author of nature can never truly know [...]. It occurred to me, most noble and most distinguished sir, when I was thinking of publishing these our physical institutions, to offer and dedicate these labours of ours, such as they are, to you; because you not only cherish and warmly love all pious and honourable men, but also burn with zeal for the liberal arts and good studies. This is certainly clear enough to those to whom the splendour of your name has come. Nor indeed has skill in warfare and arms, with which you are endowed, as were your most noble ancestors, ever been able to call you away from good letters and disciplines, or to prevent you from joining Minerva with Mars in a most skilful and close bond. Therefore I ask you, most generous and distinguished sir, to deign to accept these writings of ours, offered to you, with a willing mind and kindly, and to wish to hear in them not so much us as natural philosophy itself. And may God the Best and Greatest, the creator and lord of nature, increase you and your most splendid family day by day more and more with his most excellent gifts and every kind of ornament. Farewell. Given at Lausanne on the Kalends of March, in the year 1584.

units.la: Tuæ amplitudini addictissimusIacobus Aubertus medicus.
units.tr: Most devoted to your distinction, Iacobus Aubertus, physician.

units.la: ΕΙΣ ΤΟΝ ἈΝΔΡΑ ΛΑΜΠΡΟΤΑΤΟΝ, καὶ φιλόσοφον σοφώτατον τὸν Ἰάκωβον Ἀλέξερον Αἰμίλιος ὁ Φραγκίσκου Πορτογάλλου Κρητὸς τοῦτο τὸ ἐπίγραμμα ποίει Μαΐῳ μηνὸς δεκάτῃ φθίνοντος, ἀ τῷ ἔτει τῷ, πτῷ δ τῇ ἔτει τῆς χρισγονίας.
units.tr: To the most illustrious man, James Alexer, most wise philosopher: Aemilius, son of Franciscus, a Portuguese from Crete, made this epigram on the tenth day before the end of May, in the year of Christian reckoning.

units.la: Πᾶστις Ἀεισοτέλης θαυμάζει κῦδος, ἀεὶ δὲ Πᾶστις τοῦ ζοφίλου, τλῶ τε δημοσιῷ, Αὐταρ παυροτάτοις μυσηΐα τῦδε γοῦσα Δῶκε Θεὸς, ζῶον θαῦμα πέλει ἱρυφίων. Οὐνεκεν, ὦ Θεῖη κεφαλὴ, χάειν ἐξομβῷ αἰεὶ Σοὶ πλείστῳ πινυτῆς εἵνεκα σῆς διδαχῆς. Καὶ γὰρ ἀπεσκεδασας πυκνὸν νέφος, ἀμμι φάος τε Λαμπρὸν ἔδωκας. Ἄλλη γὰρ κλέος αἰδλον.
units.tr: Aristotle, the whole of him, is admired for his fame, and the whole of the dark-minded, and the public too. But God gave this Muse to very few, a marvel among the wise and a wonder of the age. Therefore, divine head, I shall always give you the warmest thanks for the sake of your wise teaching. For you have scattered the dense cloud and given us clear light, for another glory is manifest.

units.la: AD AUBERTUM MEDI-cum, Jani Antonij Saraceni medici
units.tr: To Aubert, physician, from Janus Antonius Saracenus, physician

units.la: αὐτοσχέδιον ἐπίγραμμα.
units.tr: An extempore epigram.

units.la: Rerum Naturam, causas ab origine prima Dum repetis, facilem reddis Aristotelem. Solis nanque prius fuerant quae peruia doctis, Jam facile cuius peruia tute facis.
units.tr: As you trace the nature of things and their causes back to the first origin, you make Aristotle easy to read. For those things which were before accessible only to the learned, you now make easily accessible, as you yourself have done.

units.la: Ergo tibi multum debet noua turba sophorum. Ipse etiam multum debet Aristoteles.
units.tr: Therefore the new crowd of wise men owes you much. Aristotle himself also owes you much.

units.la: SIMONIS GIRARDI Biturigis Iurisc.ad Medicinae & Physicae scientiae studiosos Epigramma.
units.tr: Epigram by Simon Girard of Bourges, jurist, to students of medicine and the science of natural philosophy.

units.la: Si cupis ô lector, primordia discere Mundi, Quis cœli motus, quaeue sit effigies, Quae naturales rerum causae esse feruntur, Naturae in gremio semina quotque latent: Immò qui Mundum & Naturâ condidit ipsam Si vis Naturae lumine, nosse Deum: Haec age, perlegito physicorum dogmata: quæte Aubertus breuiter perspicueque docet. Non alius quisquā hac de re, si vera fatemur, Post doctum melius scripsit Aristotelem. Aubertus facilem patefecit ad ardua callem, Abdita Naturae mente reclusa canens. Huic saltem grates persoluas, si qua referri Digna potest tantis gratia muneribus.
units.tr: O reader, if you wish to learn the beginnings of the world, what the motions of the heavens are and what their form is, what natural causes of things are said to exist, and how many seeds lie hidden in the bosom of nature; indeed, if you wish, by the light of nature, to know God, who made the world and nature itself: come, read through the doctrines of the physicists, which Aubert teaches briefly and clearly. If we speak the truth, no one else has written better on this subject since the learned Aristotle. Aubert has opened an easy path to difficult matters, singing of the hidden things of nature unlocked to the mind. To him at least give thanks, if any thanks worthy of such gifts can be rendered.

units.la: IN D. IACOBI AV-berti Medicinæ Doctoris celeberri-mi, Physici præstantissimi, institutio-nes physicas Mosis Molerij Epigramma.
units.tr: On the Physical Institutions of Jacob Aubert, the most celebrated Doctor of Medicine and most distinguished physician, an epigram by Moses Molerius.

units.la: Multos[?] astra juvat, terrásq. errasse per omnes, Lustrasse & vasto quicquid in Oceano: At vero abstrusas rerum cognoscere causas, Non datur in tanto cuique natâre freto.
units.tr: Many delight to have wandered among the stars and through every land, and to have traversed whatever lies in the vast ocean. But to know the hidden causes of things is not granted to anyone swimming in so great a sea.

units.la: Ergo (lector) ades, quid cælū, terra, quid unda, Et quis res atomos, spiritus intus alat, Quæ sit natura vis atque innata facultas, Et quæ sint animæ munera iusta tuæ, Has tibi divitias, thesauros atque latentes Subtili Aubertus dexteritate dabit.
units.tr: Therefore, reader, come: learn what heaven, earth and water are, what atoms are, and what spirit nourishes things from within, what nature is, its force and innate faculty, and what are the just duties of your soul. These riches, treasures and hidden things Aubert will give you with subtle dexterity.

units.la: Ille tibi physices claros ita sarrijt[?] hortos, Ut nullus possit sentibus esse locus.
units.tr: He has so weeded the bright gardens of physics that no place is left for thorns.

units.la: Hæc igitur grata doctissima dogmata fronte Suscipito, & vigili volue, revolue[?] manu.
units.tr: Receive, then, these most learned doctrines with a welcoming brow, and turn them over and over with a watchful hand.

units.la: ΕΙΣ ΑΛΒΕΡΤΟΝ.
units.tr: TO ALBERTUS.

units.la: [?]ΙΑΜΕΝ ὅτ' ἀρχαίοισι Θεὸς θεῖόν τε Πλάτωνα, / Καὶ μεγάλως πραπίδας φύσιν Ἀριστοτέλευς. / Αὐταρ ἐπεὶ κόνιν οἱ χθαμαλῷ ὑπέδυ ἀείσοις / Καὶ ἦκον ςυγγὺς εἰς αἰδαο δόμως, / Πολλὰ τὰ τῆς φυσικῆς ἀγνωστα πολυχρόνου ἐ- / Ὥσπερ τῷ νέφει κρυπτόμενα σκοτίῳ. / Χαίρετε ἄλλα βροτοί, εἰδυίᾳ πραπίδεσιν / Ὑμῖν Ἀλεξέρος πᾶν τόδ' ἀνέλε σκότος. / Ὦ νέε, εἰ ὠφελεῖς ἄγε, καὶ θαμὰ βίβλον / Τοιαύτην ἀσὶν ἡ ὠνῇ, χερσὶ τρίβε.
units.tr: Once God honoured the ancients, the divine Plato and Aristotle, whose mind was great by nature. But when they went down into the dust of the low earth and drew near the house of Hades, many things of natural science, long unknown, lay hidden as in a dark cloud. Rejoice, mortals, for Albertus with his knowing mind has dispelled all this darkness for you. Young man, if you are able, come, and often take this book in your hands and handle it. [Greek: ΕΙΣ ΑΛΒΕΡΤΟΝ. ΙΑΜΕΝ ὅτ' ἀρχαίοισι Θεὸς θεῖόν τε Πλάτωνα, / Καὶ μεγάλως πραπίδας φύσιν Ἀριστοτέλευς. / Αὐταρ ἐπεὶ κόνιν οἱ χθαμαλῷ ὑπέδυ ἀείσοις / Καὶ ἦκον ςυγγὺς εἰς αἰδαο δόμως, / Πολλὰ τὰ τῆς φυσικῆς ἀγνωστα πολυχρόνου ἐ- / Ὥσπερ τῷ νέφει κρυπτόμενα σκοτίῳ. / Χαίρετε ἄλλα βροτοί, εἰδυίᾳ πραπίδεσιν / Ὑμῖν Ἀλεξέρος πᾶν τόδ' ἀνέλε σκότος. / Ὦ νέε, εἰ ὠφελεῖς ἄγε, καὶ θαμὰ βίβλον / Τοιαύτην ἀσὶν ἡ ὠνῇ, χερσὶ τρίβε.]

units.la: Θεόδωρος ὁ τοῦ Νικολέω τοῦ / Κολλαδέωνος.
units.tr: Theodore, son of Nicoleos, of Kolladeon. [Greek: Θεόδωρος ὁ τοῦ Νικολέω τοῦ / Κολλαδέωνος.]

units.la: IDEM.
units.tr: BY THE SAME.

units.la: Antiquorum ætas admirandúmque Platonem, / Doctíque ingenium vidit Aristotelis. / Sed postquam invidit mortalibus Orcus, & illa / Lumina doctrinæ fata tulêre duo. / Multis natura male nota scientia seclis / Nube tenebrosa condita delituit.
units.tr: The age of the ancients saw the admirable Plato and the learned genius of Aristotle. But after Orcus envied mortals, the fates carried off those two lights of learning. For many ages natural science, ill known, lay hidden, shut up in a dark cloud.

units.la: Ast hanc Albertus nubem medicúsque, sophós-que Sustulit ingenii dexteritate sui.
units.tr: But Albertus, physician and sage, lifted this cloud by the skill of his own intellect.

units.la: Maste ergo, ô iuvenis, Physicásque accingere ad artes, Hunc librum summa sedulitate legens.
units.tr: Therefore, young man, gird yourself for the physical arts, reading this book with the utmost diligence.

units.la: IN EVNDEM.
units.tr: ON THE SAME.

units.la: Albertus fuerit Magnus, parvus tamen ecce Albertus, Magno (credite) maior adest.
units.tr: Albert was Great; yet behold, little Albert is here, greater than Magnus (believe me).

units.la: UNIVERSAE Philosophiae diuisio.
units.tr: Heading: The division of universal philosophy.

units.la: ONTEM uniuersæ philosophiæ ac principium metemhomi-nis esse, rectè Aristote-les,in primo Analytic.libro,ostendere videtur: quādoquidem homo non solùm rationis particeps est,sed etiam rerum agendarum consiliis : ex quibus vtraque humanæ mentis functio oriri videtur. Vna namque rerum æternarum meditatio est, altera in actio-ne & consilio versatur. Quare ipse Philosophus,in primo diuinæ scientiæ libro , duplex philosophiæ genus ponit , vnum quod θεωρητικὸν est, & alterū πρακτικὸν. Hu-ius ius autem finis opus est: illius ve-rò veritas. Quamobrem Aristo-teles ibidem hoc philosophiæ ge-nus, quod omnino in contempla-tione rerum divinarum & cogni-tione versatur, scientiam veritatis nominat, nec iniuria, quadoquidem in vtraque theorica intelle-ctione veritas consistit. Alterum autem philosophiæ genus, quod in virtutis actione versatur, tresin partes distribui solet, quarum v-na recte honesteque viuendi via rationemque tradit, bonosque mores sequendi, & prauos declì-nandi iubet, atque præscribit: quā obrem ἠθικὴ[?] scientia dicitur. Alia est, quæ in rei familiaris admini-stratione versatur, ac proinde οἰκο-νομικὴ[?] nominatur. Alia denique est quæ regendorum regnorum ciuitatumque omnium ac rerum publicarum rationem praeceptaque tradit, ac propterea πολιτικὰ[?] appellatur. Quarum omnium origo mens hominis ea est, quae πρακτικὴ[?] dicitur, & alicuius rei agedæ gratia ratiocinatur. At vero ea, alte-ra, cuius actio contemplatio est, proficiscitur alterū philosophiæ genus, quod θεωρητικὸν[?] nominant. Hoc autem multiplex esse dicitur: quandoquidem genera eorū quæ sunt, in quibus versatur, va-ria sunt. Quædam enim re ipsa, & ratione à sensibili materia seiuncta sunt ac separata: in quo genere primæ substantiæ consistunt, quæ diuinæ subiiciuntur philosophiæ, propterea quod immutabiles sint, & insensibiles ac æternæ. Etenim alias esse substantias primas immuta-biles, biles, & ab omni concretione li-beras,& alias secundas & mutabi-les, quod ex materia constent & forma, aperte exprimit Aristote-les primo sapientiæ libro,nec à ratione alienum est, quoniam rerum aliæ æternæ sunt & divinæ, aliæ caducæ ortui interituique obnoxiæ. Præterea τῶν ὄντων [?] quædam non reipsa,sed duntaxat ratione à materia seiunguntur, in quibus mathematica scientia consistit. Mathematicus enim cuncta quæ sub sensum cadunt, cuiusmodi est gravitas, levitas, durities, mollities, frigus,calor,humor,ariditas, atque aliæ huius generis sensiles affectiones mente ex corpore abstrahit, atque separat, ac id duntaxat, quod quantum est nudum relinquit, ac meditatur, quemadmodum ex undecimo primæ philo-sophiæ libro intelligere licet. Eorum denique quæ sunt, quædam nec actu neque[?] ipsa, nec ratione ulla à materia, concretioneque naturæ seiuncta separataque contemplamur: quo genere prima universi corpora consistunt, quæ quatuor elementa dicuntur, & a-lia omnia, quæ ex his constant, & concrescunt, quorum meditatio cognitioque physica philosophia & secunda ab Aristotele nominatur, libro divinæ philosophiæ quarto: quo in loco tot esse philosophiæ genera quot sunt rerum essentiæ perspicuè exprimit. Philosophi enim est substantiarum principia & causas meditari ac co-gnoscere, quemadmodum ibidē Aristoteles nos docet: quandoquidem proprie nullius accidetis scientia est, sed eius rei, quæ per se semper est, aut sæpissime, teste eodem Philosopho in x. metaphysicorū libro. Eius autē rei, quæ seper est, scientia metaphysica dicitur: alterius physica, quoniā subiestū eius huiusmodi est. Quare hæc reuera scietia est, non autem ea quæ dicitur, nec quæ, quoniam operibus & fine multum inter se discrepant, etsi versatur in eodē subiecto, quod quidem naturale corpus est, & mutabile. Cæterum ea ex parte tempus, reliquaque naturæ accidentia Physicus meditatur ac cognoscit, qua ipsum tempus est motus affectio, & ipse motus magnitudinis perfectæ. Nam magnitudo perfecta corpus est, cuius scientia, si mobile est, physica dicitur, sed si duntaxat quan-tum existit, & omnis affectio-nis & formæ expers, ad mathematicam spe-culationem spe-ctare vide-tur.
units.tr: Indeed, Aristotle seems rightly to show, in the first book of the Analytics, that the beginning of all philosophy and of human understanding lies in man, since man shares not only in reason but also in deliberation about things to be done, and from these two arise both functions of the human mind. One is the contemplation of eternal things; the other is concerned with action and counsel. For this reason the Philosopher himself, in the first book of the divine science, sets out two kinds of philosophy, one which is theoretical [θεωρητικὸν] and the other practical [πρακτικὸν]. The end of the latter is work, but the end of the former is truth. Accordingly Aristotle in the same place calls this kind of philosophy, which is concerned entirely with the contemplation and knowledge of divine things, the science of truth, and not without reason, since truth consists in theoretical understanding in both cases. The other kind of philosophy, which is concerned with the practice of virtue, is usually divided into three parts. The first teaches the way and method of living rightly and honourably, and commands and prescribes the following of good morals and the avoiding of bad ones; for this reason it is called ethical [ἠθικὴ] science. The second is concerned with the management of household affairs, and is therefore called economic [οἰκονομικὴ]. The third, finally, teaches the principles and precepts for governing kingdoms, cities and all commonwealths, and is therefore called political [πολιτικὰ]. The origin of all these is that mind of man which is called practical [πρακτικὴ] and reasons for the sake of doing something. But the other mind, whose activity is contemplation, gives rise to the other kind of philosophy, which they call theoretical [θεωρητικὸν]. This kind is said to be manifold, since the kinds of things that exist, with which it is concerned, are various. For some things exist in fact and by reason separated and set apart from sensible matter; in this class are the primary substances, which fall under divine philosophy, because they are immutable, insensible and eternal. Aristotle plainly states in the first book of Wisdom that there are other primary substances, immutable and free from all composition, and others secondary and mutable, which consist of matter and form; nor is this unreasonable, since some things are eternal and divine, while others are perishable and subject to coming into being and passing away. Besides, some beings are separated from matter not in fact but only in reason, and in this class mathematical science consists. For the mathematician mentally abstracts and separates from body all that falls under the senses, such as heaviness, lightness, hardness, softness, cold, heat, moisture, dryness, and other sensible affections of this kind, and leaves only that which is quantity, bare, and contemplates it, as may be understood from the eleventh book of First Philosophy. Finally, among the things that exist, some we consider neither in act nor in reason as separate from matter and from the composition of nature. To this class belong the first bodies of the universe, which are called the four elements, and all the others which are composed and compounded of these; the contemplation and knowledge of these is called physical philosophy, and by Aristotle the second philosophy, in the fourth book of the divine philosophy, where he clearly sets out that there are as many kinds of philosophy as there are kinds of essence. For it belongs to the philosopher to contemplate and know the principles and causes of substances, as Aristotle teaches us in the same place; since there is strictly no science of accidents, but only of that which always exists in itself, or most often, as the same Philosopher says in the tenth book of the Metaphysics. The science of that which always exists is called metaphysics; the science of the other is physics, since its subject is of this kind. Hence this is truly a science, but not that which is called (...), since their works and ends differ greatly, although they deal with the same subject, which is natural and mutable body. On the other hand, the natural philosopher contemplates and knows time and the remaining accidents of nature, insofar as time itself is an affection of motion, and motion itself of perfect magnitude. For perfect magnitude is body, whose science, if it is mobile, is called physical; but if it merely exists as quantity, free of every affection and form, it seems to belong to mathematical speculation.

units.la: INSTITVTIONVM PHYSICARVM PRIMA PARS, IN QVA RERVM OMNIVM, quae Natura constant, principia, causae, motus, mutationesque perspicuè explicantur. CAP. I.
units.tr: FIRST PART OF THE PHYSICAL INSTITUTES, IN WHICH THE PRINCIPLES, CAUSES, MOTIONS AND CHANGES OF ALL THINGS THAT CONSIST BY NATURE ARE CLEARLY EXPLAINED. CHAPTER I.

units.la: Rerum naturalium principia esse contraria.
units.tr: The principles of natural things are contrary.

units.la: EORVM, quae natura constat, principia esse contraria olim veteres philosophi professi sunt: alioqui nullum naturale corpus esset, mutationi obnoxium: nec vllum principium alterum pelleret. Omnium enim mutationum contrariae causae sunt. Itaque corporum naturalium principia esse contraria recte statuisse videntur prisci: in quorum sententia Aristoteles fuit, quemadmodum ex primo physicorum libro perspicuè intelligi potest. Neque vero hanc sententiam vllo modo labefactauerit quicunque obiecerit nullam esse substantiam contrariam: & principia, ex quibus naturalia corpora constant, substantias esse: quandoquidem hoc in loco contraria principia intelligutur latissima communique contrariorum significatione, per quam forma & priuatio contrariæ sunt. Nam contrarietatu omnium prima est habitus & priuatio, à qua omnes aliæ proficiscuntur, quemadmodum Aristoteles, libro primæ philosophiæ decimo perspicuè nobis demonstrat. Quòd etiam principia rerum naturalium pri ma sint contraria aperte philosophus ipse, primo physicorum libro, cap.5. innuit his verbis. Quæcunque neque ex aliis fiunt, neque ex se vicissim, sed ex eis omnia oriri oportet, illa sunt prima rerum naturalium contraria. Nam ex contrariorum genere quædam prima sunt quæ non ex aliis oriuntur, vt forma & priuatio: quædam ex aliis nascuntur, vt dulce & amarum: alia denique, elementorum affectiones sunt & qualitates, vt calor, frigus & similes huius generis. At eorum, quæ natura constant, principia nec ex aliis sunt, nec ex se vicissim, sed ex his omnia oriuntur. Si enim ex aliis essent, profecto eorum omnium, quæ natura constant, non principia essent. Si præterea ex se vicissim orientur, non prima essent principia. Simplicia autem Vniuersa corpora nimirum ignis, aer, aqua, terra, praeterea quòd vicissim ex se ipsis generentur, non prima sunt Naturæ principia, sed secundaria, ex quibus mista concrescunt omnia. Nec denique omnia naturæ prima principia esse contraria expedit: quandoquidem compositam substantiam non absoluerent.Materiam riam enim, ex qua naturale corpus oriatur, eis subiici oportuit.
units.tr: The ancient philosophers long ago professed that the principles of the things which consist by nature are contrary. Otherwise no natural body would be subject to change, and one principle would not drive out another, for all changes have contrary causes. The ancients therefore seem to have rightly held that the principles of natural bodies are contrary, and Aristotle was of this opinion, as can be clearly understood from the first book of the Physics. Nor will anyone who objects that no substance is contrary, and that the principles from which natural bodies are composed are substances, shake this opinion in any way. For in this place contrary principles are understood in the broadest and common sense of contraries, in which form and privation are contraries. For the first of all contrarieties is habit and privation, from which all the others proceed, as Aristotle clearly shows us in the tenth book of First Philosophy. That the principles of natural things are the first contraries the philosopher himself plainly hints in the fifth chapter of the first book of the Physics, in these words: "Whatever things neither arise from others nor from one another in turn, but from which all things must arise, those are the first contraries of natural things." For among the kind of contraries some are first, which do not arise from others, such as form and privation; some arise from others, such as sweet and bitter; and others finally are affections and qualities of the elements, such as hot, cold and things of this kind. But the principles of the things which consist by nature neither come from others nor from one another in turn, but all things arise from these. For if they came from others, they would certainly not be the principles of all the things which consist by nature. Moreover, if they arose from one another in turn, they would not be first principles. Simple bodies, namely fire, air, water and earth, because they are generated from one another in turn, are not the first principles of nature but secondary ones, from which all mixed things are compounded. Finally, it is not expedient that all the first principles of nature be contrary, since they would not account for a composite substance; for the matter from which a natural body arises had to be subject to them.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CAP. II.

units.la: Quot sint rerum naturalium principia.
units.tr: How many principles of natural things there are.

units.la: Principia eorum, quæ natura con- stant, vel vnum duntaxat sunt, ex quo primùm omnia oriuntur, & in quod postremò resoluuntur, vel plura. At naturalia corpora ex vno principio oriri non possunt: quoniam nihil ei aduersari potest, quod vnum est. Principia autem, omnium philosophorum consensu, contraria esse expedit. Quare plura sunt rerum naturalium principia, quæ vel infinita sunt, vel finita. At infinita esse nō possunt, plures ob causas. Primum eorum nulla esset scientia, nec consequenter eorum quæ ex his constant. Præterea quæ ex eis constaret essentia, esset infinita, quoniam suis principiis nulla res carere potest. At nulla naturalis essentia infinita est, sed omnis superficie quadam clauditur. Itaque rerum omnium, quæ natura constat, principia esse finita, necesse est. Ea autem prima sunt contraria, nempe forma & priuatio, quæ omnium mutationum causæ sunt. At quoniam absque subiecto nulla mutatio fieri potest, his necessario materia additur. Propterea in omni mutatione tribus principiis opus est, nimirum duobus contrariis, & tertio, quod eis subiicitur, & in quo vnum eorum alterū pellit. Hoc autem tertium rerum naturalium principium materia est & potestate ens, atque patibile. Verūtamen quæcunque oriuntur eodem modo oriri, non necesse est. Quædā enim vt substantiæ, simpliciter fiunt, eo quod ante fui ortū simplicitas non erant. Cum enim homo oritur, tum nondum est. Alia vero ἀπὸ τι fieri dicuntur, vt ea, quæ accidentia sunt, quorum ortus nō simpliciter sit & absolutus. Nam homo, cum musicus sit, tum est, sed non musicus. Itaque in huiusmodi generatione non acquiritur substantia, sed dunta-xat aliquod accidēs, qualis est musica ars, quę aduenit homini. Sed in substantiæ generatione non solùm comparatur accidens, sed etiā substantia. Cæterùm in vtraque generatione, vt & in illa eorū, quæ arte cōstant, semper materiam subiici, necesse est, quæ ab aliis naturæ principiis distinguitur. Est enim ens duntaxat potestate, & corporeæ substantiæ pars, atque eorum omniū quæ natura oriuntur velut mater. Priuatio verò, quanuis in ipsa infit materia, nullius substantiæ pars est, eò quòd accidens sit, & substātiæ corruptionem moliatur. Etenim corruptionis naturalium corporū maximè in causa est, propterea quòd formæ aduersetur. Est enim formæ absentia in materia. Forma verò corporis ratio & perfectio: quæ tametsi è materiæ potentia vi agentis educitur, non tamen velut in sinu eius latet, sed in ea inefle potest. Nec ipsa materies vnquam astu τὸ ὄν est, nisi in aliqua rerum specie fit, quemadmodum philosophus, libro diuinæ philosophiæ duodecimo, perspicuè demonstrat. Huius denique generis principiorum non censetur esse efficiens causa, eo quòd exterior fit: ac propterea de ea differere duntaxat primi philosophi interest, quemadmodum nobis Ariftoteles ostendit libro physicorum primo, capite nono. Physicus enim ea duntaxat quærit principia, ex quibus naturale corpus constat, quæ quidem interiora sunt & corporis partes, & priuatiõe, fine quanulla mutatio fieri potest.
units.tr: The principles of those things which consist by nature are either only one, from which all things first arise and into which they are finally resolved, or several. But natural bodies cannot arise from one principle, since nothing can oppose that which is one. The principles, however, by the agreement of all philosophers, ought to be contrary. Therefore there are several principles of natural things, which are either infinite or finite. But they cannot be infinite, for several reasons. First, there would be no knowledge of them, and consequently none of the things that consist of them. Moreover, the essence that consisted of them would be infinite, since no thing can lack its principles. But no natural essence is infinite; every one is bounded by some surface. Therefore it is necessary that the principles of all things which consist by nature are finite. Now the first of these are contraries, namely form and privation, which are the causes of all changes. But since no change can take place without a subject, matter is necessarily added to these. Hence in every change three principles are needed: two contraries, and a third which underlies them and in which one of the two drives out the other. This third principle of natural things is matter, which is being in potency and capable of being acted upon. Yet it is not necessary that all things which come to be come to be in the same way. For some things, as substances, come to be simply, because before their coming to be they were not simply. When a man comes to be, he is not yet at that time. Other things, however, are said to come to be from something (ἀπὸ τι), as accidents do, whose coming to be is not simple and absolute. For a man, when he is musical, is then, but not musical. Thus in such a generation no substance is acquired, but only some accident, such as the art of music, which comes to a man. But in the generation of a substance, not only an accident is acquired but also a substance. Moreover, in either kind of generation, as also in that of things which consist by art, matter must always be underlying, and it is distinguished from the other principles of nature. For it is being only in potency, and a part of corporeal substance, and as it were the mother of all things which arise by nature. Privation, however, although it inheres in matter itself, is no part of any substance, because it is an accident and labours toward the corruption of substance. Indeed it is chiefly the cause of the corruption of natural bodies, because it is opposed to form. For privation is the absence of form in matter. Form, however, is the reason and perfection of a body; and although it is drawn out of the potency of matter by the power of the agent, it does not lie hidden as in its bosom, but can be present in it. Nor is matter ever actually being unless it comes to be in some species of things, as the philosopher clearly demonstrates in the twelfth book of his divine philosophy. Finally, this kind of principle is not considered to have an efficient cause, because it is external; and therefore it belongs only to the first philosopher to discourse about it, as Aristotle shows us in the first book of the Physics, chapter nine. For the physicist seeks only those principles from which a natural body consists, which are indeed internal and parts of the body, and without which no change can take place.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CAP. III.

units.la: Quid natura fit, & quot eius genera.
units.tr: What nature is, and how many kinds of it there are.

units.la: ORVM quæ sunt in vniuerso, quæ dam natura constant, quædam arte: quæ omnia non parum inter fe discrepant. Nam illa in fe principium & causam motus & status habent, hæc vero extrinsecus & ab exterioribus causis mouentur & stant. Siquidè leĉtica, & quicquid aliud similis generis fit, quod ab arte fit, nullum habet insitum mutationis principium. Nihil enim à Natura habent præter materiam, quam ex quatuor elemetis accipiut, ea quæ ab arte proficiscuntur. Quæ omnia cum ita sint, perspicuum est naturam quoddam esse principium & causam motus statusque eius rei, in qua primum, & per se inest, & non per accidens & aliud: artem vero principium motionis, non per se, sed per aliud. Veluti si Medicus ægrotat, & sibi sanitatem restituit, non per se & qua ex par[?]te homo est sanatur, sed ex accidente & per aliud, quoniam homo, qui ægrotat, Medicus est. Itaque mutationis sanationisque Medic[?]prin-cipium non natura eius est, sed medica ars. Ex quo constat artem non insitum esse principium motus eius rei, in qua versatur, sed adventitium: propterea non necessario suum mouet subiectum. Cæterum Natura duplex est: altera materia, forma altera, quoniam ex utraque naturale corpus constat, & de utroque principio ipsa natura dicitur. Ex quo perspicue intelligere possumus naturam hic non esse principium mouens. Nam nec intus nec foris aliquid mouet. Si enim quicquam intus moueret, haud dubie ab anima non di-stingueretur ac omne corpus, quod natura constat, animatum esset. Nec præterea materia, cuius pati proprium est, natura esset. Adhæc natura est causa & principium motus. Atqui motus non est actus mouentis, sed mobilis, quemadmodum Aristoteles, libro physicorum tertio, aperte ostendit. Ex quibus perspicuum est, Naturam non externam esse causam, nec efficiens principium, sed internum ex naturalis corporis partem. Ea autem natura,quæ mouens est & exterius principium,ad primum spectat philosophum, de qua fere passim Ariftoteles verba facit, & maxime primo libro de cœlo, vbi Deum & Naturam nihil ꝓrorsus frustra agere,apertissime exprimit. Hæc breui de vtraque natura dicta sint, alia pergere expedit.
units.tr: Of the things that exist in the universe, some consist by nature and some by art, and these differ from one another not a little. For the former have within themselves the principle and cause of motion and of rest, whereas the latter are moved and kept at rest from outside, by external causes. For a bed, and whatever else of the same kind is made by art, has no inborn principle of change; it has from nature nothing but the matter, which it takes from the four elements, while the things that come from art proceed from art. Since all this is so, it is plain that nature is a certain principle and cause of motion and rest in that thing in which it is present first and through itself, and not by accident or through something else; whereas art is a principle of motion not through itself but through something else. For example, if a physician falls ill and restores his own health, he is cured not through himself, insofar as he is a man, but by accident and through something else, since the man who is ill is a physician. Hence the principle of the change and the cure is not his nature but the medical art. From this it is established that art is not an inborn principle of motion in the thing in which it is exercised, but an adventitious one; for that reason it does not necessarily move its own subject. Moreover, nature is twofold: one is matter, the other form, since a natural body consists of both, and nature itself is said of both principles. From this we can clearly understand that nature here is not the moving principle; for it moves nothing either within or without. For if it moved anything within, it would undoubtedly not be distinguished from the soul, and every body that consists by nature would be animate. Nor again would matter, whose proper character is to be acted upon, be nature. Furthermore, nature is the cause and principle of motion; yet motion is not the act of the mover but of the movable, as Aristotle clearly shows in the third book of the Physics. From these things it is evident that nature is not an external cause or efficient principle, but an internal principle of the natural body's parts. However, that nature which is a mover and an external principle belongs to the first philosopher, and of it Aristotle speaks almost everywhere, and most of all in the first book of On the Heavens, where he expresses most plainly that God and Nature do nothing at all in vain. These things may be said briefly about both natures; it is expedient to proceed to other matters.

units.la: CAP. IIII. De causis, & earum differentijs.
units.tr: CHAPTER 4. On causes, and their differences.

units.la: OSTHAEC quot sint caufarū ge- nera, explicandum est. Scire enim nihil ante putamus quàm prius cognitam habeamus causam. Itaque hoc faciendum est in rerum generatione & corruptione, atque (vt summatim dicam) in omni mutatione & explicanda & tradenda, vt cognitis rerum causis & principiis, ad ea, id omne, quod quæritur, referri possit. Causa igitur vna, id est ex quo aliquid sic fit, vt in eo & reipfa infit. Huiusmodi est æreæ statuæ æs, argenteæ pateræ argentum: quod quidem causæ genus materia est. Alia item est forma & ratio essentiæ rei. Tertium causæ genus, id est, vnde primum mutationis statúsque principium ducitur, & exterius est. Postremum vero finis est, & id cuius causa aliquid fit: vt valetudinis causa ambulat homo. Si enim quæratur cur quis ambulet, vt valeat, refpõdetur. Causæ igitur fere tot modis dici pofsunt. Sed earum quæ eiusdem generis sunt, alia prior est, alia posterior, & propinquior. Vt in efficientis genere medicus valetudinis causa propinquior est, quàm artifex, qui causa communis dicitur. Præterea causarum aliæ per se sunt, aliæ ex accidente, & per aliud. Per se autem illæ sunt quæ per se effectum producunt: vt statuarius per se statuam efficit. Per aliud aliæ sunt, vt Polycletus, qui nō per se causa statuæ est, sed eò quòd statuarius sit. Aliæ item quidpiam actu efficiunt, aliæ potestate, quarum hę sunt, vt architectus, qui domum ædificare potest, illæ verò, vt architectus, actu domum ædificans. Quod autem in causis expositum est, id in effectis locu habere par est. Propterea effectus quidè prior sit oportet, vt statua, quidem posterior vt hęc statua. Sed ad causarum genera explicanda redeundum est. Etenim earum quædam interdum connexa est, vt Polycletus statuarius statuam efficit: interdum diuisa & separata, vt statuarius statuam efficit. Omnes quidè huiusmodi causæ vel singulares sunt, vel generales, vel coniunctæ, aut disiunctæ, quæ omnes vel actu reque ipsa efficiunt, vel potestate. Sed actu causæ ab aliis, quæ potestate sunt hoc differunt, quòd illæ, atque earū esse ćta [?] talem inter se coniunctionem habent, vt in rerū natura simul sint, vt hic qui actu medetur, & is qui curatur, ac is qui ædificat, & id quod ædificatur: quæ verò potestate agût, non semper simul sunt. Deinde huiusmodi causæ, quæ potestate agunt, duntaxat ea efficere possunt, quæ possibilia sunt: vt aliæ quæ actu sunt, id etiam quod actu est, agunt. Aliæ denique sunt generales, vt statuarius: aliæ singulares, quæ rerum sunt singularium, vt hîc statuarius huius statuæ.
units.tr: Next, we must explain how many kinds of cause there are. For we think nothing is known until we have first grasped its cause. Therefore this must be done in the generation and corruption of things, and (to put it briefly) in every change, both in explaining and in teaching, so that once the causes and principles of things are known, all that is sought can be referred back to them. One cause, then, is that out of which something comes to be, so that it is in it and is present in the thing itself. Of this kind is the bronze of a bronze statue, or the silver of a silver bowl; this kind of cause is matter. Another is form and the rational account of the thing's essence. The third kind of cause is that from which the first principle of change and rest is derived, and it is external. The last is the end, that is, that for the sake of which something is done: as a man walks for the sake of health. For if one asks why someone walks, the answer is, so that he may be well. Causes can therefore be spoken of in about this many ways. But among causes of the same kind, one is prior and another posterior, and one is nearer. Thus in the class of efficient causes, the physician is nearer to the cause of health than the craftsman, who is called the common cause. Moreover, some causes are per se, and others are by accident and through something else. Those are per se which produce the effect directly: as the sculptor makes the statue per se. Those are through something else, as Polycletus is not the cause of the statue per se, but because he is a sculptor. Again, some cause something actually, and others potentially; of the latter kind is the architect who is able to build a house, while the former is the architect actually building a house. What has been set out concerning causes ought likewise to hold for effects. Hence the effect must indeed be prior, as the statue in general, and posterior, as this statue. But we must return to explaining the kinds of cause. For some causes are sometimes joined, as Polycletus the sculptor makes the statue; at other times they are divided and separate, as the sculptor makes the statue. All such causes are either singular, or general, or joined, or disjoined, and all of them produce either actually and in reality, or potentially. But actual causes differ from those that are potential in this: the former, and their effects, have such a mutual connection that they exist together in the nature of things, as the one who is actually healing and the one who is being healed, and the builder and the thing being built; whereas causes that act potentially are not always simultaneous with their effects. Furthermore, causes that act potentially can produce only those things that are possible, whereas causes that are actual act on what is actual. Finally, some causes are general, as the sculptor; others are singular, which belong to singular things, as this sculptor of this statue.

units.la: CAP. V. De fortuna & casu.
units.tr: Chapter 5. On fortune and chance.

units.la: F[?]ORTVNA autem & casus etiam in causis esse dicuntur, quandoqui-dem multa & esse, & fieri fortuito & casu contingunt. At vero quorumnam causæ sint, exquirendum est: quoniā alia semper & necessario fieri eodem modo cernuntur: alia raro, nec necessario. Præterea eorum, quæ fiunt, quædam ad aliquem pertinent finem, quædam minimè. At quæ alicuius causa fiunt, alia a mete & voluntate, alia a natura proficiscutur: quæ omnia cum ex accidente & aliena vi, fiunt, tum fortuitò & esse & euenire dicuntur. Quemadmodum enim quædam per se víque sua sunt, alia vero per aliud & aliena vi, sic & alia causa per se est, & alia ex accidente, veluti Architectus per se domus causa est, sed per aliud ille, qui albus est, aut Musicus. Ac ea quidem causa, quæ per se facultateque sua aliquid efficit, certa ac definita est: quæ vero aliena vi agit, incerta & indefinita, cuiusmodi fortuna est & casus. Quare nec semper necessarióque, neque eo-dem modo eueniunt, quæ forté temere, & casu fiunt. Cæterum in iis rebus fortuna est ac versatur, quæ a mentis iudicio & voluntate proficiscuntur, & alicuius causa[?] fiunt. Ete-nim nihil fortuito homini euenist, nisi quid ante sibi agendum esse alicuius causa deliberauerit. Quare si præter rationem & spem ei aliud euenerit, id fortuito contigisse dicitur. Quemadmodum si quis in forum proficisci-tur quidpiam emendi causa, & pecuniam a suo debitore accepit, quam se accepturum non sperabat, id fortuito ei euenisse dicitur. Causa certè huius euentus profectio ad forú fuit. Neque enim a suo debitore pecunia ac-cepisset, nisi ad forum profectusfuisset. Quo-niam verò huiusmodi incerta sunt, & raro eueniunt, fortunam etiam esse incertam ludi-candum est. Propterea interdú prospera dicitur, cum nimirum aliquid boni euenit: in-terdum aduersa, cum aliquid mali produxit. Verum tamen secunda infirma est & incon-stans: nec iniuria, quippe cum nec semper esse, nec plerunque euenire possit, quicquid eorum, quæ fortuna fiunt. Itaque fortuna & casus ex iis sunt causis, quæ efficere exaccidente dicuntur, atque in iis consistunt, quæ nec necessariò neque plerunque euenire possunt. Hoc autem differunt, quòd casus latius patet, quàm fortuna. Quod enim fortuna euenit, id etiam casu evenisse fertur: sed non omne quod casu fit, fortuna evenire potest. Nam quod fortuito fit & fortuna, id dunta-xat in ea omnia cadit in quibus humana actio consistit. Itaque in iis, quae homini age-da sunt, fortuna versatur, non autem in iis, in quae non voluntaria actio cadere potest. Ob eamque causam nulla res inanimata, nullae bestiae, nullusque puer quicquam facit eorum, quae fortuna evenient, eo quod iudicio mentis careant. Caeterum aduersa fortuna, aut prospera inanimatis evenit, sed quadam similitudine. Quam ob causam Protarcus dixisse fertur fortunatos beatosque esse lapides, ex quibus arae extruuntur, propterea quod eis honor tribueretur, cum alii eiusdem generis conculcarentur. At vero casus & multis animantibus, & inanimatis evenire potest. Nam cum in rebus, quae sine consilio, & voluntate agunt, aliud evenit, quam quod expectabatur, tum id casu evenisse dicitur. Quare casus ex accidente eorum est, quae raro fiunt, & absque consilio atque proposito. Ac etiā utriusque causae effecta differunt. Effectus enim casus tum fit, cum evenit aliquid praeter naturae scopum: veluti si cui sextum digitum nasci contingat. Fortuitus vero cum quid praeter propositum & voluntatem evenit, huius enim causa exterior est voluntas & propositum, illius vero interior & natura, quo-niam quae natura constant, circa quae casus versatur, principium in se habent & causam motus ac status. Causa enim cur foetui in utero sex digiti eveniant formatrix est, & interior. Quid casus, quid fortuna, quidve inter se differant, dictum est. Utrunque autem eorum ad id causae genus pertinet unde motus principium ducitur, hoc est ac efficiens, sed incertum & indefinitum. Veruntamen casus & fortuna eorum causae sunt, quae vel a mente, vel a natura proficiscuntur, sed adventitiae, & aliis posteriores quae per se agunt. Et quemadmodum huiusmodi causae improprie efficientes sunt, ita quoque in natura rerum effecta reperiuntur, quae monstrifica dici consueuerunt.
units.tr: Fortune and chance are also said to be found among causes, since many things both exist and come about by fortune and by chance. But we must inquire what kinds of things they are the causes of. Some things are always and necessarily seen to happen in the same way, while others happen rarely and not by necessity. Moreover, of the things that happen, some relate to a certain end and some do not at all. And of those things that happen for the sake of something, some proceed from the mind and will, others from nature. All of these, when they come about from an accident and from a foreign force, are said to happen and to occur by fortune and by chance. For just as some things are so by themselves, while others are so through something else and by a foreign force, so too one cause is per se and another is by accident. The architect, for example, is the cause of a house per se, but he is the cause of it through something else when he is pale or a musician. The cause that produces something by its own power and nature is certain and definite; the cause that acts by a foreign force is uncertain and indefinite, and of this kind are fortune and chance. Hence the things that happen by chance and accident do not happen always or of necessity, nor in the same way. Fortune, moreover, is found and operates in those things that proceed from the judgment and will of the mind and come about for the sake of something. For nothing happens to a man by chance unless he has first deliberated that something is to be done by him for some purpose. Therefore, if something other than he reckoned and hoped for befalls him, it is said to have happened to him by chance. Thus, if someone goes into the forum to buy something and receives money from his debtor, which he did not expect to receive, it is said to have befallen him by chance. The cause of this event is certainly the going to the forum, for he would not have received the money from his debtor unless he had gone to the forum. Since such things are uncertain and happen rarely, fortune must also be judged to be uncertain. For this reason it is sometimes called favourable, when it has produced something good, and sometimes adverse, when it has produced something bad. Yet fortune is weak and inconstant, and not without reason, since whatever things come about by fortune can neither be always nor generally the case. Thus fortune and chance belong to those causes which are said to produce their effects from an accident, and they consist in those things which can happen neither necessarily nor generally. They differ in this, that chance has a wider range than fortune. For what happens by fortune is also said to happen by chance, but not everything that happens by chance can happen by fortune. For what happens by fortune and chance pertains only to those matters in which human action consists. Thus fortune is concerned with those things that are to be done by a man, but not with those things into which non-voluntary action cannot fall. For this reason no inanimate thing, no beast, and no child does anything that could come about by fortune, because they lack the judgment of the mind. Nevertheless, adverse or favourable fortune does befall inanimate things, but by a certain likeness. This is why Protarchus is reported to have said that the stones from which altars are built are fortunate and blessed, because honour is paid to them while others of the same kind are trampled underfoot. But chance can befall both many animate things and inanimate things. For when, in things that act without counsel and will, something other than what was expected comes about, it is said to have happened by chance. Hence chance is an accident of those things that happen rarely and without counsel and purpose. Moreover, the effects of the two also differ. For the effect of chance occurs when something happens beyond the aim of nature, as when someone happens to be born with a sixth finger. The effect of fortune, however, is when something happens beyond purpose and will; for the cause of the one is external, namely will and purpose, while the cause of the other is internal and natural, since the things that consist of nature, about which chance is concerned, have within themselves the principle and cause of motion and of rest. For the cause why a sixth finger arises in a foetus in the womb is formative and internal. What chance is, what fortune is, and how they differ from one another has been said. Yet each of them belongs to that kind of cause from which the principle of motion is derived, that is, the efficient cause, but an uncertain and indefinite one. Nevertheless, chance and fortune are causes of those things that proceed either from the mind or from nature, but they are adventitious and posterior to the things which act through themselves. And just as causes of this kind are improperly efficient, so too in the nature of things there are found effects which are customarily called monstrous.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CAP. VI.

units.la: Non plures causas esse, quam quatuor.
units.tr: That there are no more causes than four.

units.la: OT esse causas & earum genera, quot iam diximus, satis perspicuum est. Nam quaestio cur quidque fit, totidem causarum genera complectitur. Haec autem[?] quadruplex est, ex quo, per quod, a quo, & cuius gratia res est. Itaque quatuor sunt causarum genera, materies, forma, efficiens, & finis, quorum tria plerunque in unum cadunt. Nam & forma & finis unum sunt, & id unde motus principium ducitur. Quod autem forma & finis unum sint & idem in rerum, quae natura constant, ge-neratione neratione, cuius finis forma est, satis perspicuum est. Efficiens vero idem esse cum forma & fine ex eo intelligi potest, quòd homo hominem gignat. Etenim gignens homo, & qui genitus est idem specie sunt. Forma etiam generantis, quæ principium est & causa motus hominis, eadem specie est, quæ geniti, quoniam perfectio eius est & ratio. Sed materia nec specie, nec numero idem esse potest, quod[?] quæ causæ dictæ sunt, propterea qꝑ potestate dūtaxat τὸ ὂν fit. Hæc sunt quatuor causarum genera, quæ physicus considerare debet, quoniam ea meditatur, quæ oriuntur & corrumpuntur, quibus necessario materia subiicitur.
units.tr: That there are causes, and kinds of causes, as many as we have already said, is quite clear. For the question why anything comes to be embraces just as many kinds of cause. This question, however, has four parts: from what, through what, by whom, and for whose sake a thing exists. There are therefore four kinds of cause: matter, form, efficient cause, and end; of these three generally fall into one. For form and end are one, and so is that from which the beginning of motion is derived. That form and end are one and the same in the generation of things that consist in nature, whose end is form, is quite clear. That the efficient cause is also the same as form and end can be understood from the fact that a man begets a man: for the begetting man and the one begotten are the same in species. The form of the one generating, which is the principle and cause of the motion, is also the same in species as that of the one begotten, since it is its perfection and pattern. But matter cannot be the same in species or in number as the causes just named; for this reason it becomes "what is" only potentially [τὸ ὂν]. These are the four kinds of cause which the natural philosopher must consider, since he studies those things which arise and perish, to which matter is necessarily subjected.

units.la: Cap. VII.
units.tr: Chapter VII.

units.la: Naturam ex eis causis esse, quæ alicuius gratia agunt.
units.tr: That nature acts from those causes which work for the sake of something.

units.la: LIM non defuerunt philosophi, qui naturam quicquam alicuius gratia agere, negarunt, quoniā(inquiebant) si quicquam propter aliquem finem ipsa ageret, id quod esset melius & commodius eam efficere, necesse est. Deus autem vel Natura pluit, non(inquiút) ut fruges augeat, sed ut interdum ipsis damnum afferat. Ex quo necessitate materiæ, quæ aqua pluvia est, pluere conclu-dunt. Vapor enim sursum elatus frigescit, dein frigefactus in nubem concrescit, quæ tandem in pluuiam resoluitur.Itaque pluuiá ob id nő euenit semper vt fruges augeat, sed interdum vt eas labefaciat. Quod fi alteru-trum fiat,id casu contingere, non natura di-cebant. Sed toto cœlo errare[?] isti videntur. Si enim quæ ab arte proficiscuntur[?], causa ali-cuius fiunt,profecto ea multo magis, quæ na-tura constant. Ars enim Naturam imitatur, quatenus potest,etsi ea interdu abfolut[?],quæ Natura perficere non potuit. Quod autem Natura in stirpibus quidpiam alicuius effi-ciat,hinc perspicuum est,quod producantur folia fructus tegendi causa : nec radices sur-sum versus agant, sed deorsum, propter ali-mentum. Ex animalibus etiam hirundo cer-nitur alicuius causa nidum construere, & a-ranea telam quasi rete. Propterea eo magis alicuius causa agi videntur omnia, quæ Na-tura constant,quàm artificialia. Præterea for-ma,quæ Natura dicitur,finis generationis na-turalis est.Itaque Natura semper propter fi-nem agit. Cæterum nihil mirari oportet, si Natura non semper suum finem consequa-tur: quandoquidem interdum in iis, quæ ar-te constant,error contingit. Nam non sem-per Grammaticus recte scribit, nec Medicus recte potionem præbet. Quod si in iis quæ arte fiunt, & in quibus recta faciendi ratio ad aliquem nitatur finem,artifex ab eo sæpe-numero aberret,profecto in iis etiam, quæ à Natura proficiscuntur idem eueniat, necesse est. Itaque Monstra errationes Naturæ sunt ab eo fine, quem ea sibi in procreando proposuerat. Cæterum in procreatione animalium ipsa non statim formata sunt, sed semel prius existat, n[?]esse est: quod quidem eo fine ne produ[?]t est, vt ex eo animal sit. In iis etiam, quæ e terra oriuntur, id cuius causa aliquid fit semper reperitur, quaquam minus distinctu[?]quibus idem euenire potest, quod in animalibus, in quibus monstra fiunt. Quæ-admodum enim ex asino & iumento animal, cui mulus nomen est, oriri potest, sic ex vitis & oleæ partibus planta, tametsi hæc in Natura videantur absurda.
units.tr: There were not lacking philosophers who denied that nature does anything for the sake of something. For (they said) if nature did anything for some end, it would necessarily do what was better and more convenient. "God, or Nature, makes it rain," they say, "not so that it may swell the crops, but sometimes so that it may do them harm. So from the necessity of matter, rain, which is rainwater, must fall. For vapour, drawn upward, cools; then, once cooled, it condenses into a cloud, which at last dissolves into rain. Therefore rain does not fall always so as to swell the crops, but sometimes so as to ruin them. If one or the other happens, they said it comes about by chance, not by nature." But these men seem to be utterly mistaken. For if things that proceed from art are made for the sake of something, then much more surely are things that exist by nature. For art imitates nature as far as it can, although art sometimes completes what nature was unable to bring to perfection. That nature does something for a purpose in plants is clear from the fact that leaves are put out to cover the fruit, and that the roots grow downward, not upward, for the sake of nourishment. Among animals too, the swallow is seen to build its nest for a purpose, and the spider its web, as if a net. For this reason all the things that exist by nature seem to be done for a purpose even more than artificial things. Moreover, the form which is called nature is the end of natural generation. Thus nature always acts for the sake of an end. Yet we should not be surprised if nature does not always attain its end, since in things made by art too error sometimes occurs. For the grammarian does not always write correctly, nor does the physician always give the right draught. If, in things done by art, where the right way of doing something is aimed at some end, the artist often misses that end, then it must necessarily happen the same way in things that proceed from nature. Thus monsters are errors of nature, departures from the end which nature had proposed to itself in producing. Moreover, in the procreation of animals the parts are not formed all at once, but something must first exist, which is brought about for the sake of the animal to come from it. In those things too which arise from the earth, that for the sake of which something is made is always found, although it is less distinct, and they may suffer the same thing that happens to animals in which monsters arise. For just as a creature called a mule can arise from an ass and a mare, so a plant can arise from parts of the vine and the olive, although such things may seem absurd in nature.

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CAP. VIII.

units.la: Qui in naturalibus necessitas infit?
units.tr: Whether necessity inheres in natural things.

units.la: [Q?]VAERITVR postea utrū necessitas ex hypothesi in rebus insit, quæ natura constant, an vel ea, quæ omnino est, & absoluta? Hoc profecto dubium perspicue diluit Aristoteles, cap. 1, libri primi de partibus animalium initio, vbi vnam esse ostendit, quæ absoluta ratione dicitur, & in æternis diuinisque inest: altera vero, quæ ex hypothesi est, caducis gignendisque omnibus tribui: quemadmodum artificialibus, vt ædibus, & aliis eiusdem generis. Nam in talibus materiam adesse necesse est, fi finis domus, aut cuiusuis alius futurus fit. In iis autem nulla necessitas est, in quibus nullus finis proponitur, nullaque est necessaria natura, hoc est Materia, in qua tum in Natura, tum in arte necessitas est. Quamobrem ipsam Materiam Ariftotele[?]s libro physico secundo, cap.9. necessitatem nominat, quoniam absque ea nec Natura, neque quiuis artifex quicqua efficere potest. Itaque vt domus abdendi quædam, & eadem c[?]nfcruan[?]di causa fit, ex lapidibus & lignis coftruatur, necesse est: quæ fi non adsint, nec etiam domus struetur. Sic quoque ferra (cuius opus sectio est) vt fit, ferrum, ex quo fiat, adesse oportet. Quod fi deest, non ferra erit, nec secabit. Est etiam huiusmodi necessitas in doctrinis scientiisque, vt & in hisce, quæ Natura constant. At in doctrinis ea perspicua est, quandoquidem non triangulus erit, nisi figura tres angulos duobus rectis pares obtineat. Sic etiam in rerum Natura, animal non erit, aut stirps, nisi adsit materia, ex qua fiat: nec etiam quicquam eorum corrumpetur, nisi ex contrariis compactum fit. Huiusmodi necessitas vt summatim dicam in materia consistit, quemadmodum finis in forma & ratione rei, quæ alicuius causa est.
units.tr: It is asked next whether necessity inheres in things that consist by nature only hypothetically, or whether there is also a necessity that is unconditional and absolute. Aristotle clearly resolves this doubt at the beginning of the first chapter of the first book of On the Parts of Animals, where he shows that there is one kind of necessity which is called absolute, and which belongs to eternal and divine things; and another, which is hypothetical, and is attributed to perishable and generable things, just as it is to artificial things such as houses and others of the same kind. For in such things matter must be present if the end of a house, or of any other thing of the kind, is to come about. In those things, however, in which no end is proposed, there is no necessity; and there is no necessity in nature, that is, in matter, in which necessity lies both in nature and in art. For this reason Aristotle, in the second chapter of the ninth book of his Physics, calls matter itself "necessity," since neither nature nor any artificer can produce anything without it. Thus, if a house is to be built for the sake of shelter and preservation, it must be built of stones and timber, and if these are not present, no house will be built. So too a saw (whose work is cutting), if it is to exist, must have the iron from which it is made; if that is lacking, there will be no saw, and nothing will be cut. There is also this kind of necessity in the disciplines and sciences, as there is in those things which consist by nature. In the disciplines it is plain, since a triangle will not exist unless its figure has three angles equal to two right angles. So too in the nature of things, an animal or a plant will not exist unless the matter from which it is made is present; nor will any of these be corrupted unless it is compounded of contraries. To put it briefly, this kind of necessity consists in matter, just as the end consists in the form and reason of a thing which is the cause of something.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: Quid motus sit, & mutatio, & quantum inter se differant.
units.tr: What motion is, and change, and how far they differ from each other.

units.la: VONAM autem motus mutatio nisi principium Natura est, quid ipse motus sit videre licet. Eo enim ignorato, Naturæ ignoratio etiam consequatur, necesse est. Itaque motus actus est rei mobilis, qua ex parte mobilis est. Sed huiusmodi actus imperfectus est, propterea quod eius subiectum, quod mobile est, & potestate τοῦ fit imperfectum. Eorum enim quæ sunt, quædam actu sunt, quædam potestate. Ea autem actu sunt, quæ formam habent, & reipsa sunt, quorum actus perfectus est, quoniam formæ rationisque est particeps. Actus vero rei mobilis quæ esse potest, imperfectus est ut ædificatio, quæ actus est rei quæ ædificari potest, & nondum ædificata est: sic alteratio eius rei est, quæ alterari potest: accretio, decretioque eorum, quæ accrescere & decrescere possunt: generatio quoque & corruptio etiam mutationes sunt eorum, quæ & generari & corrumpi queunt: sic φορά, quæ ad locum mutatio est, eorum etiam est, quæ e loco mutari possunt. Ex quibus perspicuum est omnem motum actum esse imperfectum. Cæterum in omni motu non tantum mobili opus est, quod patiatur, sed etiam aliquo movente, quod mobili motum afferat. Mouens autem huiusmodi duplex est, vnum quod naturaliter mouet, & simul a mobili mouetur: alterum quod mouet, & a mobili non mouetur, quale cœli motor est, & anima: cætera autem mouent, simul mouentur. Quoniam autem naturale agens semper in eo, quod mouetur, aliquam imprimit formam vel substantiæ, vel quantitatis, vel denique alicuius qualitatis, vt tria mutationis genera tradan[?]ur, vnum quod in substantia est, & generatio dicitur, & corruptio: alterum in quantitate, quod accretio est, & imminutio: postremum in qualitate, quod alteratio nominatur. Quod autem tot sint mutationis genera ex hoc e-tiam intelligere possumus, quod omne mutabile tribus modis mutetur. Aut enim e subiecto in subiectum: aut e nullo subiecto in subiectum, aut denique e subiecto in nullum subiectum omnis mutatio est. Sed triū harum mutationum duæ ex contradicentibus sunt, nempe generatio & corruptio. Nā hæc fit e subiecto, in id quod non subiectum est: illa verò ex nullo subiecto, quod actu sit, in subiectum actu existens. Ex repugnantibus autem & contrariis reliquæ mutationes fiunt, quæ motus proprie dicuntur. Vnde constat a mutatione motum ex eo differre, quod omnis motus mutatio sit, sed non contrà. Generatio enim & corruptio ptio mutationes quidem sunt, & non motus, quandoquidem omnis motus e contrario in contrarium, aut medium est. Adde quòd substantiæ nihil contrarium sit: vnde sequitur motum in substantiam non cadere posse, sed quantitatem, qualitatem, & locum. Verùm in omni mutatione non solum mouens requiritur, & id quod moueri potest, sed etiam tempus, quandoquidem quicquid mouetur mutatúrque in tempore moueri oportet, quoniam tempus motus mensura est & affectio. Cæterum quæstio oritur, vtrum motus in mouente sit, an verò in mobili? Huic dubio respondendum est in mobili tanquam in subiecto motum esse, & à mouente proficisci. Verùmtamen mouentis & mobilis vna & eadem motio reipsa est, sed ratione diuersa, quandoquidem agentis actus actio est, & patientis passio. Præterea vt motus, qui quantitati & qualitati conuenit, non vnus est, sed multiplex, ita e loco mutatio triplex esse dicitur. Etenim vna cœli est, & conuersio dicitur, quæ primus est ad locum motus, eò quòd perfectissimus sit, & simplicissimus. Tametsi in loco omnes motus fiant, illetamé, qui cœli est, nò in loco fit, nisi secundū partes. Altera autem ad locum mutatio recta est & simplex: postrema mista. Nam si, quæ recta est, super recta linea reflectatur composita sit, necesse est, & geminus motus. Si verò nō reflectatur imperfecta erit. Quoniam autem omne per-sectum & tempore & natura eo prius est im-perfecto, consequitur cæli conuersionem omnium motuum qui in loco fiunt esse primum. Id quod etiam ostendit eius perpetuitas. Perpetuus enim motus prior[?] est eo, qui in quietem definit. Propterea cæli[?] conuersio non solum primus est motus e loco, sed & aliarum mutationum causa: quoniam perpetua est: perpetuitatis cuius author[?] habetur[?] primus motor, qui indesinenter cælos mouere potest. Aliorum autem motuum nullus potest perpetuus esse, propterea quod omnes a contrariis ad contraria loca fiant, quæ extrema sunt. Itaque mutationis omnis eorum, quæ natura cõstant, cæli conuersio causa est: Sed primùm animalia ante generetur, necesse est quàm accretione, & ad locũ moueri possint. Propterea prima mutatio rerū naturalium generatio est, postrema verò latio ad locum, quæ in animante non simplex motus est, sed permistus, & progressio dicitur, propterea quòd misti corporis sit, quod animal est. Verum enimuero viuetium quædam instrumentis ad motum localem aptis carent: propterea non omnia e loco mouentur. Stant enim ostrea, & omnia concharum genera, sicuti plantæ. Alia verò animantia tũ loco cientur, cum perfectionem adepta sunt. Deinde quædam loci mutatio naturalis est, cuius causa & principium est Natura: quædam violenta & præter naturam, quæ ab exteriori principio oritur. Demum motus non solum motui aduersatur, sed etiā quieti, quoniam quies motus priuatio est, & fere contrarium. Quod autem motus fit motui aduersus satis apparet accretione [?] & diminutione, quæ non tanquam habitus & priuatio inter se pugnant, sed vt habitus habitui aduersatur. Atque quemadmodum naturalis mutatio violentæ contraria est, sic duplex quies eiusdem rei sibi aduersatur. Altera enim quies est naturalis, qua æther in sublimi loco naturaliter quiescit: altera coacta, per quam nostras ignis vi in imo quiescit loco.
units.tr: Since change is the principle of nature, we can see what motion itself is, for if that is unknown, ignorance of nature must necessarily follow. Motion, then, is the act of a movable thing, insofar as it is movable. But this kind of act is imperfect, because its subject, which is movable, is still in potentiality [τοῦ], and so is imperfect. Of things that exist, some are in act and some in potentiality. Those things are in act which have a form and are actually what they are, and their act is perfect because they share in form and definition. But the act of a movable thing that can be something else is imperfect, as building is the act of a thing that can be built and is not yet built. So too alteration is the act of a thing that can be altered; accretion and decretion are the acts of things that can grow and shrink; generation and corruption are changes of things that can both be generated and corrupted; and locomotion [φορά], which is change of place, belongs to things that can be moved from place to place. From these things it is clear that every motion is an imperfect act. Moreover, in every motion there is needed not only a movable thing that undergoes it, but also some mover that imparts motion to the movable. Now there are two kinds of mover: one that moves naturally and is itself moved at the same time as the movable; and another that moves without being moved by the movable, such as the mover of the heavens and the soul. All other movers are moved at the same time as they move. Since a natural agent always impresses on the thing it moves some form, either of substance, or of quantity, or finally of some quality, there are said to be three kinds of change: one in substance, called generation and corruption; another in quantity, which is accretion and diminution; and the last in quality, which is named alteration. That there are so many kinds of change we can also understand from the fact that everything changeable changes in three ways: every change is either from a subject into a subject, or from no subject into a subject, or finally from a subject into no subject. But of these three changes, two are between contradictories, namely generation and corruption, for the first passes from a subject into what is not a subject, and the second from what is not an actual subject into an actually existing subject. The remaining changes, which are properly called motions, come about between opposites and contraries. Hence it is established that motion differs from change in this, that every motion is a change, but not conversely. For generation and corruption are changes and not motions, since every motion goes from contrary to contrary or to an intermediate. Add that substance has no contrary; hence it follows that motion cannot fall upon substance, but only upon quantity, quality, and place.
