Yet in every change not only a mover and that which can be moved are required, but also time, since whatever is moved and changed must be moved in time, time being the measure and attribute of motion. But the question arises whether motion is in the mover or in the movable. To this doubt it must be answered that motion is in the movable as in its subject, and proceeds from the mover. Nevertheless, the motion of the mover and of the movable is one and the same in reality, but different in definition, since the act of the agent is action and the undergoing of the patient is passion. Furthermore, just as motion belonging to quantity and quality is not one but manifold, so change of place is said to be threefold. For there is one motion of the heavens, called rotation, which is the first motion in respect of place, because it is most perfect and most simple. Although all motions take place in place, that of the heavens does not take place in a place, except according to its parts. The second change of place is straight and simple; the last is mixed. For if what is straight is reflected upon a straight line, it is necessarily compound and a double motion; but if it is not reflected, it will be imperfect. Since every perfect thing is prior to the imperfect both in time and in nature, it follows that the rotation of the heavens is the first of all motions that take place in place. This is also shown by its perpetuity, for a perpetual motion is prior to one that ends in rest. Therefore the rotation of the heavens is not only the first motion of place but also the cause of the other changes, since it is perpetual; the author of this perpetuity is held to be the first mover, who is able to move the heavens without ceasing. But none of the other motions can be perpetual, because all of them go from contrary places to contrary places, which are the extremes. Thus the rotation of the heavens is the cause of all change among things that consist by nature. But living things must first be generated before they can grow and be moved to a place. Hence the first change among natural things is generation, and the last is motion to a place, which in an animal is not a simple motion but a mixed one, and is called progression, because it belongs to a mixed body, which an animal is. Indeed, some living things lack instruments suited to local motion, and so not all of them are moved from place to place. Oysters and all kinds of shellfish stand still, like plants. Other animals are moved from place only when they have attained their perfection. Further, one local change is natural, having nature as its cause and principle; another is violent and against nature, arising from an external principle. Finally, motion is opposed not only to motion but also to rest, since rest is a privation of motion and almost its contrary. That motion is opposed to motion is plain enough in accretion and diminution, which do not fight with each other as a habit and its privation, but as one habit is opposed to another. And just as natural change is contrary to violent change, so the twofold rest of the same thing is opposed to itself: one rest is natural, by which the aether rests naturally in a high place; the other is forced, by which our fire, by its force, rests in the lowest place.

units.la: CAP. X. De palingenesia, & mortuorum re-surrectione.
units.tr: CAP. X. On palingenesis and the resurrection of the dead.

units.la: CCVRRIT hoc loco quæstio, quæ potius ad Theologum & primum philosophi pertinet, quam ad physicum, vtrum palingenesia generatio fit, an vero alteratio? Et si alteratio fit, an vna numero & eadem, vt quæ naturalem ortum antecedit? Aristoteles, libro physicorum quinto, cap. 4. hoc mutationis genus alterationem esse perspicuis verbis explicat. Si fieri potest (inquit) vt id quod interit rursus oriatur, fiatque vnum numero, profecto ista alteratio etiam vna erit. Sed si non vna est numero, una fit specie & eadem, necesse est. His philosophi verbis perspicuum est palin-genefiam, non novam esse mortuorum generationem, sed duntaxat factam in corporibus alterationem. Huc accedit quod generatione ἐντελέχεια corporis acquiritur[?]. At in palingenefia nulla corporis ἐντελέχεια acquiritur, sed duntaxat materiae, quae in universi elementis potestate erat, forma animaque restituitur. Nam morte & interitu hominis mentem extingui abolerique nemo est qui sibi persuadeat, nisi summe fit impius & brutiffimus, quoniam mentis effentia incorporea est & simplex, nullisque corporeis affectionibus per fe obnoxia, sicuti non inscite philosophus, libro De anima tertio, perspicue demonstrat. Id quod magis magif-que sacrosanctae scripturae testimonio confirmari potest. Ibi enim Deus Abrahami esse dicitur, & Ifachi, atque Jacobi. Sed (ut rectissime noster Christus affumit) Deus viuentium est, non autem mortuorum. Itaque ipsorum patrum animae ἐντελέχειαι quae non extinctae sunt nec abolitae, sed ab ipso Deo conseruatae, donec sua repetant pristina corpora, quae in inferiori vniuerso delitescunt & consistunt. Ex quibus perspicuum est palingenefiam non mutationem esse sub-stantiae, sed qualitatis corporis humani, quam Apostolus priore epistola ad Corinthios ἀνάστασιν νεκρῶν appellat. Haec enim mortuorum excitatio nō hominum ortus est, nec a-nimarum eis nōua acquisitio, sed duntaxat mutatio qualitatis, qua hominis mortalitas inimmortalitatem commutatur.
units.tr: The following question arises here, which belongs more to the theologian and to the first philosophy than to the natural philosopher: whether palingenesis is a generation or rather an alteration? And if it is an alteration, is it one and the same in number, as it is with the natural origin that precedes it? Aristotle, in the fifth book of the Physics, chapter 4, explains in clear words that this kind of change is an alteration. "If it is possible," he says, "for that which has perished to arise again and become one in number, then this alteration will certainly also be one. But if it is not one in number, it must necessarily be one in species and the same." From these words of the philosopher it is evident that palingenesis is not a new generation of the dead, but only an alteration effected in the bodies. Moreover, in generation the entelechy [ἐντελέχεια] of the body is acquired, whereas in palingenesis no entelechy of the body is acquired; rather, only form and soul are restored to that matter which was in the power of the elements of the universe. For no one who is not utterly impious and brutish will persuade himself that the mind is extinguished and destroyed by the death and perishing of a man, since the essence of the mind is incorporeal and simple and not subject in itself to any bodily affections, as the philosopher demonstrates clearly, and not without skill, in the third book of On the Soul. This can be confirmed more and more by the testimony of Sacred Scripture. For there God is said to be the God of Abraham, and of Isaac, and of Jacob. But (as our Christ rightly argues) "God is the God of the living, not of the dead." Therefore the entelechies, that is, the souls of the fathers themselves, which are neither extinguished nor abolished, but are preserved by God himself, remain until they reclaim their former bodies, which lie hidden and abide in the lower universe. From these things it is clear that palingenesis is not a change of substance but of the quality of the human body, which the Apostle in his first epistle to the Corinthians calls the resurrection of the dead [ἀνάστασιν νεκρῶν]. For this raising of the dead is not the origin of men, nor a new acquisition of souls for them, but only a change of quality, by which the mortality of man is exchanged for immortality.

units.la: CAP. XI. Mens & motum simul esse.
units.tr: CHAPTER XI. That mind and motion are simultaneous.

units.la: Q[?]VONIAM ut tria sunt in quibus motus fiunt, quantitas, qualitas, & locus, sic tres sunt motus differentiæ, quarum prima est φορά, altera accretio & diminutio, tertia alteratio: de quibus sigillatim differeđum est, & primum de ea quæ è loco ad locum fit, quoniam pri-mus motus est. Itaque quicquid fertur, aut à se ipso mouetur, aut ab alio. Quòd si à se feratur, animal est, in quo inter mouentem & motum corpus nullum interiicitur medium, sed simul sunt. Sin vero ab alio mouetur, ipsū quatuor modis cieri, necesse est. Motionum enim, quæ ab alio & externo motore afferū-tur quatuor sunt genera, pulsio, attractio, volutatio, vectio, ad quæ omnes aliæ huiusmodi referuntur. Propterea ad pulsionem pertinent impulsio & expulsio, quoniā eius species sunt. Eo duntaxat differūt cū[?] impulsio fit cum moues id nō deserit quod mouetur: ex-pulsio verò ipsum deserit. Vectio autē ex his tribus motionibus, nēpe pulsione, tractione, volutatione una est, quadoquidè quod vehi-tur, id aut pellitur, aut attrahitur, aut deniq;[?] voluitur. Ex quo perspicuum est quod vehi-tur,id per aliud & ex accidente moueri.Mo-uetur enim,aut quia in eo est,quod mouetur, aut super ipsum. Attractio trahentis motus est,aut ad se,aut ad aliud: qui quidem motus non celerior est motu eius [quod?] trahitur, quoniam ab eo seiungi non [potest?]: quando-quidem attractio attrahentis est, & rei, quae attrahitur. Ad tractionem pertinent inspi-ratio & expiratio,expuitio, & aliae motiones huiusmodi,quibus, aut emittuntur corpora, aut assumuntur. Volutatio denique ex tra-ctatione constat & pulsione. Voluens enim partim pellit,partim trahit. Quare si pellens & trahens cum eo sunt quod pellitur & tra-hitur, perspicuum est mouens mobili conti-guum esse,nec vllum interiici medium inter vtrunque. Id quod etiam ex definitionibus motionum huiusmodi intelligere possumus. Nam pulsio aut a se est, aut ab alio in aliud motio. Tractio autem ab alio ad seipsum, vel ad aliud. Huiusmodi est compulsio, & difpulsio, vt pulsio. Sed proiectio motus est celerior naturali motione eius corporis,quod fertur, quoniam vehementior fit pulsio. Id enim quod proiicitur eousque fertur, quo-usque is motus vehementior fit. Quae cum i-ta sint perspicuum est id quod mouet, & a-liud quod mouetur simul esse,& inter vtrun-que nihil interiici. Idem de alterante, & eo quod alteratur, iudicandum est, inter quae nullum interiicitur medium. Quare id quod alterat, & quod alteratur simul sunt. Quod autem alterat, id qualitatis alicuius fit particeps, oportet, ut & quod alteratur sensile. At sensilia ea sunt, quibus corpora distinguuntur nempe gravitas, levitas, durities, mollities, sonus, silentium, albor, nigror, dulcedo, amaritudo, humor, siccitas, desitas, raritas, &c. quae huius generis sunt, & sensui subiiciuntur, ut calor & frigus, laevitas & asperitas, quibus, & horum gradibus sensilia corpora inter se differunt. Quoniam autem sensilium corpo-rum nonnulla pati possunt, idcirco non so-lum animata corpora, sed ea etiam, quae animae expertia sunt, alterari patiq; possunt. Calefiunt enim, aut refrigerantur, aut dulcescunt, amarescuntve, aut alio huiusmodi qualitatum sensilium afficiuntur. Ipsi quoque sensus alterantur, propterea quod recipien-do patiantur. Atque quibus inanimata alterantur iisdem omnibus animantia, & non contra. Nam quibus animantia alterantur, hisce inanimata alterari non possunt. Nullo enim sensu haec alterantur, nec dum alteran-tur, sentiunt. Itaque si sensilibus affectioni-bus omnis alteratio fiat, iam satis perspicuum est simul esse ipsum agens & affectum, & inter ea nihil interiici. Simili modo id quod augescit, & quod auget simul sunt, & se contingunt, quoniam accretio est additio quaedam. Idem de diminutione iudicandum est, eo quòd eius causa ablatio quædam fit.
units.tr: Since there are three things in which motions occur, quantity, quality and place, so there are three differences of motion: the first is φορά (locomotion), the second increase and decrease, the third alteration. These must be treated one by one, and first that which takes place from place to place, since it is the first motion. Therefore whatever is carried, is moved either by itself or by another. If it is carried by itself, it is an animal, in which no intervening body lies between the mover and the moved, but they are simultaneous. But if it is moved by another, it must be moved in one of four ways. For there are four kinds of motions that are brought about by another, an external mover: pulsion, attraction, rolling, and carrying, to which all other such motions are referred. Accordingly impulsion and expulsion belong to pulsion, since they are its species. They differ only in this: impulsion occurs when the mover does not leave what is moved, whereas expulsion leaves it. Carrying, however, is one of these three motions, namely pulsion, traction and rolling, since what is carried is either pushed, or drawn, or finally rolled. From this it is clear that what is carried is moved through another and by accident. For it is moved either because it is in that which is moved, or upon it. Attraction is the motion of the one who draws, either toward himself or toward another; and this motion is not swifter than the motion of that which is drawn, since it cannot be separated from it, inasmuch as attraction belongs to the one who attracts and to the thing attracted. To traction belong inspiration and expiration, spitting, and other motions of this kind, by which bodies are either sent out or taken in. Finally, rolling consists of traction and pulsion. For the thing rolling partly pushes and partly draws. Wherefore, if the pushing and drawing agents are together with that which is pushed and drawn, it is clear that the mover is contiguous to the mobile, and that nothing intervenes between them. This we can also understand from the definitions of such motions. For pulsion is a motion either from oneself or from one thing to another. Traction, however, is from another to oneself, or to another. Of this kind is compulsion and dispulsion, as is pulsion. But projection is a motion swifter than the natural motion of the body that is carried, since the pulsion becomes more vehement. For that which is projected is carried as far as that motion becomes more vehement. Since these things are so, it is clear that the mover and the other thing that is moved are simultaneous, and nothing intervenes between them. The same judgment is to be made concerning the alterer and that which is altered, between which no medium intervenes. Therefore that which alters and that which is altered are simultaneous. Now that which alters must partake of some quality, and so must that which is altered, being sensible. And the sensible things are those by which bodies are distinguished, namely heaviness, lightness, hardness, softness, sound, silence, whiteness, blackness, sweetness, bitterness, moisture, dryness, density, rarity, etc., which are of this kind and are subject to the senses, as heat and cold, smoothness and roughness, by which sensible bodies differ from one another and by their degrees. Since, however, some sensible bodies can suffer, therefore not only animate bodies but also those that are devoid of soul can be altered and suffer alteration. For they become warm, or cool, or grow sweet, or bitter, or are affected by some other sensible qualities of this kind. The senses themselves also are altered, because in receiving they suffer. And inanimate things are altered by all the same things by which animate things are altered, and not conversely. For those things by which animate things are altered cannot alter inanimate things. For these are not altered by any sense, nor do they perceive when they are altered. Therefore, if all alteration takes place through sensible affections, it is now sufficiently clear that the agent and the patient are simultaneous, and nothing intervenes between them. In a similar way, that which increases and that which causes increase are simultaneous and touch one another, since accretion is a certain addition. The same is to be judged concerning diminution, since its cause is a certain removal.

units.la: CAP. XII.
units.tr: CHAP. XII.

units.la: Definito & infinito disputatio.
units.tr: Disputation on the finite and the infinite.

units.la: VONIAM Naturæ ratio & scientia in magnitudinibus, motu, & tempore versatur, quorum quídque necesse est aut finitum esse, aut infinitum, hoc profecto consentaneum est, vt is, qui Naturæ scientiam tractat, infinitum sit necne, & quid sit, exquirat. Propterea primum an vt essentia, an vel vt accidens per se alicui Naturæ conueniat, an ne alterutri quidem infinitas insit, intelligere par est. At si essentia est, & ex iis, quæ sub sensum cadunt, profecto corpus magnitudine infinitum esse, expedit. Sed hoc esse non potest. Si enim corporis definitio id sit quod extremitate su perficieque finitum est, certè corpus infinitum nullo modo esse potest. At verò, qui magis physicas rationes adhibere volet, is nullum esse infinitum corpus demonstrabit, siue illud simplex sit, siue ex pluribus concretum. Hoc quidem infinitum non erit, si elementa, ex quibus constat, finita numero sunt. Atqui non omnia esse infinita possunt, quandoquidem in vniuerso ne plura quidem infinita esse queunt. Vnum enim omnia occupat? Deinde ex infinitis nulla infinita oriri possunt: quoniam plura esse infinita nequeunt. Si præterea unum elementorum est infinitu, & cætera finita, profecto illud unum infinitum alia,quæ finita sunt, cofumet, quoniam contraria sunt. Contraria enim se perimunt,eo quòd inter se mutuò & agant,& patiantur. Atq[?] eorum quod infinitum erit maiorem vim agendi obtinebit: ac propterea ab eo cætera abolebùtur. At contraria ef-fe elementa ostendunt eorū qualitates,& ad diuersa loca motiones. Aer enim frigidus est,ignis calidus,aqua humida, & terra sicca: ignis sublime petit, terra imum, aqua & aer in mediis consistunt locis. Quòd autè,præter hęc quatuor elemeta,aliud sit simplex corpus comune infinitū, ex quo orta sint elementa, fieri nò potest. Si enim ex eo orta essent elementa, in illud postremò omnia resoluerētur. Deinde si hoc ipsum elementorum unū esset, profecto in Universo quinque elemeta essent. Atqui plura quàm quatuor esse, non constat.
units.tr: Since the science of nature deals with magnitudes, motion and time, and each of these must be either finite or infinite, it follows that the one who treats the science of nature should inquire whether the infinite exists, and what it is. First, then, we should understand whether infinity belongs to some nature as an essence, or as an accident belonging to it per se, or whether it belongs to neither. If it is an essence, then, judging from the things that fall under the senses, it is clear that body is infinite in magnitude. But this cannot be. For if the definition of body is that which is finite by its extremity and surface, then certainly an infinite body is in no way possible. Whoever wishes to use the more physical arguments will also demonstrate that there is no infinite body, whether it is simple or compounded of several. A body would not be infinite if the elements of which it consists are finite in number. But not all of them can be infinite, since in the universe not even several things can be infinite. For would one thing fill everything? Further, no infinite can arise from infinites, since several infinites cannot exist. Moreover, if one of the elements were infinite and the others finite, then that one infinite would surely consume the other, finite ones, since they are contraries. For contraries destroy one another, since they act upon and are acted upon by each other. And that which is infinite will have the greater power of acting, so the rest will be abolished by it. But that the elements are contraries is shown by their qualities and by their motions to different places. Air is cold, fire hot, water moist, and earth dry; fire seeks the heights, earth the lowest place, and water and air remain in intermediate places. But that, besides these four elements, there should be some other simple, common, infinite body from which the elements arose, cannot happen. For if the elements arose from it, all things would finally be resolved back into it. Further, if this very thing were one of the elements, then in the universe there would be five elements. But it is not agreed that there are more than four.

units.la: Præterea nullum omnino esse Corpus infinitū, quod sub sensum cadat, facilè ex his perspici potest. Primùm omne corpus sensile alicubi, natura duce, sit, oportet. Est enim suus cuique datus à Natura locus, qui idè est & partis, & totius: ut totius terræ & uni° glebæ, ignis itè, & eius scintillæ idè locus est. Sed infinito corpori nullus locus attribui potest. Fieri neqt qn paria sint locus & corpus. Neq; etiā ullus maior locus est, q̃ quātū satis sit ad corpus recipiēdum: nęc corpus maius loco: alioqui aut vacuum erit, aut huiusmodi cor-pus suapte natura nullum occupabit locum. Deinde omnis locus aliquo in corpore sit o-portet. Nam vbi nullum corpus est, ibi nul-lus locus. Sed si aliquod corpus esset, in quo infinitus esset locus, profecto [illegible, ~4 letters]ul duo infi-nita essent corpora. Fieri enim non potest, ut simul & infinitum corpus dicatur, & aliquis locus corpore definitus sit. Præterea omne corpus, quod sub sensum cadit, vel grave est, vel leue. Quod si quidem graue sit, deorsum suo pondere feretur, sin leue, sursum natura. At fieri non potest, si infinitum est, ut deorsum feratur, & sursum. Qui(quæso)fieri potest, ut rei infinitæ alia pars in superiore loco sit, alia in inferiore, alia denique in medio? Ex quibus constat nullum locum corpus, quod infinitum est, occupare posse. Sed si nulla res plane infinita sit, multa con-sequi incommoda videbuntur. Temporis enim principium quoddam erit & finis, ac ma-gnitudines in alias magnitudines non diuidi poterunt, nec numerus erit infinitus. Sed hęc omnia sunt infinita, non actu, sed potentia. Nulla enim magnitudo actu ac reipsa est infinita, sed duntaxat diuisione. Numerus etiā sit potestate infinitus, adiectione. Quod si dixerit quispiam idem esse infinitum potesta-te, & infinitum actu, propterea quod in æternis esse, & posse esse non differant: ei respondendum erit quidpiam potestate esse duobus modis, uno cùm ipsa potestas in actum redu-citur: sic æs potestate statua est, propterea quòd statua futurum sit artificis opera: altero, cum ipsa potestas cum imperfecto actu semper coniuncta est, quomodo infinitum potestate dicitur[?]. Huiusmodi autem potestate infinitas in iis omnibus inest, quæ esse dicuntur, non solùm quòd sint actu, sed etiam perpetuò fiant, cuiusmodi dies festi sunt, qui nō tantùm esse dicuntur cum celebrantur, sed quòd in posterum celebrandi sint, in quibus præsens actus futuri initium est. Omnino etiam infinitum potestate ex eo dicitur, quòd aliud semper & aliud accipiatur: atque id quod ex eo accipitur semper infinitum est. Ac tale infinitum non quasi certa quædam ac definita natura accipi debet, qualis homo est, sed quemadmodum dies festus, quem esse dicimus, non quòd aliquam habeat essentiam constantem & permanentem, sed quia perpetua quadam successione & vicissitudi-ne & oriatur & occidat: ac quanquam id fi-nitum est quod accipitur, semper ei aliud succedit. Hoc tamen interest inter infinitatem magnitudinis, numeri, temporis & rerum naturalium generationis, quòd in magnitudine id semper remanet quod ex ea sumptū est: sed in tempore & generatione non remanet, sed effluit. Nihil enim ex tempore remanet præter momentum, quod nunc di-citur: & in generatione id quod generatum est,corrumpitur. Ac semper generatio rerū, quæ natura constant, perdurat, propterea cp[?] unius corruptio,alterius generatio est, & vice versa. Nunquā etiam tempus deficit,quoniam de motu,id quod posterius est, semper priori succedit. Præterea magnitudo[?] infinita est diuisione: numerus vero adiectione: quoniam detractione in unitatem terminatur. Ad hæc infinitum potentia non idem est in motu,magnitudine,& tempore[?]Motus enim propter magnitudine, quæ eo prior est, infinitus dicitur: tempus vero propter motum,quę sequitur,& cuius affectio est. Quoniam autem id infinitum est, cuius semper aliquid restat, præter id quod sumptum est, ideo nonnulli annulum esse infinitum dicut; quod semper aliquid præterea in illo sumi possit: sed non proprie imò quadam simili-tudine. Nam in vero proprioque infinito nunquā idem accipi potest,sed semper quod diuersum est. At in circulo semper idem re-sumitur,ac recurrit. Itaque infinitum ratio-ne quantitatis sumptum, id est, cuius semper aliquid extrà est. Cuius autem nihil extra accipi potest,id non infinitum est,sed perfectū & totum. Sic enim totū,id est,cui nulla pars deest,vt homo,vt arca. Totum igitur & vniuersum id sit,extra quod nihil est: cui verò aliquid deest,id totum non est, quoniam totum aut idem est quod perfectū , aut vtrius-que natura finitima est. Perfectum porro ni-
units.tr: Moreover, it can easily be seen from these points that no infinite body exists which falls under the senses. First, every sensible body must be somewhere, under the guidance of nature. For nature gives each thing its own place, which is the same for a part and for the whole: as the place of the whole earth and of a single clod is the same, and likewise the place of fire and of its spark is the same. But no place can be assigned to an infinite body. Nor can place and body be equal, nor is there any place larger than is sufficient to receive a body, nor a body larger than its place; otherwise either there will be a void, or such a body by its nature will occupy no place. Further, every place must be in some body, for where there is no body there is no place. But if there were some body in which the place was infinite, then surely there would be two infinite bodies. For it cannot be that one infinite body is spoken of while some place is still bounded by a body. Moreover, every body that falls under the senses is either heavy or light. If it is heavy, it is carried downward by its weight; if light, upward by nature. But it cannot happen, if it is infinite, that it is carried both downward and upward. How, I ask, can it happen that one part of an infinite thing is in a higher place, another in a lower, and another finally in the middle? From these considerations it is clear that a body which is infinite cannot occupy any place. [illegible] But if no thing at all were infinite, many inconveniences would seem to follow. For time would have some beginning and end, magnitudes could not be divided into other magnitudes, and number would not be infinite. Yet all of these are infinite, not actually but potentially. For no magnitude is actually and in reality infinite, but only by division; number too is potentially infinite, by addition. But if someone should say that the infinite in potency and the infinite in act are the same, since in eternal things being and being able to be do not differ, then it must be answered that something is in potency in two ways. In one way, when the potency is reduced into act, as bronze is potentially a statue, because it will become a statue through the work of the craftsman. In the other way, when the potency is always joined with an imperfect act; in this way the infinite is said to be in potency. Infinity in potency is found in all those things which are said to exist, not only because they are actual, but because they are continually coming into being, such as festival days, which are said to exist not only while they are being celebrated, but because they are to be celebrated in the future, and in them the present act is the beginning of what is to come. Altogether, the infinite is also said to be in potency from this, that always one thing after another is taken, and that which is taken from it is always infinite. Such an infinite must be understood not as some certain and definite nature, such as a man is, but as a festival day, which we say exists not because it has some constant and permanent essence, but because by a perpetual succession and alternation it both rises and sets; and although what is taken is finite, another always succeeds it. Yet there is this difference between the infinity of magnitude, of number, of time, and of the generation of natural things: in magnitude what has been taken from it remains, but in time and generation it does not remain, but flows away. For nothing of time remains except the moment that is now called present; and in generation, what has been generated is corrupted. Yet the generation of things which consist by nature always endures, so that the corruption of one is the generation of another, and vice versa. Nor does time ever fail, since in motion what is later always succeeds what is earlier. Moreover, magnitude is infinite by division, number by addition, since by subtraction number ends in unity. Besides, the infinite in potency is not the same in motion, in magnitude and in time. For motion is called infinite on account of the magnitude which is prior to it; time is called infinite on account of the motion which follows it and of which it is an affection. Since that is infinite of which something always remains beyond what has been taken, some say that a ring is infinite, because something further can always be taken from it; but this is not properly so, only by a certain likeness. For in the true and proper infinite the same thing can never be taken, but always something different; whereas in a circle the same thing is always taken again and recurs. Therefore the infinite, taken with respect to quantity, is that of which something always lies outside. But that of which nothing can be taken outside is not infinite but perfect and whole. For the whole, that is, that to which no part is lacking, is like a man or a chest. Therefore the whole and the universal is that outside of which nothing exists; but that to which something is lacking is not a whole, since the whole is either the same as the perfect or is of a nature bordering on it. units.la: De loco.
units.tr: On place.

units.la: CORPORA quæcunque mouetur mutuò sibi succedunt, & è loco in locum mo- uetur, alicubi esse necesse est. Propterea eorum quædam sursum feruntur, alia verò deorsum: quandoquidem sursum & deorsum loci genera sunt, ac reliquæ differentiæ, nempe dextrorsum, sinistrorsum, ante & pone, in quibus corpora conseruantur. Vnum quodque enim corpus natura in suum fertur locum, vt ab eo conseruetur, & ibi quiescat. Vis autem loci, etsi attractrix est, non sic corpus attrahit, vt magnes ferrum, sed vt finis. Itaque in rerum natura locus est, id in quo aliquod corpus collocatur, vt conseruetur. Vt autem magis ac magis loci ratio innotescat, quot modis aliquid in aliquo esse dicatur, explicandum est. Vno quidem modo, vt digitus in manu, pars in toto. Alio, vt totū in partibus. Deinde vt species in genere, homo in animali. Posthæc vt genus in specie. Præterea vt valetudo in calidis naturis, & frigidis. Quinetiam, vt forma in materia. Adhæc, vt res Galliæ in Gallorum Rege: & id quod primùm mouetur in primo mouente. Insuper, id quod alicuius gratia est, atque fit in bono consistit, atque omnino in fine. Maxime autem omnium, & proprie id in aliquo est, quod in vase consistit, & omnino in loco. Hinc tamen oritur quæstio an aliquid in se post esse, necne, an vero nihil prorsus in se sit, quod vis, aut nusquam, aut in alio sit? Diluetur hoc dubium, si id in se esse dixerimus, cuius vna pars in alia est. Hoc enim pacto totum in se est, eo quod ex partibus constat. Verum quod hoc modo in se est, id non per se, sed ex accidente, & per aliud, nempe per suas partes, quæ non per se in loco sunt, quoniam vna in alia est. Sic homo in se est, propterea quod totus ex anima & corpore constet. Nihil igitur per se in se esse potest. Verumtamen locus non in alio est tanquam in loco, sed vt in naturis calidis valetudo & in frigidis, in quibus vt habitus est, vel vt terminus in eo, quod terminatur. Cæterum vt eorum quæ sunt, quædam potestate esse dicuntur, quædam actu, ita quædam potestate in loco sunt, vt partes corporis similares: aliæ reipsa, cuiusmodi ea sunt, quæ se contingunt, vt in cumulo fit. Vnum quodque etiam naturale corpus, propterea quod, & loco, & accretione moueri potest, per se alicubi est. Cœlum autem nusquam totum in loco est, quandoquidem ab alio nullo corpore continetur. Sed quatenus mouetur, eatenus in loco est, non ratione totius essentiæ ipsius, sed partium, quarum aliæ aliis cohærent. Propterea omnes cœli partes quodámodo, & ex accidente in loco sunt, propterea quòd in illius orbe alia aliam continet & ampleċtitur. Etsi Cœlū in loco est, non tamen alicubi situs est mundus. Quod enim alicubi profecto id extra se aliud habeat in quo contineatur, necesse est. Sed extra Mundum nihil est corporeum. Quam ob causam cœlum omnia suo complexu corpo-ra continet. Verum tamen non locus cœli est, sed eius superficies, quæ id contingit corpus quod moueri potest. Ob eamque cau-sam aqua terram, aër aquam, ignis aërem, cœlum ignem ampleċtitur. Ex quibus perspicuum est non quòduis in loco esse, sed dutaxat ipsum corpus, quod mobile est. Hæc breui de iis quæ in loco esse possunt, dicta sint. Quid deinceps locus sit, explicare licet. Verum in primis ea sunt assumenda, quæ in eum cadere possunt, quorum hoc primum esse debet, nempe locum id, cuius locus est ambire cotinereque, nec aliquid esse eius rei, quæ continetur. Itaque locus nec materia est, neque forma, quæ partes sunt ipsum corpus constituentes, quod in loco continetur. Alterum autem est, locum proprium nec maiorem esse, nec minorem illo corpore, quod continetur, sed æqualem, quoniam extrinsecus eam omnino ambit, & contingit. Tertium est a nullo corpore locum deseri. Nam quemadmodum omne corpus in loco mouetur, sic in omni loco quoddam corpus est, quandoquidem rerū natura ab inani abhorret. Nihil tamē obstat quōd à corpore locus seiungi possit. Quartum sequitur, quod innuit locū natura loco moueri non posse. Nā si moueri posset, profecto a[illegible, ~3 letters] loci locus esset. Ex quo fieret multa simul esse loca vnius collocati corporis. Id quod proculdubio natura fieri non potest. Postremum est in omni loco superum, vel inferum esse, & natura o[?]-mne corpus ad locum suæ naturæ accommodatum propriūmque ferri: atque in eo vel supero, vel infero quiescere. Cæterum quemadmodum qnædam per se dicuntur, esse nonnulla per accides & aliud, ita alius locus per se dicitur, vt qui proprius est & primus corpus ambit, alius ex accidente, qui communis est & multa simul ambit corpora, vt cœlum, quod cuncta inferiora amplectitur corpora. His autem ita positis constat locum nec materiam esse, nec formam, nec denique corpus vllum, sed corporis continetis superficiem. Si enim continens corpus locus esset, profecto locus non esset immobilis, sed in alium moueri locum posset. Deinde fieret vt locus relocata maior esset. Sed continentis corporis superficies, quæ primo contentum corpus ambit, æqualis est extremæ superficiei corporis locati. Quare locus extremum accidens est non locati corporis, sed continentis. Duæ nanque superficies extremitremitatésque sunt, quæ vnumquodque corpus naturale concludunt & ampleƈtuntur (dempta cœli superficie, quam nullum aliud corpus ambit) vna quidem ipsius loca-ti corporis, altera ambientis, quæ vere proprieque locu⁠s⁠t.
units.tr: Whatever bodies are moved succeed one another in turn and pass from place to place, so they must be somewhere. For this reason some of them are carried upwards and others downwards, since up and down are kinds of place, as are the remaining differences, namely right, left, before and behind, in which bodies are preserved. Each body is carried by nature to its own place, so that it may be preserved there and rest. The power of place, though it is attractive, does not draw a body as a magnet draws iron, but as an end does. Thus in the nature of things, place is that in which a body is situated so that it may be preserved. To make the account of place clearer, we must explain in how many ways something is said to be in something. In one way, as a finger is in the hand, a part in a whole. In another way, as the whole is in its parts. Then, as a species is in its genus, man in animal. Afterwards, as a genus is in its species. Again, as health is in hot and cold natures. Moreover, as form is in matter. In addition, as the affairs of Gaul are in the King of the Gauls, and as that which is first moved is in the first mover. Further, that which exists for the sake of something, and which is made, consists in the good, and altogether in the end. But most of all, and properly, that is in something which is contained in a vessel, and altogether in a place. From this, however, arises the question whether anything can be in itself or not; or whether nothing at all is in itself, but whatever it is, it is either nowhere or in another. This doubt is resolved if we say that a thing is in itself when one of its parts is in another. For in this way the whole is in itself, because it consists of parts. But what is in itself in this way is not so per se, but accidentally and through another, namely through its parts, which are not per se in place, since one is in another. Thus man is in himself, because as a whole he consists of soul and body. Nothing therefore can be per se in itself. Yet place is not in another as in a place, but as health is in hot and cold natures, in which it is as a state, or as a limit is in that which it bounds. Moreover, as some of the things that exist are said to be in potency and others in act, so some things are in place potentially, like the similar parts of a body, and others actually, such as those things which touch one another, as happens in a heap. Every natural body also, since it can be moved both by place and by growth, is per se somewhere. The heaven, however, is not wholly in place anywhere, since no other body contains it. But insofar as it is moved, so far it is in place, not in respect of the whole of its essence, but of its parts, some of which cohere with others. Therefore all the parts of the heaven are in place in a certain way and accidentally, because in its sphere one part contains and embraces another. Although the heaven is in place, the world is not situated anywhere. For whatever is somewhere must necessarily have outside itself something else in which it is contained. But outside the World there is nothing corporeal. For this reason the heaven contains all bodies in its embrace. Yet the place of the heaven is not the heaven itself, but its surface, which touches the body that can be moved. And for this reason water embraces earth, air embraces water, fire embraces air, and heaven embraces fire. From these things it is clear that not just anything is in place, but only the body itself which is mobile. Let these things be said briefly about what can be in place. Now we may explain what place is. First, however, those things must be assumed which can fall under it. Of these, the first must be this: that place is that which surrounds and contains the thing of which it is the place, and is not any part of what is contained. Thus place is neither matter nor form, which are the parts constituting the body itself that is contained in place. The second is that the proper place is neither greater nor smaller than the body it contains, but equal to it, since it entirely surrounds and touches it on the outside. The third is that place is never vacated by a body. For just as every body is moved in place, so in every place there is some body, since the nature of things abhors the void. Nevertheless, nothing prevents place from being separated from a body. The fourth follows, which implies that place cannot by nature be moved in place. For if it could be moved, it would certainly be the place of a place. From this it would follow that one placed body would have many places at once, which without doubt cannot happen by nature. The last is that in every place there is an up or a down, and that by nature every body is carried to the place suited and proper to its nature, and rests there, whether above or below. But just as some things are said to be per se and others per accidens and through another, so one place is said to be per se, namely the proper and first place which surrounds the body, and another accidentally, which is common and surrounds many bodies at once, such as the heaven, which embraces all the lower bodies. With these points laid down, it is established that place is neither matter, nor form, nor finally any body at all, but the surface of the containing body. For if the containing body were place, then place would certainly not be immobile, but could be moved into another place. Then it would follow that the place would be greater when relocated. But the surface of the containing body, which first surrounds the contained body, is equal to the extreme surface of the located body. Therefore place is an extreme accident not of the located body, but of the containing body. For there are two surfaces, or extremities, which enclose and surround each natural body (excepting the surface of the heaven, which no other body surrounds): one belonging to the located body itself, the other to the surrounding body, and this second one is truly and properly place.

units.la: CAP. XIIII.
units.tr: CAP. XIIII.

units.la: De vacuo ex Veterum philosophorum sententia.
units.tr: On the void according to the opinion of the ancient philosophers.

units.la: Lim motum ad locum, accretionem decretionémque nó fieri posse absque vacuo, nonnulli veterum philosophorum existimabát, propterea quòd nihil præterea accipere possit, quod plenum est. Si enim aliquid acciperet (inquiebant) non solùm duo corpora, sed etiam plura, simul in eodem esse, futurum est. Præterea quod corpus crescit, id maiorem locum occupet, necesse est. Id quod sane, nisi in vacuo fieri non potest. Deinde alimentū, quod corpus est in pleno non accipitur, alioqui corpus in corpus subiret. Id quod natura fieri nò potest. Itaque vacuum, in quo alimentum recipiatur, adsit, necesse est. Idem ex cinere, quo plenum aliquod vas est, perspici posse dicebant, qui tantum aquę recipit, quantum vas inane. Sed ante explicandum est, quid per vacuum intellexerint, quàm eorū rationes refellere oporteat. Existimabant enim omne corpus in loco ef-fe, & locum, ubi nullum corpus est, nomina-bant vacuum, dicebantque ibi nihil esse, ubi non effet corpus. Itaque uno modo vacuum illis id erat quod tractabilis corporis nō ple-num est. Sed tractabile corp[illegible, ~2 letters]omne leuita-tis grauitatisque particeps est. Quare necef-sario in loco est. Altero modo vacuu id esse dicebant, in quo nulla effet effentia corpo-rea. Quamobrem corporum materiam vacuum esse exiftimarunt, sed male quidem, quoniam materia a corporibus, quibus sub-iicitur, ut sint, non separatur. Vacuum igitur a corporibus feparabile quaerebant, & cor-porum spatium, in quo moveretur ipsa. Sed primum adversus veterum rationes, dicimus vacuum in rerum natura non necessarium esse: quandoquidem in motu ad locum corpora mutuo sibi cedunt, nec ullum est interea fe-parabile spatium. Possunt etiam corpora, quae densa sunt, tenuia extrudere, & eorum loco succedere. Propterea aerem aqua pel-lit, & eius locum occupat. Quod autem di-xerint corpus, quod crescit, maiorem locum occupare, nihil demonstrarunt, quoniam cor-pora non solum alius corporis additione, quod alimentum est, sed etiam alteratione crescunt. Nisi enim alimentum alteraretur, & in substantiam eius, quod alitur, mutare-tur, procul dubio in se subirent duo corpora, & simul in eodem loco essent. Aqua denique,quam ipsi proponebant,aut in totum cinerem infunditur, aut minimè. At fi in totû cinerem infundatur, duo corpora in eodem loco sint,necefle est. Id quod profecto huiusmodi philosophis absurdum fuit. Igitur non in totum circumfem[?] aqua infunditur, sed tota ab eo imbibitur absorbetúrque, propterea quòd cinis corpus admodum fit siccum. Propinde nihil mirum est, fi tantum aquæ absorbeat, quantum inane vas continet.
units.tr: Some of the ancient philosophers thought that motion to a place, and increase and decrease, cannot happen without a void, because a body cannot receive anything else when it is already full. For (they said) if it received something, not only two bodies but several would be in the same place at once, which is impossible. Moreover, a body that grows must occupy a larger place, and this, surely, cannot happen except in a void. Again, nourishment, which is a body, is not received into a full body, since otherwise one body would pass into another; and nature cannot bring this about. Therefore a void must be present in which the nourishment may be received. They also said that the same can be seen from ashes in a vessel which is full: it receives as much water as an empty vessel does. But before refuting their arguments we must explain what they meant by the void. For they held that every body is in a place, and they called a place where no body is a void, and they said that there is nothing where there is no body. Thus in one sense the void for them was that which is not filled by a tangible body. But every tangible body partakes of lightness or heaviness, and so it is necessarily in a place. In another sense they said the void is that in which there is no corporeal essence at all. For this reason they thought the matter of bodies was a void, but wrongly, since matter is not separated from the bodies to which it is subject in order to exist. Therefore they sought a void separable from bodies, and a space of bodies in which the void itself might move. But first, against the arguments of the ancients, we say that a void is not necessary in the nature of things: since in motion to a place bodies yield to one another, and in the meantime there is no separable space. Dense bodies can also push out thin ones and take their place; thus water drives out air and occupies its place. As for their claim that a body which grows occupies a larger place, they proved nothing, since bodies grow not only by the addition of another body, which is nourishment, but also by alteration. For unless the nourishment were altered and changed into the substance of what is nourished, undoubtedly two bodies would pass into one another and be in the same place at once. Finally, the water which they themselves proposed is either poured into the whole of the ashes or not at all. But if it is poured into the whole of the ashes, two bodies must be in the same place, which is certainly absurd for philosophers of this sort. Therefore the water is not poured around the ashes as a whole, but is wholly soaked up and absorbed by them, because ash is a very dry body. Hence it is no wonder if it absorbs as much water as an empty vessel holds.

units.la: CAP. XV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XV.

units.la: Motum ad locum Vacuum esse, non satis ostendere.
units.tr: That motion does not sufficiently show the void to be a place.

units.la: POSTHAEC vacuum nō locum esse his rationibus cōstat. Primum fi vacuū locus est, profecto id causa eius erit,quod mouetur. Sed vacuum nullius corporis motus causam esse ex his constat. Primùm motus elementorum causa esse non potest. Unicuique enim simplicium corporum motus a Natura tributus est,ut igni in sublime ferri,terræ deorsum & ad medium. Quòd si elementis motum non adferat vacuum, concreta ex eis ab eo moueri non possunt. Præterea si vacuum locus est corpore carens,quónam (quæso) ferretur id quod in eo collocatur? Neque profecto magis hanc in partem, quàm in illam mouebitur. Atque hoc modo corporum, quæ natura constant, nullus erit motus. Deinde omnis motus qui ad locum e loco est, aut sursum sit, aut deorsum. Atqui omnibus loci differentiis vacuum caret. Propterea in vacuo nullum corpus moueri potest. Quòd si in vacuo nullus natura motus est, nec profecto is erit, qui vi, & contra naturam fit: quandoquidem quod natura est id prius eo est, quod contra naturam existit. Imò verò tantum abest vt in vacuo corpora moueantur, cùm quietis eorum magis ipsum causa sit. Nihil enim in eo est, quo magis, aut minus corpus aliquod moueatur: quandoquidem vacuum & infinitum reipsa non distiuguuntur. Propterea quò infinitum est, eò nihil infrà, nihil supra, nihil denique medij loci relinquitur. Quò præterea vacuum est, eò inter superum & inferum nihil interest. Nam quèmadmodum nihili nulla est differentia, sic vacuum omnino non τὸ ὄν est, sed eius priuatio. Præterea φορά, aut nulla est vsquam natura: aut si qua est, profecto vacuum in rerum natura non est. Sed corporum, quæ natura constat, mutatio ad locum est. Igitur nullum vacuum. Itaque ex iis, quæ commemorata sunt, perspicuum est, nullum à corporibus separatum esse vacuum, nec ipsum in raro corpore, neque potestate alibi, nisi quispiam id omnino vacuum appellari velit, quod mutationis è loco in causa est. Sed hoc modo gratuis & leuis corporis materia, quà ex parte huiushuiusmodi est, vacuum erit. Materia autem huiusmodi vna est contrariorum caloris (inquam) & frigoris, & aliarum contrarietatum, quae τὸ ὂν potestate est, & ex qua τὸ ὂν actu fit. Sed huiusmodi materia à nullo corpore separabilis est, sed duntaxat ab eo ratione diuersa. Estque vna numero caloris & frigoris, magni & parui corporis, densi & rari, grauis atque leuis, duri & mollis, & aliorum huiusmodi. Hæc quidem de vacuo, quatenus id sit, & non sit, hoc modo paucis explicata sunt.
units.tr: Furthermore, that the void is not a place is established by the following reasons. First, if the void is a place, then surely it will be the cause of that which is moved. But that the void is the cause of no body's motion is clear from these points. First, it cannot be the cause of the motion of the elements. For nature has assigned to each of the simple bodies its own motion: fire to be carried upwards, earth downwards and towards the centre. And if the void does not impart motion to the elements, the compounds made from them cannot be moved by it. Moreover, if the void is a place lacking body, whither (I ask) would that which is placed in it be carried? It would certainly move no more in this direction than in that. In this way there would be no motion of bodies which consist by nature. Next, every motion from place to place is either upward or downward. But the void lacks all the differences of place. Therefore no body can be moved in the void. And if in the void there is no natural motion, then surely there will be no motion that happens by force and against nature, since what is according to nature is prior to what exists against nature. Indeed, far from bodies being moved in the void, the void is rather the cause of their rest. For there is nothing in it by which a body is moved more or less, since the void and the infinite are not really distinguished. For because it is infinite, nothing lies below, nothing above, and finally nothing of the middle place is left. Moreover, insofar as it is void, there is no difference between above and below. For just as there is no difference in nothing, so the void is not being [τὸ ὄν] at all, but its privation. Furthermore, locomotion [φορά] either is nowhere in nature, or, if there is any, the void certainly is not in the nature of things. But the change of bodies which consist by nature is a change of place. Therefore there is no void. Thus from what has been recalled it is evident that no void is separated from bodies, nor is it in a rare body, nor in potentiality elsewhere, unless someone wishes to call that void which is the cause of change of place. But in this way the matter of a heavy and light body, insofar as it is of this kind, would be void. Matter of this kind is one, of contraries (I mean heat and cold, and other contrarieties), which is being [τὸ ὄν] in potentiality and from which being in actuality [τὸ ὄν] comes about. But such matter cannot be separated from any body; it differs from it only in definition. And it is one in number: of heat and cold, of large and small body, dense and rare, heavy and light, hard and soft, and others of this kind. These things have been briefly explained about the void, insofar as it is and is not.

units.la: De tempore.
units.tr: On time.

units.la: EQVITVR deinceps vt de tem-pore differamus, quandoquidem omnis motus & mutatio in tem-pore fit. Verum in primis quærendum est sitne tempus in iis, quæ sunt, an vero in iis, quæ non sunt. Deinde quænam eius natura sit. At illud quidem omnino esse, aut vix, his rationibus quispiam suspicabitur. Aliud enim eius fuit, & non est, aliud futurum, & nondum existit. Atqui nihil in rerum natura esse potest, quod ex iis constet, quæ non sunt. Præterea si quid sit tempus, quod in partes diuidi possit, certè cum est, tum aut omnes eius partes esse, aut nonnullas, par est.
units.tr: Next, we proceed to discuss time, since every motion and change takes place in time. First, however, we must ask whether time is among the things that exist or among those that do not, and then what its nature is. Some will suspect, on these grounds, that time does not exist at all, or hardly exists. One part of it has been and is no more; another is future and does not yet exist. But nothing in the nature of things can consist of things that do not exist. Moreover, if time is something that can be divided into parts, then when it exists, all of its parts, or some of them, must surely exist as well.

units.la: Sed temporis partes aliæ sunt præteritæ, futuræ aliæ,ita vt nulla adsit.Ipsum autè nunc, & momentum,partem temporis non esse,sed tis perspicuum est. Nam totum pars metitur. At ipsum nunc nihil metitur, quoniam indiuiduum est. Præterea totum ex partibus constet,necesse est. Sed tempus ex pluribus nunc constare non potest, quoniam simul nō sunt plura momenta,sed vnū duntaxat,quod præteritum à futuro distinguit. Adhæc si plures res simul partes temporis essent, profecto vna ab alia necessario contineretur, perinde atque minus à maiori. At simul esse nequeunt illud nunc quod corruptum est & antea fuit, & aliud nunc,quod præsens est. Nec fieri potest, vt id nunc, quod præteritum est, & iam abiit,in alio nunc infit,quod est. Adde quod plura nunc veluti plura puncta sunt. Et quemadmodum plura puncta simul esse non possunt in linea,ita in tempore plura nunc simul non cohærent, igitur nunc non metitur tempus,nec constituit. Deinde si in eodem nunc prius esset & posterius,profecto ea quæ ante plura annorum milia fuerunt facta, cum iis simul erunt, quæ hodie sunt, nec quicquam alio prius erit, nec posterius. Hæ sunt quidem dubitationes, quæ de tempore, afferri possunt. Quidnam autem tempus sit, non minus obscurum multis videtur. Nonnulli enim veterum tempus esse cœli conuersionem dixerunt,alij sphæram,quorum sententia non vera ra est. Nam tempus non est conuersio & motus, sed quidpiam eius. Si enim tempus esset conuersio, profecto plura simul essent tepo-ra, quoniam plures sunt orbium cœli conuersiones. Neque etiam tepus ulla mutatio est. Omnis enim mutatio in eo est, quod mutatur & mouetur. At tempus non solum est in iis quæ mouetur, sed ubique & apud omnia, quæ natura constant. Præterea omnis muta-tio aut celerior esse potest, aut tardior: id quod tempori nō euenit, imo vero quod tardum est, & velox tempore definitur. Nam id velox dicitur, quod breui tempore magnum percurrit spatium: tardum contra, quod lōgo paruum. Eorū etiam sententia, qui tempus esse vniuersi sphæram dixerunt, adeo insulsa est & ridicula, ut ne ulla quidem refutatione digna videatur. Iam vero quid tempus sit, videndum est. At, in primis tempus absque motu mutationeque non esse nec intelligi, scire nobis licet: quandoquidem tempus motus affectio est. Ac motus omnis in a-liqua magnitudine fit. Quoniam autem ma-gnitudo omnis continua est, motus etiam con-tinuus fit, necesse est, & consequenter tepus.
units.tr: But the parts of time are some past and others future, so that none is present. That the now itself, or the moment, is not a part of time, but as is clear: a whole is measured by its part, whereas the now measures nothing, since it is indivisible. Moreover, a whole must necessarily consist of parts, yet time cannot consist of several nows, since several moments do not exist together; there is only one, which separates the past from the future. Besides, if several things were parts of time at once, one of them would necessarily be contained by another, just as the less is contained by the greater. But that now which has perished and was before, and another now which is present, cannot exist together. Nor can that now which is past and has already gone, come to be within another now which is present. Add that several nows are like several points. Just as several points cannot be together in a line, so several nows cannot cohere together in time. Therefore the now neither measures nor constitutes time. Again, if there were a before and an after in the same now, then those things that were done many thousands of years ago would exist together with those that are today, and nothing would be before or after anything else. These are the doubts that can be raised about time. What time is, however, seems no less obscure to many. Some of the ancients said that time is the revolution of the heavens, others that it is the sphere of the heavens, but their opinion is not true. For time is not the revolution or motion itself, but something of it. If time were the revolution, then several times would exist at once, since there are many revolutions of the heavenly spheres. Nor is time any change. For every change is in that which is changed and moved, whereas time is not only in what moves, but everywhere and among all things that have natural existence. Moreover, every change can be faster or slower, which does not happen with time; rather, the slow and the swift are defined by time. For that is called swift which traverses a great space in a short time, and slow, on the contrary, which traverses a small space in a long time. The opinion of those who said that time is the sphere of the universe is so foolish and ridiculous that it does not seem worthy of any refutation. Now we must see what time is. First of all, we may know that time cannot exist or be understood without motion and change, since time is an affection of motion. And all motion takes place in some magnitude. Since every magnitude is continuous, motion too must necessarily be continuous, and consequently time.

units.la: Præterea omnis magnitudo diuidua est, cuius una pars prior est, altera posterior. Proinde simili ratione motus duæ sunt partes, quarum una prior est, & altera posterior, quę in temporis constitutione per nunc coniun-guntur. Si enim utranque partem motus n[?] animadvertimus proculdubio nullum tem-pus intercessisse putamus, quemadmodū eis euenit à somno expergefactis, qui nullâ fuisse factam mutationem percipiunt. Tales enim per nunc prius & posterius non coniun-gunt, nec unum ex his duobus constituunt, quod tempus est. Itaque cum in motu prius & posterius numeramus, tum naturam tem-poris & explicamus & percipimus. Proinde tempus numerus est motus secundū prius & posterius: numerus (inquā) numeratus. Duplex enim numerus est, vnus quo numeramus, vt binarius, ternarius: alter numeratus, cuius vnitates non simplices sunt, sed rei alicuius definito generi coniunctæ, veluti ea sunt quæ numeramus, vt decem viri. In motu prius & posterius, quæ per nunc continuantur, & tempus constituunt, sunt huiusmodi. Nam in motu tempus nihil aliud est, quàm prius & posterius, quoniam eius partes sunt. Qua autem ex parte tempus numerus est, eadem multum ac paucū dicitur. Ex qua verò continuum, ex ea longum, & breue. Non autem velox dicitur, neque tardū, quoniam nullus est velox numerus, aut tardus. Præterea vt idem motus ac vnus iterum atque iterum esse potest, sic idem tempus vnumque redit, vt annus, ver, autumnus. Nec solum tempore motum metimur, sed etiam motu tempus, propterea quod se mutuo definiant: quandoquidem tempus motum definit, quoniam numerus eius est. Motus etiā ipsum tempus. Nam multum, paucum tempus dicimus ipsum motu metientes. Quod autem motu tempore, & tempus motu metiamur absque ratione fieri non videtur. Magnitudinem enim motus sequitur, & motum tempus, propterea quod haec omnia quanta sunt cōtinua & diuidua. Quare tempus motu[?] metimur, magnitudinem motu, & motum magnitudine. Vt si ambulatio multa fit, viā quoque esse multam expedit, & ambulationem esse multam, si multa fit via. Similiter & tempus multum sit oportet, si multus est motus, & vice versa si multus est motus, multum etiam tempus esse, necesse est. Itaque patet tempus mensuram esse motus. Atque sic ipsum motum metiri, sicut motus magnitudinem, & vlna longitudinem. Ex quo etiam apparet motum in tempore esse, vt & cætera omnia quæ mutantur. Quæcunque autem in tempore sunt, ab eo continentur, necesse est, vt conseruentur. Patiuntur etiam quicquam ab ipso tempore. Quamobrem omnia consumi tempore, & senescere, ac memoriam deleri, homines dicere solent, non autem discere, adolescere, pulchrum euadere: quoniam tempus per se magis corruptionis causa est quàm generationis, quoniā numerus motus est: motus auctus autē id quod inest, extrudit.
units.tr: Moreover, every magnitude is divisible, having one part prior and another posterior. In the same way, motion has two parts, one prior and the other posterior, which are joined by the now in the constitution of time. For if we notice neither part of a motion, we undoubtedly think that no time has intervened, as happens to those awakened from sleep, who perceive that no change was made. For such things do not join before and after through a now, nor do they constitute one of the two, which is time. Therefore, when we count the before and after in motion, we both explain and perceive the nature of time. Thus time is the number of motion according to before and after: a number, I say, that is numbered. For there are two kinds of number: one by which we count, such as two or three, and another that is numbered, whose units are not simple but joined to some definite kind of thing, as the things we count are, for example ten men. The before and after in motion, which are continued through the now and constitute time, are of this kind. For in motion, time is nothing other than before and after, since these are its parts. In so far as time is a number, it is said to be much or little; in so far as it is continuous, it is said to be long or short. It is not called swift or slow, since no number is swift or slow. Moreover, just as the same motion and the same one can recur again and again, so the same time and the same unit return, such as a year, spring, or autumn. We measure not only motion by time but also time by motion, because they define each other: time defines motion, since it is its number, and motion defines time, for we say that time is much or little when we measure it by motion. That we measure motion by time and time by motion does not seem to happen without reason, for time follows the magnitude of motion, and motion follows time, because all these things are continuous and divisible quantities. Thus we measure time by motion, magnitude by motion, and motion by magnitude. Just as, if a walk is long, the road too must be long, and the walk is long if the road is long, so time must be much if motion is much, and conversely, if motion is much, time must also be much. So it is clear that time is the measure of motion, and in this way motion is measured by time, as magnitude is measured by motion, and length by the ell. From this it also appears that motion is in time, as are all other things that change. Moreover, whatever is in time must necessarily be contained by it in order to be preserved. They also suffer something from time itself. Therefore people commonly say that all things are consumed by time, grow old, and their memory is erased, but not that they learn, grow up, or become beautiful, since time is by its nature more a cause of corruption than of generation, because it is the number of motion, and increased motion drives out what is within it.

units.la: CAP. XVII. Universum esse perfectum.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVII. That the universe is perfect.

units.la: HYSICA ratio, & scientia in magnitudinibus, & corporibus, eorumque affectionibus ac mutationibus, & prętercain principiis, quę huiusmodi essentię sunt, tota fere versari videtur[?]. Eorum enim quæ natura constant[?], alia sunt corpora & magnitudines, alia eorum omnium principia. Magnitudines autem & corpora dividi possunt, propterea quodCon-tinuata sint. Nihil enim natura dividi potest, nisi continuatum sit. Continuatum quidem, id est, quod in ea, quæ semper & infinite dividi possunt, dividuum est. At vero huiusmodi omnes magnitudines sunt, quarum duæ dicuntur imperfectæ, nimirum linea & superficies, una perfecta, quæ corpus est. Linea autem in unam dimensionem dividi potest, in duas superficies, in tres corpus, nempe in longitudinem, latitudinem & altitudinem, propterea quod omnibus constet dimensionibus. Nec præter has magnitudines alia invenitur, quoniam ipsum universum tribus duntaxat definitum est, nimirum fine, medio & principio, quæ universi ac totius numerū absolvunt, complectuntur[?]que. Universum autem & totum, atque perfectum non forma & specie differunt, sed duntaxat subiecto & materia. teria. Nam omne discretæ quantitatis est; totum continuæ,perfectum vtriusque. Quod autem omnes magnitudines sint continuatæ & diuiduæ, satis constat. Alia enim, vt linea, ex vna parte diuidua est: quædam vt superficies, ex duabus: tertia ex tribus. Nam corpus, omni ex parte diuiduum est: linea autem in longitudinem, superficies vero in longitudinem & latitudine diuidi potest. Omnes igitur magnitudines diuiduæ sunt, & continuatæ, quoniam omnes earum partes in vnū cohærent. Itaque vnumquodque corporum, quæ partis speciem habent, nedum totius, omnes habeat dimensiones, necesse est. Ex quo perspicue constat ipsum omne ac vniuersum esse perfectum.
units.tr: Natural philosophy and science are concerned almost entirely with magnitudes and bodies, with their affections and changes, and besides these with the principles which are of this kind of being. For of the things that consist by nature, some are bodies and magnitudes, and others are the principles of all of them. Now magnitudes and bodies can be divided, because they are continuous; for nothing can be divided by nature unless it is continuous. Continuous, that is, that which is divisible in such a way that it can be divided always and without end. Indeed, all magnitudes of this kind are such that two of them are called imperfect, namely the line and the surface, while one is perfect, which is the body. A line can be divided in one dimension, a surface into two, and a body into three, namely length, breadth and height, because it consists of all dimensions. Nor is any other magnitude found besides these, since the universe itself is defined by three things only, namely end, middle and beginning, which complete and embrace the number of the universe and of the whole. The universe, the whole and the perfect do not differ in form or kind, but only in subject and matter. For everything belongs to discrete quantity, the whole to continuous quantity, and the perfect to both. Now that all magnitudes are continuous and divisible is quite clear. For some, like the line, are divisible in one direction; some, like the surface, in two; a third kind in three. For a body is divisible on every side; a line only in length, and a surface in length and breadth. Therefore all magnitudes are divisible and continuous, since all their parts cohere in one. Thus it is necessary that each of the bodies, which have the appearance of a part, let alone of a whole, should have all dimensions. From this it is plainly clear that the all and the universe itself is perfect.

units.la: Cap. XVIII.
units.tr: Chapter 18.

units.la: Motum cœli omnium aliorum primum & causam esse.
units.tr: That the motion of the heavens is the first and cause of all others.

units.la: OSTHAEC de Vniuersi mundique natura, vtrum magnitudine infinita sit, ne finita, videdum est. Verum in primis de partibus eius speciatim dicendum nobis a motu incipietibus, esse videtur. Omnia nanque corpora, quæ natura constant, moueri possunt. Etenim eis natura est principium motus & status. At vero omnis motus, quo per locum quid moue tur, aut rectus est, aut rotundus, aut denique ex utroque mistus. Rotundus autem is est, qui circum medium fit, & conuersio dicitur. Rectus verò, quo sursum aliquid fertur, aut deorsum. Atque is, quo sursum itur, e medio universi oritur, qui verò deorsum fit, in ipsū medium vergit. Quare simplicium huiusmodi motuum alium e medio, alium ad ipsum medium, tertium circum idem medium fieri expedit. Quoniam autē corporum alia sunt simplicia, alia ex his concreta, motus quoque quibus ad locum ea mouentur, alij simplices sint, alij compositi, necesse est: quorum simplices corporum sunt simplicium, compositi verò concretorum, quae quodammodo mouentur vi ipsius simplicis, quod in eis dominatur, & vincit. Itaque simplicium corporū aliquod est, quod suapte natura circum medium voluitur & coelum est: caetera verò vel e medio in sublime feruntur, vel in medium & deorsum. Ut ignis & aer sursum mouetur, terra verò & aqua deorsum. Coelum autem solum circum universi medium versatur, cuius motio caeterarum prima est, & perfectis-fima, propterea quod in sphaera fiat, omnium figurarum, quae in solidis sunt, perfectissima. Id enim quod perfectū est, natura prius imperfecto sit, necesse est. Itaque Coeli motus aliorum omnium primus est, & causa.
units.tr: Next, we must consider whether the universe and the nature of the world are infinite or finite in magnitude. But first it seems right to speak of its parts in particular, beginning from motion. For all bodies that consist by nature can be moved, since nature is for them the principle of motion and of rest. Now every motion by which something is moved through place is either straight, or circular, or finally a mixture of both. A circular motion is that which takes place around a middle point, and is called revolution. A straight motion is that by which something is carried upwards or downwards. The upward motion arises from the centre of the universe, while the downward motion tends towards the centre itself. Hence it is fitting to recognise that of such simple motions, one is from the centre, another towards the centre, and a third around the same centre. Since some bodies are simple and others compounded from these, the motions by which they are moved to place must also be some simple and some compound, which is necessarily so: the simple motions belong to simple bodies, the compound to compounded bodies, which are moved in a certain way by the power of the simple element that rules and prevails in them. Thus there is one simple body which by its own nature revolves around the centre, and this is the heaven; the others are carried either upwards from the centre or downwards towards the centre. Thus fire and air move upwards, while earth and water move downwards. The heaven alone turns around the middle of the universe, and its motion is the first of the others and the most perfect, because it takes place in a sphere, which is the most perfect of all the figures that are in solids. For what is perfect must necessarily be prior by nature to what is imperfect. Therefore the motion of the heaven is the first and the cause of all the others.

units.la: CAP. XIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIX.

units.la: Cœlestis corporis, & aliorum simplicium discrimen.
units.tr: The difference between the celestial body and the other simple bodies.

units.la: XIS quæ dicta sunt, perspicuum est, non in omni corpore gravitatem ineße, aut levitatem, sed duntaxat in eo, quod vel sursum movetur, vel deorsum. Tale næque aut leve sit, aut grave, aut utraque qualitate præditum, necesse est. Id autem grave est quod naturæ vi ad medium fertur, leve vero quod e medio sursum, gravissimum quod omnibus, quæ deorsum mouentur, substernitur: levissimum quod omnibus, quæ supera capessunt, eminet ac extat. Cæterum quædam gravia sunt & levia non solum simpliciter, sed comparatè, cum videlicet corpora quædam inter se conferuntur: ut si aër conferatur cum aqua, profecto aër levis erit & aqua gravis, quæ etiam levis est, si terræ coparetur. Sed ipsum corpus quod circum medium versatur nec grave, neque leve vllo modo esse potest, propterea qp motus is, quo recta ducitur linea, ei corpori à Natura non tributus sit. Quod si nec grave neque leve sit, vllis aliis mutationibus obnoxium esse non potest. Quicquid enim generatur semper ex aliquo contradicente oriatur, oportet, ut & id, quod corrum pitur, in alterum quod enti actu aduersatur. Deinde quicquid crescit, accessione eius, quod eiusdem generis & naturæ est, crescere debet: ut & id quod imminuitur eiusdem rei abscessione decrescit. Atqui nihil est, ex quo tanquam ex repugnante oriatur cœlum, nec consequenter a quo augeatur[?]. Propterea si generationis corruptionisque cœlum expers sit, & augmetationis & diminutionis, ipsum nullis affectionibus affici potest consequens est. Quam ob rem existimauit Aristoteles[?], ipsum sempiternum esse. Ex his constat simplicium corporum non plura esse quàm quinque, quorum unum circumuoluitur: cætera quatuor recta feruntur linea, quorum omnium motiones sunt simplices, & numero duæ, una conuersio, quæ nulli alteri repugnare potest. Si enim motus alius ei aduersaretur, is profecto rectus esset, quoniam uterque simplex est, & simplicium corporum. Atqui rectus motus conuersioni citra maximum incommodum repugnare non potest. Uni nanque motui nempe recto plures alij aduersarentur. Nam qui rectis lineis motus fiunt, ij propter loca inter se contraria, sint contrarij, necesse est. Sursum autem & deorsum, per quæ recti duo motus fiunt, aduersa esse loca, nulli dubium est. Itaque ex his constat conuersionis cœli motum rectum non aduersari. Præterea perpetuo motui nullus alius repugnare potest. At vero cœli conuersione esse perennem, satis perspicuum est. Denique contrarij motus semper ab extremis, quæ aduersa fasunt, incipere solent. Sed nulla cæli couersio ab extremis incipit. Ex quo perspicuum est couersioni nullum esse contrarium motum.
units.tr: From what has been said it is clear that gravity or levity does not belong to every body, but only to that which is moved either upward or downward. Such a body must necessarily be either light, or heavy, or endowed with both qualities. That is heavy which by the force of its nature is carried towards the centre; light, which is carried from the centre upward. The heaviest is that which lies beneath all things moving downward; the lightest is that which rises above and stands out over all things that reach upward. Moreover, some things are heavy and light not only absolutely but comparatively, namely when certain bodies are compared with one another: thus if air is compared with water, air will certainly be light and water heavy, yet water is also light if it is compared with earth. But the body which revolves about the centre can be neither heavy nor light in any way, because that motion by which a straight line is traced was not assigned to that body by Nature. And if it is neither heavy nor light, it cannot be subject to any other changes. For whatever is generated must always arise from some contrary, so that that which is corrupted passes into the other, which is actually opposed to it. Again, whatever grows must increase by the addition of that which is of the same kind and nature, just as that which is diminished decreases by the removal of the same thing. But there is nothing from which the heaven could arise as from a contrary, nor consequently anything by which it could be increased. Therefore, if the heaven is free of generation and corruption, and of augmentation and diminution, it follows that it cannot be affected by any changes. For this reason Aristotle judged that it is everlasting. From these considerations it is established that there are not more than five simple bodies, of which one revolves in a circle, while the other four are carried in straight lines; the motions of all of them are simple, and two in number: one circular motion, which can be opposed by no other. For if another motion were opposed to it, that would certainly be a straight motion, since each is simple and belongs to simple bodies. But a straight motion cannot oppose circular motion without the greatest inconvenience. For many other motions would be opposed to the one straight motion. Indeed, those motions which take place in straight lines must necessarily be contrary to one another because of their contrary places. That upward and downward, by which the two straight motions take place, are opposed places, is beyond doubt. Thus it is established from these considerations that the straight motion does not oppose the circular motion of the heaven. Moreover, no other motion can oppose a perpetual motion. But that the circular motion of the heaven is perpetual is sufficiently clear. Finally, contrary motions usually begin from the extremes that are opposed. But no circular motion of the heaven begins from extremes. From this it is clear that there is no contrary motion to the circular motion.

units.la: CAP. XX. Mundum nec magnitudine neque numero infinitum esse.
units.tr: CHAPTER XX. That the world is infinite neither in magnitude nor in number.

units.la: OSTMODVM demonstrandum est mundum non infinitum esse, à primo corpore, quòd cælum est, sumpto exordio. Si igitur ipsum corpus, quod in orbem fertur, magnitudine infinitum est, lineæ etiam à medio ad ipsum ductæ infinitæ erunt, & consequenter interuallum infinitum erit, extra quod nulla est alia magnitudo hisce lineis adiuncta finitimáq;. Quamobrem ipsum interuallum nullo motu peragrari poterit, nec cælum uersabitur. At uersari cernitur, propterea non magnitudine infinitum est. Adhæc omne rotundum corpus finitum est. Orbis enim figura, quæ omnium alia in perfectissima est, extremitate superficieque concluditur, & finita est. Ex quibus constat primum corpus non infinitum esse. Reliqua etiam simplicia corpora non esse infinita his rationibus demonstratur. Primum enim id infinitum esse non potest, quod à medio, vel ad medium mouetur. Sed hoc modo quatuor prima vniuersi elementa mouentur. Ignis enim & aer superiora petunt, & a medio sursum feruntur: terra vero & aqua ad medium & in inferiora loca mouentur. Deinde contrarij motus sunt inferior & superior, propterea quod ad contraria loca fiunt, quorum si unus definitus sit[?], alterum etiam definitum esse oportet. At elementorum motus contrarij sunt. Quod si determinata loca sunt, ea corpora, quae in eis sita sunt, necessario determinata erunt. Sed loca vbi elementa mouentur finita sunt. Praeterea si superior locus & inferior terminatus est, medium quoque terminatum esse, necesse est. Nisi enim terminatum esset medium, motus, qui ab eo, & ad eum fit, infinitus erit. Sed huiusmodi motus infinitus esse non potest, quoniam in statum definit & finitur. Itaque definitum medium est, & consequenter omne corpus, quod in eo est situm. Adhæc si corpus leue est, in sublime feratur, necesse est: sin graue deorsum. At tale infinitum esse non potest.
units.tr: First it must be shown that the world is not infinite, beginning from the first body, which is the heaven. If, then, the body itself which is carried in a circle is infinite in magnitude, the lines drawn from the middle to it will also be infinite, and consequently the interval will be infinite, outside which there is no other magnitude joined to these lines and adjacent to them. Therefore that interval itself could not be traversed by any motion, and the heaven would not revolve. But it is seen to revolve; therefore it is not infinite in magnitude.
