Moreover, every round body is finite. For the figure of a sphere, which is the most perfect of all figures, is bounded by an extremity and surface, and is finite. From these things it is established that the first body is not infinite. The remaining simple bodies are also shown not to be infinite by these arguments. For first, that cannot be infinite which is moved from the middle or towards the middle. But in this way the four first elements of the universe are moved: fire and air seek the higher places and are carried upward from the middle, while earth and water are moved towards the middle and into the lower places. Next, lower and higher are contrary motions, because they proceed to contrary places, and if one of these is limited, the other too must be limited. But the motions of the elements are contrary. And if the places are determined, the bodies situated in them will necessarily be determined. But the places where the elements are moved are finite. Furthermore, if the upper place and the lower place are bounded, the middle must also be bounded, of necessity. For unless the middle were bounded, the motion which goes from it and towards it would be infinite. But a motion of this kind cannot be infinite, since it ends in a state of rest and is limited. Therefore the middle is determined, and consequently every body which is situated in it. Moreover, if a body is light, it must be carried aloft; if heavy, downward. But such a thing cannot be infinite.

units.la: Quare nullum Mundi elementum infinitum est. Praeterea si nulla est infinita grauitas, nec vllu quidem horū corporū est futurū infinitū, præsertim cum infiniti corporis, interminatam esse grauitatem, expediat. Similis est ratio leuitatis. Si enim infinita est grauitas, fit etiam huiusmodi leuitas, oportet. Sed nulla est infinita leuitas. Si qua enim esset, ei profecto inesset[?] corpori, quod omnibus eminet & circumagi cernitur. At ipsum nec leue esse neque graue,fatis manifestum est. Si praeter-ea quodpiam pondus infinitum eflet, haud-dubiè corpus pondere præditu moueri non posset. Quicquid enim mouetur in loco fit, oportet. Sed enim infinitum pondus nusquā est. Propterea[?] omne pondus finitū est. Quin-etiam omne simplex corpus rotundo motu, vel recto cietur. Sed neutro id cieri potest, quod est infinitum. Poftmodū naturali motu, vel violento omne corpus agitatur. Neutro autem id mouetur, quod infinitum est: quandoquidem ex accidente, & fecundo fit violentus motus. Si præterea in ratione rerū est infinitum corpus, id profecto fit partium similium aut dissimilium, necesse est: At fi dissimilium est, aut ex partibus specie finitis, aut infinitis necessario constabit. Sed ex infinitis ipsum non constare, iam fatis perfpicuū est. Plura enim simul infinita effent. Ergo ex finitis est. Sed ex finitis partibus nullum nasci corpus infinitum, tam certum est quàm quod certissimum. Si item in vniuerso corpora effent infinitæ naturæ, certe eorum loca, magnitudine infinita esse expediret, & illorum motus infinitos. Sed hæc incommoda sunt. Quod etiam deorsum fertur, vel sursum, id non infinitè moueri potest. At omne corpus naturale simplex vel è medio sursum fertur, vel deorsum ad medium: Adhæc omne sensile corpus vim agendi habet,vel patiendi,vel utranque[?]. Corpus autem,quod infinitum est,nec agendi vim,nec patiendi habet. Secus enim infinitum a finito pateretur, aut in id quod finitum est, ageret. Sed quod infinitum est, id a finito pati non potest: quandoquidem semper a debiliori perpessio proficiscitur, ut a valentiori actio. Itaque nullum est naturale corpus infinitum. Quicquid insuper in orbem fertur, circum medium cieri, necesse[?] est. At in infinito corpore nec medium est ullū, neque extremum. Propterea quod in orbem fertur corpus, id non infinitum est. Nec etiā ullo motu recto id cieri potest, quod infinitum est, quandoquidem rectus motus semper in quietem definit & finitur. Atque si quod infinitum est, moueri contingat, motu eius infinitū esse par est. Praeterea quicquid mouetur, vel vi sua, vel aliena cietur. Sed si vi sua mouetur, animal est. Atqui omne animal certam definitamque habet magnitudinem, non autem interminatam. Atqui si id quod mouetur animal non sit, id ab alio moueri expedit, quod vel finitum est, vel infinitum. Sed si infinitum est id ab alio, quod etiā infinitum sit, non mouebitur, quoniam tum duo simul infinita erunt. Si denique infinitū corpus graue sit, aut leue, profecto aut universi aliquod extremum est, aut medium. Id quod nullo modo fieri potest. Ubi enim omnino nihil inest medium, neque extremū, nec ibi sursum erit aut deorsum. Sublato enim loco omni corporibus nullus erit motus. Sed omnia moueri corpora vel suapte natura, vel vi & contra naturam, certissimum est. Definita igitur sunt omnia vel propriis locis, vel alienis. Ex quibus perspicuum in vniuerso nullum esse infinitum corpus, nec omnia corpora esse grauia aut leuia, aut vtraque qualitate praedita.
units.tr: Therefore no element of the world is infinite. Furthermore, if there is no infinite heaviness, then none of these bodies will be infinite either, especially since it would be absurd for heaviness to be unbounded for an infinite body. The same reasoning applies to lightness. For if there is an infinite heaviness, there must also be a corresponding infinite lightness. But there is no infinite lightness. For if there were any, it would certainly belong to that body which rises above all and is seen to be carried round; but that body is plainly neither light nor heavy. Again, if any weight were infinite, a body endowed with that weight could undoubtedly not be moved; for whatever is moved must be moved in a place. But an infinite weight is nowhere. Therefore every weight is finite. Moreover, every simple body is moved either with a circular motion or a straight one; but an infinite thing can be moved by neither. Again, every body is moved either by a natural motion or a violent one; but that which is infinite is moved by neither, since a violent motion arises from an accident and is secondary. Further, if an infinite body exists in the nature of things, it must necessarily be made of similar or dissimilar parts. If of dissimilar parts, it will necessarily be composed either of parts finite in kind or of infinite ones. But that it is not composed of infinite parts is already sufficiently clear, for then several infinites would exist at once. Therefore it is composed of finite parts. But that no infinite body is born from finite parts is as certain as anything most certain. Likewise, if there were bodies of infinite nature in the universe, it would surely follow that their places would be infinite in magnitude, and their motions infinite. But these are absurd. What is carried downward or upward cannot be moved infinitely. Yet every simple natural body is either carried upward from the middle or downward to the middle. Moreover, every sensible body has a power of acting or of being acted upon, or both. But an infinite body has neither the power of acting nor of being acted upon. For otherwise the infinite would be acted upon by the finite, or would act upon what is finite. But what is infinite cannot be acted upon by the finite, since passion always proceeds from the weaker, as action from the stronger. Therefore no natural body is infinite. Whatever is carried in a circle must necessarily revolve about a middle; but in an infinite body there is neither a middle nor an extremity. Therefore a body that is carried in a circle is not infinite. Nor can anything that is infinite be moved by any straight motion, since a straight motion always ends and is limited in rest. And if anything infinite should happen to be moved, its motion must be infinite as well. Furthermore, whatever is moved is moved either by its own power or by another's. But if it is moved by its own power, it is an animal. Yet every animal has a definite and determinate magnitude, not an unbounded one. And if what is moved is not an animal, it must be moved by something else, which is either finite or infinite. But if it is moved by an infinite thing, that thing too, being infinite, would not be moved, since then two infinites would exist at once. Finally, if an infinite body were heavy or light, it would certainly have either some extremity or middle of the universe; and this can in no way happen. For where there is absolutely no middle and no extremity, there will be neither up nor down. For when all place is taken away, there will be no motion for bodies. But that all bodies are moved either by their own nature or by force and against nature is most certain. Therefore all things are determined either by their proper places or by alien ones. From which it is plain that in the universe there is no infinite body, nor are all bodies heavy or light, or endowed with both qualities.

units.la: CAP. XXI.
units.tr: CHAP. XXI.

units.la: Plures mundos non esse.
units.tr: That there are not several worlds.

units.la: NTEQVAM plures non esse Mundos oftedamus, quaedam adeo certa firmaque sunt proponenda, vt nullo modo refelli possint. Primum est, corpora & quiescere & moueri, tum natura, tum vi, quaeque vbi natura mouentur, ibi etiam natura quiescere: & in quem locum vi feruntur, in eo etiam vi manere: atque in quo vi stant, in eum etiam vi ferri. Praeterea motum ad locum vi factum naturali contrarium esse. Deinde si terra ex alius Mundi medio ad medium huius vi feratur, huic illuc ea suapte natura ferri. Si insuper hic no vi quiescit, illic etiam natura moueri. Si quoque plures mundi sunt, eos ex iisdem corporibus constare, quoniam omnes eiusdem naturae sunt. Quinetiam vnumquodque corpus cuiusuis Mundi eandem vim habere. Atque eorum quidem corporum, quæ simplicia sunt, quædam necessario & natura è medio sur-sum ferri, vt ignem & aërem, quæda ad medium, vt aquam, & terræ partes. Denique motus huiusmodi corporum finitos esse, & quodlibet ex vnoquoque motu nobis significari. Quare si in pluribus mundis iidem motus sunt, in singulis, eadem esse elementa, necesse est. Propterea terra, quæ in alio[?] est vniuerso, ad hoc nostrum medium ferri potest, & ignis, qui illic est, ad extremum huius Mundi defertur. Sed hoc nullo modo fieri potest. Si enim hoc fiat, terra etiā suo in Mundo sur-sum efferri, & ignem deorsum ad medium moueri, expediet. Propterea terra, quæ hic est, è medio huius Mundi in Medium alius, moueri poterit, propterea quod Mundi ita inter se siti sint. Nam aut eadem natura simplicium corporum in pluribus Mundis non ponenda est (quod sane absurdè dictum erit) aut si eadem omnibus natura sit, profecto & vnum medium & extremum vnum in singulis ponenda sunt? Quod si hoc absurdum est, certè Mundi plures vno esse nō possunt. Præ-terea partes Mundi, quæ tum hic, tum alio in Mundo sunt eandem habent ratione & vim, nec specie differunt, sed numero. Propterea cùm eorum omnium vna eademque sit natura, vnus etiam motus eis sit, necesse est. Itaq; grauia corpora alius Mundi ad hoc nostrum medium mouebuntur, vt leuia ad extremu. Sed hæc natura fieri nó possunt. Quare duo Mudi,non dicam plures,esse non possunt. Id quod certé rationibus, & disciplinis, quæ ex prima petuntur philosophia, demoftrari potest. Etenim omne[?] mobile,cuius motor proprius numero vnus est,vnum numero esse oportet. Atqui cœli motor vnus numero est. Ergo vnum est cœlum, quod non pluribus Mundis,sed vni duntaxat sufficere potest. Si præterea alius effet Mundus præter hunc, profecto ille supra nostrum aut infra locatus effet. Sed alium esse Mundum supra hunc, non rationi consentaneum videtur: quandoquidem pars illius grauior supra cœlum nostri Mundi sita effet. Id quod tam absurdum est, quàm quod abfurdiffimum. Nec etiam alium esse Mundum infra nostrum credibile est,quoniam leuitas eius infra grauitate huius nostri effet. Sed hoc incommodum tantum est, vt nulla ratione perferri possit. Si insuper aliquod naturale corpus extra hunc nostrum Mundum fit, istud profecto aut simplex erit, aut ex simplicibus compactum & concretu: illicque aut natura, aut vi continebitur. Quod autem simplex nullum fit, his rationibus perspicuum est. In primis cœlum, quod omnium corporum est primum, a suis sedibus discedere non potest. Nec etiam vllum eorum, quæ sursum e medio, & deorsum ad medium feruntur, extra coelum suapte natura consi-stere potest. Etenim infra coelum suis in lo-cis contineantur, & quiescant, necesse est. Neque vero illic extraque hunc mundu con-tineri possunt, quandoquidem nihil contra naturam continetur, nisi ibi natura consiste-re possit.Quod si extra hoc nostrum vniuer-sum nec coelu,nec aliud simplex corpus con-stat,nullum aliud ex his concretu illic con-tineri potest: quoniam nullum corpus mistu absque simplicibus consistit. Conflat igitur vnum duntaxat vniuersum esse, & extra coe-lum mundumque nec locum haberi vllum, nec vacuum,neque tempus: quoniam haec om-nia absque naturali corpore esse non pos-sunt. Nam vbi nullum corpus est,ibi nec lo-cus,nec motus,nec denique tempus. Omnis enim motus semper alicubi fit, & in aliquo tempore: quandoquidem tempus mensura motus est.
units.tr: Before we show that there are not several worlds, certain propositions must be set out which are so certain and firm that they can in no way be refuted. The first is that bodies both rest and move, both by nature and by force; and those bodies which move by nature rest there by nature too, and the place to which they are carried by force they also remain in by force, and the place in which they stand by force they are also carried to by force. Moreover, motion to a place brought about by force is contrary to natural motion. Next, if earth is forced from the middle of another world to the middle of this one, it is carried there by its own nature. If, further, earth here rests without force, it is also moved there by nature. Again, if there are several worlds, they must be made of the same bodies, since all are of the same nature. Indeed, every body of any world has the same power. Of those bodies which are simple, some are carried necessarily and by nature from the centre upwards, such as fire and air, and some towards the centre, such as water and the parts of earth. Finally, the motions of such bodies are finite, and from any one motion we are told what the others are. Therefore, if the same motions occur in several worlds, it is necessary that the elements in each be the same. Accordingly, the earth which is in another universe could be carried to this our centre, and the fire which is there would be carried to the extremity of this world. But this cannot happen in any way. For if it did, it would be expedient for earth to be borne upwards in its own world, and fire to be moved downwards to the centre. Therefore the earth which is here can be moved from the centre of this world to the centre of another, since the worlds are situated thus relative to one another. For either the same nature of simple bodies must not be posited in several worlds (which would certainly be said absurdly), or, if the nature is the same in all, then surely one centre and one extremity must be posited in each? But if this is absurd, certainly there cannot be several worlds rather than one. Moreover, the parts of the world which are here and those which are in another world have the same reason and power, and differ not in kind but in number. Therefore, since the nature of all of them is one and the same, it is necessary that their motion also be one. Thus heavy bodies of another world would be moved towards this our centre, just as light ones towards the extremity. But these things cannot happen by nature. Therefore two worlds, let alone several, cannot exist. This can certainly be demonstrated from arguments and doctrines drawn from first philosophy. For every mobile thing whose proper mover is numerically one must be numerically one. But the mover of the heaven is numerically one. Therefore the heaven is one, which can suffice not for several worlds but for one alone. Moreover, if there were another world besides this one, it would surely be placed either above or below ours. But that another world should be above this one does not seem consistent with reason, since its heavier part would lie above the heaven of our world. This is as absurd as anything could be. Nor is it credible that there is another world below ours, since its lightness would be below the weight of this our world. But this inconvenience is so great that it cannot be endured on any account. Furthermore, if some natural body exists outside this our world, it will surely be either simple, or compounded and concrete out of simple bodies; and it will be held there either by nature or by force. That no such body is simple is clear from these reasons. In the first place, the heaven, which is the first of all bodies, cannot depart from its seats. Nor can any of those things which are carried upwards from the centre and downwards to the centre by their own nature stand outside the heaven. For they must necessarily be contained and rest in their places below the heaven. Nor indeed can they be contained there, outside this world, since nothing is contained contrary to nature unless it can naturally stand there. But if neither the heaven nor any other simple body exists outside this our universe, then no compound concrete body can be contained there, since no mixed body subsists without simple bodies. It follows, therefore, that there is only one universe, and that outside the heaven and the world there is no place, no void, and no time, since none of these can exist without a natural body. For where there is no body, there is no place, no motion, and finally no time. For all motion always takes place somewhere and in some time, since time is the measure of motion.

units.la: CAP. XXII. Vtrum Mundus originem habuerit, & tandem non intereat?
units.tr: Chapter 22. Whether the world had an origin, and whether it will at last not perish?

units.la: VPERBST, vt deinceps quaera-mus vtrum Mundus nullam habuerit vnquam originem, an vero ortus sit,& interire tandem non possit? Veterum enim philosophorum quidem mundum originem habuisse tradiderunt, alij vero ipsum esse æternum, nonnulli interitu-rum docuerunt. Nam Mundum fuisse ortu, nec tamen interiturū esse existimarunt Empedocles Agrigentinus, & Heraclitus Ephe-sius. Sed quæcunque natura constant, posse corrumpi, & extingui, satis perspicuum est. Nihil enim in rerum natura ortum & perpe-tuum esse potest. Aristoteles autem, libro se-cundo de cœlo, capite primo de cœlo, & universo, Mundum nec[?] ortum fuisse, neque interiturū esse, his rationibus ostendere contendit. In primis id æternum est, cuius motus est infinitus. Cœli autem cœversio infinita est, quoniam motor eius æternus est. Deinde sedes Dei æterna est, nec unquam corrupi poterit. Sed sedem ac domicilium Dei cœlum esse, omnes hactenus existimarunt. Adde quod omnes Deum deprecaturi sursum natura ma-nus efferentes sedem eius cœlum esse, testan-tur. Præterea quicquid contrario caret, & o-mni difficultate, prorsus corruptionis est expers. Quicquid enim corrumpitur semper in contrarium & a contrario corrumpitur. Cœlum autem omni difficultate & contrario vacat. Nullius enim sensilis mutabilisq; qualitatis est particeps. Quinetiam quicquid est temporis causa, æternum fit, oportet. Cœlum autem temporis est causa. Nam tempus est conversionis cœli mensura & affectio. Omne denique corpus divinum sempiternum est. Divini enim nullum est naturale principium. Sed cœli corpus divinum esse à philosophis traditur. Non enim naturale esse, nec naturæ ullis legibus devinctum existimarunt. Ex quibus constat cœlum esse sempiternum. Sed cœlum originem habuisse testatur Moses, libri Geneseos statim initio, qui Christianis maiorem facit fidem, quàm omnium philosophorum princeps Aristoteles.
units.tr: It remains to inquire whether the world never had any origin, or whether it did come into being and cannot in the end perish. Among the ancient philosophers, some have taught that the world had an origin, others that it is eternal, and some that it will perish. Empedocles of Agrigentum and Heraclitus of Ephesus thought that the world did come into being but would not perish. Yet it is quite plain that whatever things consist of a nature can be corrupted and extinguished. Nothing in the nature of things can be both generated and perpetual. Aristotle, however, in the first chapter of the second book of his work On the Heavens, On the Heavens and the Universe, argues that the world neither came into being nor will perish, and he tries to show this by the following reasons. First, that is eternal whose motion is infinite. The revolution of the heaven is infinite, since its mover is eternal. Next, the seat of God is eternal and can never be corrupted. All men until now have held that the seat and dwelling of God is the heaven. Add that all who are about to pray to God, lifting their hands naturally upward, bear witness that his seat is heaven. Moreover, whatever lacks a contrary and all difficulty is wholly free from corruption. For whatever is corrupted is always corrupted into its contrary and by its contrary. But the heaven lacks all difficulty and contrariety; it partakes of no sensible or changeable quality. Furthermore, whatever is the cause of time must necessarily be eternal. But the heaven is the cause of time, for time is the measure and attribute of the heaven's revolution. Finally, every divine body is everlasting, for the divine has no natural principle. But the philosophers teach that the body of the heaven is divine; for they thought it was not natural, nor bound by any laws of nature. From these things it is established that the heaven is everlasting. But Moses, at the very beginning of the book of Genesis, testifies that the heaven had an origin; and this gives Christians greater credence than Aristotle, the prince of all philosophers, does.

units.la: Cap. XXIII.
units.tr: Chapter 23.

units.la: Utrum in universo duntaxat sint dex-trum & sinistrum.
units.tr: Whether in the universe there really are only right and left.

units.la: Q[?]VONIAM olim Pythagorei dun-taxat dextrum & sinistrum mundo ponebant, oritur hæc quæstio, utrum ita sit, an secus potius? Sed si in Mundo dextrum sit & sinistrum, ea etiam quæ hæc priora sunt, nempe superum, inferum, ante & post, ei esse existimandum est.
units.tr: Since the Pythagoreans once assigned only right and left to the world, the question arises whether it is so or rather otherwise. But if there is right and left in the world, then those things which are prior to these, namely above and below, before and behind, must also be thought to exist in it.

units.la: Hæc autem omnia in omnibus perfectis animantibus insunt: in plantis vero duntaxat superum & inferum. At in inanimatis quorum quædam non omnino mov• entur, quædam moventur, non proprie sunt superum & inferum, dextrum & sinistrum, sed duntaxat in eis esse dicuntur, cum ad nos referuntur: eis enim quidpiam dextrum esse dicimus, quod nostro opponitur sinistro, & sinistrum, quod nostro dextro adversum est. anticum quod cum nostro postico ex diametro pugnat. Itaque non in omni corpore, atque natura pars superior & inferior, dextra & sinistra antica & postica quærenda est, sed in iis tatum naturis, quæ animatæ sunt, & in fe mo tus principium habent. Propterea Mundus Pythagoreis animatus videbatur. Sed quispiam dubitabit quis possit superior coeli pars esse & inferior, dextra & sinistra, cùm rotunda fit eius figura, semperque moueatur. Hoc autem sic intelligendum esse docet Ariftoteles, vt si quis in iis corporibus, in quibus inter dextrum & sinistrum discrimen est, sphæram circumponat, in hæc certè vim dextri & sinistri diuersam habere videbuntur: quauis propter sphericæ figuræ similitudinem, minimè appareant. Dextra igitur pars cœli ea est, è qua stellæ nobis oriuntur, sinistra, vbi occidunt. Vtraque enim latitudine ipsius cœli constituit, quæ inter vtrumque verticem intercedit. Itaque si a dextra parte conuersio cœli incipiat, & ad eandem procedat, profecto eum verticem, qui antarcticus dicitur, superam esse cœli partem, necesse est. Si enim is esset, qui nobis apparet, haud dubiè conuersio cœli ad sinistram partem pertineret. Sed id esse non potest, eo quòd a dextra parte cælū potius moueri incipiat, q; a sinistra. Cùm igitur is vertex, q; antarticus est, supera cœli mudiue pars sit, consequens est eos, qui illic habitat in superiore hemisphærio esse, & in dextra cœli parte, nos verò in inferiore, & sinistra, contra ac Pythagorei censebant, quibus nos in su-pera dextráque vniuersi parte habitare videbatur, alios vero in infera & sinistra.
units.tr: All these distinctions are found in all perfect living beings, and in plants only above and below. In inanimate things, some of which do not move at all and others of which do move, there is not strictly an above and below, a right and left, a front and back, but these are said to be in them only when they are referred to us. For we call a thing right when it lies opposite our left, and left when it faces our right, and front when it is diametrically opposed to our back. Therefore the upper and lower part, the right and left, the front and back, are not to be sought in every body and every nature, but only in those natures which are animate and have the principle of motion within themselves. For this reason the world seemed animate to the Pythagoreans. But someone may doubt how the heaven can have an upper and lower part, a right and left, since its figure is round and it is always moving. Aristotle teaches that this must be understood thus: if someone were to place a sphere around bodies in which there is a distinction between right and left, these bodies would certainly appear to have a different power of right and left, although on account of the likeness of the spherical figure they do not appear so at all. The right part of the heaven, then, is that from which the stars rise for us, and the left is where they set. For both are fixed by the breadth of the heaven itself, which lies between the two poles. Accordingly, if the rotation of the heaven begins from the right part and proceeds toward the same side, it is necessary that the pole which is called antarctic is the upper part of the heaven. For if it were the pole visible to us, the rotation of the heaven would undoubtedly be toward the left part. But this cannot be, because the heaven begins to move from the right part rather than from the left. Since, then, that pole which is antarctic is the upper part of the heavenly world, it follows that those who live there are in the upper hemisphere and in the right part of the heaven, while we are in the lower and in the left, contrary to what the Pythagoreans thought, for they believed that we lived in the upper and right part of the universe, and others in the lower and left.

units.la: CAP. XXIIII.
units.tr: CAP. XXIIII.

units.la: Cur duntaxat quatuor sint vniuersi elementa, & cur item orbium cæli plures conuersiones, & diuersa?
units.tr: Why there are only four elements of the universe, and why there are likewise several revolutions of the spheres of heaven, and different ones?

units.la: OELVM quandam esse diuina naturam eo philosophus demostrat, quòd ei rotundum corpus tributū sit, vt suapte natura perpetuò cir-cumagatur. Quod tamen fieri non potest, nisi in eius medio aliquid stet. Medium autem quiescens, circa quod perpetuò cœlum voluitur, terra est: quæ si sit, & ignis etiā est, quoniam si vnum est contrarium, sit alterū, necesse est. Eadem enim est contrariorū materia. Si præterea terra & ignis sunt, ea etiam corpora sint oportet, quæ medium eorū locum obtinent, nempe aër & terra. Constat iam quatuor esse elementa, quæ inter se vicissim repugnant, ex quibus, eorum quæ natura constant, generatio est, & corruptio. Res enim naturales non solum generantur, sed etiam corrumpuntur, propterea quòd earū nihil æternum esse possit. Generantur quidē & corrumpuntur mutua actione & perpef-sione ipsorum quatuor elementorum, quæ suis qualitatibus contrariis mutuò inter se agunt & patiuntur. Vt autem perpetua sit corporum, quæ natura constant, generatio & corruptio motu opus est, qui etiā sit perpetuus, & causa huiusmodi mutationum in vniuerso. At[?]is motus non potest elementorum esse, quoniam perpetuo moueri nō possunt. Motus enim, qui per rectam fiunt lineam, æterni non sunt, sed in statum desinut. Alius igitur requiritur ad locum motus, qui æternus sit, & generationis corruptionisque causa. Hic autem conuersio cœli sit oportet, quæ vel vna est, vel multiplex. Sed vno & eadem esse non potest. Nam si cœli conuersio vna esset, profecto elementa vniuersi semper eodem modo se haberent, nec mutarentur, nihilque ex eis oriretur. Adde quòd temporum nulla esset vicissitudo mutatioque, nec rerum, quæ natura constant, varietas vlla: quæ non aliunde nisi à varia multorum orbium conuersione, promanare potest.
units.tr: That there is a certain fifth nature, the philosopher demonstrates from the fact that a round body is assigned to it, so that it may by its own nature be turned in a perpetual circle. This, however, cannot happen unless something stands in its middle. The motionless middle, around which the heaven is perpetually rolled, is the earth; and if there is earth, there is also fire, since if one of two contraries exists, the other must necessarily exist too; for the matter of contraries is the same. Moreover, if earth and fire exist, there must also be those bodies which hold the place between them, namely air and water. It is now established that there are four elements, which mutually oppose one another in turn, and from whose action and reaction come the generation and corruption of those things which consist in nature. For natural things are not only generated but also corrupted, because nothing of them can be eternal. They are indeed generated and corrupted by the mutual action and passion of the four elements themselves, which act and are acted upon among one another by their contrary qualities. But in order that the generation and corruption of bodies consisting in nature may be perpetual, there is need of a motion which is also perpetual, and which is the cause of such changes in the universe. Now this motion cannot belong to the elements, since they cannot be moved perpetually; for motions which proceed in a straight line are not eternal, but come to an end in rest. Another motion is therefore required for the place of motion, one which is eternal and is the cause of generation and corruption. This must be the revolution of the heaven, which is either one or many. But it cannot be one and the same. For if the revolution of the heaven were single, the elements of the universe would always be in the same condition, and would not change, and nothing would arise from them. Add that there would be no alternation or change of seasons, nor any variety of natural things, which can arise from nothing other than the varied revolution of many spheres.

units.la: CAP. XXV.
units.tr: CAP. XXV.

units.la: Simplicium corporum figuras simplices esse, & rotundas.
units.tr: That the simple bodies have simple figures, and are round.

units.la: NTEQ;VAM de cœli figura, & a- liorum simplicium corporum tra- ctemus, primùm de toto figurarum genere, quænam prima sit tam in planis, quàm in solidis, explicandum est. At in vno quoque genere quod vnum est, id naturæ ordine prius est & antiquius multis. Quare Circulus prima est figura eorū, quæ ad plana pertinent. At Circulus non pluribus lineis in rectitudinem ductis, circunscribitur, sed vna duntaxat in orbe reflexa. Hæc autem, quoniam ei nihil addi potest, perfecta est: Recta vero, quòd ei semper aliquid addi possit, imperfecta. Duæ igitur perfectæ sunt figuræ, quarum vna planorum prima est, quæ circulus dicitur: altera solidorum, quæ globus nominatur, & eorum prima est, & perfecta. Solidorum autem primum cœli corpus est, cui propterea globosa figura & rotunda maximè conuenit. Quoniam etiam primi corporis prima est figura, & prima motio, profecto ipsum sit rotundum, vt in orbem feratur, necesse est. Atque quod corpori rotundo coniunctum est id etiam sphæricum esse oportet. Eadem est ratio eorum, quæ in huiusmodi rotundorum medio sita sunt. Quæ enim ab eo, quod rotundum est, continentur, ea sint omnino rotūda, expedit. At ea corpora, quæ sunt sub errantium stellarum orbibus supremam contingunt sphærā. Proinde ea esse rotūda, necesse est, & confequeter vniuersum: quandoquidē cælestes sphæras inferiora corpora contingunt, ac cum eis cohærent. Quòd etiam vniuersum sit rotundum ex eo maximè constat, quòd extra summum orbem nullum sit vacuum. Nam si figura eius rectarum[?] lineārum esset, profecto extra ipsum & locus effet, & corpus, aut vacuum. Præterea corpus, quod celerrime mo-vetur, rotundum est. Cœlum autem celerrime cieri hac ratione constat. Nam id quod in vno quoque genere principium est, id minimum habet. Atqui omnium aliorum motuum conuersio cœli, principium est & causa, eo quod sola fit æquabilis motus & perpetuus. Quare conuersio cœli omnium motionum minima & celerrima est. Postremo cœlum esse rotundum hinc facile intelligi potest, quod quemadmodum aqua terram ambit, aquam aer, aerem ignis: ita cœli orbes se complectuntur, quoniam non continuata sunt, sed contigua coniunctaque veluti ipsa elementa. Quæ cum ita sint, vniuersum esse rotundum, facile intelligi potest.
units.tr: Now that we are to treat of the figure of the heavens and of the other simple bodies, we must first explain, concerning the whole kind of figures, which is the first both among plane figures and among solid ones. In every kind, that which is one is prior and older in the order of nature than the many. Therefore the circle is the first of the figures that belong to planes. But a circle is not bounded by several lines drawn straight, but by one only, bent back into a ring. And since nothing can be added to it, it is perfect; whereas the straight line is imperfect, because something can always be added to it. There are therefore two perfect figures: of planes the first is that called the circle, and of solids the one called the globe, which is both the first and the perfect solid. Now the body of the heavens is the first of solids, and so the globular and round figure most of all suits it. Since the first body has the first figure and the first motion, it must necessarily be round, so that it may be carried in a circle. And whatever is joined to a round body must also be spherical. The same reasoning applies to those things that lie in the middle of such round bodies. For it is fitting that those things which are contained by what is round should themselves be wholly round. But those bodies which lie beneath the orbits of the wandering stars touch the uppermost sphere. Therefore they must be round, and consequently the whole universe is round, since the heavenly spheres touch the lower bodies and cohere with them. That the universe is round is also shown chiefly by this, that there is no void outside the highest orbit. For if its figure were of straight lines, then beyond it there would necessarily be either a place and a body, or a void. Moreover, the body that moves most swiftly is round. Now that the heavens are moved most swiftly is established by this reasoning: that which is the principle in any kind has the least of it. But the rotation of the heavens is the principle and cause of all the other motions, inasmuch as it alone is uniform and perpetual. Therefore the rotation of the heavens is the least and the swiftest of all motions. Lastly, that the heavens are round can easily be understood from this: just as water surrounds the earth, air the water, and fire the air, so the orbs of the heavens embrace one another, since they are not continuous but contiguous and joined together, like the elements themselves. These things being so, it can easily be understood that the universe is round.

units.la: CAP. XXVI.
units.tr: CAP. XXVI.

units.la: Cur cœlum potius ab oriente in occidentem, quàm ab occidente in orientem vertatur.
units.tr: Why the heavens turn from east to west rather than from west to east.

units.la: VONIAM[?] autem rebus æternis nihil casu & fortuna euenit, & cœ-lum, nostri philosophi sententia, æternum est, vt & eius motio, quæritur cur potius ab oriente in occidente circumferatur partem, quam ab occidente in orientem? Proculdubio huius rei exacta demonstratio omnino reddi non potest. Atque insignis audacia est, magnáque temeritas & stultitia de omnibus suo interponere iudicium, ac nihil praetermittere. Propterea id duntaxat, quod probabile est, producere licebit. Natura enim eorū, quā fieri possunt, id semper efficit quod optimum est. Idcirco quemadmodum eorum motuum, qui rectis fiunt lineis, is, qui in sublimi est, aliis praestatior habetur, quoniam superior locus inferiore diuinior est: ita coeli couersio, quae ante fit longe praestat ea, quae pone est: quandoquidem ante & pone eandem inter se habent rationem, quam dextrum & sinistrum. Ante enim ut coeli dextra pars est, pone vero ut sinistra. Quoniam autem optimum coelo est motu simplici & perenni cieri, atque in id, quod praestantissimum est, nimirum in se ipsum, cuius naturam esse diuinam Plato & Aristoteles tradiderunt, stellae ab oriente tanquam a praestantiore coeli parte nobis oriri videntur.
units.tr: Since nothing happens by chance or fortune to eternal things, and the heavens, in the opinion of our philosophers, are eternal, as is their motion, the question is raised why the heavens are carried around from east to west rather than from west to east. Certainly an exact demonstration of this matter cannot be given in full. It is a remarkable audacity, and great rashness and foolishness, to interpose one's own judgment on all things and leave nothing unexamined. Therefore we shall be permitted to put forward only what is probable. For nature, in those things that can come about, always produces what is best. Accordingly, just as among motions that take place in straight lines, that which is above is regarded as more excellent than the others, since a higher place is more divine than a lower one, so the revolution of the heavens that begins in the east far surpasses that which is behind it; for before and behind bear the same relation to one another as right and left. For the front of the heavens is like their right side, and the rear like their left. Since, moreover, it is best for the heavens to be moved by a simple and perpetual motion, and towards that which is most excellent, namely themselves, whose nature Plato and Aristotle taught is divine, the stars appear to us to rise from the east, as from the more excellent part of the heavens.

units.la: CAP. XXVII.
units.tr: CAP. XXVII.

units.la: An cœli motus æquabilis sit.
units.tr: Whether the motion of the heavens is uniform.

units.la: P[?]ORRO de Cœli prima couersione, quæ æquabilis est, sequitur, ut differamus. Si enim non æquabilis esset, non dubium est, quin aut velocior, aut tardior ea fieret: quoniam ad locum mutatio, quæ non æquabilis est, retardari, dari, & stare potest. Status autem motionis est, vel unde mobile ferri incipit, aut ibi, quò fertur, aut in medio. Sed cœlesti conuersioni, nec unde sit, nec quo statio fiat, datum est[?]. Neque enim ipsius[?] principiū est, neque terminus, nec omnino medium. Nam & tempore perpetua est, & nec natura sua interrupi potest. Quare si cœli conuersioni nullus sit[?] status, nec retardatio, nulla etiam ei erit inæquabilitas. Nam tum inæquabilitas motus fieri solet, cum aliquando celerior est, aliquando tardior. Præterea motus inæquabilitas, aut ab eo est quod mouet, aut ab eo quod mouetur, aut ab utroque. Sed nec a motore, nec a mobili proficiscitur conuersionis cœli inæquabilitas. Quod enim cœlum mouet, id eadem vi pollet, quam cœli conuersio requirit: nec fieri potest, ut moueatur, eo.qp[?] incorporeum sit. Quare cœlestis conuersio inæquabilis esse non potest. Quinetiam cœli conuersio inæquabilis esset, & astrorum unum celerius, aliud tardius moueretur, iam eorum infinito tempore factum fuisset interuallum. At eorum nullum interuallis mutatum fuisse, satis constat. Deinde uniuscuiusque rei remissio ab aliqua imbecillitate oritur. Omnis autem imbecillitas a natura aliena est. Omnes enim imbecillitates in animantibus, ut ea quæ senectutis est, & diminutionis corporis, contra naturam sunt. Sed primo corpori nulla est imbecillitas, quandoquidem simplex est,nec quicquahabet,quod suæ aduersetur naturæ. Itaque in eo non dominatur imbecillitas,nec remissio motus, vt & neque intentio. Si enim ei motus cotentio esset, & etiam remissio. Hactenus de æquabilitate conuersionis cœli: superest, vt ad alia pergamus.
units.tr: Next, after the first revolution of the heavens, which is uniform, we must consider what follows. For if it were not uniform, there is no doubt it would become either faster or slower, since a change of place that is not uniform can be slowed, halted, and brought to rest. Now a state of motion is either the point from which the moving body begins to be carried, or the point to which it is carried, or the middle. But for the celestial revolution neither a point of departure nor a point of rest has been given. For it has neither a beginning, nor an end, nor indeed any middle. For it is both perpetual in time and by its nature cannot be interrupted. Therefore, if the revolution of the heavens has no state of rest, and no slowing, then it will have no non-uniformity either. For non-uniformity of motion usually arises when a motion is at one time faster and at another slower. Moreover, the non-uniformity of a motion comes either from that which moves, or from that which is moved, or from both. But the non-uniformity of the heavenly revolution proceeds neither from the mover nor from the moved. For that which moves the heavens possesses the same power that the revolution of the heavens requires, nor can it be moved, if it is incorporeal. Therefore the celestial revolution cannot be non-uniform. Furthermore, if the revolution of the heavens were non-uniform, and one of the stars moved faster and another more slowly, then by now an interval would have been produced between them over infinite time. But it is quite certain that none of them has been changed in its intervals. Again, the slackening of anything arises from some weakness. Yet every weakness is foreign to nature. For all weaknesses in living things, such as those of old age and the wasting of the body, are contrary to nature. But the first body has no weakness, since it is simple and has nothing that opposes its nature. Therefore weakness does not rule in it, nor does slackening of motion, any more than intensification. For if there were intensification of its motion, there would also be slackening. So much concerning the uniformity of the revolution of the heavens; it remains that we proceed to other matters.

units.la: CAP. XXVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVIII.

units.la: Quænam sit astrorum essentia. * *
units.tr: What the essence of the stars is.

units.la: EQUITUR deinceps vt de astris differamus, & ex quibus constant, quas habeant figuras, quíque eorum motus sint, inquiramus. Primum rationi consentaneum est unumquodque astrum ex eo orbe constare, in quo mouetur.
units.tr: Next it follows that we should discuss the stars, and inquire of what they consist, what shapes they have, and what their motions are. First, it is consonant with reason that each star consists of that orb in which it moves.

units.la: Quæcunque enim eodem motu cientur, eandem habere naturam, par est. At vero astra eodem motu agitatur,quo ipsi orbes,in quibus insunt. Deinde ex quibus oritur calor,& lumen,ea cœlestem habere naturam consentaneum est. Sed ab astris lumen est & calor, sicut satis testantur Sol & Luna. Quam ob causam olim nonnulli fuerūt, qui altissimum corpus ignem esse dixerunt? Quare quodque astrorum ex orbe suo cöstare nihil fuerit in-commodum. At aerem calefaciunt, non sua essentia,veluti ignis & omnia ignea, sed motu. Motus enim & ligna & lapides, atq; terram accedere solet. Quare quod vicinius est regio in ignis,id ab astris inflammari, magis conconfentaneũ est. Propior autem igni aer est: id quod in eis stellis, quæ in ipso aere feruntur, cernere licet. Hæ enim ipsæ adeò incalescunt, ignescúntque, vt ab eis plumbū liquescat. Atq; cũ in eis hoc fiat, aer etiã, qui cir cumfusus est, idẽ patiatur, necesse est. Aere igitur calefaciunt, propterea qp[?] per eũ feruatur. Is enim istu pulsus & conflictu igneus reddᵗur[?]. Etsi tamen superiorum corporum vnumquodque sua in sphæra mouetur, non ignescit, sed ipse aer, propterea quòd ab eis cœli orbibus, & à Sole maximè, cui inhæret, moueatur. Itaque Solis accessu, & ortu, & cum supra nos est, tum in aere calor fit.
units.tr: For things moved by the same motion ought to have the same nature. But the stars are moved by the same motion as the orbs in which they are fixed. Again, it is consonant that those things from which heat and light arise have a heavenly nature. But light and heat come from the stars, as the Sun and Moon sufficiently bear witness. For this reason, have there not been some who said that the highest body is fire? Wherefore it would be no inconvenience to say that each of the stars consists of its own orb. They warm the air, however, not by their essence, as fire and all fiery things do, but by motion. For motion is wont to heat wood, stones and earth too. Therefore it is more consonant that the region nearer to fire is set alight by the stars. The air is nearer to fire; this can be seen in those stars which are carried in the air itself. For these very stars become so hot and so aflame that lead is melted by them. And since this happens in them, the air which surrounds them must necessarily suffer the same. Therefore they warm the air, and for that reason it is preserved by it. For it is rendered fiery by this push and collision. Although each of the superior bodies is moved in its own sphere, it does not itself catch fire, but the air itself is moved by the orbs of heaven, and above all by the Sun, to which it adheres. Thus at the Sun's approach, and at its rising, and when it is above us, heat arises in the air.

units.la: CAP. XXIX.
units.tr: CAP. XXIX.

units.la: Astra non suo motu fieri, sed secundum vniuscuiusque orbis motum.
units.tr: That the stars do not move by their own motion, but according to the motion of each sphere.

units.la: OELVM & astra stare, terra quiescente, in rerū natura fieri non potest. Propterea sistat terra, cœlum & astra mouentur: aut si hæc duntaxat mouentur, illud stat: aut contra. Atqui astra moueri, cœlo stante, non rationi cõsentaneũ videtur. Itaq; cœlu & astra mouetur. Atque si propriis motionibus mouetur, eadē eorū celeritas erit: Sed stellarū & orbiū non eadē & par potest esse celeritas, quòniā non easdē habet magnitudines. Propterea celerior sit ea stella, oportet, q p maiore orbe fertur, quam quæ per minorem. Etenim orbem esse minorem, & astrum celerius moueri rationi non consonum est. Quod cum ita fit astra nō proprio motu cieri, sed orbibus quæque suis circunferri, necessarium videtur[?]. Itaque alia celerius, alia tardius mouentur prout maior minorve est ille orbis, quo quodque fertur. Quod autem orbes stent & astra moueatur, nulla ratio est. Sic enim fieret ea celerius moueri, quæ superiora sunt, & eorum celeritates ex orbium suorum magnitudine prouenire. Id quod omnino falsum est. Quoniam igitur astra non proprio motu cientur, relinquitur orbes per fe duntaxat moueri, & astra, fixa ipsis orbibus ferri: ita enim nihil absurdum eueniet. Cæterum forte quispiam dixerit astra per fe moueri voluique, quod rotunda sint. Sed nihil minus. Nam fi versarentur, omnia eode motu mouerentur. At variis motibus cientur prout varie voluuntur orbes. Quod etiam non voluantur in Luna facile conspici potest. Si enim ea volueretur eius facies, in qua maculæ sunt, non semper nobis appareret. Nam ea, quæ voluuntur omnes suas partes ostendunt. Quamobrem luna nō voluitur, nec vllum aliorum astrorum. Itaque astra per fe non mouentur, sed, eorum orbium motu, quibus inhærent.
units.tr: That the heavens and the stars should stand still while the earth is at rest cannot happen in the nature of things. Therefore, either the earth stands still and the heavens and stars move, or, if only these move, the earth stands still, or the reverse. But that the stars should move while the heavens stand still does not seem consonant with reason. Therefore the heavens and the stars move. And if they move by their own proper motions, their speed would be the same; but the stars and the spheres cannot have the same and an equal speed, since they do not have the same magnitudes. Therefore a star that is carried through a larger sphere must be swifter than one that is carried through a smaller. For it is not consistent with reason that the sphere should be smaller and the star move more swiftly. Since this is so, it seems necessary that the stars are not moved by their own proper motion, but that each is carried round by its own sphere. Accordingly, some move more swiftly and others more slowly, according as the sphere by which each is carried is larger or smaller. But there is no reason why the spheres should stand still and the stars move. For in that case those stars that are higher would be moved more swiftly, and their speeds would arise from the magnitude of their spheres, which is altogether false. Since, therefore, the stars are not moved by a proper motion, it remains that the spheres alone move of themselves, and the stars, fixed to the spheres themselves, are carried along; for in this way nothing absurd follows. But perhaps someone will say that the stars move and roll of themselves because they are round. But this is by no means so. For if they rotated, all would be moved by the same motion; yet they are moved by various motions, according as the spheres roll in various ways. That they do not roll in the case of the Moon can also be easily seen: for if its face, on which the spots are, rolled, it would not always appear to us. For things that roll show all their parts. Wherefore the Moon does not roll, nor does any other of the stars. Therefore the stars do not move of themselves, but by the motion of those spheres to which they are attached.

units.la: CAP. XXX.
units.tr: CAP. XXX.

units.la: Corporum cœlestium conuersiones nullam efficere harmoniam.
units.tr: The heavenly bodies' revolutions produce no harmony.

units.la: Jam[?] Pythagorei dixerunt quen- dam concetum impulsu motuque cœlestium orbium effici, hac ratione ducti, quòd ea quæ hic apud nos mouentur, sonum edant: quæ quidem nec tam magna sunt, quàm Sol & Luna, nec tanta celeritate mouentur: quódque fieri nō posset quin astra, quæ tanta sunt & multitudine & magnitudine, atque tanta celeritate cientur sonum quendam admirabile & magnum conficiant. Quòd autem eorum sonū non audiamus id causæ esse dixerunt, quòd à primo ortu nostro aures nostræ hoc sonitu ita oppleantur, vt à contrario silentio non internoscatur. Sed hæc ita esse nullo modo possunt. Non enim solùm modò absurdum est, nihil nos sonum audire omnium maximum, sed etiam ab eo nihil sensu affici. Imò verò vehementes soni inanimatorum corporum moles ac magnitudines dirimunt, ita vt tonitru & saxa & alia robustissima corpora diuidat. Præterea non omnia corpora, quæ magna mole sunt sonum efficere possunt, sed ea duntaxat, quæ colliduntur, & consequen-ter dura sunt. Sed huiusmodi cœlestia corpora non sunt. Non enim colliduntur, nec vlla duritie prædita sunt. Quare nullum efficere sonum & concentum possunt.
units.tr: The Pythagoreans said that a certain harmony is produced by the impulse and motion of the heavenly spheres, led to this view because the things that are moved here among us give out a sound; and the heavenly bodies, which are not as large as the Sun and Moon nor move with such speed, indeed could not fail, being so great in number and size and moved with such speed, to produce some wonderful and great sound. They said that the reason we do not hear their sound is that from our very first coming into being our ears are so filled with this sound that it cannot be distinguished from the silence to which we are contrary. But these things cannot be so in any way. For it is not only absurd that we hear no sound at all, though it is the greatest of all, but also that we are not affected by it in any way to our senses. Indeed, the violent sounds of inanimate bodies, and their masses and magnitudes, do split things apart, so that thunder splits rocks and other very solid bodies. Moreover, not all bodies that are large in mass can produce a sound, but only those that collide and are consequently hard. But heavenly bodies of this kind are not such: for they do not collide, nor are they endowed with any hardness. Wherefore they cannot produce any sound or harmony.

units.la: CAP. XXXI. Quis sit astrorum ordo.
units.tr: CAP. XXXI. What the order of the stars is.

units.la: P[?]ORRO de astrorum ordine, quemadmodum vnumquodque dispositum fit, & quòd alia aliis priora sint, alia posteriora, & interuallis inter se disiuncta, iis, quæ in Astrologia traduntur, cognoscendum est. Primùm autem consentaneum est, vt singulorum motiones pro interuallorum ratione aliæ aliis celeriores sint, aliæ tardiores. Verùm quoniam extima cœli conuersio ponitur esse simplex & celerrima, aliorúmque orbium motiones tartiores[?], atque plures (vnumquodque enim astrum in suo orbe fertur motu contrario extimæ conuersioni cœli, & è regione illius) iam hoc consentaneum est, vt quæ conuersio proxima est extimæ & simplici longissimo tempore perficiatur, & quæ remotissima breuissimo: cæterarum autem, ea quæ ipsi primæ propinquior est, longiori tempore, quæ remotior, breuiori suum absoluat cursum. Quæ enim proxima est conuersio maximè à prima superatur, quæ verò remotissima minimè omnium propter maximam remotionem. Mediam autem ab extima etiam superari pro interualli ratione Mathematici demonstrant.
units.tr: Next, concerning the order of the stars: how each one is arranged, and how some are prior to others and some posterior, and how they are separated from one another by intervals, must be learned from those things that are taught in Astrology. First, then, it is reasonable that the motions of the individual bodies should be some faster and some slower, according to the proportion of their intervals. But since the outermost revolution of the heaven is held to be simple and most rapid, while the motions of the other spheres are slower and more numerous (for each star is carried in its own sphere by a motion contrary to the outermost revolution of the heaven, and in the opposite direction to it), it follows that the revolution nearest to the outermost and simple one is completed in the longest time, and the most remote in the shortest time; and of the rest, the one nearer to the first completes its course in a longer time, and the more remote in a shorter time. For the revolution that is nearest is most strongly overcome by the first, while the most remote is least overcome of all, on account of its very great distance. The mathematicians also demonstrate that the middle one is overcome by the outermost too, in proportion to the interval.

units.la: CAP. XXXII.
units.tr: CAP. XXXII.

units.la: Quænam sit astrorum figura.
units.tr: What the shape of the stars is.

units.la: INGULORUM autem astrorum figuram esse sphæricam, ex eo intelligere possumus quòd Natura, quæ nihil frustra facit, ac sine causa, eis figuram huiusmodi tribuisse, quæ ad φο-ρὰν minimè apta sit. At sphærica figura huiusmodi est: quandoquidem instrumentis, quibus aliquod corpus seipsum loco promoueat, omnibus caret. Itaque rotunda sunt omnia astra. Id quòd profecto in Luna perspicuum est. Neque enim cùm crescit & decre-scit curua ex vtraque parte videretur, & fe-micircularis, nisi rotunda esset eius figura. Id quodtum magis apparet, cum ea plena est. Deinde Solis rotunditas, dum mane nobis exoritur, & cum sudum est cœlum, satis omnibus conspicua est. Nec etiam cùm deficit nobis curuus appareret, nisi rotundus esset. Quare astra sphæricam habent figuram,pro-pterea quòd ad motum inepta sint. Cœlū etiā non natura versatur mouetúrque,sed diuinitus: quadoquidem motor eius diuinus est, & sempiternus. Quare ipsius cœli motus etiam æternus Aristoteli visus est.
units.tr: That the figure of the individual stars is spherical we can understand from this: Nature, which makes nothing in vain or without cause, has given them a figure of such a kind as is least suited to motion. But a spherical figure is of this kind, since it lacks all the instruments by which a body moves itself from place to place. Therefore all the stars are round. This is clearly evident in the Moon. For when it waxes and wanes, it would not appear curved on either side, and semicircular, unless its figure were round. This appears all the more when it is full. Next, the roundness of the Sun, as it rises for us in the morning, and when the sky is clear, is sufficiently visible to everyone. Nor would it appear curved to us when it is eclipsed, unless it were round. Hence the stars have a spherical figure, because they are unfit for motion. Nor is the heaven itself moved by nature, but by divine power, since its mover is divine and everlasting. Hence Aristotle also thought the motion of the heaven itself to be eternal.

units.la: CAP. XXXIII.
units.tr: CAP. XXXIII.

units.la: Cur orbes astrorum errantium nō eo pluribus motionibus cientur, quò longius à primo cœli corpore absunt. Ite cur in primo orbe infinita pro pemodū sit astrorū multitudo, in reliquis dun-taxat unum?
units.tr: Why the orbs of the wandering stars are not moved by more motions the farther they are from the first body of the heavens; and why, in the first orb, there is an almost infinite multitude of stars, but in the rest only one?

units.la: VAE hîc proponuntur quæstiones, quarū prima est, quam ob causam non semper hæc astra, quæ lōgius à primo orbe distát, pluribus motionibus cientur, cum medi{a}plurimis ferantur. Etenim rationi consentaneum videtur, vt si primum corpus vna tantum conuersione moueatur, id quod ei proximum est duabus, & quæ deinceps consequuntur pluribus huiusmodi motionibus tali ordine dispositis cientur. Sed contrà euenire Aristoteles censuit, Ægyptiorum Babyloniorumque obseruationibus ducts. Paucioribus enim motionibus Solem & Lunam cieri ait, quàm quædam aliorum errantium, quæ primo corporeri propinquiora sunt, & à medio longiùs distant. Non etiam iniuria quæri potest, cur in primo corpore tàta sit astrorum multitudo, & in vno quoque reliquorum cœlestium vnum duntaxat. Oportet haud dubie nos de hisce corporibus ita cogitare, vt si viuerent: quandoquidem vim agendi habent. Agunt enim vt bonum consequuntur, quod profecto ei naturæ, quæ optima est & diuina, sine vlla actioneinesse videtur. Ei verò, quæ illi proxima est, vna tantum & exigua: aliis autem, quæ ab ea longissimè absunt pluribus, vt corporibus euenit. Quemadmodũ enim absque vlla exercitatione aliud valet: aliud leui ambulatione: aliud cursu & luctatione, aut alia huiuscemodi motione, ita astrorum actioactionem talem esse existimandum est, qua-lis ea est animaliu & stirpium. Nam hic homi-nis actiones plurimae sunt, quandoquidé multa cosequi bona ille potest. Ei vero quod optimum est,[?] nulla actione opus est. Id enim est cuius gratia cætera agunt. Sed aliæ animantes pauciora agunt: stirpes vnam duntaxat actionem edunt. Vnum enim est, quod consequi possunt. Itaque aliud illius optimi absque ulla[?] actione particeps est: aliud ad id ipsum paucis peruenit: aliud vero multis: aliud denique nullo modo ipsum consequitur, sed ei satis est, si aliquousque accedat. O-mnibus enim maxime optimum est ipsum co-sequi finem & ultimum, quod optimum est. Quod quidem si non euenìat, semper id melius est, quod ipsi optimo propinquius accedit. Terra autem ipsum optimum non consequitur, propterea omnino non mouetur. Sed, quæ ei propinqua sunt, paucis motionibus cietur, quoniam non ad ipsum ultimum peruenìunt, sed eousque pergunt, quousque diuinissimum istud principiū consequi possint. Primum autem corpus illud ipsum una motione assequitur: Alij vero orbes inter ipsum & postremum interiecti motionibus multis ad ipsum perueniunt optimum. Posterior tandem quæstio, qua quæritur, cur in primo corpore tāta sit astrorum multitudo, & in unoquoque unum duntaxat, eodé quasi modo explicari potest, quo prior. Primum
units.tr: Here two questions are put forward. The first is why those stars that lie farther from the first orb are not always moved by more motions, since the ones in the middle are carried around by very many. For it seems reasonable that if the first body is moved by a single revolution, the body next to it should be moved by two, and those that follow in order should be moved by more such motions, arranged in this order. Aristotle, however, held that the opposite happens, led by the observations of the Egyptians and Babylonians. He says that the Sun and Moon are moved by fewer motions than certain other wandering stars, which are nearer the first body and farther from the middle. Nor can it be asked without reason why there is such a multitude of stars in the first body, and only one in each of the other heavenly bodies. We must undoubtedly think of these bodies as if they were alive, since they have a power of acting. For they act in order to obtain something good, which seems to belong to that nature which is best and divine, without any activity. But the body nearest to it has one motion only, and a small one; others, which are farthest from it, have more, as happens with bodies. For just as one thing has strength without any exercise, another by light walking, another by running and wrestling, or some other such motion, so we must judge that the activity of the stars is of the same kind as that of animals and plants. For man has many actions, since he can obtain many goods. But for that which is best, no action is needed at all, since it is that for the sake of which the other things act. Other living things act less, and plants perform only one action, for there is only one thing they can obtain. So one thing shares in that best thing without any action; another reaches it by few; another by many; and finally another does not obtain it in any way, but it is enough for it to approach it to some extent. For it is greatest good for all things to attain the final end, which is the best. If this does not happen, that is always better which comes nearer to the best itself. The earth, however, does not attain the best, and therefore is not moved at all. But those bodies that are near to it are moved by few motions, because they do not reach the ultimate end itself, but proceed only so far as they can attain that most divine principle. The first body attains it by one motion alone; but the other orbs, placed between it and the last, reach the best by many motions. The final question, why there is such a multitude of stars in the first body, and only one in each of the others, can be explained in much the same way as the former. The first

units.la: CAP. XXXIIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXIV.

units.la: De terra.
units.tr: On the earth.

units.la: ESTAT deinceps utile [?] terra di-camus, ubi locata sit, & utrum stet, ánne moveatur nécne, & denique de eius figura. De situ quidem eius non omnes philosophi olim consentiebant.
units.tr: Next it is useful to say where the earth is located, whether it stands still or moves, and finally what its shape is. The ancient philosophers did not all agree about its position.

units.la: Plurimi enim eam in Mundi medio esse collocatam dicebat, alij negabant, & præsertim Pythagorei, qui ignem in medio situm esse statuebant, & terram unum astrorum, quod motu suo noctem efficit, & diem. Dicebant enim ei corpori, quod omnium præstantissimum est locum præcipuum tribui: ac proinde ignem, quòd terra præstaret, in medio Universi locatum esse iudicabant. Fuerút alij, quibus placuit ipsam terram in Universi medio sitam esse, & circú axem, qui per ipsum universum extensus est, versari. Alij vero eam in aqua collocata esse voluerút, ubi quiescat & sustineatur, perinde ac lignu innatás, quod quidè nó in aere cósistit. Alij denique eandé in aere stare dicebat, ut Anaxagoras atq; Democritus, propterea quòd eum non diuidat & secet sua planitie ( ea enim plana esse cen-febant)sed operiat. Hocipfum terra sua latitudine & planitie facere iudicabant contra vim subiecti aeris,qui cū nihilhabeat, quo apte locū mutare possit,coarctatusinfra terra stat & cohibetur, quemadmodū aqua in clepsydriis. De figura eiufde terrę variæ etia fuerunt veterū sententiæ. Aliis enim rotuda videbatur, aliis plana & lata. Posteriores id huic perspici dicebat, quod cū Sol occidit atque oritur,tū per recta linea,nō aute per curuam abscōdi videatur,etiafi oporteret, si terra esset rotuda,diuisione eius curua fieri. Hæ sunt propemodū omnes veterū philosophorum sententiæ,motu & figura,quas omnes singulatim refellere licet. Primum enim terra circū axem in medio moueri non posse, perspicere licet hinc sumpto principio. Si terra mouetur siue in medio vniuersi, siue extra ipsū,ea violeter moueri,necesse est. Neque enim terræ proprius motus est. Nā si natura moueretur: profecto vnaquæque pars eius hoc naturali motu cieretur. Sed omnes eius partes rectis feruntur lineis in medium, si forte eas moueri contingat. Quod si violenta fit terræ commotio, ea esse perpetua non potest, quoniam nullus violentus motus, & qui a natura alienus est,perpetuus esse potest. Ordo autem Mundi continuus est. præterea si terra in orbem moueretur,haud dubie pluribus cieretur motionibus siue circum Mediū,siue in eo locata sit: quandoquidem quæcunque in orbem feruntur à prima motione primi orbis pluribus motionibus cieri cernuntur. Id quod sane in vagis astris, quæ ab ipso pri-mo orbe variis motionibus agitantur[?], perspicuum satis est. Si præterea absque[?] externa vi pars nulla terræ sursum moueri possit, con-sequens est terram natura stabilem omnino esse. Quo enim quæque pars suapte natura moueri apta est, eo etiam ipsum eius totum[?]. Posthæc quam infirma sit eorum ratio, qui terram in aqua sitam esse voluerunt, viden-dum est. Vt enim aer aqua leuior est, sic aqua ipsam terram leuitate superat. At non con-sentaneum est, vt quod leue est, id in inferio-re sede potius quam graue collocetur. Præ-terea si hoc toti naturæ terræ largitum sit vt in aqua stet, non id quidem dubium est, quin etiam vnicuique partiu eius naturaidem tri-buerit. At quæuis pars terræ ad infimum eius loci mouetur, eoque celerius, quo amplior fuerit. Ex quibus perspicuum est in Mundi medio terram sitam esse: id quod ex omnium ipsius terræ partium motione facile intelligi potest. Hæ enim ad medium ferri cernuntur. Vtrum autem ad medium Mundi ferantur, anne ad medium ipsius terræ, nihil interest. Mundi enim & terræ idem medium est. Pro-pterea ad terræ medium grauia feruntur, sed ex accidete, quoniam in ipso vniuersi medio terra sita est, & suum habet medium. Grauia
units.tr: Many held that it is placed in the middle of the world, while others denied this, especially the Pythagoreans. They held that fire is situated in the middle, and that the earth is one of the stars, which by its motion produces night and day. For they thought that the chief place should be given to the body that is most excellent of all, and so they judged that fire, which is superior to earth, was placed in the middle of the universe. Others have thought that the earth itself lies in the middle of the universe and turns about the axis that extends through the whole universe. Others have wished that the earth is set in water, where it rests and is supported, just as wood floats, though it does not stand in air. Others, finally, said that it stands in air, as Anaxagoras and Democritus did, because it does not cut or divide the air with its flat surface (for they thought it was flat) but covers it. They judged that the earth does this by its breadth and flatness, against the force of the air beneath it, which, having no room to move freely, is compressed and held in beneath the earth, just as water is held in water clocks. There were also various ancient opinions about the shape of the earth. For some thought it round, others flat and broad. Later writers said this could be seen because when the sun sets and rises it is hidden by a straight line and not by a curve, although if the earth were round, its division would have to make a curve. These are almost all the opinions of the ancient philosophers about motion and shape, and each of them can be refuted separately. First, that the earth cannot move in a circle about an axis in the middle may be seen from the following principle. If the earth moves, whether in the middle of the universe or outside it, it must necessarily be moved violently. For motion is not proper to the earth. If it moved by nature, then each part of it would certainly be carried by this natural motion. But all its parts are borne in straight lines towards the middle, if they happen to be moved at all. If the earth's motion is violent, it cannot be perpetual, since no violent motion, which is contrary to nature, can be perpetual. But the order of the world is continuous. Moreover, if the earth were moved in a circle, it would undoubtedly be carried by several motions, whether it were located around the middle or in it, since whatever is carried in a circle is seen to be moved by several motions from the first motion of the first sphere. This is quite plain in the wandering stars, which are moved by various motions from the first sphere itself. Furthermore, if no part of the earth can be moved upward without external force, it follows that the earth is by nature wholly stable. For just as each part is by its own nature apt to be moved in a certain way, so too is the whole of it. Next, we must see how weak is the reasoning of those who wished the earth to be set in water. For just as air is lighter than water, so water surpasses the earth in lightness. But it is not consistent that what is light should be placed in a lower seat rather than what is heavy. Moreover, if this has been granted to the whole nature of the earth, that it stands in water, there is no doubt that it has also granted the same nature to each of its parts. But every part of the earth is moved to the lowest point of that place, and the more quickly the larger it is. From these things it is plain that the earth is placed in the middle of the world, which can easily be understood from the motion of all its parts. For these are seen to be carried towards the middle. Whether they are carried towards the middle of the world or towards the middle of the earth itself makes no difference. For the middle of the world and of the earth is the same. Therefore heavy bodies are carried towards the middle of the earth, but by accident, since the earth is situated in the very middle of the universe and has its own middle.

units.la: autem ad ipsum terrę medium ferri,huic sci- ri potest, quòd ad pares angulos omnia hu- iufmodi moueantur, tamétsi non æquè di- stent. Hæc de terræ situ & statu paucis dicta sint. Quænam sutem fit eius figura etiam ex- plicare conuenit. Verùm in primis non au- diendi sunt, qui terram planam latámque ef- fe asseruerunt, quòd sol, cùm occidit atque oritur, per rectam linea, non autem per cur- uam abscoisdatur. Solis enim interuallum à terræ, & ambitus magnitudinem non rectè isti animaduertebant. Itaque hac specie non eos adduci opportuit, vt terram non esse ro- tundam crederent. Quòd autem rotunda fit hac ratione ducimur: quòd quæque partium eius vsque ad medium delata fit grauis: cu- ius grauitate maior minorem pellere nō po- teft,sed duntaxat comprimit. Ex quo fit, vt ambæ conglobentur, & figuram acquirant sphæricam. Præterea si vndique ab extremis Mundi vsque ad eius medii omnia, quæ gra- uia sunt,deferuntur, ea rotunda fiant,neces- se est. Deinde quod sphæricam efficit vm- bram,aut pyramidatam,id rotundum est.Sed vmbram terræ talem esse lunæ defectio- nibus, satis perspicuum est. Quoniam e- tiam terræ obiectu Luna deficit, aliter fieri non potest, quin ipsius terræ ambitus sit ro- tundus.
units.tr: Moreover, it can be known that heavy bodies moving to the very middle of the earth move to equal angles, although they are not equally distant. This is said briefly about the position and state of the earth. But it is fitting to explain what its shape is. First, we must not listen to those who have asserted that the earth is flat and broad, because the sun is hidden when it sets and rises by a straight line and not by a curve. For they did not correctly consider the distance of the sun from the earth and the greatness of the earth's circumference. Hence they ought not to have been led by this appearance into believing that the earth is not round. But we are led to conclude that it is round by this reasoning: each of its parts is carried heavily down to the middle, and the greater heaviness cannot drive away the smaller but only compresses it. From this it follows that both are gathered into a ball and acquire a spherical shape. Moreover, if all heavy things are carried from the extremities of the world to its middle, they must necessarily become round. Next, whatever casts a spherical or pyramidal shadow is round. But that the shadow of the earth is of this kind is plain enough from the eclipses of the moon. Since the moon is eclipsed by the interposition of the earth, it cannot happen otherwise than that the circumference of the earth itself is round.

units.la: CAP. XXV. Nullum corpus ex foliis superficiebus conflatum esse.
units.tr: Chapter 25. That no body is composed of surfaces.

units.la: ORUM autem, quæ in natura esse dicuntur, quædam substantiæ sunt, quædam earum opera & affectiones. Substantias dicimus simplicia corpora, ut cœlum & eius partes, ignem, ter-ram, aera & aquam, & rursus animantia, stir-pes, & eorum omnium partes. Affectiones autem & functiones vocamus motiones v-niuscuiusque horum corporum, & aliorum, quorum elementa vi sua causæ sunt & principia: ac præterea ipsorum quatuor elementorum mutuas inter se alterationes. Omnes item naturales substantiæ, aut corpora sunt, aut cum corporibus magnitudinibusque na-scuntur, ut rerum species & formæ. De primo corpore & quale natura sit, iam explica-tum est, de aliis restat differere: quod simul fiet cum de generatione & corruptione di-sputabimus. Verum utramque mutationem nonnulli veterum philosophorum funditus sustulerunt. Nulla enim rem gigni, nec cor-rumpi volebant, sed tantummodo videri: in qua hæresi fuit Melissus & Parmenides. Alij autem fuerunt, qui nihil origine & ortu va-care dixerunt, quorum maxime fuit Hesio-dus, & alij, qui primum de Natura disputa-runt. Alij quoque omnia, quæ natura con-stant; stant,& gigni & labi,nihilque stabile esse,as-seruerunt, sed vnum quiddam duntaxat per manere, ex quo omnia natura formari pos-sint. Alij denique fuerunt, qui omne corpus genitum esse,ex[?] superficiebus,&in eastandē[?] resolui putarunt. Quod si ita esset, profecto nullus[?] haberetur graue corpus. Atqui omnia sensilia corpora,vel nonnulla, sunt gra-uia,vt terra& aqua. Quod autem nihil eorū corporum,quæ ex superficiebus constant, graue sit,his rationibus intelligi potest. Pri-mum superficies ex lineis constat,lineæ ex puncto. Atqui nullius ponderis est pun-ctum, nec consequenter lineæ, quæ exeo constant. Deinde omnes habitus intendi & remitti possuut. Quare si punctum graue es-set, certè aliquo grauius esse posset. Ex quo consequeretur ipsum esse diuiduum. Atqui punctum indiuiduum esse statuitur. Præter-ea si omne punctum graue esset ipsum que-que densum esse posset : quàdoquidem quod graue est,id etiam densum,vt tenue ac rarum quod leue est. At quod densum est, id diuidi potest, vt & rarum. Punctum autem indiui-duum est. Adhæc quicquid graue est, sit e-tiam molle,aut durum, necesse est. Molle,id quod tactui cedit,durum,contrà id quod no cedit. Quod autem cedit, id secari potest. Sed punctum secari diuidíque nequit. Ita-que punctum nec densum est,nec rarum,nec durum,nec molle, nec denique graue, aut leue.' Ex quibus constat nullum corpus ex superficiebus compositum graue esse.
units.tr: Of the things that are said to exist in nature, some are substances and some are their works and affections. By substances we mean simple bodies, such as the heavens and their parts, fire, earth, air and water, and again living things, plants, and all their parts. By affections and functions we mean the motions of each of these bodies, and of others whose elements are the causes and principles of their powers; and besides, the mutual alterations of the four elements themselves. Likewise all natural substances are either bodies, or are born together with bodies and magnitudes, like the species and forms of things. About the first body, and what its nature is, we have already explained; the rest remains to be discussed, and this will be done together with our disputation on generation and corruption. Yet some of the ancient philosophers utterly abolished both kinds of change. For they held that nothing is generated or corrupted, but only seems to be so; in this heresy were Melissus and Parmenides. Others said that nothing lacks origin and birth, and among these was chiefly Hesiod, and others who first disputed about nature. Others again asserted that all things which consist in nature both come into being and perish, and that nothing is stable, but that only one thing remains through all, from which all natural things can be formed. Finally there were others who thought that every body is generated from surfaces and resolved again into them. If that were so, certainly no body would be regarded as heavy. Yet all sensible bodies, or some of them, are heavy, as earth and water. That none of those bodies which consist of surfaces is heavy can be understood from these reasons. First, a surface consists of lines, and lines of points. But a point has no weight at all, nor consequently the lines which consist of it. Next, all qualities can be intensified and remitted. Therefore if a point were heavy, it could certainly be heavier than something else. From this it would follow that it is divisible. But a point is established to be indivisible. Moreover, if every point were heavy, it could also be dense; since what is heavy is also dense, just as what is light is thin and rare. But what is dense can be divided, as also what is rare. A point, however, is indivisible. Besides, whatever is heavy must also be either soft or hard. Soft is that which yields to touch, hard, on the contrary, that which does not yield. But what yields can be cut. Yet a point cannot be cut or divided. Therefore a point is neither dense nor rare, neither hard nor soft, and finally neither heavy nor light. From these things it is established that no body composed of surfaces is heavy.

units.la: CAP. XXXVI. Simplicium corporum motiones ostendere corpora ex superficiebus non conflari.
units.tr: CAP. XXXVI. That the motions of simple bodies show that bodies are not formed from surfaces.

units.la: Omnibus autem simplicibus corporibus aliquam motionem à Natura necessario datam esse, ex his intelligi potest. Quæcunque enim moueri videntur, vi moueantur, necesse est, nisi proprio motu cientur. Vi autem moueri & contra naturam idem sunt. Sed motus contra naturam nullus esse potest, nisi alius sit ei aduersus, qui naturalis est. Nam, quanuis simplicium corporum plures motus contra naturam sint, vnum habeant necesse est, qui secundum Naturam sit. Itaque Democriti sectatores nunc respondeant, quonam motu atomi cientur, quas semper in vacuo & infinitate moueri ipse dicebat.
