Si enim aliud elementum ab alio moueri dicant, alium esse motum naturæ cuiusque concedant, oportet. Nam primus motus non est violentus, sed secundum Naturam : atque in infinitum progressus fiet, si non sit aliquid primum Naturale mouens, a quo primus motus sit. Hoc fere pacto refelleda erit eorum sententia, qui ante vniuersi originem elementa in-ordiordinatè moueri, dicebant. Nam si sponte Naturæ mouebatur,tum Mundum fuisse,expedit,& omnia corpora iam sua & naturalia loca occupasse: quoniam hunc ordine Mundus obtinet. Præterea si vnum id esset, quod elementa moueret, profecto vno motu ea cieri oportuit. Itaque non inordinatè moue-bantur. Si insuper ea tum infinita erant, quæ ipsis elementis motum afferebant, infinitos quoque motus eis fuisse, necesse fuit. Sed elementis Natura vnum duntaxat motum dedit. Sin fuerint, ante Mundi ortum,tum illis ordo quidem motus fuit. Nam inordinatè moueri nihil est aliud, quàm contra Naturā. Propterea proprius ordo corporum, quæ sen[?] filia sunt,secundū naturam est. Quare quendam esse motum naturalem vnicuique corporum,quo non vi,nec contra naturam mo-uetur,necesse est. Nam si quod natura moue-tur id nec graue fit, nec leue, profecto haud-quaquam ad vniuersi medium, aut è medio moueri poterit. Atqui omne corpus natura-le vel è medio Vniuersi,vel in medium & in-ferum locum Natura fertur. Quare omne corpus naturale aut graue est, aut leue. Cæ-terum naturalis motus à violento ex eo di-stinguitur quòd illius principium interius sit,& ipsa Natura, quæ causa motus est & sta-tus:huius verò exterius: Vt iactus lapidis sursum, causa in homine[?] est, sed deambulatio-nis natura hominis.
units.tr: From these points it can be understood that every simple body is necessarily given some motion by Nature. For whatever seems to be moved is either moved by force or moved by its own motion. To be moved by force and to be moved contrary to nature are the same thing. But there can be no motion contrary to nature unless there is some opposing motion that is natural. For although simple bodies have several motions contrary to nature, they must have one that accords with nature. Let the followers of Democritus therefore now say by what motion the atoms are moved, which he himself said were always moving in the void and in infinity. For if they say that one element is moved by another, they must concede that each element has a motion of its own nature. The first motion is not violent but according to nature, and there would be an infinite regress unless there were some first natural mover from which the first motion comes. In much the same way the opinion of those who said that the elements were moved in disorder before the origin of the universe should be refuted. For if they were moved by the will of Nature, then the world would have been already in existence and all bodies would already occupy their natural places, since the world holds this order. Furthermore, if there were only one thing that moved the elements, it must surely have moved them by one motion. Therefore they were not moved in disorder. If moreover the things that gave motion to the elements were infinite, it must follow that the motions too were infinite. But Nature gave the elements only one motion. If, however, they existed before the birth of the world, then they had indeed an order of motion, for to be moved in disorder is nothing other than to be moved contrary to nature. Therefore the proper order of those bodies which are simple is according to nature. Hence it is necessary that each body have a certain natural motion, by which it is moved not by force nor contrary to nature. For if a thing moved by nature is neither heavy nor light, it certainly cannot be moved at all towards the centre of the universe or away from it. Yet every natural body is carried by nature either from the centre of the universe or towards the central and lowest place. Therefore every natural body is either heavy or light. Moreover, natural motion is distinguished from violent motion in this, that the principle of the former is internal and is Nature itself, which is the cause of motion and rest, whereas the principle of the latter is external. Thus when a stone is thrown upwards, the cause lies in the man, but the walking of a man comes from the nature of man.

units.la: CAP. XXXVII. Quænam sit elementi natura ?
units.tr: CAP. XXXVII. What is the nature of an element?

units.la: Estat ut quorum corporum generatio fit, & cur sit dicamus. Quoniam autem in omnibus cognitio per prima nobis est; ideo quæ prima sunt corpora primum explicare licet. Hæc autem universi elementa sunt, quæ mistorum corporum principia dicuntur. Quare quænam sit elementi natura dicendum est.{*} Est autem id in quod cætera diuiduntur corpora, in quibus potestate inest vel actu: nec in ea, quæ specie differunt, diuidi potest. Quod si hoc elementum est, id corpus esse oportet. Propterea in carne & in ligno, atque in unoquo-que eiusdem generis, potestas materiaque ignis & terræ, aeris & aquæ inest: quæ perspicuè ex eis secernuntur.
units.tr: Next we should say how and why the generation of bodies takes place. Since, however, knowledge of everything comes to us through what is first, it is permissible to explain first the bodies that are first. These are the elements of the universe, which are called the principles of mixed bodies. Therefore we must say what the nature of an element is. An element is that into which other bodies are divided, and which is contained in them either potentially or actually, and which cannot be divided into things that differ in species. If this is an element, it must be a body. Accordingly, in flesh and in wood, and in each thing of the same kind, the potential and the matter of fire, earth, air and water are present, and these are clearly separated out of them.

units.la: CAP. XXXVIII. An universi elementa infinita sint, anne finita ?
units.tr: Chapter 38. Are the elements of the universe infinite, or finite?

units.la: Etiam[?] quidem non defuerunt, qui Mundi elemeta esse innumerabilia dixerunt, ut Leucippus & Democritus Abderites, qui atomos primas esse magnitudines multitudine infinitas, & magnitudine indiuiduas esse existimauerunt: atque ex earu omniu complexu omnia genera corpora. Sed si omniu corporum differentiae sunt finitæ, profecto numerus elementorum, rum, ex quibus concrescunt cætera corpora, quæ natura constant, non infinitus erit. Fue-runt etiam alij, qui elementa Mundi esse indiuidua posuerunt: sed hos similiter errasse ex eo colligat, quod si ita esset, proculdubio ignis, aer, aqua & terra, non se mutuo generarent. Alij quoque omnes corporis partes, quæ inter se sunt similes, elementa fecerunt, vt Anaxagoras. Sed multa videntur corpora eorum, quæ mixta sunt[?], vt caro, os, ligni cortex, lapis, metallum, & similia in partes eiusdem generis & naturæ distribui, quæ non elementa sunt, quoniam ex aliis concreta fuerunt. Elementum enim nullum ex alio concrescit, quandoquidem, id est, quod in alias partes specie diuersas diuidi non potest. Quibus autem elementa vniuersi infinita esse visum fuit, non parum errarunt. Nam si cuiusque corporis proprius quidem motus est, profecto simplicis corporis simplex motus est proprius. Sed motus simplices non infiniti sunt, propterea quod simplices lationes duabus plures non sint. Præterea cuique simplicium corporum suus est locus. Sed nullius corporis locus est infinitus. Quare elementorum numerus non infinitus est. Restat igitur vt videam, vtrum vnum sit, an plura. Quidā[?] enim vnum dumtaxat in natura statuerunt; quorum alij aquam, alij aerem, quidam ignem esse dicebant: Alij vero aliud ponebant, aquā tenuius, & aere densius, quod cælos suo amplexu continet. Sed commune peccatum omnium hoc fuit, ex eo quod unum solumque naturale motum eundemque corporum omnium fecerint. At si omnium corporum unus duntaxat motus esset, profecto omnia corpora unum quiddam essent. Sed plures corporum motus esse, sa-tis iam demonstratum est. Erraruntetiam non minus qui quoddam aliud corpus esse aqua tenuius, & aere densius statuerunt omnium aliorum corporum principium. Si enim ex uno duntaxat elemento mista corpora constarent, haud dubie omnia vel calida essent, vel frigida prout natura esset: illius elementi, ex quo constarent. Sed alia esse calida, alia frigida tam verum est, quam quod verissi-mum. Quare pluribus elementis inter se pugnantibus omne mistum corpus constat.
units.tr: Indeed, there were not lacking some who said that the elements of the world are innumerable, such as Leucippus and Democritus of Abdera, who thought that atoms are the first magnitudes, infinite in number and indivisible in size, and that all kinds of bodies arise from the combination of all of them. But if the differences of all bodies are finite, then surely the number of the elements, out of which the other bodies that consist by nature are compounded, will not be infinite. There were also others who held that the elements of the world are indivisible; but it is inferred that these erred in the same way, because if it were so, without doubt fire, air, water and earth would not generate one another. Others too made the elements out of all the parts of a body that are alike among themselves, as Anaxagoras did. But many bodies, of those that are mixed, such as flesh, bone, the bark of wood, stone, metal and the like, are seen to be divided into parts of the same kind and nature, and these are not elements, since they were formed out of other things. For no element is formed out of another, since it is that which cannot be divided into parts differing in kind. Yet those to whom it seemed that the elements of the universe are infinite erred not a little. For if each body has its own motion, then surely a simple body has a simple proper motion. But simple motions are not infinite, because there are not more simple motions than two. Besides, each of the simple bodies has its own place. But the place of no body is infinite. Therefore the number of the elements is not infinite. It remains, then, for me to see whether there is one or several. For some have posited only one thing in nature: of these, some said that it was water, others air, some fire. Others, however, put forward something else, a body finer than water and denser than air, which embraces the heavens in its embrace. But the common error of all of them was this, that they made one and the same natural motion for all bodies. But if all bodies had only one motion, then surely all bodies would be one thing. But that there are several motions of bodies has already been sufficiently demonstrated. Those who held that some other body, finer than water and denser than air, is the principle of all other bodies erred no less. For if mixed bodies consisted of only one element, then without doubt all of them would be either hot or cold, according to the nature of that element out of which they were composed. But that some things are hot and others cold is as true as anything can be. Therefore every mixed body consists of several elements that are opposed to one another.

units.la: CAP. XXXIX.
units.tr: CAP. XXXIX.

units.la: Elementa Mundi non esse æterna, sed seipsa mutuo generare.
units.tr: The elements of the world are not eternal, but generate one another in turn.

units.la: P[?]OST HÆC utrum Mundi elementa æterna sint, an vero generentur, & corrumpantur, videndum est. Hoc enim demonstrato, & quot sint, & qualia, perspicuum erit. Æterna quidem esse non possunt. Nam & ignem & aquam, ac unumquodque simplex corpus, præter cœlum, dissolui cernimus. Ignis enim duobus modis dissoluitur, uno consumptione marcoreque, altero corruptione. At à contrario tum corrumpitur, cum extinguitur, & à sea seipso tabescit. Itaque cum vniuersi elementa generari & dissolui possint, eorum generatio aut ex incorporeo, aut ex corpore fit, necesse est. At si ex corpore oriatur, aut ex alio, aut ex seipsis originem ducunt. Deinde si ex incorporeo sint, certe in vacuo generantur. Sed in aliquo sit[?] corporeo oportet, id quod generatur. Igitur id, in quo generatio fit, corpus est. Atqui corpus esse non potest, quoniam duo simul in eodem erunt corpora, vnum quod generatur, & alterum, vbi o-rigo est. Deinde si incorporeum sit, admittendum erit vacuum. Sed in Natura nullum esse vacuum, iam satis demonstratum est. Itaque vniuersi elementa non ex incorporeo oriuntur, neque ex corpore. Si enim ex alio corpore orirentur, eis proculdubio aliud esset corpus & prius & antiquius, quod graue ef-set aut leue. Sed hoc in Natura esse non potest. Propterea ex nullo corpore elementa oriuntur. Praeterea quod gignitur, & id ex quo, & vbi gignitur simul sint, necesse est. Sed duo corpora simul & in eodem nō sunt. Quare elementa nec ex incorporeis, neque ex corpore gigni possunt, sed ex seipsis vicissim.
units.tr: After these things, it must be examined whether the elements of the world are eternal, or whether they are generated and corrupted. For once this has been demonstrated, both how many there are and what they are like will be plain. Indeed they cannot be eternal. For we see that fire and water, and every simple body except the heavens, are dissolved. Fire is dissolved in two ways: one by consumption and wasting away, the other by corruption. On the contrary, it is corrupted when it is extinguished, and it wastes away from itself. Therefore, since the elements of the universe can be generated and dissolved, their generation must come either from the incorporeal or from a body. But if they arise from a body, they derive their origin either from another body or from themselves. Next, if they come from the incorporeal, they are certainly generated in a void. But that which is generated must be in some corporeal place. Therefore the place in which the generation occurs is a body. Yet it cannot be a body, since two bodies would then be together in the same place, the one which is generated and the other where the origin is. Next, if it is incorporeal, a void must be admitted. But it has already been sufficiently demonstrated that there is no void in Nature. Therefore the elements of the universe do not arise from the incorporeal, nor from a body. For if they arose from another body, that body would undoubtedly be prior and older than them, and it would be either heavy or light. But this cannot be in Nature. Therefore the elements arise from no body. Moreover, that which is generated, and that from which it is generated, and the place where it is generated, must necessarily exist together. But two bodies do not exist together in the same place. Therefore the elements can be generated neither from incorporeal things nor from a body, but from one another in turn.

units.la: CAP. XL.
units.tr: CAP. XL.

units.la: Mutuam esse elementorum ge-nerationem.
units.tr: That the generation of the elements is mutual.

units.la: VRSVS igitur videndum est, quisnam fit mutuæ generationis elemetorum modus & ratio, vtru quemadmodu Empedocli & Democrito placuit, an vero vt iis, qu̶ corpora fieri mutatione figuræ in figuram dixerút, an denique alius quispiam, præter hos, modus fit. Empedocles quidem & Democritus suam prodiderunt ignorationem, quando non mutuam elementorum generationem inter se esse, fecerunt, sed quandam duntaxat originis speciem. Dixerunt enim quæque naturalia esse, ac quasi ex aliquo vase educi, & absque vlla oriri materia, & mutatione. Sed horum sententiam multa sequuntur incommoda. Primum enim eadem magnitudo, si condensetur, non grauior reddetur. At quæ ex densato aere aqua gignitur, grauior ipso aere est, & minorem locum occupat. Quod enim ex tenuioribus constat partibus, id in maiore loco situm esse oportet: id quod in euaporatione rei humidæ, & turgente spiritu, perspici licet. Cum nanque humidum expirat, aut flatus turget, tum propter loci angustiam, vasa rumpuntur, quæ ipsa corpora continent. Deinde si generatio est corporis velut ex vase excretio, proculdubio cum aqua ex terra oritur, tum ex ea terra aliquid efferri, necesse est, ex quo aqua gignitur. Quod si semper ex terra fiat corporum excretio, tandem terra deficiet. Ex quo constat mutuam elementorum rum generationem non corporum excretionem esse, sed mutuam eorum mutationem. Si praeterea mutatione figurae in figura mutuae elementorum generationes inter se fiant, necessario individua ipsorum elementorum corpora. Aut si diuidua sint, profecto ignis pars non ignis erit, neque terrae pars terra, propterea quod pyramidis pars, no pyramis est, neque tesserae tessera. Quare certissimis scientiis quae mathematicae dicuntur, aduersati fuerunt, quippe quae quod in intellectu cadit, id diuiduum esse demonstrant. Quod autem figuris duntaxat simplicia corpora inter se differat, ut huiusmodi philosophis placuit, omnino absurdum videtur. Sic enim fiet, ut non plenus sit Mundus nec perfectus. Etenim in planis tres figurae nimirum triangulus, quadragulus & sexangulus locu implere videtur: in solidis autem duae duntaxat esse possunt pyramis & tessera. Sed in vniuerso plures his duabus fumatur, necesse est, quoniam multo plura his elementa sunt. Corpora item omnia, quae simplicia sunt in continete loco sua mutare figura, nec ea tame corrupi videntur, maxime aer & aqua. Quare elementorum figura no perpetuo permanere poterit. Postmodum si aqua ab aere dutaxat figura differt, certe id esse quod erat, desinet, si in alia vertatur figura. Sed hoc no fit. Proinde figuris no distinguuntur elementa, nec definitas figuras habet, Id quod ipsa natura nobis significatu voluit. Quemadmodum enim id quod generationi & corruptioni subiicitur, & omnium corporum formas induere potest, propria figura caret, & ita elementa, quæ corporum mis-torum sunt materia, non determinatam[?] habet figuram. Quapropter in se mutuo mutatur, non mutatis eorum figuris, sed affectionibus, ac patibilibus qualitatibus.
units.tr: We must therefore consider what the manner and principle of the mutual generation of the elements is: whether it is as it pleased Empedocles and Democritus, or rather as it pleased those who said that bodies come to be by a change of figure into figure, or finally whether there is some other manner apart from these. Empedocles and Democritus indeed revealed their ignorance, since they made the elements not mutually generated from one another, but only a certain kind of origin. For they said that each thing is natural and, as it were, drawn out of some vessel, and arises without any matter or change. But many inconveniences follow from their opinion. First, the same magnitude, if it is condensed, does not become heavier. Yet water generated from condensed air is heavier than the air itself and occupies a smaller place. For what consists of finer parts must be situated in a larger place, as can be seen in the evaporation of a moist thing and in a swelling breath. For when moisture is breathed out, or a blast swells, then, because of the narrowness of the place, the vessels that contain those bodies are burst. Next, if generation is an excretion of a body, as it were out of a vessel, then surely when water arises from earth, something must necessarily be drawn out of that earth from which the water is generated. And if the excretion of bodies always took place from the earth, the earth would at last be exhausted. From which it is clear that the mutual generation of the elements is not an excretion of bodies but their mutual change. Further, if the mutual generations of the elements take place by a change of figure into figure, then the bodies of the elements themselves must necessarily be indivisible. Or if they are divisible, then surely a part of fire will not be fire, nor a part of earth earth, since a part of a pyramid is not a pyramid, nor a part of a cube a cube. Therefore they have opposed the most certain sciences, which are called mathematical, since these demonstrate that whatever falls under the intellect is divisible. But that simple bodies differ from one another only in figures, as this has pleased such philosophers, seems wholly absurd. For thus it would come about that the world would be neither full nor perfect. Indeed, among plane figures, three, namely the triangle, the quadrangle and the hexagon, seem to fill space; among solids, however, only two can exist, the pyramid and the cube. But in the universe, since there are far more elements than these, more than these two must necessarily be assumed. Likewise, all simple bodies seem to change their figure in the surrounding place, and yet they do not seem to be corrupted by this, most of all air and water. Therefore the figure of the elements cannot remain perpetually the same. Moreover, if water differs from air only in figure, then surely it will cease to be what it was if it is turned into another figure. But this does not happen. Therefore the elements are not distinguished by figures, nor do they have fixed figures, which nature itself meant to signify to us. For just as that which is subject to generation and corruption, and can take on the forms of all bodies, lacks a proper figure, so the elements, which are the matter of mixed bodies, have no determined figure. Hence they are changed into one another not by a change of their figures, but by their affections and passible qualities.

units.la: CAP. XLI. Quæ sit grauitatis & leuitatis natura.
units.tr: CHAP. XLI. What the nature of heaviness and lightness is.

units.la: VIDNAM aute[?] graue sit, & quid leue, ac quænam utriusque natura sit ante videndum est quam elemen-torum numerum ostendamus, quo-niam facultates sunt a quibus naturalium corporum motiones proficiscuntur. Graue igitur & leue duobus modis dicutur, vno sim-pliciter & altero comparate. Leue aute[?] ab-solute, id est, quod sursum & extremum in locum fertur: graue omnino, id quod deorsum & in medium movetur. Graue etiam & leue comparate dicta pondus habent, quorum aliud leuius est, & aliud grauius. Ut si duo leuia sint mole paria, quod sursum celerius fertur, id leuius est: sic de duobus grauibus pari mole iudicandum est. De iis autem, quæ omnino grauia sunt & leuia nihil a priscis, præ-terquam ab vno Aristotele, disputatum est: sed de aliis, quæ comparate dicuntur dunta-xat disseruerunt. At inter eos de huiusmodi facultatibus non plane constabat. Alij enim, vt Timeus,id grauius esse dixerunt,quod ex pluribus eiusdem naturæ partibus compa-ctum est : leuius vero quod ex paucioribus. Alij autem differebant ex triagulis quodque corpus constare, atque ob triangulorū pau-citatem sursum ignem ferri, quorū omnium ratio nullo pacto consentanea videtur. Sic enim maior ignis moles grauior esset, atque minimus dutaxat in sublime extolletur, quā-doquidem ex paucioribus triangulis costat: At contrà fieri,satis perspicuum est. Quò e-nim maior est ignis eo celerius sursum fer-tur, & leuius est: ac è superiore loco exiguus ignis minori negotio, quàm magnus,detur-batur. Perquàm absurda etiam eorum sen-tentia est, qui id leuius esse dicebant, quod minus eoiu habet, quæ eiusdem generis sunt, & naturæ : & contra id grauius, quo plus hu-iusmodi participest. Semper enim faci-lius maior aer sursum fertur,quàm minor:& omnino queuis aëris pars ex aqua eleuatur. Fuerunt denique alij, vt Leucippus & Democritus,qui id leuius esse dixerunt, in quo plus vacui inesset. Ob eámque causam ignem, eo quòd plurimum vacui haberet, leuissimum esse asserebant. Sed si ob vacuum feratur quidpiam sursum, etiam vacuum sursum ef-ferri,& plenum deorsum,necesse erit. Atqui vacuum moueri non potest. Nam si moueretur, profecto ei locus esset, quoniam omnis φορὰ in loco fit. Sed vacuo nullum esse locu, satis perspicuum est. Sin mouetur, quidnam (quæsó) motionis eius causa erit? Nihil enim seipsum mouet, nisi animal sit. Itaque vacuū non leuitatis causa est, nec ponderis, quod plenum est. Præterea illius grauitatis & leuitatis absolutę, non vna est subiecta materia: Ea enim, si absolutè grauis esset, nullum corpus leue esse posset. Nec etiam illius materię magnitudo, grauitatis causa est, neque leuitatis paucitas: propterea quod aer & ignis sua magnitudine aquam & terram grauitate superarent.
units.tr: Before we set out the number of the elements, we must first see what the heavy is, and what the light is, and what the nature of each is, since these are the powers from which the motions of natural bodies proceed. Heavy and light are spoken of in two ways: one absolutely, the other comparatively. Absolutely light is that which is carried upward and toward the extremity; absolutely heavy is that which is moved downward and toward the centre. Heavy and light in the comparative sense have weight, so that one of two things is lighter and the other heavier. Thus, if two light things are equal in bulk, the one carried upward more quickly is the lighter; and the same judgement must be made of two heavy things of equal bulk. Of things that are absolutely heavy and light, the ancients disputed nothing, except Aristotle alone; they discussed only those things that are called heavy and light comparatively. Even among them there was no clear agreement about such powers. For some, as Timaeus, said that the heavier thing is that which is composed of more parts of the same nature, and the lighter that which is composed of fewer. Others held that every body consists of triangles, and that fire is carried upward because of the fewness of its triangles; none of these opinions seems in any way consistent. For on this view a greater mass of fire would be heavier, and the smallest amount would be raised aloft, since it is made of fewer triangles; yet the opposite is quite plainly the case. For the greater the mass of fire, the more quickly it is carried upward and the lighter it is; and a small fire is extinguished from a high place with less effort than a large one. Also very absurd is the opinion of those who said that the thing is lighter which has less of what belongs to the same kind and nature, and conversely heavier the more of such a thing it partakes. For a larger mass of air is always carried upward more easily than a smaller, and in general any part of air is lifted up out of water. Finally there were others, such as Leucippus and Democritus, who said that the thing is lighter in which there is more void. For this reason they asserted that fire, because it has the most void, is the lightest of all. But if something is carried upward on account of the void, then of necessity the void too would be carried upward, and the full downward. Yet the void cannot be moved. For if it were moved, it would surely have a place, since every motion [φορὰ] takes place in a place; but it is quite plain that the void has no place. And if it is moved, what (I ask) would be the cause of its motion? For nothing moves itself unless it is an animal. Therefore the void is the cause neither of lightness nor of weight, which belongs to the full. Moreover, absolute heaviness and lightness do not have one single underlying matter; for if that matter were absolutely heavy, no body could be light. Nor is the magnitude of that matter the cause of heaviness, nor the smallness of it the cause of lightness, since air and fire by their magnitude would surpass water and earth in weight.

units.la: CAP. XLII. Cur corporum quædam semper sursum, alia deorsum natura feruntur?
units.tr: CHAPTER XLII. Why are some bodies by nature always carried upward, and others downward?

units.la: UR postbæc[?] corporum alia naturæ vi semper in sublime feruntur, alia deorsum, explicandum est. Sed primum de illo motu, quo vnumquodque naturale corpus in suum fertur locum, tractare conuenit. Porrò omnis motus tria sunt genera, vnum in magnitudine fit, aliud in forma & qualitate, tertium in loco. At in horum vnoquoque mutatio ex contrariis in contraria, aut media fit: non enim cuius vis in quo vis vlla mutatio est. Ac quemadmodum, quæ natura mobilia sunt distin-guuntur, ita etiam mouetia. Non enim quid-uis vis rem quamlibet mouere potest : sed vt id quod alterari potest, ab eo discrepat quod crescendi vim habet:ita alterans causa,ab augente distinguitur. Idem etiam de iis,quæ ad locum moueri iudicare licet. Non enim quídvis a quouis ad locu moueri potest, sed quod natura mobile est,quod graue est,& leue. Hoc enim in suum fertur locum,hoc est, in suam quasi adducitur formam: quandoquidem locus quodammodo forma est, & locati corporis perfectio. Quare veteres philosophi recte a simili simile ferri dicebant.
units.tr: Why some bodies are always carried upward by the force of nature and others downward must now be explained. But first it is fitting to treat of that motion by which every natural body is carried to its own place. Now every motion is of three kinds: one takes place in magnitude, another in form and quality, and the third in place. In each of these, change occurs from contraries into contraries, or through intermediates; for there is no change in that which has no contrary in which it may be. And just as things that are naturally movable are distinguished, so too are the things that cause motion. For not just anything can move just anything; rather, what can be altered differs from what has the power of growing, and so the altering cause is distinguished from the augmenting cause. The same may also be judged of those things which are moved to a place. For not just anything can be moved from anywhere to a place, but only that which is by nature movable, namely what is heavy and light. For this is carried to its own place, that is, is as it were brought to its own form, since place is in a certain way a form and the perfection of the body placed. Hence the ancient philosophers rightly said that like is carried to like.

units.la: Propterea quæcunque sunt similia, nec differunt, eodem motu cieri, expedit. Quamobrem quocunque aliqua pars suapte natu-ra fertur, eo etiam totum ferri, necesse est.
units.tr: For this reason, whatever things are alike and do not differ are rightly said to be moved by the same motion. Therefore, wherever any part is carried by its own nature, the whole too must necessarily be carried there.

units.la: Cæterum quærere, cur ignis ad superiora fertur,& terra ad inferiora: idem est, quod petere, cur quod curatur, fi moueatur, & mutetur, conualescit, & non redditur album.
units.tr: But to ask why fire is carried upward and earth downward is the same as asking why a sick man, if he is moved and changed, recovers, and why what is black is not made white.

units.la: Eodem modo de omni mobili existi-mandum est. Vt enim quod augeri potest, fi augescit non conualescere dicitur, sed maiorem accipere molem & magnitudinem: sic vnumquodque aliorum mobiliu m, partim in qualitatem, partim in quantitatem & partim denique in locum mutatur: vt quod graue est, & leue.
units.tr: In the same way one must think about every movable thing. For just as what can be increased, if it grows, is not said to recover but to take on a greater mass and size, so each of the other movable things is changed partly in quality, partly in quantity, and finally in place, as is the case with what is heavy and light.

units.la: Hoc tamen interest, quòd grauia & leuia in fe mutationis principium habeat: alia vero aliúde, & extrinf cús, atq; ab eo, quod alterandi & augedi vim obtinet. Quare φορὰ[?] primus est motus, alteratio verò & accretio secundus, & imperfectorum corporum.
units.tr: Yet there is this difference: that heavy and light things have the principle of their change within themselves, whereas other things have it from elsewhere, externally, and from that which possesses the power of altering and increasing. Hence local motion is the first motion, while alteration and accretion are the second, belonging to imperfect bodies.

units.la: CAP. XLIII. Elementa Mundi grauitate & leuitate distingui.
units.tr: Chapter 43. That the elements are distinguished by heaviness and lightness.

units.la: SUPEREST autem ut leuis & grauis dissimilitudines explicemus. Graue quidem id absolutè est, quod omnibus aliis corporibus subiici-tur: leue omnino, quod super omnia extat, & eminet. Itaq; ignis simpliciter leuis est, quàdoquidem quaelibet eius pars ad supremum locū fertur. Terra etiam simpliciter est gra-uis, quoniam quaelibet eius pars deorsum mo-uetur. Ac quò maior fuerit, eò celerius. Aqua autem & aër absolutè grauia nō sunt, nec leuia, propterea quòd utrúque terra leuius sit, & igne grauius. Cæterum si inter se hæc duo elementa comparentur, certè aqua simpliciter erit grauis, & aër leuis. Aqua enim aëri substernitur, aër verò quantuscunque sit, su-per aquam perpetuò effertur. Ex quibus perspicuum est, corpora, quæ ex quatuor elemen-tis conflata sunt pondere & leuitate esse prædita: quanuis alia aliis grauiora, alia leuiora videantur. Verùm non ubique grauia cer-nuntur & leuia, quæcunque ex quatuor ele-mentis concreta sunt, propter primarū na-turarū dissimilitudines: Veluti lignū, quod librarū centum est,in aere grauius erit,quàm plumbum unius librae, sed in aqua leuius est.
units.tr: It remains now to explain the differences between light and heavy. That is absolutely heavy which is carried down beneath all other bodies; that is absolutely light which rises above and stands out over all things. Thus fire is simply light, since every part of it is carried toward the highest place. Earth too is simply heavy, since every part of it moves downward, and the greater it is, the more swiftly it moves. Water and air, however, are not absolutely heavy nor light, because both are lighter than earth and heavier than fire. Yet if these two elements are compared with each other, water will certainly be heavy simply, and air light. For water is placed beneath air, while air, however great its quantity, is always borne up above water. From these things it is clear that bodies compounded of the four elements are endowed with weight and lightness, although some seem heavier and others lighter. Yet compounds of the four elements are not everywhere seen to be heavy and light, on account of the differences of their primary natures. For example, a piece of wood weighing a hundred pounds will be heavier in air than a lead weight of one pound, but in water it is lighter.

units.la: Id quidè ex eo fit,quòd omnia corpora præter ignem & terram,pondus & leuitatem simul habeant. Terra autem,& quæ terræ plurimum habent,ubique grauia sunt. Aqua etiam ubique grauis est,præterquàm in terra: sic & aer, nisi in aqua sit,aut in terra, ex quibus sua leuitate effertur. Quídque ( ut summatim dicam) suo in loco,præter ignem,gra-ue est. Quare si quid plus aeris quàm aquæ & terræ habet,id quidem in aqua leuis est,& in aere grauis,ut lignum. Proinde in aqua natat, & in aere non consistit. Ex quibus constat aliquid absolutè gratiæ esse, & omnino leue : atque hoc natura semper in sublime ferri,illud verò deorsum. Nam ignis nullum pondus habet,ut nec terra leuitatem. Hæc enim,universis corporibus subsidit, & in medium fertur: ignis verò super omnia eminet, & sursum fertur, in aere pacato & quiescente. Ipsum autem medium,id est,ad quod motus grauium fit, & à quo leuia sursum efferuntur, & universi & terræ commune est. Quoniam igitur simplicium corporum duo sunt leuia,& duo grauia, perspicuum est elementorum universi contraria esse. Id quod etiam declarant eorum loca,quæ adversa sunt. Alius enim medius est, & extremus alius. Duo igitur elementa sunt,quorum unum ad extremum fertur, alterum ad medium: duo caetera in horum medio collocata sunt, quæ ad vtrunque relata vtriusque vim obtinent: ob eamque causam aliud graue est, vt aqua, aliud leue, vt aër. Hæc autem quatuor vniuersi elementa inter se ita coniectuntur, & naturæ quadam societate coniunguntur, vt superiora quasi formæ & species inferiorum sint, inferiora vero instar materiæ eorum subiiciantur. Verum graui & leui subiicitur materia, quæ reipsa vna & eadem est sed ratione diuersa: quandoquidem non actu ens est, sed potentia, quod quidem densitate grauitatis, & raritate leuitatis actu efficitur. Propterea singulis elementis sua est materia tantummodo densitate, & raritate distincta. Veruntamen omnium vna communis est, alioqui non ex se ipsa mutuo generarent. Itaque ex his perspicuum est, quatuor esse vniuersi simplicia corpora: quorum vnum absolute leue est, vt ignis, alterum omnino graue, vt terra: duo reliqua pondus & leuitatem habent, propterea quod extremorum media sint interiecta, quanuis verius grauia dicantur, quàm leuia, eo quòd igni subiiciantur. Quòd autem duobus extremis, nempe igni & terræ, plura interiiciantur media, vt aër & aqua nihil mirari oportet, cum albori & nigrori plures alij colores medij interponantur. Grauia quoque omnia sunt alia corpora & leuia, vt moueantur: sed vt celeriore motu, vel tardiore cieantur plurimum valet eorum rum figura. Propterea ferrum, quod latum est, & in tenuissimas laminas ductum, in aqua natare cernitur: alia vero minus eo grauia si rotunda sunt, aut oblongae figurae, qualis est acus, submerguntur: Ea vero, quae lata sunt, in aqua natant, non solum quod plurimum aquae comprehendant, sed etiam quod ipsius aquae superficiem diuidere non possint. Alia denique grauia, quae latis contrarias habent figuras, parum aquae comprehendunt. Propterea in aqua submerguntur, & in fundum eius delabuntur, quod facile eam diuidant, & in aere multo celerius deorsum feruntur, eo quod eum facilius quam aquam disrumpant.
units.tr: This happens because all bodies except fire and earth have weight and lightness at the same time. Earth, and things that have much earth in them, are heavy everywhere. Water too is heavy everywhere, except in earth; likewise air, unless it is in water or in earth, is carried up by its own lightness. And (to sum up briefly) everything, except fire, is heavy in its own place. Hence if something has more air than water and earth, it is light in water and heavy in air, like wood; therefore it floats on water and does not stay in air. From these things it is established that some things are absolutely heavy and others wholly light; by nature the one is always carried upward, the other downward. For fire has no weight, just as earth has no lightness: earth sinks beneath all bodies and is carried to the middle, while fire stands out above all things and is carried upward in calm and quiet air. Moreover, the middle itself, that is, the place toward which the motion of heavy things tends and from which light things are raised upward, is common to the whole universe and to earth. Since therefore there are two simple bodies that are light and two that are heavy, it is clear that the elements of the universe are contrary to one another. Their places, which are opposite, also show this: one occupies the middle, the other the extremity. Thus there are two elements, one of which is carried to the extremity and the other to the middle; the two remaining elements are placed between these, and, being related to both, they take on the power of each: for this reason one is heavy, like water, and the other light, like air. These four elements of the universe are so joined to one another and bound together by a certain natural fellowship that the higher ones are, as it were, the forms and species of the lower, and the lower are placed beneath them in the manner of matter. Now matter underlies the heavy and the light; it is really one and the same, but differs in aspect, since it is not actually existing but potential, and it is made actual as heavy by density and as light by rarity. Therefore each element has its own matter, distinguished only by density and rarity, yet there is one matter common to all, otherwise they would not generate one another mutually. Thus it is clear from these things that there are four simple bodies of the universe: of these, one is absolutely light, like fire, another wholly heavy, like earth; the two remaining have weight and lightness, because they are placed between the extremes, although they are more rightly called heavy than light, since they lie beneath fire. That more intermediate elements are interposed between the two extremes, fire and earth, such as air and water, is no cause for wonder, since many other intermediate colours are placed between white and black. Moreover, all bodies are heavy and light, so that they may be moved; but their figure contributes greatly to whether they are moved with a swifter or slower motion. Therefore iron, when it is broad and beaten into very thin plates, is seen to float on water; other things, less heavy than it, if they are round or of oblong shape, such as a needle, sink. Those things which are broad float on water not only because they take up a great deal of water, but also because they cannot divide the surface of the water itself. Finally, other heavy things, which have shapes contrary to broad ones, take up little water; therefore they sink in water and drop to its bottom, because they easily cleave it, and in air they are carried downward much more swiftly, because they break through air more easily than water.

units.la: Cap. XLIII.
units.tr: Cap. XLIII.

units.la: Causæ generationis, corruptionis, accretionis, diminutionis & alterationis corporum naturalium.
units.tr: The causes of generation, corruption, accretion, diminution and alteration of natural bodies.

units.la: GENERATIONIS autem, & cor- ruptionis eorum omnium, quæ na-tura generantur & corrumpuntur, tum causæ tum rationes primum explicandæ sunt. Deinde de accretione diminutioneque, & alteratione disputandum est, ac dicendum quid vtrunque sit, ac vtrum vna eademque natura sit statuenda alterationis & generationis, an diuersa diuersifq. nominibus exprimeda. Nā veterū nonulli eam generationem, quae simplex appellatur, alterationem esse dixerunt, alii eam ab alteratione distinxerunt. Qui autem generationem simplicem & alterationem idem esse voluerunt, omnia ex uno fonte & principio oriri statuere fuerunt coacti, eo quod rebus naturalibus unum duntaxat sit subiectum & idem. Propterea id praecipue alterari existimaverunt, quod gignitur. Qui vero materiam rerum, quae natura constant, non ver[?]am[?] esse[?], sed multiplicem posuerunt, generationem ab alteratione distinguebant, censebantque ex atomorum concretione, & earundem dissipatione res naturales generari & corrumpi.
units.tr: First of all, the causes and principles of the generation and corruption of all those things that are generated and corrupted by nature must be explained. Next we must discuss accretion, diminution and alteration, and say what each of them is, and whether alteration and generation are to be taken as one and the same nature or as different natures to be named differently. For some of the ancients said that the generation called simple is alteration, while others distinguished it from alteration. Those who wanted simple generation and alteration to be the same were forced to hold that all things arise from one source and principle, since natural things have only one and the same subject. For this reason they thought that whatever is generated is especially altered. Those who held that the matter of natural things is not one but many distinguished generation from alteration, and believed that natural things are generated and corrupted by the coming together and the dispersal of atoms.

units.la: Quanquam hi recte senserunt, generationem ab alteratione distinguentes, non propterea suam tueri sententiam potuerunt, alterationem prorsus ab ortu tollentes. Ut enim in ea mutatione, quae accretio est & decretio, remanet eadem substantia mutationibus obnoxia: ita in alteratione fit, sine qua nulla potest esse generatio & corruptio, nec accretio.
units.tr: Although these men were right to distinguish generation from alteration, they could not on that account defend their view, since they removed alteration altogether from coming into being. For just as, in that change which is increase and decrease, the same substance remains subject to changes, so in alteration, without which there can be no generation, corruption or increase, something happens.

units.la: Affectiones autem quibus alterationem eve-nire oportet, sunt elementorum differentiae: nempe calor, frigus, ariditas, humor, candor, nigror, durities, mollities, & unaquaeque caeterarum huius generis. Quamobrem si alterari elementa non possunt, nec ex igne aqua generabitur, nec ex aqua terra: nec etiam ex albo quicquam nigrum, neque ex molli durum fiet. Quare ex elementis conflata cocrescere non possunt nisi prius alterata fuerint ipsa elementa. Empedocles etiam elementa alterari negabat, quod ea non se mutuo gignere arbitrabatur. Existimauit enim nullam subiici materiam formis elementorum commune, sine qua ne vlla quidem elementa & alterari & vicissim generari possunt. Sed falsa fuit illius sententia. Nam elementorum qualitates sunt mutabiles, atque tolli possunt, eo quod aduenatitiae[?] affectiones sunt. Propterea ex aqua terra, & aqua ex terra, mutatis duntaxat eorum qualitatibus fieri potest. Quod autem ex atomis tanquam ex elementis nulla corpora concrescere possint, ex his intelligi potest. Primum enim atomi corpora non sunt. Nam omne corpus superficie terminatur: sed atomi nulla superficie clauduntur. Deinde vt linea in indiuiduas lineas diuidi non potest, sic nec superficies in indiuiduas superficies diuiditur. Quod si nec superficies, neque linea in partes indiuiduas distribui possunt, multo adhuc minus corpus in indiuidua alia corpora, cuiusmodi atomi sunt, diuiditur. Profecto nulla pars lineae dari potest, quae non linea sit, ac proinde diuidua, quantacunque progressio in diuisione fiat. Quare atomi corpora esse non possunt, nec ad vllum continuatae quantitatis genus referuntur. Praeterea ex atomis, etiamsi corpora sint nisi alterentur, nulla erit generatio, sed duntaxat coaceruatio, quae potius ad locum mutatio est, quàm substantiæ. Itaque ex atomis nulla corpora concrescere possunt[?]. His autem definitis, videndum est vtrum quidpiam simpliciter & plane significatur & corrumpatur, annon omnino? Quicquid certè fit & generatur, ex contrario generari & efficì, necesse est: vt ex ægro valentem, ex valente ægrum, aut ex paruo magnum, & magnum ex paruo. Atque hoc modo omnia ex contrario fiunt. Ex quo nullam esse generationem rerum absolutam consequi videtur.
units.tr: The affections that must come about through alteration are the differences of the elements: namely heat, cold, dryness, moisture, whiteness, blackness, hardness, softness, and each of the others of this kind. Therefore, if the elements cannot be altered, water will not be generated from fire, nor earth from water, nor will anything black come from white, or hard from soft. Hence bodies compounded of the elements cannot grow, unless the elements themselves have first been altered. Empedocles also denied that the elements are altered, because he thought they do not generate one another. For he thought that there is no common matter underlying the forms of the elements, without which the elements cannot be either altered or generated in turn. But his opinion was false. For the qualities of the elements are changeable and can be removed, since they are adventitious affections. So earth can come from water, and water from earth, by a change of their qualities alone. That bodies cannot be compounded out of atoms as if out of elements can be understood from the following. First, atoms are not bodies. For every body is bounded by a surface, but atoms are enclosed by no surface. Next, just as a line cannot be divided into indivisible lines, so a surface is not divided into indivisible surfaces. If neither surface nor line can be distributed into indivisible parts, much less is a body divided into other indivisible bodies, such as atoms are. Indeed, no part of a line can be given which is not itself a line, and therefore divisible, however far the division is carried. Therefore atoms cannot be bodies, nor do they belong to any kind of continuous quantity. Moreover, if atoms were bodies, there would be no generation from them unless they were altered, but only an aggregation, which is a change of place rather than of substance. So no bodies can be compounded out of atoms. Having settled these points, we must consider whether something is simply generated and corrupted, or not at all? Surely whatever comes to be and is generated must necessarily be generated and made from its opposite: as the healthy man from the sick, the sick from the healthy, or the large from the small, and the small from the large. And in this way all things come to be from their opposites. From this it seems to follow that there is no absolute generation of things.

units.la: Præterea quod absolutè generatur, id absolutè non ens est. Quare si non ens absolutè dictum de prima ex categoriis intelligatur, profectò substantiæ generatio, ex eo erit, quod simpliciter substantia non est. At quod non substantia est, ei nulla attribuitur alia categoria, neque quantitas, neque qualitas, neque vbi, neque aliud huius generis, quoniam huiusmodi categoriæ eam haberent naturam: vt à sua substantia seiungi possent. Ex quibus constat, quod simpliciter generatur, id ex nihilo generari: quod plane absurdum est.
units.tr: Furthermore, what is absolutely generated is absolutely not being. Therefore, if "non-being" said absolutely is understood in the first of the categories, then the generation of a substance will be from that which is simply not a substance. But to what is not a substance no other category is attributed, neither quantity, nor quality, nor place, nor anything else of this kind, since such categories would have the nature of being separable from their substance. From these points it is clear that what is simply generated is generated from nothing, which is plainly absurd.

units.la: Etenim ex nihilo nihil fit. Sed facile hoc dubium diluemus, si aliquid ex nihilo fieri intelligerimus, hoc est, ex eo, quod non absolutè ens est, nempe ex materia, quæ semper subsistit substernitúrque omnium substantiarum generationi, & duntaxat potestate ens est, quod omnem præcedit generationem, pro-pterea ꝑ[?] id quod esse potest, necessariò prius est eo,quod actu & reipsa existit. Quod autem potestate τὸ ὂν[?] est,& semper subsistit,materia prima dicitur. Propterea quod simpliciter generatur id ex eo fit, quod nō actu ens est,sed esse potest. Superest tādē ut causam exquiramus,cur sit generatio perpetua,& corruptio. Hæc autē duplex esse videtur una,unde motʼ proficiscitur altera materia: quandoquidem omnis mutationis semper duo principia sūt, unū immotū, alterū mobile: quorū prius, id est,à quo motʼprincipiū proficiscitur & motor est primus, de quo pertractare ad primū philosophū pertinet. Posterius verò materia est & mobile principiū, quod omnibus mutationibus subiicitur, facitq; ut generatio & corruptio nunquā Naturā deserant. Cæterū magna quædā quæstio expediatur oportet, qua quæritur,cur rerū generatio quadā con-sequentia perpetuetur: siquidē quod corrū-pitur semper in id quod nō est ens, reducitur. Atqui quod nō ens est,nihil est prorsus: nec enim substantia est, nec quantitas, nec qualitas, neque vbi. Quamobrē mirari quis poterit: cur non iam olim consumpta sit, & inanis reddita rerum vniuersitas. Siquidem id finitum est, ex quo vnumquodque eorum, quæ siunt,generatur. Nulla sanè magnitudo actu infinita est,etiam si potestate & diuisione sit immensa. Ad hoc autem respondendū est omnē mutatione,quæ in materia sit, perpetuā esse, quoniā vnius generatio alterius corruptio est, & vice versa. Atque hæc quidem causa fatis idonea est, cur cuiusque substantiæ generatio & corruptio perpetuo fiat. Cæterum rursus quæritur, quam ob causam quædam simpliciter tum generari, tum corrumpi dicantur : quædam verò non omnino cum vnius generatio alterius corruptio fit, & contrà. Ad hoc etiam respondetur in substantiarum ordine generationem vnius corruptionem alterius esse,& contrà: sed in aliis cathegoriis non ita fieri, nec quicquam eorum simpliciter gigni, sed κ̓ τί. Qui enim scientiam discit aliquam,non simpliciter homo fit,sed dutaxat peritus. Itaque duplicem esse generationem fatis perspicuum est. Vna enim simplex est quæ essentiam materiæ tribuit, & eam ad absolutum ens perducit, cui opponitur simplex corruptio,quæ ad nō ens via est. Altera autem duntaxat in substantia aliquod accidens efficit, nec absoluta est, sed fecundum aliquid generatio dicitur. At verò in priore generatur aliquid ex eo,quod non actu ens est,sed potentia:hoc est, ex materia, in qua formæ recipiendæ priuatio adest: vt,exempli causa, homo ex eo quod non actu homo est, gignitur. Aliquid etiam tum absolute gigni dicitur, cùm nobiliorem acquirit formam , vt cùm ex femine,vel fit animal,vel planta: Sic etiam terra tum nobiliorem acquirit formam,cùm ex ea ignis fit. At ex terra ignis fieri potest, quoniam omnium eleelementorum ea infimum est, & propemodum non ens. Quaré Parmenides terram & ignem non esse τὰ ὄντα tradidit. Seme quoque, si cum animal comparetur, ens imperfectum est: animal vero, & planta perfectum.
units.tr: Indeed, nothing comes from nothing. But we shall easily resolve this doubt if we understand that something comes from nothing, that is, from that which is not absolutely being, namely from matter, which always underlies and serves as the substrate for the generation of all substances, and which is being only in potency. What precedes every generation is that which can be, and so what can be is necessarily prior to what actually and really exists. What is in potency [τὸ ὂν] and always underlies is called prime matter. Therefore what is simply generated arises from that which is not actually being but can be. It remains finally to inquire into the cause why generation and corruption are perpetual. This cause seems to be twofold: one is the source from which motion proceeds, the other is matter; for every change always has two principles, one unmoved and one movable. Of these, the first, that is, the principle from which motion proceeds, is the first mover, and to treat of it belongs to the first philosopher. The second, however, is matter, the movable principle that underlies all changes and makes generation and corruption never abandon nature. But a great question must be settled, namely why the generation of things is perpetuated by a certain succession: since what is corrupted is always reduced to that which is not being. Yet what is not being is absolutely nothing: for it is neither substance, nor quantity, nor quality, nor place. Hence someone may wonder why the totality of things has not long since been used up and reduced to emptiness. For that is finite from which each of the things that come to be is generated. Indeed no magnitude is actually infinite, even if it is immense in potency and by division. To this it must be answered that every change that takes place in matter is perpetual, since the generation of one thing is the corruption of another, and vice versa. And this is indeed a sufficiently suitable cause why the generation and corruption of each substance take place perpetually. However, it is again asked why some things are said to be both generated and corrupted absolutely, while others are not so absolutely, since the generation of one is the corruption of another, and conversely. To this too it is answered that in the order of substances the generation of one is the corruption of another, and conversely; but in the other categories this does not happen, and nothing of them is generated absolutely, but only [κατά τι], in some respect. For he who learns some science does not become a man absolutely, but only skilled. It is therefore quite clear that there are two kinds of generation. The one is simple, which gives matter its essence and brings it to absolute being, and is opposed to simple corruption, which is the way to non-being. The other produces only some accident in a substance; it is not absolute, but is called generation in some respect. In the former, something is generated from that which is not actually being but potentially, that is, from matter in which there is the privation of the form to be received; for example, a man is generated from that which is not actually a man. Something is also said to be generated absolutely when it acquires a nobler form, as when an animal or a plant arises from seed. So too earth acquires a nobler form when fire is made from it. But fire can be made from earth, since of all the elements earth is the lowest and almost non-being. Hence Parmenides taught that earth and fire are not beings [τὰ ὄντα]. Seed too, when compared with an animal, is an imperfect being; but the animal and the plant are perfect.

units.la: Cap. XLV. Generationis alterationis & accretionis discrimina.
units.tr: Chapter 45. The differences between generation, alteration and accretion.

units.la: OSTH[?] AEC quid inter generatione & alterationem interfit, explicandum est. Has enim mutationes inter fe differre, ex eo intelligi potest, quòd subiectum, & eius affectio, atque qualitas magnopere discrepent. Itaque alteratio est affectionum sensilis corporis mutatio, ipso remanente subiecto. Ut cùm animalis corpus idem permanens, modò ægrotat, modò valet: ac cùm idem æs modò rotundù est, modò angulatum. Cùm verò totum mutatur fubiectù, & nihil sensile eius remanet, tum hoc mutationis genus, partim generatio dicitur, partim corruptio. Ut cùm ex aqua aer gignitur, & ex aere aqua: quoniam unius generatio alterius corruptio est. Tum enim aer, vel aqua plane sensu non percipitur, cum alterutrum mutatum est. Itaque si duntaxat subiecti corporis affectio mutetur, alteratio erit: ut si musicæ artis imperitus fiat musicus:in quo mutationis genere homo remanet. Cùm verò in magnitudine animati corporis mutatio fit, tũ accretio inducitur, vel diminutio : quod mutationis genus etiã à generatione & corruptione differt. Generatio enim mutatio est illius substantiæ, quæ potestate ens est, in aliam, quæ actu existit[?]. Accretio verò & diminutio unius magnitudinis in aliam motio. Differt etiam hoc mutationis genus ab alteratione & generatione hunc in modum. Neque enim quod alteratur, aut gignitur necessariè loco mouetur, sed id quod crescit, vel imminuitur, alio tamen modo, quàm ea, quæ feruntur. Hæc enim tota locum mutat: illud verò quod crescit, aut minuitur, sic locum mutat ut id quod procuditur. Etenim quod augescit id ex minore angustioreque loco in latiorem promouetur, etsi permanet. Quod verò decrescit, contrà id minorem angustioremque locum occupat. Sed eorum, quæ feruntur quædam in nouum recipiuntur locum, priore relicto. Huiusmodi ea sunt, quæ recta linea sursum, deorsum, ante, pone, ad dextrum & sinistrum mouentur. Ea verò, quæ circunuoluuntur, ut cœli orbes, in suo permanent loco, & eorū partes duntaxat alicubi mouentur. Ex his perspicuum est, generationem, alterationè, & augmentationem, diminutionéque diuersas mutationes esse, non solùm subiecto, sed etiam modo, quo fiunt. Subiectum enim, in quo accretionis & diminutionis mutatio est, magnitudo actu existit, quale corpus est, nō mathematicum, quod quidem, etsi magnitudo perfecta est, à naturali distinguitur, quoniam naturali forma caret, qua alterum necessario prædítum est. Generatio vero mutatio eius rei, quæ potestate magnitudo est. Præterea crescit corpus accessione rei adventitiæ, & imminuitur eiusdem decessione.
units.tr: Next we must explain what lies between generation and alteration. That these changes differ from one another can be understood from the fact that the subject, its affection and its quality differ greatly. Alteration, then, is a change in the sensible affections of a body while the subject itself remains. For example, the same animal body remains and now falls ill, now is well; and the same bronze is now round, now angular. But when the whole subject is changed and nothing sensible of it remains, this kind of change is called partly generation and partly corruption. Thus when air is produced from water, and water from air, the generation of one is the corruption of the other: neither air nor water is perceived by the senses at all once one has been changed into the other. So if only the affection of the body that is the subject is changed, it is alteration, as when someone unskilled in music becomes a musician; in this kind of change the man remains the same. But when the change takes place in the magnitude of an animate body, accretion or diminution is brought about, and this kind of change also differs from generation and corruption. For generation is the change of that substance which exists potentially into another which exists actually, whereas accretion and diminution are the motion of one magnitude into another. This kind of change also differs from alteration and generation in the following way. What is altered or generated does not necessarily move from its place, but what grows or shrinks changes place in a different manner from things that are carried along. For the latter move as a whole, whereas what grows or shrinks changes place in the way that metal beaten out thin does. What increases passes from a smaller and narrower place into a larger and wider one, though it remains the same; what decreases, conversely, occupies a smaller and narrower place. Of things that are carried, some are received into a new place once the old one is left. Such are those that move in a straight line upward, downward, forward, backward, to the right and to the left. Those that revolve, like the spheres of heaven, remain in their place, and only their parts are moved somewhere. From this it is clear that generation, alteration, and augmentation and diminution are different changes, not only in their subject but also in the manner in which they occur. For the subject in which accretion and diminution take place is an actually existing magnitude, a body that is not mathematical; although it is a perfect magnitude, it is distinguished from a natural body, since it lacks the natural form which the latter necessarily possesses. Generation, however, is the change of that which is potentially a magnitude. Moreover, a body grows by the addition of an extraneous thing and diminishes by the removal of one.

units.la: Hæc autem aduentitia res vel incorporea est, vel corporea. At si incorporea est, id quod commune est, nempe materia, à magnitudine separari poterit. Id quod absurdum est. Materia enim natura à magnitudine nullo modo separari potest, alioqui in rerum natura vacuum esset. Sin corpore accretio fiat, duo corpora simul eodem in loco erunt, vnum quod augetur, & alterum quod auget: Id quod etiam in ipsa natura fieri non potest. Adhæc autem omnia respondendum est, id augeri, cui aliquid additur, quod actu est. Quamuis enim sensilis pars corporis nutrione maior reddatur, non propterea id corpus, quod augescit, vacuum est, nec duo corpora simul in eodem[?] sunt: nec denique corpus re incorporea augescit.
units.tr: This added thing is either incorporeal or corporeal. If it is incorporeal, then what is common to it, namely matter, could be separated from the magnitude. This is absurd. For matter by its nature can in no way be separated from magnitude; otherwise there would be a void in nature. If, however, accretion takes place through a body, then two bodies will be in the same place at once: the one that grows and the one that causes the growth. This too cannot happen in nature itself. Moreover, to all these objections the answer must be that what grows is that to which something is added that is actually existing. For although a sensible part of a body becomes larger through nourishment, the body that grows is not on that account empty, nor are two bodies in the same place at once, nor, finally, does a body grow by means of something incorporeal.

units.la: Nam animatorum corpora similibus dissimilibúsque partibus constant. Quare etiam quæ dissimiles sunt, augentur, cum similes crescunt.Ea nanque quæ ex materia constant & forma,non secundum materiam crescunt, sed secundum formam, quæ quamlibet partem materiæ appositam assimulat & perficit. Maius enim totum corpus redditur accessione rei alicuius, quod alimetum vocamus cū eā-de in formā quā habet ipsum corpus, muta-tum est. Cæterum simile partim à simili par-tim à dissimili augescit. Id enim, quo auge-scit corpus, tale potestate esse debet{*}, quale est,quod actu augetur. Quare alimentum si-mile potestate carni est, quæ ex eo crescere debet,& actu diversum. At vero accretio nō est,cum id,quod potetia caro est, carnis for-mam assumit:tu enim generatio est, sed cū ipsa caro ex pane & vino orta crescit. Nam accretio sine generatione non est. Cæterum generalis quantitas non augescit, quemad-modum nec animal,quod nec homo est, nec quidpiam singulare: sed quemadmodum hu-ius hominis generatio est, ita huius quantæ carnis accretio. Caro igitur & os, aut ner-uus,atque partes, quæ eiusdem generis sunt, non accessione carnis quantæ crescunt,sed a-licuius rei quantæ. Ex his perspicuum est ac-cretionem absque nutritione fieri posse, atque tantum modo huiusmodi mutationes ra-tione differre, non autè subiecto & materia: Tametsi enim animantia,quandiu vivunt,nu-triantur,nec propterea crescunt. Ea nanque dūtaxat,ut stirpes omnes, eousque augescūt, dodonec ad definitam vsque[?] magnitudine peruenerint, quam natura cunctis anima prædiditis tribui,statuit. Atque tatisper animati corporis instrumentum crescit,dum vis eius tantum alimenti vincere potest, quatum ad crescendum requiritur. Contra tum decrescit, cum alimentum in suam substantiam non omni ex parte conuertere potest.
units.tr: For the bodies of animate things consist of like and unlike parts. Therefore, unlike parts also grow, just as like parts do. For things that consist of matter and form do not grow according to matter but according to form, which assimilates and perfects whatever portion of matter is applied to it. For the whole body is made larger by the addition of something which, once it has been changed into the same form that the body itself has, we call nourishment. Moreover, a like thing grows partly from a like and partly from an unlike thing. For that by which a body grows must be potentially of the same kind as that which is actually growing. Thus the nourishment must be potentially similar to flesh, since it is from it that the flesh is to grow, yet actually different from it. But there is no accretion when what is potentially flesh takes on the form of flesh; that is generation. Rather, the flesh itself grows when it arises from bread and wine. For there is no accretion without generation. Nor does a general quantity grow, just as an animal that is neither man nor anything singular does not grow; but just as there is the generation of this particular man, so there is the accretion of this particular quantity of flesh. Flesh, therefore, and bone or sinew, and the parts that are of the same kind, grow not by the addition of a quantity of flesh but by the addition of a quantity of some thing. From this it is clear that accretion can take place without nourishment, and that such changes differ only in their account and not in their subject and matter. For although living things are nourished as long as they live, they do not on that account grow. Only plants, like all stocks, grow until they reach a fixed magnitude, which nature has determined to be assigned to every animate being. And the instrument of an animate body grows for as long as its power can overcome the amount of nourishment required for growth. On the contrary, it diminishes when it cannot convert the nourishment into its own substance in every respect.

units.la: CAP. XLVI. Quid contactus sit.
units.tr: CHAPTER XLVI. What contact is.

units.la: AM vero dictis mutationibus sen-silem materiam subiici,quæ necessario ex simplicibus corporibus constet, necesse est, quoniam mistorum corporum elementa principia sunt: ex quibus nihil concrescere cogique potest, nisi alterentur. Sed nec alterabuntur, nisi vicissim agant & patiantur. Atque ea vicissim agere & pati non possunt, quæ non se contingunt, & permiscentur. Nec vero permisceri possunt, nisi cohæreant, & se contingant. Itaque quid contactus sit, quid permissio, & quid affectio, explicandum est. Porro contactus duobus modis dicitur, proprie & communiter: Qui proprie dicitur iis conuenit, quæ situm habent, & quibus locus conuenit. Quoniam autem prima loci differetia est superus & inferus, cæteraque eiusdem generis, perspicuum est omnia, quæ se mutuo contingunt, aut grauitate aut leuitate, aut utroque prædita esse, atque vim in se agendi & patiendi habere. Quapropter contactus proprie dictus iis convenit, quæ distinctam habent magnitudinem, & superficies coniunctas, ut mutuo & se movere, & à se moveri possint.
units.tr: Now, since the changes just described require an insensible matter underlying them, which must necessarily consist of simple bodies (for the elements are the principles of mixed bodies), it is necessary to say this: nothing can grow together and be compacted out of these unless they are altered. But they cannot be altered unless they act and are acted upon in turn. Yet things that do not touch one another and mix cannot act and be acted upon in turn, and they cannot mix unless they cohere and touch. Therefore it must be explained what contact is, what mixture is, and what affection is. Now contact is spoken of in two ways, properly and in common usage. That which is properly called contact belongs to those things which have position and to which place belongs. Since the first difference of place is above and below, and the others of the same kind, it is clear that all things which touch one another are endowed with weight, or lightness, or both, and have the power of acting and being acted upon. Wherefore contact properly so called belongs to those things which have a distinct magnitude and conjoined surfaces, so that they can both move one another and be moved by one another.

units.la: Eorum autem, quæ movent duplex genus est: alia enim movent, & vicissim moventur, alia movent, nec moventur. Sed illud duntaxat movet simul & movetur, cuius motus est affectio & alteratio. Quare cotactus[?] pro-prie dictus iis convenit, quæ agendi & patiendi vim habent, cuiusmodi sunt hæc inferiora corpora, quorum moventia contingut ea, quæ moventur. Superiora verò, quæ cælestia sunt non proprie ea contingunt, quæ movent, quoniam agendo vicissim non patiuntur. Ea quidem ultro citroque afficiendi & patiendi vim habent, quorum aliud tangit, & aliud tangitur. Etenim quæ ferè omnia in nostrum cadunt aspectum, quæque generantur & corrumpuntur, cùm moventur, vicissim movent: quandoquidem, quod tangit, id quod tangitur percipiat necesse est. Hæc autem de iis, quæ suas habent superficies coniunctas facilè intelligi potest. Cælestia verò corpora, tandem si inferiora moveant, non moventur, nec patiuntur, quoniam his, ut nec mathematicis magnitudinibus, proprius contactus non convenit.
units.tr: Now there are two kinds of things that move: some move and in turn are moved, others move and are not moved. But only that which moves and is moved at the same time is the subject of motion and alteration. Hence contact properly so called belongs to those things which have the power of acting and being acted upon, such as these lower bodies, whose moving parts touch those that are moved. The higher bodies, however, which are heavenly, do not properly touch what they move, since in acting they are not in turn acted upon. Those things indeed which have the power of affecting and being affected from either side, of which one touches and the other is touched, are the ones that do so. For nearly all the things that fall under our sight, and that are generated and corrupted, when they are moved, move in turn; since whatever touches must perceive that which is touched. This can easily be understood about those things which have conjoined surfaces. But the heavenly bodies, although they move the lower ones, are not themselves moved nor acted upon, since proper contact does not belong to them, just as it does not belong to mathematical magnitudes.

units.la: CAP. XLVII.
units.tr: CAP. XLVII.

units.la: Quæ agunt & patiuntur mutuò.
units.tr: What things act and suffer mutually.

units.la: O[?]MNIA quæ in se mutuò agunt at-que patiuntur, aliquo modo simi-lia sunt, & quodammodo dissimi-lia. Genere enim similia sunt atque eadem, sed specie contraria, aut contrariorum media: Optima igitur ratione frigidum in calidum agit, ac omnino agens ad sui similitudinem reddit id quod patitur. Agens enim & patibile contraria sunt: quamobrem necessario patibile in agens permutatur. Porrò ipsum movens agénsque duplex est, unum, in quo motionis principium consistit, cuiusmodi est omnium causarum principium & maximè primum. Alterum autem quod in ea re cōtinetur, quæ aut mobilis est, aut gignitur. Medicus & vinum (exempli causa) leuandi morbum vim habent, sed medicus ut primum movens, vinum ut postremum, quod cum reo quæ fit, coniungitur. Itaque primum movens immotum est: postremum verò nihil movet, nisi antè moueatur, hoc est, primum movens impatibile est, postremum verò patibile. Verumtamè quæ eiusdè materiæ expertia sunt, ea nihil agendo patiùtur. Propterea curandorum morborum ars, quæ tametsi curet, nihil tamen ab eo patitur, quod curatur. Sed cibus, cùm in animatum corpus inditur, tum aliquid ab eo patitur. Nam aut calescit, aut refrigeratur, aut aliquod huiusmodi pa-titur. Igitur ab eo differt medicina, quoniam hęc ut primarium agens est, & motionis prin-cipium: ille vero ut postremum, & quod pa-tibile est. Omnia igitur agentia, quæ cum ma-teria, quæ patitur, non copulata sunt, in age-do nihil patiuntur: alia vero, quæ materiæ iunguntur, agunt & patiuntur. Quamobrem agentium alia impatibilia sunt, & alia pa-tibi-lia. Ac quemadmodum primum mouens o-mni motione vacat, ita primum agens pas-sionis expers est. Hactenus de iis, circa quæ omnis actio est, & passio. Restat ut qui hoc fiat, explicemus, omissis quorudam veterum philosophorum opinionibus, ab entis diui-sione incipientes. Quicquid enim est, aut po-testate, aut actu & forma est: quorum quod potestate τὸ ὄν[?] est, patitur: id vero, quod actu existit, vim agendi habet. Atque quod pati-tur, id magis minúsve ad patiendum aptum est, prout maiore minoreve ipsa potestate præditum est. Cæterum quæ vicissim inter se agunt & patiùtur separata esse oportet: quā-doquidem continuata eiusdem naturæ sunt, nec à seipsis pati possunt. Verùmtamen neque adeo ea separata esse oportet, ut se mu-tuò contingere, aut alia habere interiecta media, nequeant, quæ à primis agentibus af-secta, iterum alia afficiant. Ut (exempli cau-sa) ignis non ita à nobis procul est, quin per interiectum aërem nostra calefaciat corpo-ra. ra. Aer enim ab eo affectus, cocalefactúsque mox igneum calorem in nostra transfert corpora.
units.tr: All things which mutually act upon and suffer from one another are in some respects similar, and in some respects dissimilar. For they are similar and the same in genus, but contrary in species, or the intermediates of contraries. By the best reasoning, therefore, the cold acts upon the hot, and in general the agent renders what it suffers upon into its own likeness. For the agent and the patient are contraries; for this reason the patient is necessarily changed into the agent. Moreover, the mover and the thing which moves are of two kinds: one, in which the principle of motion resides, such as the principle of all causes and especially the first; and another, which is contained in that thing which is either movable or generated. A physician and wine (for example) have the power of relieving disease, but the physician as the first mover, the wine as the last, which is joined to the patient when the cure takes place. Thus the first mover is unmoved; the last moves nothing unless it has first been moved; that is, the first mover is impassible, but the last is passible. Yet those things which are free of matter suffer nothing while they act. For this reason the art of healing diseases, although it cures, suffers nothing from that which is cured. But food, when it is put into an animate body, also suffers something from it: for it either grows warm, or is cooled, or suffers something of this kind. Medicine therefore differs from food, since the former is the principal agent and the principle of motion, but the latter is the last agent and that which is passible. Therefore all agents which are not joined to the matter that suffers do not suffer in acting; but those which are joined to matter both act and suffer. Hence some agents are impassible and others passible. And just as the first mover is free from all motion, so the first agent is free from passion. So far concerning those things in which all action and passion occurs. It remains that we explain how this takes place, setting aside the opinions of certain ancient philosophers and beginning from the division of being. For whatever exists is either in potency or in act and form: of these, that which is in potency (τὸ ὄν) suffers, while that which exists in act has the power of acting. And that which suffers is more or less apt for suffering, according as it is endowed with greater or lesser power. Moreover, those things which act and suffer upon one another must be separate; since things continuous in the same nature cannot suffer from themselves. Yet they must not be so separated that they cannot touch one another, or have other intervening media, which, affected by the first agents, in turn affect others. Thus (for example) fire is not so far from us that it does not warm our bodies through the intervening air. For the air, affected and warmed by it, soon transfers the fiery heat into our bodies.

units.la: CAP. XLVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XLVIII.

units.la: Quid sit naturalis permissio?
units.tr: What is natural mixture?

units.la: ESTAT deinceps vt eadem ratio- ne & via, de naturali permistione instituatur disputatio, & quantum a generatione corruptioneque differat, quidq; res mistiles ab eis, quæ generari & corrumpi possunt, discrepent, explicemus.
units.tr: Next, in the same manner and by the same method, we shall set out a discussion of natural mixture, and explain how far it differs from generation and corruption, and how mixable things differ from those which can be generated and corrupted.

units.la: Neque enim dubium est quin ea inter se multum differant. Nam in generatione ignis ex ligno, profecto lignum igni non admiscetur, sed ex eo ipse ignis efficitur. Eodem modo nec corpori alimentum in accretione admiscetur: nec affectiones & habitus cum ipsis rebus permisceri possunt in alteratione. Ca-dor[?] enim & disciplina, atque ea, quæ a subiectis summoueri possunt, a permissione sunt aliena. Quiduis namque cum quouis non permisceri potest, sed vnumquodque eorum, quæ permiscentur, aliquid esse oportet, quod a misto separari possit. Atqui affectio a nulla re, cui euenit, seiungi potest. Quoniam autem eorum quę sunt alia potestate, alia actu, fit vt in misto mistilia sint, & quodammodo non sint. Sunt enim entia potestate, & non actu, propterea quod eorum formæ non eodem modo se habeant, quo antequam permiscerentur, sed omnia vni formæ deuincta sunt. Itaque non aƿtu mistitia in misto remanent, nec prorsus obolentur, quoniam eorum vis salua remanet. Propterea quæritur, sitne sensus iudicio, permistio, vel an quæuis particula eorum, quæ inter se permiscentur, cuiuis proxima sit? Vt autem hæc diluatur quæstio, dicendum est permistionem, per quam mista generantur eam non esse, in qua quæuis particula eorum, quæ inter se miscentur, cui vis proxima est, quoniam ea aceruatio similis est ei, per quam hordeum cum tritico permiscetur. Nam in propria & naturali permistione quæque misti particula eandem habet rationem & formam quàm ipsum totum: quandoquidem mistū corpus similes sibi partes habet. Quare quemadmodum aquæ pars aqua est, ita temperati mistíque corporis pars temperatum quiddam est & mistum.
