Quod si ex particulis compositio esset naturalis permistio, profecto misti partes non ipsi toti similes essent. Itaque permistio eorum duntaxat est, quæ vnam eandémque materiam habent, & mutuo inter se aguńt & patiuntur. Aliorum vero, quæ illæsa agunt, nec eandem habent materiam, nulla permistio est. Quapropter medicina à sanitate, quam efficit, nihil patitur, nec cum ea permiscetur. Ea quoque, quibus agendi & patiendi vis est, & quæ diuidi possunt, si multa cum paucis, magna cum paruis copulentur, permistionem non efficiunt, sed tantum amplificationem.
units.tr: There is no doubt that these differ greatly from one another. For in the generation of fire from wood, the wood is certainly not mixed with the fire; rather, the fire itself is produced from it. In the same way, nourishment is not mixed with the body in growth, nor are affections and habits able to be mixed with the things themselves in alteration. For quality[?] and discipline, and whatever can be removed from their subjects, are foreign to mixture. For anything at all cannot be mixed with anything at all; rather, each of the things that are mixed must be something that can be separated from the mixture. But an affection cannot be separated from the thing to which it happens. Since, moreover, some of the things that are have potential existence and others actual existence, it follows that in a mixture the mixables are and in a way are not. For they are beings in potency and not in act, because their forms do not stand in the same condition as before they were mixed, but all are bound to one form. Thus the mixables do not remain in the mixture in act, nor are they utterly destroyed, since their power remains intact. Hence the question arises whether mixture is a matter of judgement of the senses, or whether any particle of those things which are mixed together is close to any other. To resolve this question, it must be said that the mixture by which mixed things are generated is not that in which any particle of the things mixed together is close to whatever power it has, since that aggregation is like the one by which barley is mixed with wheat. For in a proper and natural mixture every particle of the mixed body has the same nature and form as the whole itself, since a mixed body has parts similar to itself. Therefore, just as a part of water is water, so a part of a tempered and mixed body is itself something tempered and mixed. But if natural mixture were a composition of particles, the parts of the mixed body would certainly not be similar to the whole. Thus mixture belongs only to those things which have one and the same matter and act and are acted upon mutually among themselves. Of those which act without being harmed, and do not have the same matter, there is no mixture. Hence medicine, which produces health, suffers nothing from it and is not mixed with it. Likewise, those things which have the power of acting and being acted upon, and which can be divided, if many are joined with few or great with small, do not produce a mixture but only an enlargement.

units.la: Veruntamen fit vt quod exiguum est, in id, quod superat, mutetur: veluti gutta vini decem millibus cyathis aquæ non admiscetur, sed ipsius vini forma difflatur, aboleturque & omnino vinum in aquam vertitur.
units.tr: Nevertheless it happens that what is small is changed into what is greater: for example, a drop of wine is not mixed into ten thousand cups of water, but the form of the wine is dissipated and destroyed, and the wine is wholly turned into water.

units.la: Cùm autem vis vtriusque æquatur, tum vnum non in alterum mutatur, sed quoddam medium fit, & crama.
units.tr: When, however, the power of each is equal, then neither is changed into the other, but something intermediate comes into being, a blend.

units.la: Itaque permistio eorum est, quæ inter se permisceri possunt, & in se vicissim agunt, & afficiuntur: quorum tamen parua paruis apposita facilius admisceri possunt, propterea quòd facilius ac celerius in se mutuò insinuent, quàm quæ maiora sunt. Ea quoque quæ patibilem habent naturam, & quæ facilè terminari possunt, mistitia sunt, quoniam facilè in minimas partes diuidantur, cuiusmodi omnia sunt humida, nisi lenta sint.
units.tr: Thus mixture belongs to those things which can be mixed together, and which act upon and are affected by one another in turn; yet small things placed next to small things can be mixed more easily, because they penetrate one another more readily and quickly than larger things. Those also which have a passible nature, and which can easily be bounded, are mixable, since they are easily divided into the smallest parts; of this kind are all liquids, unless they are viscous.

units.la: Veruntamen cùm eorum vnum admodum, aut omnino patibile est, & alterum paruam agendi vim habet, tum id quod ex vtroque consurgit, parum fit permistum necesse est: id quod in stanno vtroque & ære animaduertere licet. Ex his igitur, quæ disputata sunt, constat permistionem nihil aliud esse, nisi mistilium alteratorum in vnum concretionem.
units.tr: Yet when one of two things is very or wholly passible, and the other has only a small power of acting, then what arises from both must necessarily be only slightly mixed; this can be observed in tin and bronze together. From these things which have been discussed, it is established that mixture is nothing other than the concretion into one of altered mixables.

units.la: CAP. XLIX. Quatuor Mundi elementorum principia esse qualitates tractabiles.
units.tr: CAP. XLIX. The four elements of the world are tangible qualities.

units.la: VONIAM sensilis corporis & trt[?]-ctabilis principia quærimus, ac id tractabile est, quod sensu tactus affici potest: constat non omnia contraria esse corporum principia, sed ea duntaxat, quæ qualitates dicuntur tractabiles. Qua-doquidem prima Naturæ corpora, quorum originem quærimus, contrariis qualitatibus, & iis quidem tractabilibus differunt. Itaque nec candor, nec nigror, nec dulcedo, nec amaror, itemque nec vlla aliarum huiusmodi sensilium qualitatum contrariarum vllum efficit elementum, sed quæ tractabiles dicuntur, quarum differentiæ sunt omnium sensilium primæ. Hæ autem sunt calor, frigus, a-riditas, humor, grauitas, leuitas, durities, mollities, lentor, friabilitas, læuitas, quarum grauitas & leuitas nec faciendi, neque patiendi vim habent. Calor autem & frigus maxime vim efficiendi habent, ariditas verò & humor patiendi. Quare ea calor cogit quæ sunt eiusdem generis, eaque etiam secernit, quæ heterogenea sunt & diuersi generis. Frigus ve-rò tam ea cogit quæ sunt eiusdem generis, quam quæ alieni. Ac humor non suis termi-nis, sed alienis probè coercetur, ac circun-scribitur. Siccitas contrà se habet. Tenuitas porro & crassitudo, lentor, friabilitas, duritiēs, molities, caeteraeq. ex his oriuntur. Na tenuitas ad humore, crassitudo ad siccitate pertinet: Lentor etiam humoris est, qui aliquid est perpessus, ut oleum: Friabilitas, eo quòd omnino sicca sit ad siccitatem pertinere videtur. Quod enim tale est propter humoris pennriam cogitur & condensatur. Iam verò mollities humoris est, ut durities siccitatis. Mole enim in se cedit, nec obnititur, neque sibi resistit. Quamobrem humidum non est molle, quanuis mollities ad humorem referatur, & durities ad siccitatem: quonia quod coactum est, id duritie continetur, & siccum est.
units.tr: Since we are seeking the principles of the sensible and tangible body, and that is tangible which can be affected by the sense of touch, it is agreed that the principles of bodies are not all contraries, but only those called tangible qualities. For the primary bodies of nature, whose origin we are seeking, differ by contrary qualities, and indeed by tangible ones. So whiteness, blackness, sweetness, bitterness, and any other contrary sensible qualities of this kind make no element. Rather, the tangible qualities make the elements, and their differences are the first of all sensible differences. These are heat, cold, dryness, moisture, heaviness, lightness, hardness, softness, viscosity, friability, and smoothness; of these, heaviness and lightness have neither the power of acting nor of being acted upon. Heat and cold have the greatest power of acting, but dryness and moisture the power of being acted upon. Hence heat gathers together things of the same kind, and also separates those that are heterogeneous and of different kinds. Cold, however, gathers together both things of the same kind and those that are foreign. Moisture is not confined by its own limits but is properly held in and bounded by alien ones. Dryness behaves the opposite way. Next come thinness and thickness, viscosity, friability, hardness, softness, and the other qualities that arise from these. For thinness pertains to moisture, and thickness to dryness. Viscosity also belongs to moisture, being a moisture that has undergone some change, as oil does. Friability seems to pertain to dryness, since whatever is wholly dry is, on account of the lack of moisture, compressed and condensed. Softness indeed belongs to moisture, as hardness does to dryness. For what yields to pressure gives way within itself, neither resists nor holds its own. Therefore the moist is not soft, although softness is referred to moisture and hardness to dryness, since what has been compressed is held together by hardness and is dry.

units.la: CAP. XLIX. Elementa Mundi quatuor esse.
units.tr: CHAPTER 49. That the elements of the world are four.

units.la: ORUM autem, qui simplicia cor- pora esse elementa statuerunt, alij unum, ut Tales qui aquam; Anaximenes qui aerem, Heraclius qui ignem: alij duo, ut Parmenides, qui ignem & terram, quidam tria ut Plato, nonnulli quatuor ut Empedocles, qui igni caetera omnia opposuit. Sed quatuor esse Mundi elementa ex copulationibus primarum quatuor qualitatum tractabilium intelligi licet: Una enim est calidi & humidi, altera calidi & sicci, tertia frigidi & humidi, quarta frigidi & sicci. Copulari hae quidem possunt, eo quod contrariæ sint. Contraria enim coniungi nõ possunt, vt calidum & frigidũ, siccum & humidum. Cum igitur calidum cum sicco copulatur,tum fit ignis. Si vero calidum cum humido aër. Si præterea frigidum cum sicco coniungitur,terra est: sin cum humido aqua. Ac sic tot simplicia inueniuntur corpora, quæ natura constant, ex quibus ignis & aër eiusdem loci sunt,qui sursum est,terra & aqua e-ius, qui in vniuersi medio consistit: quorum extrema nimirum ignis & terra purissima sunt: media vero nempe aqua & aër minus pura, sed quodammodo permista. Eorum autem natura est contraria: Nam igni contraria est aqua, aëri terra, quoniam ex contrariis qualitatibus, proprietatibusque con-stant, quæ cum sint omnino quatuor, calor, frigus,ariditas, & humor in quoque elemento vna reperiatur,necesse est. Propterea ariditas terræ magis est propria, quàm frigus, & aquæ frigus,magis,quàm humor, & aëris humor magis quàm calor, ac denique ignis calor magis quàm ariditas.
units.tr: Of those who held that the simple bodies are the elements, some, like Thales, posited one, namely water; Anaximenes posited air; Heraclitus fire. Others posited two: Parmenides, fire and earth; some three, like Plato; some four, like Empedocles, who set all the other things over against fire. But that the elements of the world are four can be understood from the combinations of the four primary tangible qualities: for one is of hot and moist, another of hot and dry, a third of cold and moist, a fourth of cold and dry. These can indeed be combined, because they are not contraries; for contraries cannot be joined, such as hot and cold, or dry and moist. Therefore, when the hot is joined with the dry, fire comes to be; if the hot is joined with the moist, air. Moreover, if the cold is joined with the dry, earth; but if with the moist, water. And so there are found as many simple bodies, which exist by nature, from which fire and air belong to the place which is above, and earth and water to that which lies in the middle of the universe. Of these, the extremes, namely fire and earth, are most pure; the middle ones, namely water and air, are less pure, but in a certain way mixed. Their nature is contrary: for water is contrary to fire, earth to air, since they consist of contrary qualities and properties; and since these are four in all, heat, cold, dryness and moisture, it is necessary that one be found in each element. Hence dryness is more proper to earth than cold is, and cold more than moisture is to water, and moisture more than heat is to air, and finally the heat of fire more than dryness.

units.la: CAP. L.
units.tr: CHAP. L.

units.la: Quoduis elementum ex quouis generari.
units.tr: That any element can be generated from any other.

units.la: IMPLICIA corpora, quæ natura constant, ex se mutuo oriri, supra iam satis demonstratum est. Nam nisi vicissim ex se ipsa generaretur, nulla profecto esset alteratio, quæ fit ex affectiosectionibus eorum, quæ se contingunt. Nunc autem quænam sit mutuæ eorum corporum mutationis & vicissitudinis ratio dicendum est. Quoduis sane elementum ex quoque oriri posse, ex eo constat, quòd generatio ex contradicentibus in contradicentia tendat.
units.tr: That mixed bodies, which are composed of natures, arise from one another has already been sufficiently demonstrated above. For unless each were generated in turn from the others, there would certainly be no alteration, which comes about through the affections and sections of those things that touch one another. Now we must say what the manner of this mutual change and interchange of those bodies is. That any element can arise from any other is clear from the fact that generation proceeds from contraries into contraries.

units.la: Elementa autem omnia aut qualitate una, aut duabus inter se pugnant, & se mutuò afficiunt. Utraque enim repugnantia igni & aquæ inest, quandoquidem ille calidus est & siccus, hæc frigida & humida: aëri verò & aquæ altera tantum est. Hæc enim frigida est & humida, illæ verò humidus & calidus. Itaque quoduis elementum ex quouis suapte natura oriri, mutatis duntaxat ipsis qualitatibus, quibus prædita sunt, ex his satis perspicuum est. Iam verò nec magnum erit negotium animaduertere qui id fiat, etiamsi maiore celeritate & tarditate, facilitateque, ac difficultate differant. Quæ enim inter se cognatione quadam communicant, & qualitatis communione coniuncta sunt, eorum velox admodum est mutatio: aliorum autem, quæ hac caret, tarda, propterea quòd una qualitas facilius, quam duæ, mutatur: veluti facilius ex aëre fit ignis, quàm ex aqua: quandoquidem aër & ignis calore communicant, & aqua omnibus suis qualitatibus igni repugnat: aër verò & ignis duntaxat siccitate & humore discrepant. Ignis enim calidus est & siccus: aër calidus & humidus. Quare si ab humore siccitas vincatur, aer erit. Rursus autem ex aere aqua oritur, si calor à frigore superetur. Eodémque modo aqua in terram & in ignem terra vertitur. Vtraque enim cum vtrisque aliqua societate coniunguntur: quandoquidem aqua frigore & humore prædita est, terra verò frigore ac siccitate. Itaque si humor aquæ vincatur, terra erit. Rursúsque quoniam in igne siccitas inest & calor, terra verò frigidæ est & sicca, si frigus à calore consumatur, ex ea gignetur ignis. Ex quibus constat corporum simplicium generationem vicissitudine quadam esse mutuam, propterea quòd eorum cognatio magna sit. Cæterùm ex igne aqua, & ex aere terra, rursúsque ex aqua & terra aër & ignis procreari possunt, sed difficilius, quòd plures qualitates mutandæ sint. Si enim ex aqua futurus sit ignis, & frigus mutari & humorem, expedit: rursúsque si ex terra aër, frigus siccitatémque consumi. Eadémque ratione, si ex igne & aëre aqua & terra generentur, vtráque qualitatem mutari, necesse erit. Atque hæc generatio longior est. Si verò vtriusque qualitatis altera tollatur, facilior quidem & breuior erit mutatio. Cùm enim frigus aquę, & siccitas ignis sublatæ erunt, tum aër erit, quandoquidem huius calor remanet, & illius humor. Cùm autem ignis calor, & aquæ humor tolluntur tum terra generatur, propterea quòd illius siccitas, & huius frigus relinquanquantur. Eodem modo ex aëre ac terra ignis & aqua oriuntur. Porrò[?] cùm aëris humor & terræ frigus mutatur tum ignis est, quoniam illius calor, remanet, & huius siccitas, quæ quidem qualitates ignis propriæ sunt. Non solùm in sublimi fit ignis, sed etiam hîc in i-mo, & nostro aspectu flamma, quæ ignis est & ardens fumus, quæque ex aëre & terra con-stant[?], expirat.
units.tr: Now all the elements struggle either in one quality or in two, and they act upon one another. For both kinds of opposition are present in fire and water, since the one is hot and dry, the other cold and moist; but air and water have only one opposition between them. For water is cold and moist, while air is moist and hot. Thus it is quite plain from these facts that any element can arise from any other by its own nature, the qualities with which they are endowed being merely changed. Nor will it be a great task to see how this happens, even though the processes differ in speed, slowness and ease or difficulty. Those things which share a certain kinship with one another and are joined by a common quality change very quickly, whereas those which lack this change slowly, because one quality is changed more easily than two. For example, fire is made from air more easily than from water, since air and fire share heat, while water is opposed to fire in all its qualities; but air and fire differ only in dryness and moisture. For fire is hot and dry, air hot and moist. Therefore, if dryness is overcome by moisture, there will be air. Conversely, water arises from air if heat is overcome by cold. In the same way, earth is turned into water and into fire from water. For each of these is joined with each of the others by some affinity: water is endowed with cold and moisture, earth with cold and dryness. So if the moisture of water is overcome, there will be earth. And again, since fire contains dryness and heat, and earth is cold and dry, if the cold is consumed by heat, fire will be generated from earth. From these facts it is established that the generation of simple bodies is mutual by a certain interchange, because their kinship is great. Yet fire can produce water, and air earth, and again water and earth can produce air and fire, but with more difficulty, because more qualities must be changed. For if fire is to become water, its cold and moisture must be changed, which is a matter of ease; and again, if air is to become earth, its cold and dryness must be consumed. By the same reasoning, if water and earth are to be generated from fire and air, both qualities must necessarily be changed. And this generation is longer. But if one of the two qualities is removed, the change will be easier and quicker. For when the cold of water and the dryness of fire are removed, there will be air, since the heat of the one and the moisture of the other remain. But when the heat of fire and the moisture of water are removed, earth is generated, because the dryness of the one and the cold of the other remain. In the same way fire and water arise from air and earth. Moreover, when the moisture of air and the cold of earth are changed, there is fire, since the heat of the one remains and the dryness of the other, which qualities are indeed proper to fire. Fire is produced not only on high, but also here below, and before our eyes the flame, which is fire and burning smoke, and which consists of air and earth, breathes out.

units.la: CAP. LI.
units.tr: CHAPTER 51.

units.la: Quatuor elementa, non esse primum corporum naturalium materiam, nec elementum elementi.
units.tr: That the four elements are not the first matter of natural bodies, nor an element of an element.

units.la: VOdvis[?] elementum ex quouis oriri, fatis iam perspicuum esse ar-bitramur, sed quo in subiecto id fiat, ostendere restat. Nonnullis quidem philosophis olim placuit aërem, & a-quam, quæque eiusdem generis sunt, pro materia subiici, quam alij unum esse elementum, alij plura dicebant. Sed si unum duntaxat est, profecto omnia unum erunt, aut nihil generabitur: quandoquidem generatio in contradictione est. Atque si aër ea sit materia, aut aliud quoduis elementorum, cuius substantia in generatione corporum remaneat, haud dubiè non generatio erit, sed duntaxat alteratio, quoniam sola illius elementi mutabitur qualitas. Adde quòd si illius elementi, quòd aliorum origini subiicitur, substantia non mutetur, necessario simul in eodem loco erunt duo corpora, nempe, quod subii-citur, & quod generatur. Sed hoc non con-sentaneum est, nec Naturæ comodum. Præ-terea si ex ignis substatia generetur aer dun-taxat mutatione caloris, in contrarium facta, certè aer quiddam frigidum erit, aut simul i-dem erit & calidum & frigidum. Atqui hoc tam absurdum est, quàm quod absurdissimū. Quare præter elementum generationi na-turalium corporum aliud principium subii-citur, quod quædam communis materia est, quæ si vnum elementorū esse non possit, mul-to adhuc minus plura eorum. Nam si ex plu-ribus, quæ simul actu sunt, naturale corpus o-riretur, profecto quæ contraria sunt, simul in eodem subiecto inessent. Constat igitur ex his generationi corporum nullum subiici elementum, nec aliud, quod medium sit cor-pus inter aerem & aquam, aut aerem & igne interiectum aere crassius, & aqua & terra ra-rius: quandoquidem hoc calidum sit oportet, aut frigidum. Quod si calidum est, & ex eo gignatur ignis, profecto ignem frigi-dum esse, expediet: quoniam vnumquodque ex suo oritur contrario. Si rursus ex eodem aqua fiat, ea necessario calida erit, aut v-numquodque corpus simul calidum erit & frigidum, ac repugnantiæ particeps: Quod fieri non potest. Quare nec tale corpus, nec vllum aliud ex elemetis generationi naturalium corporum subiici potest, sed alia quæ-dam est communis materia, omnium quali-tatum expers, quæ dutaxat potestate τὸ ὄν[?] est.
units.tr: We think it has already been made sufficiently clear that an element arises from any of the others; it remains to show in what substrate this happens. Some philosophers long ago held that air and water, and things of the same kind, are to be put forward as matter, some saying that this is one element, others that there are several. But if there is only one, then surely everything will be one, or nothing will be generated, since generation involves contradiction. And if air is that matter, or any other of the elements, whose substance remains in the generation of bodies, then without doubt there will be no generation at all, but merely alteration, since only the quality of that element will change. Add that if the substance of that element which underlies the origin of the others does not change, then two bodies will necessarily be in the same place at once, namely the one that underlies and the one that is generated. But this is not consistent, nor to the advantage of Nature. Moreover, if air were generated from the substance of fire merely by a change of heat into its opposite, then air will certainly be something cold, or else the same thing will be at once both hot and cold. Yet this is as absurd as anything could be. Therefore, besides the element, another principle is put forward as underlying the generation of natural bodies, which is a certain common matter; and if it cannot be one of the elements, much less can it be several of them. For if a natural body arose from several things that are actually present together, then surely contraries would be present together in the same subject. It is clear, then, from these considerations, that no element underlies the generation of bodies, nor any other body intermediate between air and water, or between air and fire, a body denser than air and rarer than water and earth; since this must be either hot or cold. But if it is hot, and fire is generated from it, then it will follow that fire is cold, since each thing arises from its contrary. If again water is made from the same, it will necessarily be hot, or else each body will at once be both hot and cold, and share in a contradiction; which cannot happen. Therefore neither such a body nor any other of the elements can underlie the generation of natural bodies, but there is some other common matter, free of all qualities, which is only in potency what is [τὸ ὄν].

units.la: CAP. LII. Quænam mistorum corporum origo.
units.tr: CHAPTER 52. What is the origin of mixed bodies?

units.la: NATVRAM elementorum, ex quibus mista constant corpora, non eodem modo olim philosophi explicarunt. Eorum enim quidem aliquid commune eis subiici, in quo inter se vicissim mutentur, ce-fuerunt: alij verò vllam elementorum fieri mutationem negarunt, sed ea quæ natura constant, eo modo ex eis produci tradiderunt, quo ex cemento & lapidibus murus cōstruitur, nimirum ex minutissimis elementorum partibus inter se cohærentibus, absque vlla substantiarum mutatione. Sed hoc modo ex his nunquam caro, ossa, nervi, aliàque eius-dem generis efformari possunt, propterea quod nulla ipsorum elementorum particula sit, quæ non suam retineat formam. Quatenus enim elementa actu sunt, eatenus nihil aliud esse possunt, quàm id quod sunt. Quapropter vere permista nō sunt, sed duntaxat, ita coniunguntur, vt grana tritici & hordei, quæ aceruum faciunt. Itaque in mistorum corporum generatione elemen-ta quatuor, ita tota totis permiscentur, vt nulla sit misti particula, ex qua tandem secretione omnia regenerari possint eleme-ta, primarum quatuor qualitatum tractabi-lium opera. Nam in misti corporis genera-tione quatuor elementa ita inter se miscen-tur, vt posthac integras qualitates suas non retineant, nec omnino eas etiam perdant, sed retusæ sint. Nec etiam eorum substantiæ omnino abolentur, sed in aliam misti corporis substantiam conuertentur. Quare in misti corporibus quatuor elementa non solum ratione suæ materiæ insunt, sed etiam formarum, quæ tamen non syncerę sunt, sed vni entelechiæ subiectæ. Itaque in misto corpore terra actu non est, sed potestate, & ratione suarum qualitatum, quæ remanent quantu-uis remissæ. Eadem ratione de aliis elementis, quæ in misti corporibus insunt, indicare licet.
units.tr: The nature of the elements, out of which mixed bodies are composed, was not explained in the same way by the philosophers of old. For some of them held that there is something common underlying the elements, in which they are mutually changed into one another; but others denied that any change of the elements takes place, and taught instead that the things which have a natural constitution are produced from the elements in the way a wall is built from cement and stones, namely from the tiniest particles of the elements cohering with one another, without any change of substances. But in this way flesh, bones, sinews and other things of the same kind could never be formed from these, because there is no particle of the elements which does not retain its own form. For insofar as the elements are actual, they can be nothing other than what they are. Therefore they are not truly mixed, but are only joined together, as the grains of wheat and barley which make up a heap. Thus in the generation of mixed bodies the four elements are blended whole with whole, so that there is no particle of the mixed body from whose secretion all the elements could finally be regenerated, by the working of the four tangible primary qualities. For in the generation of a mixed body the four elements are so blended with one another that afterwards they keep neither their entire qualities, nor do they wholly lose them, but they are blunted. Nor are their substances wholly abolished, but they are converted into another substance of the mixed body. Therefore in mixed bodies the four elements are present not only in respect of their matter but also of their forms, which however are not pure, but subject to a single entelechy. Thus in a mixed body earth is not actually present but potentially, and in respect of its qualities, which remain however much they are weakened. By the same reasoning one may state the position of the other elements which are present in mixed bodies.

units.la: CAP. LIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER LIII.

units.la: Tria esse generationis principia.
units.tr: That there are three principles of generation.

units.la: Q[?]oniam generatio eorum, quæ natu-ra constat & mortalia sunt, in medio vniuersi excitari solet, de illius prin-cipiis, & quot sint & qualia oratio habenda est. Illa autem tria esse dicuntur, quorum a-liud vt materies est, aliud vt forma, quibus tertium addere par est: quandoquidem ad rerum generationem duo non satis sunt. Materies igitur genitis causa ascribitur, mate-ries (inquam) quæ ens esse potest. Etenim eorum quæ sunt quædam, necessario sunt, vt æterna, & perpetua: alia non necessario, sed esse & non esse possunt, vt ea quæ generantur, quorum originem mors consequitur. Hæc enim partim desiderantur, partim non desi-derantur, & sunt. Quare generationem & corruptionem iis euenire, quæ esse & non esse possunt, necesse est. Propterea genitis materies vt causa requiritur, & id,cuius gratia, aliquid esse & dici consueuit, nempe species & forma, qua quidem ratio vnicuique essentiæ redditur. Verum duabus his causis tertiam adiungere, expedit, quam tametsi omnes prisci philosophi somniauerint, nullus tamen eorum, præter vnum Aristotelem, re-cte[?] eam expressit. Alij præterea ipsam formarum naturam ad res procreandas, satis idoneam esse causam arbitrati fuerunt, vt in Phædone Socrates, qui cum reliquis philosophis succensuisset[?], vt de hoc principio nihil locutis, statutum voluit, eorum quæ sunt, alia formas esse, alia per communionem capacia formarum haberi, & per formas consistere, atque per earum amissionem corrumpi. Quibus boni senis verbis formas tum generationis, tum corruptionis causas esse, satis perspicuum est. Sed hoc ipsum alij materiei attribuerunt, propterea quòd mutatio in ea fiat. At neutros perite philosophatos fuisse, sic Aristoteles demonstrat. Si (inquit) formæ pro causis efficientibus habeantur, cur non continuo generationis causæ sunt? Semper enim ea suggeruntur, quæ earum capacia sunt. Imo vero quod alterandi, & transformandi vim habet, id rerum gignedarum magis causa est quam ea, quæ ab ipsis posita fuit. Id autem in naturæ & artis operibus efficientis nomen habet, cui facultas mouendi inest. Quare qui hoc materiei tribuerunt, non recte sensisse videntur. Proprium enim materiei affici est, & moueri: efficientis vero afficere & mouere, id quod perspicue ea declarant, quæ tum natura, tum arte constant. Quapropter aut elementa per se nullum animal format, nec solum lignum lecticam efficit, sed hæc ab arte, illud vero a Natura fit. Qui vero corpora, quæ natura constant ex quatuor elementis nasci dixerunt, eo quod calor ea dissi-[?]pet & secernat, quæ diuersi generis sunt, & frigus eadem omnia cogat, eandem causam efficientem perinde rebus eis naturalibus attribuerunt, atque in rebus, quæ arte constat, quæ sine instrumentis fieri non possunt. Propterea in iis, quæ sunt naturalia, causa alia prior est, quæ instrumentorum vires dispensat atque gubernat. Hæc autem Aristoteli conuersio cœli est, quæ cum perpetua sit, etiam rerum naturalium generationem (si adsit materies) perpetuam esse expedit. Cœlestis enim motus continuam excitat generationem, propterea quod æternus sit, & omnium aliarum mutationum princeps causa, si philofopho credere fas est. Hæc denique cœli conuersio necessariè generationem antecedit, quoniam quod mouetur id in natura rerum iā est, sed id quod generatur & fit, nondum in ea est. Posterior autem causa calor est & frigus, quibus rerum generatio fit.
units.tr: Since the generation of those things which consist by nature and are mortal is usually discussed in the middle of the universe, we must give an account of its principles: what they are and of what kind. These are said to be three: of these one is matter, another form, and it is fitting to add a third, since two are not sufficient for the generation of things. Matter, then, is assigned as the cause of things that are generated: matter, I say, which can be or not be. For of things that exist, some necessarily exist, such as the eternal and perpetual; others do not necessarily exist, but can both be and not be, such as things that are generated, whose origin is followed by death. For these are partly desired and partly not desired, and they exist. Hence it must be that generation and corruption befall those things which can be and not be. Therefore matter is required as the cause of things generated; and that for the sake of which a thing is and is called, namely species and form, which indeed gives its account to every essence. But it is useful to add a third cause to these two, which, although all the ancient philosophers dreamed of it, yet none of them, except Aristotle alone, expressed it rightly. Others moreover thought the very nature of forms was a sufficient cause for producing things, as Socrates in the Phaedo, who, being angry with the other philosophers because they had said nothing about this principle, laid down that of the things that exist, some are forms, others are held to be capable of forms by participation, and subsist through forms, and are corrupted by the loss of them. From these words of the good old man it is quite clear that forms are the causes both of generation and of corruption. But others assigned this very thing to matter, because change takes place in it. Yet that neither of these philosophised skilfully is shown thus by Aristotle: If (he says) forms are regarded as efficient causes, why are they not continually the causes of generation? For those things are always supplied which are capable of them. Indeed, that which has the power of altering and transforming is more truly the cause of the things to be generated than that which was posited by them. Now this, in the works of nature and of art, has the name of efficient cause, and possesses the faculty of moving. Hence those who assigned this to matter do not seem to have judged rightly. For it is the proper character of matter to be affected and moved, but of the efficient cause to affect and move; which things are plainly shown by those that are produced both by nature and by art. Wherefore either the elements by themselves form no animal, nor does wood alone make a couch, but the one is made by art, the other by Nature. But those who said that bodies which consist by nature arise from the four elements, because heat separates and sifts those things which are of different kinds, and cold compresses all of them together, have assigned the same efficient cause to those natural things in the same way as in things that are made by art, which cannot be made without instruments. Therefore among natural things there is another, prior cause, which distributes and governs the powers of the instruments. Now this is the revolution of the heavens according to Aristotle, which, since it is perpetual, makes it fitting that the generation of natural things also be perpetual (if matter be present). For the celestial motion excites continual generation, because it is eternal, and is the chief cause of all other changes, if it is right to believe the philosopher. Finally, this revolution of the heavens necessarily precedes generation, since that which is moved already exists in the nature of things, but that which is generated and comes to be does not yet exist in it. The later cause, however, is heat and cold, by which the generation of things takes place.

units.la: CAP. LIIII. Serie generationis & corruptionis esse continua.
units.tr: Chapter 54. That the series of generation and corruption is continuous.

units.la: A autem, quæ Natura constant, & generari & corrumpi absque intermissione ex his, quæ sequuntur, facile intelligemus. Primùm enim si rerum naturaliū generatio & corruptio perpetuò futura est, causam eius esse perpetuā, necesse est. Itaque ea causa est obliqui orbis conuersio, quòd perennis sit. Nam ipse obliquus orbis profectionis Solis ad nos, & à nobis discessionis author est. Propterea Solis aduentu ad nos & propinquitate, quæ natura constant, generari consentaneum est, & discessu eius ac remotione, eadem corrumpi.
units.tr: That natural things can be generated and corrupted without interruption we shall easily understand from what follows. First, if the generation and corruption of natural things is to be perpetual, its cause must also be perpetual. That cause is the revolution of the oblique orb, because it is everlasting. For the oblique orb itself is the author of the Sun's advance toward us and of its withdrawal from us. Therefore, with the Sun's approach and nearness to us, natural things are reasonably generated, and with its departure and remoteness, the same things are corrupted.

units.la: Quoniā autem crebro Solis aduentu ad nos, ea quæ natura constant, ad ætatis vigore vsque crescunt, & crebro etiam eius discessu à nobis, eadè ad interitū vsque diminuatur & attenuetur (quoniā contrariorū, contrariæ sunt causæ) euenit vt animantium vita cæterorumque omnium tempora suis claudatur terminis, ac numeris. Plerunque tamè vsuenit vt animalia quædam propter inæqualem elementorum concretionem celerius aliis intereant.
units.tr: Since, however, through the Sun's frequent approach to us, natural things grow until they reach the vigour of their age, and through its frequent departure from us they are diminished and worn down even to destruction (for contrary things have contrary causes), it comes about that the life of animals and the durations of all other things are bounded by their fixed limits and numbers. Yet it commonly happens that some animals perish more quickly than others, on account of the unequal mixture of the elements.

units.la: Cùm enim inæqualis materia est, nec vbiqu[?] eadem substernitur, tum rerū generationes inæquales esse, atque alias maturiùs, alias tardiùs effici, necesse est. Eadem corruptionis ratio est, quandoquidem huiusmodi muta-tiones, haudquaquam intermittitur. Id quod profecto optima ratione evenit. Natura e-nimid semper in omnibus rebus, quod melius est, appetit. Sed res ipsas esse, quàm non esse melius est. Nam hoc modo rerum [?] connectitur, quoniam perpetua generatio proximè ad substantiam æternam accedit, cuius rei causa est continua cæli conuersio. Itaque quæcunque affectiones perpessiones-que ac facultates vicissim fiunt, cuiusmodi in simplicibus corporibus sunt, cœlestium corporum conuersionem imitantur. Propterea cùm ex aqua aër generatur, ex aëre ignis, & rursus ex igne aqua, tum generatio velut in orbem voluitur, & in se recurrit. Cæterum dubium occurrit, cur simplicia corpora iampridè non diuulsa sint, cùm eorū quod vis ab immenso tempore in suum contendat locum? At diuulsa non sunt, cuius rei causa est eorū vicissitudo. Nam si suis in locis singula semper se continerent, & a proximis nō mutarentur, iam olim destructa essent. Quà-obrem vicissim inter se mutantur: ac propter mutuam illorum mutationem nullum suo in loco contineri potest, præter terrâ, quæ propter vniuersi medium, in quo consistit, permanet. Præterea perpetuæ generationis causa est perpetuus motor, qui semper adest. Perpetuo enim ipsum coelum mouet. Deinde tempus, in qua fit ea, perenne est, & rei continuæ numerus ac mensura. Itaque ad coeli conversione refertur, quæ perpetuitate corporis mobilis continuatur. Quomodo (quę-so) perpetuabitur affectio, nisi id cuiꝰ ea est, perpetuetur? At corpus huiusmodi coelum est quod semper in orbe voluitur. Propterea tempus perpetuum est.
units.tr: For since the matter is unequal and is not everywhere the same beneath, the generations of things must be unequal, some brought about sooner and others later. The reason for corruption is the same, since such changes are never interrupted. This certainly happens for the best of reasons. For nature in all things always seeks what is better, and it is better for things to exist than not to exist. In this way the continuity of things is maintained, since perpetual generation comes closest to eternal substance, and the cause of this is the continuous revolution of the heavens. Therefore whatever affections, passions and faculties arise in turn, such as those found in simple bodies, imitate the revolution of the heavenly bodies. Hence, when air is generated from water, fire from air, and again water from fire, generation as it were rolls in a circle and returns upon itself. But a doubt arises: why have the simple bodies not long ago been torn apart, since each, through immense time, strives toward its own place? They are not torn apart, and the cause is their interchange. For if each always remained in its own place and were not changed by its neighbours, they would have been destroyed long ago. Therefore they change among themselves in turn, and because of this mutual change none can be held in its own place, except earth, which remains because of the middle of the universe in which it sits. Moreover, the cause of perpetual generation is a perpetual mover, which is always present, for the heaven itself moves perpetually. Then the time in which generation takes place is everlasting, being the number and measure of a continuous thing. Thus it is referred to the revolution of the heaven, which is continued by the perpetuity of the moving body. How, I ask, could an affection be made perpetual unless that to which it belongs were perpetual? But a body of this kind is the heaven, which always revolves in its orb. Therefore time is perpetual.

units.la: INSTITUTIONUM PHYSICARUM SECUNDA PARS, QUAE meteorologia est. CAP. I.
units.tr: INSTITUTIONUM PHYSICARUM SECUNDA PARS, QUAE meteorologia est. CAP. I.

units.la: DE PRIMIS naturæ causis, ac omni motu naturali, & præterea de syderibus, quæ in summo orbe distincta sunt, & eorum vicissitudine, denique de communi origine & corruptione, iam ante disputatum est. Restat ut ea physices pars differenda suscipiatur, quam veteres Naturæ interpretes Meteorogiam no-minarunt. Hæc autem scientia eorum omnium disciplinam profitetur, quæ in eo loco eueniunt, qui est orbi Lunæ proximus. Ea autem sunt circulus Lacteus, Cometæ, eaque omnia, quæ in superiore loco aeris, tum ardere, tum moueri cernuntur, & quæcunque communes aeris & aquæ affectiones statuuntur: itemque ea omnia, quæ terræ species sunt, & partes, partiumque eius affectiones, ex quibus ventorum ac terræ motuum causas cognoscemus: & ea denique omnia, quæ horum agitationibus efficiuntur. Ex his etiam fiunt[?] fulminum iactus, typhones, prætereres[?], accensique turbines, ac alia, quæ orbiculata sunt, & horum ipsorum affectiones affectusque, qui cocretione per gelu ac frigus gignuntur.
units.tr: We have already discussed the first causes of nature, all natural motion, the stars set in the highest sphere and their alternation, and finally common origin and corruption. It remains to take up that part of physics which the ancient interpreters of nature called meteorology. This science deals with all those things that occur in the region nearest the orbit of the Moon. These are the Milky Way, comets, and everything seen to burn or move in the upper region of the air; and whatever common affections of air and water are established; likewise all those things which are kinds and parts of the earth, and the affections of its parts, from which we shall learn the causes of winds and earthquakes; and finally all those things which are brought about by the agitation of these. From these also come about the hurlings of thunderbolts, prester [πρηστῆρες] (fiery whirlwinds), kindled whirlwinds, and other things that are round in shape, and the affections and conditions of these same things, which arise from congealing through frost and cold.

units.la: {a}Eorum autem causæ sunt duæ, quarum vna materies est ex quatuor elementis orta: altera ex qua motus principium proficiscitur, quæ facultati eorum, quæ semper mouetur, tribuenda est. Huiusmodi autem ea sunt cœlestia corpora, quæ motu suo meteororum omnium materiam excitant.
units.tr: {a}Now there are two causes of these. One is the matter, arising from the four elements; the other is the source of motion, which is to be attributed to the power of that which moves always. Such bodies are the heavenly bodies, which by their motion stir up the matter of all meteors.

units.la: CAP. II. Cur syderum calor in ima aeris parte feruidior sit quam in media? Cur que in suprema non formentur nubes?
units.tr: CHAPTER II. Why is the heat of the stars greater in the lowest part of the air than in the middle? And why are clouds not formed in the highest part?

units.la: Ost[?] summos orbes corpora sunt alia quatuor, quorum alia sunt calida, alia frigida, quædam sicca, quædam humida, quorum vnum grauissimum est, & terra dicitur, aliud fluens frigidissimum, quod aqua est: circum utrunque cohærent aër & ignis, quorum hic caloris exuperatia est, ille verò tres habet partes unam, quæ terram & aquam ambit calida & humidam vapores excipiens & exhalationes omnes: alteram mediam, quæ frigida est, & humida: tertiam supremam calidam & siccâ. Halitus autem, qui ex aqua & terra effertur, duplex [?] est, unus vapor, cuius causa humor est [?] & calor, alter fumus, qui à calore est, & ex ariditate. Præterea vapor potestate tanquam aqua est, fumus verò perinde ac ignis. Propterea in summo aëris loco nubes minimè coguntur: quippe cùm illic non solus aër sit, sed & ignis, qui ex aëre procreatur. Ibi enim aër in ignem facilè vertitur. Ac eo in loco ipse aër in orbem fluit, propterea quòd unà cùm cœli conuersione trahatur, atque eò magis quòd ætheri, hoc est, igneo cœlo iungatur. Itaque aëris supremi & ignis motus prohibet, quominus illic nubes concrescant, sed in ea aëris parte coguntur, quæ inter imà & suprema interiecta est. Hæc enim necessariò frigida est & humida, propterea qp [?] à cœli conuersione nō calescat, nec radij Solis, & reliquorum syderū reflexi eo usque pertingant. Adde quòd calor undique circunstans frigus intendit. Ex quo fit, ut æstate hæc pars frigidior sit quàm hyeme. Principium porrò, quòd meteororum materiam movet, calor est, cuius causa ipse Sol est. Sed de calore disputatio in tractatu de sensu aptior est, quàm hoc in loco: quandoquidem calor quædam affectio sensus tactus est. Nunc verò duntaxat exponendum est, cur calor in cœlo excitetur, cùm nulla astra huiusmodi qualitate naturáque prædita sint. At à cœli conuersione & syderum id euenire ea satis declarant, quæ in aëre commoto colli quiescere videntur. Etenim si qua vi ipse aër circumfusus impellatur, maximè calescit, nec iniuria. Rei enim solidæ motus, hoc est, Solis & reliquorum astrorum ipsum aërem dis-sipat. Propterea motus Solis, reliquorúm-que syderum vna est causa, per quam huc ad nos calor perueniat: altera autem ignis est totum aërem amplectens, qui tum crebro a-strorum motu secernitur, tum vi deorsum de-turbatur. Cæterùm errantium astrorum vagatio, corpus cœli nec calidum esse, neque accendi posse satis aperte demonstrat. Si enim esset calidum, profecto quò astra celerius moueretur, eò magis ignesceret. Adde quòd Sol, qui maximè calidus videtur, & specie cadidus apparet, non igneus est. Igitur cœlum non calidum est.
units.tr: Beneath the highest spheres lie four other bodies, some hot, some cold, some dry, some moist. Of these, one is the heaviest and is called earth; another, the fluid and coldest, is water. Air and fire surround each of them. Of these, fire has an excess of heat, while the air has three parts: the first, which is warm and moist, surrounds earth and water and receives all the vapours and exhalations; the middle, which is cold and moist; and the third, the highest, which is warm and dry. The exhalation that rises from water and earth is twofold: one is vapour, whose cause is moisture and heat; the other is smoke, which comes from heat and dryness. Moreover, vapour is in potency like water, while smoke is like fire. Therefore clouds are least likely to gather in the highest region of the air, since there is not only air but also fire, which is produced from air, and air is easily turned into fire there. In that place the air itself flows in a circle, because it is carried along with the rotation of the heavens, and all the more because it is joined to the ether, that is, the fiery heaven. Thus the motion of the highest air and of the fire prevents clouds from gathering there, and they gather instead in that part of the air which lies between the lowest and the highest. For this part is necessarily cold and moist. It is not warmed by the rotation of the heavens, and the reflected rays of the sun and the other stars do not reach it. Add that the heat surrounding it on every side intensifies its cold. Hence it comes about that this part is colder in summer than in winter. Now the principle that moves the matter of meteors is heat, whose cause is the sun itself. But a discussion of heat is more fitting in the treatise on sense than here, since heat is a certain affection of the sense of touch. For now it must only be explained why heat is produced in the heavens, since no stars are endowed with this quality and nature. That this comes about from the rotation of the heavens and of the stars is sufficiently shown by those things which seem to be at rest in air that is set in motion. For if the surrounding air is struck by some force, it becomes very hot, and rightly so: the motion of a solid body, namely of the sun and the other stars, disperses the air itself. Therefore the motion of the sun and of the other stars is one cause by which heat reaches us here below; the other is the fire that embraces the whole air, which is both separated by the frequent motion of the stars and driven downward by force. Moreover, the wandering of the planets clearly shows that the heavenly body is neither hot nor capable of being kindled. For if it were hot, surely the faster the stars moved, the more they would be set on fire. Add that the sun, which seems to be the hottest, also appears white in colour and is not fiery. Therefore the heaven is not hot.

units.la: CAP. III. Cur flamma in summa parte aeris appareant.
units.tr: CAP. III. Why flames appear in the upper part of the air.

units.la: Is autem expositis, dicamus, cur in aëre tum flammæ accensæ videantur, tum traiicientes stellæ, atque faces, & capræ saltantes. Hæc omsiia[?] profecto ex eadem causa sunt, & duntaxat magnitudine paucitateque differunt. Horum quidem atque aliorum multorum idè principium est. Cùm enim à radiis Solis terra calescit, tum exhalationem excitari, necesse est, non simplicem, vt quidam putarunt, sed duplicem vnam, quæ vapor est, & alteram fumus, quarum hic propter calorem sursum ef[?]ferтur. Ille verò quia humidus est, suo pondere subsidit. Quoniam autem infra cœli conuersionem ignis, qui calidus est & siccus, collocatur, ac infra hanc ignis naturam aer locum tenetur, fit vt ignis velut caloris formes succedens circum ambitum terræ rotundù, ita extendatur, vt simulac paruus motus fieri cœperit, sæpe flamma in aëre fiat, & quasi fumus succendi videatur. Est enim flamma feruor aridi spiritus. Itaque huiusmodi inflammatio ignis ab orbis cœlestis conuersione & agitatur, & incenditur, quæ plerunque talis cernitur, qualis est ea flamma, quæ fit, cùm in agris stipula comburitur. Si verò duntaxat longa appareat, faces videbuntur, atque trabes, & caprae saltantes. Si præterea magis in longitudinem, quàm in latitudinem distendatur, atque simul id scintillet, quod ardore corripitur (hoc autem vsuuenit, dum id quod ignescit à principio modum excedit) caprae saltantes, faces & trabes magis ac magis apparebunt. Si denique huiusmodi siccae exhalationes & inflammatae secundum longitudidine paulatim ac multis in locis diffusæ sint, & longitudine & latitudine conueniant tra-iicientes stellæ videbuntur, quarum motio iaculationi similis est. Nam in media aeris parte huiusmodi ignea exhalatio ob circunftans frigus densatur, & ab ipso frigore copreffa protruditur, perinde ac fi quis nucleu digitis elidat. Deorsum aute decidunt, propterea quod densa sint. Ob eamque causam fulmina deorsum impelluntur decidúntque, eoque magis, quod horum omnium formatio non solùm ab ardore fit, sed & à difplo-fione atque dissipatione, quam caloris & frigoris conflictus attritusque affert: quandoquidem quicquid calidum est naturali propensione in sublime effertur: contrà omne frigidum inferiora petit. Quare quæ in su-periore aeris loco coguntur, ea ex accenso fumo gignuntur: quæ vero in inferiore ex vapore, vbi cogitur refrigeratúrque. Vapor enim cùm ibi cogitur, & suo pondere deorsum propendet, tum ab eo quod calidum est impellitur, & deorsum deturbatur. Præterea huiusmodi meteora, vel sursum feruntur, vel deorsum, vel denique in latus, pro exhalatio-nis situ, latitudine ac altitudine: sed fere in latus, propterea quod duplici motus genere agitentur, nempe vi deorsum, & natura sursum. Impelluntur enim hæc omnia vel per dimetientem linea, vel transuersam, quæ media est. Quamobrè stellarum, quæ traiiciuntur & transcurrunt, motus fere obliquus est: Horum ergo omnium materies est exhalatio sicca, efficiens vero partim motus, quo in sublime feruntur, partim aeris densitas. Haec autem omnia infra Lunae orbem producì, factis declarat eorum celeritas, quae non absimilis est rebus, quas iacimus. Quoniam autem huiusmodi traiicientes stellae nobis proximae super, celerius moueri quàm Sol & Luna proficiuntur, quaeanuis earum motus tardior fit.
units.tr: Having set out these matters, let us now say why, in the air, both burning flames and shooting stars, torches, and leaping goats appear. All of these certainly arise from the same cause and differ only in size and number. The principle of these and of many others is as follows. When the earth is warmed by the rays of the Sun, an exhalation must be stirred up, and this is not simple, as some have thought, but double: one part is vapour, the other smoke. Of these, the smoke is carried upward by the heat, while the vapour, because it is moist, sinks down by its own weight. Since fire, which is hot and dry, lies beneath the revolution of the heavens, and air occupies the place beneath this fiery nature, it comes about that the fire, as it were following on the form of heat, extends itself round the circuit of the rounded earth, so that as soon as a slight motion begins, a flame often forms in the air and seems to be kindled like smoke. For a flame is the glow of a dry vapour. Such an ignition of fire is therefore both moved and kindled by the revolution of the celestial sphere, and it usually looks like the flame that arises when stubble burns in the fields. If it appears only long, it will look like torches and beams, and like leaping goats. If, moreover, it is stretched more in length than in breadth, and at the same time that which catches fire sparkles (this happens when that which is igniting exceeds its proper measure from the start), the leaping goats, torches and beams will appear more and more. Finally, if such dry and inflamed exhalations are spread out gradually along their length and in many places, and they agree in length and breadth, they will appear as shooting stars, whose motion is like that of a thrown missile. For in the middle part of the air such a fiery exhalation is condensed by the surrounding cold, and being pressed together by that very cold, it is driven out, just as when someone squeezes a nut between his fingers. They fall downward because they are dense. For this reason thunderbolts are also driven down and fall, all the more because the formation of all these things comes not only from heat but also from the explosion and dispersal that the conflict and friction of heat and cold bring about; for whatever is hot is carried upward by its natural tendency, whereas everything cold seeks what is lower. Therefore, those things that are gathered in the upper region of the air are produced from kindled smoke, while those gathered in the lower region come from vapour, where it is condensed and cooled. For when the vapour gathers there, it inclines downward by its own weight, and it is also pushed by what is hot and driven down. Moreover, such meteors are carried either upward, or downward, or finally sideways, according to the position, breadth and height of the exhalation; but mostly sideways, because they are moved by a double kind of motion, namely the force pushing downward and their nature pushing upward. For all these things are impelled either along a diagonal line or along a transverse one, which lies in the middle. Hence the motion of the stars that are darted through and run across is mostly oblique. The matter of all these things is therefore a dry exhalation, while the efficient cause is partly the motion by which they are carried upward and partly the density of the air. That all these things are produced below the orbit of the Moon is shown by their speed, which is not unlike that of things we throw. Since, moreover, these darting stars nearest to us are seen to move more quickly than the Sun and Moon, whatever their motion is, it is slower.

units.la: CAP. IIII. Causa multarum imaginum, velut hiatuum, fouearum, & colorum cruentorum, quae noctu apparent in coelo.
units.tr: CAP. IIII. The cause of many appearances, such as gaps, pits, and blood-coloured hues, which are seen in the sky at night.

units.la: VLTA etiam imaginum genera noctè serena in coelo sæpe cernuntur, quorum eadem est causa. Cum enim superior aeris pars ignescit, & eius ardor talis est, ut perinde atque flamma ardere videatur, tum interdum quasi faces, aut stellae traiicientes conspiciuntur. Cùm vero idem aër simul & densatur & inflammatur, tum variis coloribus praeditus videtur. Lux enim per densiorem aërem minus transflucet. Ob eamque causam ipse varios colores praebet, sed maximè phoenicei, ceu purpureum, vel rubrum, propterea quòd hi potissimum ex ignei coloris & candidi temperatione sint. Ac huiusmodi coloris sunt sydera cum nobis oriuntur, & occidunt. fi tum æstus fit,aut perfumū videantur.Cum etiam supremus aer densatur & accenditur, non solum varij colores in cœlo apparent, sed etiam velut fossa cernitur.Nam aeris desitas obscuritasque illustrata fumi inflammati lumine,quadam in cœlo cauitatem præ fe fert: quæ fi magna est, hiatus nominatur: sin parua apparet, fossa. Quod fi fumus magis concreuerit, & densior redditus fuerit, trabes e cœlo decidere videbuntur. Sed fi vndiquaque sibi similis fuerit, & inflammatione illustretur, tum cœlum conspicietur sanguineum. Eadem est causa varietatis colorum, qui in nubibus cernuntur, prout fumus inflammatus vel superat, vel superatur. Ac stellarum quidem quæ traiiciuntur & ardet, & præterea earum imaginum, quæ fui afpe-ctum admodum celerem præbent, hæ sunt putandæ causæ.
units.tr: Often also kinds of images are seen in the clear night sky, and they have the same cause. For when the upper part of the air catches fire, and its burning is such that it seems to blaze like a flame, then sometimes torch-like or shooting stars are seen. But when the same air both thickens and is set alight, it appears endowed with various colours. For light passes less easily through denser air, and for this reason the air displays various colours, but especially the purple-red hues, such as purple or red, because these arise chiefly from a mixture of fiery and white colour. Stars of this kind of colour are those which we see when they rise and set; if then there is heat, or they appear ... When the highest air also thickens and is kindled, not only do various colours appear in the sky, but something like a ditch is also seen. For the density and darkness of the air, lit up by the light of the kindled smoke, presents a certain hollow in the sky: if this is large it is called a gap (hiatus), but if it appears small, a ditch (fossa). If the smoke has gathered more densely and become thicker, beams will seem to fall from the sky. But if it is everywhere alike and is illuminated by the burning, then the sky will be seen blood-red. The same cause accounts for the variety of colours seen in clouds, according as the burning smoke either prevails or is overcome. These are to be regarded as the causes of the stars that shoot across and burn, and likewise of those appearances which present a very swift aspect.

units.la: CAP. V. Cometarum causæ & differentiæ.
units.tr: CHAPTER V. The causes and differences of comets.

units.la: E crinitis stellis orbéque lacteo di-cemus, fi prius contra quorundam veterum sententias diffleruerimus. Nam Anaxagoras & Democritus tradiderunt cometas esse ex earum stellarum coniunctione, quæ errantes dicuntur: propterea quod eis prope accedant, & fe contingere videantur. Pythagorei etiam, qui Itali-ci fuerunt philosophi, atque Hippocrates Chius,& auditor eius Æschylus idem sentie-runt. Sed omnes stellæ errantes in signorum orbe relinquuntur, suumque illic cursum & proprium motum peragunt, cùm & permul-tæ crinitæ extra illum orbem visæ animad-uersæque sint,& plures simul effulserint. Ad-hæc si cometes ex errantibus astris vnum ef-set, profecto nullus euanesceret. At omnem cometen euanescere, sariis[?] omnibus perspi-cuum est. Nec vero illud verum est, quod olim nonnulli dixerunt, nimirum cometen in eo tantum loco, qui ad Septentriones pertinet, ardere simul cum Sol ad vtrunque solsti-tium cursum suum perficit. Nam circa æquinoctia interdum oriri videtur: ac in Australi regione plures apparere philosophus testatur. Itaque cometes fit cùm in tertia aeris parte ardens exhalatio est & arida, atque interdum cùm infra aliquam stellam ex iis, quæ vagę dicutur eadem sicca exhalatio cogitur.
units.tr: We shall speak of the bearded stars and the Milky Way, provided that we first argue against the opinions of certain ancients. For Anaxagoras and Democritus taught that comets arise from the conjunction of those stars which are called wandering (planets), because they approach them and seem to touch them. The Pythagoreans also, who were Italian philosophers, and Hippocrates of Chios, and his pupil Aeschylus, held the same view. But all the wandering stars are left within the zodiac, and carry out their own course and proper motion there, since very many bearded stars have been seen and observed outside that zodiac, and several have shone at the same time. Moreover, if the comet were one of the wandering stars, certainly none would vanish; yet it is plain to all that every comet vanishes. Nor is it true what some have said long ago, namely that a comet burns only in that part of the sky which belongs to the North, at the time when the Sun completes its course to either solstice. For it sometimes appears around the equinoxes, and the philosopher testifies that more of them appear in the southern region. Thus a comet comes to be when a dry and burning exhalation is in the third part of the air, and sometimes when this same dry exhalation is gathered beneath one of those stars which are called wandering.

units.la: Nec vero ipsis astris cometarum crines adhærent, sed ad ipsas errantes stellas eam habent rationem, quam area & corona ad Solem & lunam. Cæterum cometarum concretionem naturamque esse igneam, hinc perspici potest, quòd si plures eodem tempore appareant, ventos, & siccitates fore, iudicium est. Cùm vero rari sunt, & obscuri, tum hæc raro eueniunt. Attamen fere pro ratione temporis ac magnitudinis ipsorum cometarum nimia ventorum vis, aut paruis sæuit. Cometarum autem variæ sunt formæ propter eam figuram, quam exhalatio huiusmodi adepta fuerit. Si enim omni ex parte fumus ille sibi sit æqualis in aere, stella formabitur crinita: quæ si longè pateat & producatur, pogonia erit. Variant quoque cometarum colores: quandoquidem alij apparent nobis candidi & argentei propter fumi raritatem: alij verò rubicundi propter eiusdem denfitu[illegible, ~3 letters] crassitudinem. Ex quibus constat cometen non quandam esse orbis reflexionem, qualis corona est circu Solem & Lunam, aut circu aliud sydus facta, quemadmodumHippocrates Chius existimauit.
units.tr: Nor indeed do the tails of comets cling to the stars themselves; rather they stand to the wandering stars in the same relation as a halo and corona stand to the Sun and Moon. Moreover, that the substance and nature of comets is fiery can be seen from this: if several appear at the same time, it is a sign that winds and droughts will follow. When they are rare and dim, these things seldom happen. Nevertheless, for the most part, in proportion to the duration and size of the comets themselves, an excessive violence of winds rages, or slight ones. The forms of comets are various, on account of the shape which such an exhalation has taken on. For if that smoke is everywhere equal in the air, a star is formed with a tail (crinita); but if it stretches out and extends far, it will be a pogonia (bearded star). The colours of comets also vary: some appear to us white and silvery on account of the thinness of the smoke, while others appear reddish on account of the thickness of its density. From these things it is clear that a comet is not a reflection of a circle, such as a corona around the Sun and Moon, or one formed around another star, as Hippocrates of Chios thought.

units.la: CAP. VI. Quid sit Lacteus circulus, & qua eius causa.
units.tr: CAP. VI. What the Milky Way is, and its cause.

units.la: OSTHAEC quid circulus lacteus fit, & quam ob causam oriatur, dicemus, si prius quorundam veterum opiniones de illo exposuerimus. Eorum enim nonnulli, vt Pythagorei ipsum esse viam Solis censuerunt: alij aliquod sydus delapsum esse in ea deflagratione, quæ Phaetótis tempore fuisse facta dicitur. Quidam verò Solem in hoc ipso orbe aliquando suum confecisse cursum tradiderunt: ob eámque causam hunc locum conflagrasse: aut ab illius lustratione & motu aliquid aliud tale accepisse. Alij denique, vt Anaxagoras, & Democritus ipsum circulum quorundam sydesyderum lumen esse dicebant, ob eamque causam non interdiu apparere, quod a Solis radiis prohibeatur, sed noctu: quoniam cum sub terram Sol fertur, tum quaedam sy-dera non aspicit. Sed hoc fieri non posse, ex eo intelligi poterit, quod Sol magnitudine supramodum terram superet, & illud interuallum, quo astra fixa a terra distant, multo maius [?] sit, quam illud quo terra a sole. Qua-e vmbra terræ, quæ nox dicitur, nullis sy-deribus, sive fixa sint, sive errantia, obducitur, sed haec omnia a Sole aspectari & lustrari, nec ulli fixorum terram obiici, necesse est. Ex quo patet id falsum esse, quod ipsi afferebant, nempe quaedam sydera Solem cum sub terram fertur, non aspicere. Constat etiam ex his eos non recte probasse galaxiam quorundam astrorum lumen esse: ut & nec alij, qui eam esse nostri visus reflexionem ad Solem. Nam tum temporis noster aspectus ad Solem reflecti non poterat. Quid autem fit Lacteus circulus dicemus, si prius id principium repetierimus, quod a nobis propositum est, nempe supremam aeris partem ignescere posse. Quare cum ipse aer conuersione coeli agitatur, dissipatúrque, tum talis exhalationum concretio emicat, qualis ea, quae cometarum est, quorum inflammatio ab aliquo sydere fixo, vel vago excitatur. Propterea cometarum vnusquisque tum effulget, cum aridarum exhalationu[?] concretio aliquod ipsorum fyderum consequitur, veluti solem & lunam corona. Itaque quod in singulis fyderibus fieri contingit, idem etiam toti cœli cuenire, existimandum est. Etenim fi vnius astri motus aliquam supremi aëris partem incendit ad cometarum conformationem, consentaneum est motum omnium aliquid tale efficere ignemque excitare, & maximè vbi creberrima, p[illegible, ~6 letters]que & maxima sunt sydera. Veruntamen[?] sub signifero orbe pauci cometę oriuntur, neque galaxia fit, quoniam motu solis aliorumque errantium astrorum hæc ipsa exhalationum concretio dissipatur, sed vltra solstitiorum orbes galaxia apparet, & ipsi cometæ, vt plu-rimùm ardere cernuntur, non autem circa solem & lunam, propterea quòd ibidem celerius huiusmodi aridæ exhalationes dissoluntur quàm vt talis concretio cogi possit. Orbis autem ille continuus est, eo quòd continenter cogatur omnis hæc concretio, ex qua constat.
units.tr: Now we shall say what the Milky Way is and why it arises, but first we shall set out the opinions of some of the ancients about it. Some of them, like the Pythagoreans, thought it was the path of the Sun. Others held that some star fell into that conflagration which is said to have happened in the time of Phaethon. Some have handed down that the Sun once completed its course through this very circle, and that for this reason the place was set on fire, or received something of the kind from the Sun's passage and motion. Finally, Anaxagoras and Democritus said that the circle itself is the light of certain stars, and that it does not appear by day because it is blocked by the rays of the Sun, but appears at night, since when the Sun is carried beneath the earth, it no longer looks upon certain stars. But this cannot be so, as may be understood from the fact that the Sun far exceeds the earth in size, and that the interval by which the fixed stars are distant from the earth is much greater than that by which the earth is distant from the sun. For the shadow of the earth, which is called night, does not cover any stars, whether fixed or wandering; rather, all of them must be seen and illuminated by the Sun, and none of the fixed stars can be hidden from the earth. From this it is clear that what they asserted is false, namely that certain stars do not look upon the Sun when it is carried beneath the earth. It is also clear from these points that they did not rightly prove the Milky Way to be the light of certain stars, nor did the others who held it to be a reflection of our sight back to the Sun; for at that time our sight could not be reflected back to the Sun. Now we shall say what the Milky Way is, if we first return to the principle we have proposed, namely that the highest part of the air can catch fire. Hence, when the air itself is stirred and scattered by the revolution of the heavens, such a gathering of exhalations flashes out as that which makes up comets, whose ignition is kindled by some fixed or wandering star. For this reason each comet shines forth when a gathering of dry exhalations follows upon one of the stars, just as a corona surrounds the Sun and the Moon. Therefore, what happens with individual stars must be thought to happen for the whole heaven as well. For if the motion of a single star sets fire to some part of the highest air so as to form a comet, it is consistent that the motion of all the stars produces something of this kind and kindles fire, and most of all where the stars are most numerous and largest. However, few comets arise beneath the zodiac, and the Milky Way is not formed there, because this very gathering of exhalations is dispersed by the motion of the Sun and of the other wandering stars; but the Milky Way appears beyond the orbits of the solstices, and comets themselves are for the most part seen to burn there, not around the Sun and the Moon, because in those places such dry exhalations are dissolved more quickly than such a gathering can be compelled. That circle, moreover, is continuous, because all this gathering, of which it consists, is continually compressed.

units.la: CAP. VII. Pluuiarum causæ, & nubium nebularumque differentia.
units.tr: CAP. VII. The causes of rain, and the difference between clouds and mists.

units.la: ACTENVS de iis, quæ supremo in loco aëris oriuntur, disputatum est: nunc ad alia, quæ in medio & imo generantur, pergere tempesti-uum est. Horum autem omnium eodem modo tum principia, tum causæ sunt fumendæ. Primum quidem ac summum principium, mouens est Sol, qui suo motu exhalationes & dissipat & cogit, prout magis, aut minus à nobis recedit, vel ad nos accedit. Humor enim, qui stabilem firmámque terram circundit, à Solis radiis, & à superiore calore expressus, ac vapor factus in sublime fertur, u-bi postea[?] caloris extinctione, & mediæ aëris partis frigore, in nubem cogitur, quæ rursus inferioris aëris calore in aquam dissoluitur; atque ita tum ex vapore aëréque crasso aqua oritur, quæ rursus in terram delabitur & refluit. Est autem vapor spiritus ex mutatione aquæ ortus. Nubes verò ex vapore & aëre crasso fit, & tandem in aquam mutatur. Caligo seu nebula, excrementum ipsius nubis est in aquam concretum. Propterea serenitatem potius quàm pluuiam prænuntiat, quoniam nebula quasi sterilis nubes est? Pluuia autem, tum est, cum humor, vi caloris in sublime fertur, rursumque frigore mediæ aëris partis in nubem cogitur, ex qua paulatim aquæ guttæ in terram destillant ac defluunt. Pluuiæ enim & vaporis origo velut orbis est, ac Solis orbem imitatur. Quare pluuia ex vapore in sublime elato à Sole, generatur: rursùsque vicissim ex pluuia, quæ tandem frigore in terram refluit, vapor oritur.
units.tr: Thus far we have discussed what arises in the highest part of the air; now it is time to proceed to the other things that are generated in the middle and lowest regions. The principles and causes of all of these must be taken in the same way. The first and chief principle, the moving cause, is the Sun, which by its motion both disperses and gathers the exhalations, according as it withdraws from us or draws near to us. For the moisture which surrounds the firm and stable earth is squeezed out by the rays of the Sun and by the heat from above, and, once turned to vapour, is carried upwards; then, when the heat is extinguished and the middle part of the air grows cold, it is gathered into a cloud, which in turn is dissolved into water by the heat of the lower air. And so water arises both from vapour and from thick air, and falls back down to the earth and flows back again. Vapour is a spirit arising from a change of water. A cloud, however, is formed from vapour and thick air, and at last is changed into water. Mist or fog is the excrement of the cloud itself, condensed into water. For this reason it foretells fair weather rather than rain, since a mist is, as it were, a barren cloud. Rain, however, occurs when the moisture, carried up on high by the force of heat, is again gathered into a cloud by the cold of the middle part of the air, from which drops of water gradually trickle and run down to the earth. For the origin of rain and of vapour is like a circle, imitating the circle of the Sun. Thus rain is generated from vapour raised on high by the Sun, and conversely vapour in turn arises from rain, which at last flows back to the earth by cold.

units.la: CAP. VIII. Roris, pruinæ, niuis & pluuiæ causa, & origo.
units.tr: CAP. VIII. The causes and origin of dew, hoarfrost, snow and rain.

units.la: Res etiam fit, sed noctu, dum vapor ipse refrigeratur, qui interdiu excitatus nō in sublime fertur propter caloris efferentis imbecillitatem. Etenim tum calor non tantus est, vt id etiam quod in sublime elatum est, exsiccari [?] possit, nec frigus adeo sæuit, vt ipsum vaporem cogat. Propterea cū ros fit, tum nulla cogitur pluuia. Fit autem ros cœlo sereno, & potissimum iis in locis, in quibus serenitas est. Prima vero hyeme, & præsertim frigidis in locis, atque cœli serenitate, & tranquillitate, cum videlicet vapor congelatur, antequam in aquam vertatur. Maiore enim frigore vapor cogitur in pruinam quam aqua, propterea quod in se calorem efferentem contineat, & naturæ tenuis fit. Quamobrem ad superiora non effertur, nisi adlit [?] serenitas, neque cogi potest, si ventus flat. Vtrunque autem non procul a nobis fieri hinc sciri potest, quod pruina in excelsis montibus non oriatur duas ob causas, primum quod ex eorum concauis, & aquarum receptaculis vaporem excitatum calor, qui vim efferendi habet, tanquam onus grauius ferens quam vires eius ferre possint, in locum admodum excelsum ferre non potest, sed in proximo rursus demittit. Deinde aer, qui excelsum tenet locum, maxime diffluit agitatur, atque talé vaporū concretione dissipat. Ros autē ubique, Austro flante, oritur, & temperato serenoque cœlo, nō autem alio. Auster quidem serenum temperatumque cœlum reddit. Aquilo verò, quoniam frigidus est, hyemem affert, ac tempestate. Itaque suo frigore vaporis calorem restinguit. Cæterum eo ex loco, qui nubibus assignatus nos corpora decidunt, quæ frigore coguntur, pluuia, nix & grando, quorum duo iisdem ex causis sunt, ex quibus ea, quæ infrà oriuntur, ac duntaxat intentione & remissione, multitudine paucitateque differunt. Nix igitur & pruina idem sunt, ut & ros atque pluvia. Hæc duntaxat ab illo discrepat, ꝙ pluviæ[?] maior fit copia, roris minor. Nam pluvia ex plurimo vapore, qui refrigeratur, originem habet: cuius causa etiam est loci amplitudo & temporis diuturnitas, qua vapor ipse exsurgit & cogitur. Sed vaporis copia, ex quo ros oritur, minor est, propterea quòd unius diei ortus eius fit, & in loco cogatur angusto. Similis est pruinæ & nivis ratio. Nix enim fit cum congelatur nubes: pruina verò cum vapor concrescit in gelu. Grando etiam ibi oritur, ubi nix: pruina autem ubi pluvia. Ros denique hic apud nos & super herbas.
units.tr: This also happens, but at night, when the vapour that was drawn up during the day is cooled, and it is not carried aloft because the heat that lifts it is too weak. For at that time the heat is not so great that it can dry up even what has been raised aloft, nor is the cold so fierce that it forces the vapour together. Therefore when dew forms, no rain is gathered. Dew forms under a clear sky, and especially in those places where the air is calm. In early winter, and especially in cold places, with a clear and still sky, the vapour freezes before it turns into water. For the vapour is condensed into hoarfrost by a greater cold than is needed to turn it into water, because it contains heat that tends to lift it and it is of a thin nature. Therefore it is not carried upward unless the sky is clear, and it cannot be condensed if the wind blows. That both of these happen not far from us can be known from this: hoarfrost does not form on the high mountains, for two reasons. First, the vapour drawn up from their hollows and the reservoirs of waters, where the heat that has the power of lifting it is present, cannot carry it to a very high place, like a load heavier than its strength can bear, but it sinks it again nearby. Second, the air that holds the high place is greatly stirred and dispersed, and so it scatters the gathering of vapour. Dew, however, arises everywhere when the south wind blows, and under a mild and clear sky, but not otherwise. The south wind indeed makes the sky clear and temperate. The north wind, however, since it is cold, brings winter and storms; and so by its cold it quenches the heat of the vapour. Moreover, from that region which is assigned to the clouds, bodies fall that are condensed by cold: rain, snow and hail. Of these, two arise from the same causes as those which arise below, and they differ only in intensity and remission, in quantity and scarcity. Snow and hoarfrost are therefore the same, as are dew and rain. The only difference between the latter and the former is that rain comes in greater quantity and dew in less. For rain has its origin in a great deal of vapour that is cooled; its cause is also the vastness of the region and the long duration of time in which the vapour itself rises and is condensed. But the quantity of vapour from which dew arises is smaller, because it arises for only one day and is condensed in a narrow place. The reasoning for hoarfrost and snow is similar. For snow forms when the cloud freezes, while hoarfrost forms when the vapour congeals into frost. Hail also forms where snow does, but hoarfrost where rain does. Dew, finally, forms here among us and upon the grass.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CAP. IX.

units.la: Quomodo, & ubi grando oritur?
units.tr: How and where does hail arise?
