units.la: A deinceps cognosceda sunt, quæ in grandinum ortu contingunt, & ea consequuntur. Verum earum naturam primum exponere licet. Est igitur grando gelu, & sicut aqua, quæ hyeme congelatur. Oriuntur autem grandines vere potissimum & autumno, deinde æstate, minus & rarius hyeme, propterea quod tum vis frigoris in medio aere, vbi fiunt, [illegible, ~6 letters]. Omninoque grandines magis in locis temperatis, niues vero in frigidioribus formantur. Causa autem & origo earum est cum nubis in mediam aeris partem depulsæ aqua congelatur. Ibi enim aer frigidus est, quoniā radij Solis illic reflexi desinunt. Propterea æ-state, & in prouinciis, quæ magis temperatæ sunt, grandines decidunt maiores, quoniam calor nebulas ex inferiore aere in superiore depellit. Veruntamen in locis admodum editis minime grandines oriuntur, quanquam earum causa ibi adest, quemadmodum nix, quæ in excelsis locis nasci cernitur. Imò verò interdum non procul a terra concrescit grando admirabili magnitudine, & figura minus rotunda decidit, quoniā gelu est. Quæ autem grandines è remotiore loco decidunt, eæ, quoniam longo interuallo feruntur, paruæ & rotundæ formantur. Ex quo perspicuum est grandine non propterea cogi, quòd duntaxat frigus in superiorem locum repellatur, sed quòd etiam in inferiore sit. Vbicunque enim contrariorum repugnantia est, ibi etiā grando cogi formarīque potest. Quòd autē in inferiore aëris parte calor & frigus inter se confligant,satis aperte experientia demonstrat. Vt enim æstate inferiores terræ partes algent,& hyeme calent:ita in superiore loco fieri existimandum est. Itaque in summo æstu frigus propter circūstantem calorem interdum[?] grandinem in media aëris parte fa-cit. Ob eamque[?] causam æstate & multò maiores pluuiarum guttæ, & nimbi, quàm hyeme cadunt. Veruntamen æstate rarius grando fit, quàm vere & autumno, eo quòd tum aër siccior fit, & tamen sæpius quàm hyeme. Vere autem sæpe fit, quòd aër adhuc humidus sit,vt & autumno,qui tum iam humescit.
units.tr: Next, we must consider what happens in the formation of hail and what follows from it. Let us first set out its nature. Hail, then, is ice, like water that freezes in winter. Hailstones form mostly in spring and autumn, then in summer, and less often and rarely in winter, since then the force of cold in the middle air, where they form, is weaker. Hail generally forms in temperate regions, while snow forms in colder ones. The cause and origin of hail is that water from a cloud, driven into the middle part of the air, freezes. For the air there is cold, because the rays of the sun reflected there fail. So in summer, and in regions that are more temperate, larger hailstones fall, since heat drives the clouds from the lower air up into the higher air. Yet in very high places hail hardly arises at all, although its cause is present there, just as snow is seen to be born on mountain heights. Indeed, sometimes hail of remarkable size condenses not far from the ground and falls less round in shape, because it is ice. But hailstones that fall from a more distant place are formed small and round, since they are carried over a long interval. From this it is plain that hail is not formed merely because cold is driven back into the higher place, but also because cold is present in the lower place. For wherever there is conflict between opposites, there hail can also be produced and formed. That in the lower part of the air heat and cold clash with each other, experience demonstrates quite clearly. For just as in summer the lower parts of the earth are cold, and in winter warm, so it must be thought to happen in the higher place. Thus at the height of summer heat, the cold, owing to the surrounding heat, sometimes makes hail in the middle part of the air. For that reason, drops of rain and storm showers fall in summer much larger than in winter. Yet hail forms less often in summer than in spring and autumn, because the air then becomes drier, and yet more often than in winter. In spring it often happens because the air is still moist, as in autumn too, when it is by then becoming damp.

units.la: Calor etiam circunstantis aëris concretione aquæ nubis in grandinem adiuuat: quandoquidem aqua ante calefacta celerius refrigeratur,eo quòd magis attenuata sit. Quamobrem multi cùm celeriter aquam refrigerare volunt,eam ante ad Solem ponunt. Citò enim refrigeratur cotrario conatu & nixu.
units.tr: The heat of the surrounding air also helps the water of the cloud to turn into hail by congealing, since water that has been warmed beforehand cools more quickly, because it has been made more thin. For this reason many people, when they want to cool water quickly, first set it out in the sun. For it cools quickly by a contrary effort and striving.

units.la: CAP. X. Ventorum, sluuiorum, & fontium causæ & origines.
units.tr: CHAPTER 10. The causes and origins of winds, rivers and springs.

units.la: E ventis autem, & omni flatus ge-nere,ac etiā de fluminibus, & mari disputandum est. Olim nonnulli fuerunt,qui aërem,cùm pellitur,ac fluit ventū esse dixerunt: cūmque etiam cogitur, rursus nubem efficit & aquam. Quasi vero eadem sit natura aquæ & venti, & ipse ventus aëris motio. Fuerunt etiam alij, qui omnes ventos vnum esse professi sunt, eo quòd omnis aër vnus & idem esse videatur, itaque ex locis vnde fluit, duntaxat differat. Sed perinde dixerunt, ac si quis omnes fluuios vnum esse, assereret. At quàm absurda fuerit eorum sententia, facile quisque intelliget, si prius de fluuiorum ortu disseruerimus. Primùm autem ex eadem causa aquam in terræ visceribus oriri, ex qua super terram, & in aëre oritur, consentaneum est. Deinde si foris aër frigore in aquam cogitur, ab eo etiam frigore, quod in terra latet, hoc ipsum euenire, existimandum est: ac non solùm aqua quæ in terra secreta est, oritur, sed etiam continenter fluit, nec vllo modo generatio eius intermittitur, propterea quòd ibi semper vapor & frigus adsint. Ac quemadmodum supra terram exiguæ nubis stillæ cohærent, aliæque cum aliis coeunt, ita vt tandem magna aquæ pluuiæ copia decidat: sic in terra ex tenuibus admodum stillis aqua initio emanat, fluxionesque aquarum, & fluminum scaturigines, ac principia fiunt. Id quod res ipsa satis declarat. Qui enim aquæ ductus constituunt, ij scrobibus aquam colligunt, quam ab excelsis locis terra quasi sudans, effudit. Quamobrem obrem ex terrae partibus maximè montes & excelsa loca ex se aquam fundunt, & quasi destillant. Propterea fontes ac maximi fluuij ab altissimis montibus defluunt. In campis autem patentibus flumina omnino pauca ac fontes fluunt, propterea quòd minus aquae illa loca diffundant. Nec verò absurdum est quaedam loca reperiri huiusmodi aquarum copia affluant, vt lacus & stagna, à quibus non vniuersa aqua profluit. Caeterum omnia fere flumina à fontibus suam ducunt originem, quorum quae absorbentur, & rursus aliis in locis redduntur, terram tum anfractibus, tum cauernis hiare, fatis declarant. Amnes etiam, qui pleni sunt, nec locum habent, in quem effundantur, sibi exitum in terrae altitudine reperiunt vi aquae, quae ex superiore loco impetu magno defluit.
units.tr: We must now discuss winds, every kind of blast, and also rivers and the sea. Long ago some men held that air, when it is driven and flows, is wind; and when it is again condensed, it produces cloud and water. As if the nature of water and of wind were the same, and wind were merely a motion of air. Others again declared that all winds are one, since all air seems one and the same, and differs only according to the places from which it flows. But they spoke as if someone were to assert that all rivers are one. How absurd their opinion is, anyone will readily understand if we first discuss the origin of rivers. Now it is consistent that water is generated in the bowels of the earth from the same cause from which it arises above the earth and in the air. Next, if outside the air is condensed into water by cold, we must think that the same thing happens from the cold that lies hidden in the earth; and water is not only produced in the places where it is hidden in the ground, but also flows continuously, and its generation is never interrupted in any way, because there is always vapour and cold there. And just as in the open air the small drops of a thin cloud cling together and join with one another, so that at last a great quantity of rainwater falls, so in the earth water first flows out from very fine drops, and the flows of waters, the springs of rivers, and their beginnings come into being. The thing itself makes this plain enough. For those who construct aqueducts collect the water in trenches, which the earth, as it were sweating, has poured out from high places. Hence it is that chiefly from the parts of the earth mountains and high places pour out water from themselves, and as it were drip. For this reason springs and the largest rivers flow down from the highest mountains. But in wide plains few rivers and springs flow at all, because those places spread out less water. Nor is it absurd that some places are found to which such a quantity of waters flows, as lakes and ponds, from which not all the water flows out. Moreover, almost all rivers take their origin from springs; and that some of them are swallowed up and given back again in other places, the earth gaping with winding passages and caverns, clearly shows. Even rivers that are full, and have no place into which to pour themselves, find an outlet for themselves in the depth of the earth, by the force of the water which flows down with great impetus from a higher place.

units.la: CAP. XI.
units.tr: CAP. XI.

units.la: Cur interdum flumina & exsiccari & refluere possint?
units.tr: Why can rivers sometimes both dry up and flow back?

units.la: E c vero semper eadem terrae loca sunt humida vel arida, sed pro flumi-nu ortu, aut defectu mutantur. Quare quae terrae continenti finitima sunt & maris, ea mutari videntur. Interdum enim vbi terra patuit, ibi nunc mare superfunditur: & ubi nunc mare est, alibi rursus terra appa-rebit. Hæc autem omnia quædam ordine & ambitu fieri existimandum est, propterea qp omnium harum rerum principium & causa ex eo ducitur, quod interiores terræ partes tanquam stirpium & animantium corpora juve-nescant & senescant. Sed hoc interest, quod hæc stirpibus & animantibus per partes non evenire solet, sed simul omnia eorum corpora, & vigeant, & senescant. terræ hæc omnia vi frigoris calorisque per partes eveniunt. Animantia igitur ut augescendi, & decrescendi causam à Sole eiusque conver-sione accipiunt: sicab eodem partes terræ diversam adipiscuntur natutam & conditionem, ita ut humidæ per aliquod tempus esse possint, post exiccentur, & quasi senescant. Proinde alia loca per eandem Solis operam ad animantium vitam accommodantur, propterea quod humida per partes reddantur. Cum vero loca terræ arida redduntur, tum aquarum principia & fontes aboleri, necesse est. Quæ cum huiusmodi eveniunt, primum flumina ex magnis parua necessario fiunt. Deinde exhausta tandem exarescunt. Itaque cum sic flumina mutentur & exarescant, ac ex aliis locis in alia suum contorqueant cursum & deflectant, tum in mari mutationem consequi, expedit. Eum enim locum, in quo fluviorum effusione mare redundabat, necessarie ipsius maris recessus aridum reddit: ac quo
units.tr: And indeed the same places of the earth are not always wet or always dry, but they change according to the rising or failing of the rivers. Hence the lands bordering on the mainland and on the sea seem to change. For sometimes where land was open, there the sea now spreads out, and where there is now sea, land will appear again elsewhere. All these things must be thought to happen in a certain order and cycle, because the principle and cause of all of them is derived from this: that the inner parts of the earth grow young and grow old, like the bodies of plants and animals. But there is this difference: that this does not usually happen to plants and animals part by part, but their whole bodies together both flourish and grow old. These things happen to the earth part by part, through the force of cold and heat. Animals therefore receive the cause of their growing and diminishing from the Sun and its revolution; in the same way, the parts of the earth acquire from it a different nature and condition, so that they may be wet for some time and afterwards dry out, and as it were grow old. Accordingly, other places, by the same work of the Sun, are fitted for the life of animals, because they are made moist in their turn. But when the places of the earth are made dry, the sources and springs of waters must necessarily be destroyed. When these things happen, first the rivers necessarily shrink from great to small. Then, at last, drained, they dry up. Therefore, since rivers are thus changed and dried up, and turn their course and bend it from one region to another, it is fitting that a change in the sea should follow. For the place where the sea overflowed through the outpouring of the rivers is necessarily made dry by the withdrawal of the sea itself; and the place where the sea, teeming with its tides, was drying up, it now washes with its advance.

units.la: [?] Reading of "qp" uncertain; possibly a contraction mark (cf. ꝑ). "sicab" printed as one word. quo in loco mare fluxionibus scatens exare-scebat, eundem suo accessu nunc alluit.
units.tr: ...and in the place where the sea, teeming with its tides, was drying up, it now washes with its approach.

units.la: CAP. XII.
units.tr: CAP. XII.

units.la: Quae fit maris natura & origo ?
units.tr: What is the nature and origin of the sea?

units.la: Emaris origine olim non eadem[?] fuit omnium veterum philosopho-rum sententia. Nonnulli enim fontes esse eius principia statuerunt, quorum opinio sic ab Aristotele refellitur. Aquarum enim, quae terra alluunt, aliae profluunt, aliae stant: quarum omnes quae profluunt, a fontibus manant & oriuntur. Earum autem, quae manent, & coercentur: quaedam colliguntur, ut palustres, lacus & stagna, quae omnia duntaxat copia & paucitate differunt. Sed quae fontanae sunt, opera industriaque hominum omnes coparantur, veluti eae sunt, quae puteis continentur. Atque profluentium scaturigo altior esse debet, quam locus unde earum riui oriuntur. At in neutro horti[?] generum mare esse potest. Nec enim profluit per se, nec opere industriaque hominum ad fluxum praeparatum est. Quod autem alicubi fluere videatur, id evenit propter angusta loca, sicubi situ terrae continentis ex vasto in arctum concluditur: ac propterea saepe vltro citroque libratur: id quod profecto in vasto mari fieri non videtur. Nihil obstat, quod non pauca maria, ob magnorum fluminum multitudinem, quae per terrae cauitates effunduntur, fluant. Hac de causa Mæotis in Pontum influit, & Pontus in Ægeum. Sic enim fluunt propter magnorum fluminum numerum. Simili modo plures fluvij in Euxinum Pontum, & Mœotim influunt, quàm in patentiora interioris altiorisque maris loca. Fluunt igitur hæc maria, propterea quòd nô multùm alta sint. Veruntamen in altiores gurgites mare moveri videtur. Quare Mæo-tis in Pontum influit, quòd hic illi profun-dior sit. Quemadmodum enim ex excelsis terræ partibus amnes fluere videntur, sic ex altioribus locis, quæ ad Septentriones spectant maior aquæ copia delabitur. Partes autem terræ, quæ ad Septentriones pertinet altiores esse, hinc perspici potest, quòd Sol illic non sub terram feratur, sed circum eam delitescat, cùm noctem efficit: Id quod sanè non fieret, nisi Septentrionalis pars altior esset. Hoc paucis explicatum oportuit, ut mare nullos fontes habere, à quibus oriretur, perspicuum esset.
units.tr: Concerning the origin of the sea, the opinion of all the ancient philosophers was not once the same. For some held that springs are its sources, and Aristotle refutes this view as follows. Of the waters that wash the land, some flow onward and others stand still. All those that flow arise and issue from springs. Of those that remain and are confined, some are gathered together, such as marshes, lakes and pools, and all these differ only in quantity and scarcity. But those that are fed by springs are all collected by human effort and industry, as are those kept in wells. The spring of running waters must also lie higher than the place from which their streams arise. But the sea can be neither kind: it does not flow of its own accord, nor has it been prepared for flowing by human effort and industry. That it seems to flow in some places happens because of narrow channels, wherever the shape of the mainland squeezes it from a vast expanse into a narrow passage, and for this reason it is often driven back and forth. This certainly does not seem to happen in the open sea. Nor is it an objection that not a few seas flow, because of the multitude of great rivers poured through the hollows of the earth. For this reason the Maeotis flows into the Pontus, and the Pontus into the Aegean. They flow in this way because of the number of great rivers. In a similar way more rivers flow into the Euxine Pontus and the Maeotis than into the wider and deeper parts of the interior sea. These seas therefore flow because they are not very deep. Yet the sea seems to be moved toward deeper whirlpools. Hence the Maeotis flows into the Pontus because the latter is deeper than it. For just as rivers seem to flow down from the high parts of the land, so a greater quantity of water descends from the higher places that face the north. That the parts of the earth which lie toward the north are higher can be seen from this: the sun does not pass under the earth there, but lingers around it when it makes night. This certainly would not happen unless the northern part were higher. This had to be explained briefly, so that it would be clear that the sea has no springs from which it arises.

units.la: CAP. XIII.
units.tr: CAP. XIII.

units.la: An mare sit aquæ elementum? Cur non augescit mare omnibus fluvijs, qui in ipsum influunt?
units.tr: Whether the sea is the element of water? Why does the sea not grow larger from all the rivers that flow into it?

units.la: AVSA quidem, quæ veteres Philosophos ad iudicandum impulit mare principium vniversæ aquæ esse, hæc videtur, quòd consentaneum fit, ut quemadmodum caeterorum elementorum principium ibi consistit, ubi maior eorum vis & copia est: sic ubi maior est aquae moles conglobata, illic etiam sit aquae principium, necesse est. At constat ignem in supremo esse loco, & aëris vim & copiam in loco igni proximo, terrae corpus in infimo, cui illa omnia interiecta sunt. Propterea idem de aqua iudicandum esse censuerunt. Nam nullum aliud corpus confertim situm esse videtur, velut alia elementa, praeter ipsius maris molem. Quare & humidorum, & universae aquae principium mare esse videtur. Propterea fluvios omnes non solum in ipsum mare influere, sed etiam effluere, nonnulli (& recte quidem) censuerunt, & quod in eo salsum est, id dulce reddi, cum colatur, aut in sublime effertur. Sed adversus hanc posteriorem sententiam, quaeri potest, quid sit, & quamobrem haec maris aqua non sit dulcis sed tota salsa, si universae aquae elementum principium-que sit? Causa nimirum ea reddi potest, quae huiusce controversiae explicatio erit. Sol enim continua conversione sui orbis, id quod ex mari tenuius est & dulcius quotidie in sublime effert, ubi postquam rursus in aquam concretum est, in terram defluit, refunditurque, ac dulce redditur: quod vero ardore Solis continuo crassum adustamque salsum est, id relinquitur, ex quo totum mare salsum efficitur. Ea quidem aqua, quae dulcis est, & potui apta leuitate sua omnis, vi caloreque Solis in sublime effertur: sed quæ salsa est, grauitate sua in proprio subsi-dit loco, quæ maris est, quod suo pondere substernitur. Ea vero quæ dulcis est sua le-uitate superiora capessit, quemadmodum in animantium corporibus fieri constat, in quibus reliquiæ alimenti, quod dulce est, amaræ aut salsæ percipiuntur: quandoquidem id quod dulce est, ab infito calore corporis[?] al-lectum in carnem & alias corporis partes diffundi vertique solet. Præterea mare ini-tium aquarum esse, ex eo intelligere possu-mus, quod in ipsum omnes amnes influunt.
units.tr: The reason that led the ancient philosophers to judge the sea to be the source of all water seems to be this: it is reasonable that, just as the source of the other elements lies where their greatest force and quantity is, so where the greatest mass of water is gathered together, there too must be the source of water. But it is agreed that fire lies in the highest place, the force and quantity of air in the place nearest to fire, and the body of earth in the lowest place, with all those others lying between. Therefore they thought the same must be judged of water. For no other body seems to lie in a massed heap, like the other elements, apart from the mass of the sea itself. Hence the sea seems to be the source both of moist things and of all water. For this reason some (and rightly so) have thought that all rivers not only flow into the sea but also flow out of it, and that what is salt in the sea becomes sweet when it is strained or lifted up on high. But against this latter opinion one may ask: what is it, and why is this sea water not sweet but wholly salt, if the sea is the element and source of all water? The cause, no doubt, can be given, and this will be the explanation of the controversy. For the sun, by the continual revolution of its orbit, draws up from the sea each day what is thinner and sweeter, and when this has again condensed into water, it flows down onto the land, is poured out, and is made sweet; but what is thick and salted by the constant heat of the sun is left behind, and from this the whole sea becomes salt. Indeed, that water which is sweet, and entirely fit for drinking, is by its lightness raised aloft by the force and heat of the sun; but that which is salt settles by its own weight into its proper place, the sea, which lies beneath because of its weight. And the water that is sweet, by its lightness, seizes the higher places, just as is known to happen in the bodies of animals, in which the remains of food that are bitter or salt are separated out, since what is sweet is drawn in by the innate heat of the body and is wont to be spread through the flesh and other parts of the body and turned into them. Moreover, we can understand from this that the sea is the beginning of waters, because all streams flow into it.

units.la: Verum præcipuus eius locus is est, vbi ma-jor aquarum vis delabitur, qui quidem ea est terræ pars, quæ maxima habet caua & aluëos plures. Oritur rursus quæstio cur non semper mare crescit, cum quotidie fluuij multitudine innumerabiles, & magnitudine propemodum immensi in ipsum influant? At ei, qui diligenter rem considerauerit, causam animaduertere, non difficile erit. Eadem enim vis ac copia aquæ, quæ late effundi-tur, & collecta est non pari temporis spa-tio exhauritur: sed dissimilitudo tanta inest, vt toto die vna pars eius permanere possit, & altera statim ex spectantium oculis evanescit, nec amplius apparet, perinde ac si quis in latam mensam cyathum aquæ effuderit. Cum igitur vniuersa flumina conti-nennenter in mare labantur, semper id aquæ, quod in vastissima latissimáque maris spatia confluit, tum celeriter (licet obscurè) exhauritur. Adde quod quantum aquæ in mare influit, tantum eius à continuo calore Solis in sublime attollitur.
units.tr: But its chief place is where the greater force of waters flows down, which is indeed that part of the earth which has the largest hollows and many channels. Again the question arises why the sea does not always grow, since rivers flow into it every day, innumerable in number and almost immense in size? But for one who has considered the matter carefully, it will not be difficult to perceive the cause. For the same force and quantity of water which is spread out widely and gathered together is drained away not over an equal span of time; rather there is such a difference that one part of it may remain all day, while another vanishes at once from the eyes of onlookers and no longer appears, just as if someone had poured a cup of water onto a broad table. Therefore, since all the rivers flow continually into the sea, the water that pours into the vast and very broad spaces of the sea is always quickly drained away, though obscurely. Add that as much water flows into the sea, so much of it is lifted up on high by the continual heat of the sun.

units.la: CAP. XIIII. Causa[?] salsuginis maris, & thermarum origo.
units.tr: CAP. XIV. The cause of the saltness of the sea, and the origin of hot springs.

units.la: VONIAM[?] autem duplicem esse ex-halationem positum est, nempe unâ humidam, quæ vapor est, & alteram aridam, quæ fumus nominatur, ex alterutra salsuginem maris oriri, necesse est. Sed à vapore non est: quandoquidem salsus sapor ex adustione quadam & admistione necessario evenit. Id quod ex alimenti reliquis, quæ in vesicam delabuntur, percipere possumus. Nam salsam esse urinam gustus satis arguit. Deinde in iis rebus, quę comburuntur salsedinem animadvertere licet, sicut in cinere apparet, ex quo sal effici potest. Id enim, quod densarum rerum remanet terra est, nullaqua-si concoctione domita. Quamobrem maris salsedo ab adustione est. Quòd autem maris corpus admistum quidpiam sit, satis ostendit crassitudo eius, qua in eo feliciter natant, quæ secus in fluviis demergi solent, quanuis pari rerum pondere vehantur.Id quod etiam ostendit ea aqua,cui multum falis additum est, in qua possunt ea oua natare, quæ plena sunt. Qui demum amnium fontiumque cursus falsi sunt, eos aliquando calidos fuisse, existimandum est: & terram, per quam fluunt, quasi calcem esse & cinerem. Propterea plerisque in locis sunt fontes ac fluuij, qui varia saporis genera retinet, quorum omnium causa ad insitam v[illegible, ~4 letters] referenda est. Terra enim cum*nimium, aut parum exuritur, tum colorum & saporum varia recipit genera. Adde quòd [?]magnam in fe vim & copiam aluminis,calcis, & cætero-rum huius generis continet, per quam dulces aquæ, aut insipidæ fluentes alterari solet, quarum aliæ acescunt, aliæ amarescunt,aliæ denique alia saporum genera adipiscuntur.
units.tr: Since it has been laid down that there are two kinds of exhalation, one moist, which is vapour, and the other dry, which is called smoke, the saltness of the sea must arise from one or the other. But it does not come from vapour, since a salty taste necessarily arises from a certain scorching and admixture. We can perceive this from the residues of food that pass into the bladder, for the taste shows well enough that urine is salty. Next, in things that are burned, saltiness can be noticed, as it appears in ash, from which salt can be made. For what remains of dense things is earth, not subdued by any concoction. Therefore the saltness of the sea comes from scorching. That the body of the sea is somewhat mixed is sufficiently shown by its thickness, in which things float easily that would otherwise sink in rivers, although they are carried with the same weight of material. This is also shown by water to which much salt has been added, in which those eggs can float which are full. Finally, the courses of rivers and springs that are salty must be thought to have been hot at some time, and the earth through which they flow to be like lime and ash. For this reason, in many places there are springs and rivers that retain various kinds of taste, and the cause of all of them is to be referred to the innate power of the earth. For the earth, when it is burned too much or too little, takes on various kinds of colours and tastes. Add that it contains a great power and quantity of alum, lime and other things of this kind, by which sweet or tasteless waters flowing through it are usually altered: some turn sour, some turn bitter, and others finally acquire other kinds of taste.

units.la: CAP. XV.
units.tr: CAP. XV.

units.la: Ventorum causa & origo.
units.tr: The cause and origin of the winds.

units.la: E ventis autem nunc dicamus principium repetentes, a quo iam su-pra exorsi sumus. Exhalationum enim duo esse genera demonstratum est, quorum vnum est humidum, alterum aridum, quanuis vnum absque altero esse non possit: sed hæc, ex eo quod exuperat, dici solent. Itaque ea exhalatio, in qua multum humoris inest, pluuiæ principium est: arida vero omnium ventorum materia. Propterea non eadem est natura & venti & plu-uiæ. Quoniam autem interdum vapor multis partibus largior est, interdū fumus, fit ut nonnunquā aliis annis maxima pluuiarum vis & copia decidat: aliis vero venti & siccitates infestent. Nonnunquam tamen in una regione maior vis & copia siccæ exhalationis inest, in alia maior eius, quæ humida; propterea fit ut una multos imbres recipiat: altera siccitate[?] horrescat, ventisque agitatur, ac paucis imbribus, aut nullis perfundatur. Venti etiam tum imbrem consequi solent, cum terra ipso imbre perfusa ab interno calore, & a superiore concalefacta exhalationes illas reddit, in quibus vis ventorum inest: atque hoc modo venti excitantur: quibus sedatis vapor refrigeratus cogitur, ac in aquam pluuiam vertitur. Propterea imbres cum eueniunt, ventos reprimunt ac sedant, & iis sedatis, propter has causas exoriuntur imbres, qui siccas exhalationes refrigerant. Caeterum ab iis locis venti flare non solent, ad quæ Sol suum inflectit cursum, sed a quibus deflectit, hoc est a Septentrionibus & Meridie. Vbi etiam maximam aquæ copia terra excipit, ibi exhalationes frequetiffimę eleuantur, non secus atque ex accessis viridibus lignis fumus. Itaque ex huiusmodi aridis halitibus venti plurimi, & quidè praecipui oriri solent, quorū ij qui à Septentrionibus flant Aquilones, qui à Meridie Austri nominantur. Etsi in rectum fumus progreditur, tamen motus ventorum inflexus est & obliquus, propterea quòd circumfusus aër conuersione orbium cœli consequitur. Quare ex hoc perspicuum est principium motionis ventorum à superiore loco proficisci, vt causam materiæ ab inferiore. Propterea antequam venti flare incipiunt, aër illustrari solet, siue antea in æo nubes fuerit, siue caligo. Ac vnde venti flare incipiunt, ibi eorum vis imbecilla est, & quò longius progrediuntur, eo insignior est, & maior. Quare in Septentrionibus minimè venti flat maximi, quanquam illic facti, & sensim spirantes, tandem longiùs progressi euadunt vehementissimi. Sic de aliis ventis, vnde flare incipiunt, existimare licet.
units.tr: Now, returning to the starting point from which we began above, let us speak of the winds. It has been shown that there are two kinds of exhalations, one moist and the other dry, although the one cannot exist without the other; but they are named after whichever predominates. Thus the exhalation in which much moisture is present is the source of rain, whereas the dry exhalation is the material of all winds. For this reason the nature of the wind and the nature of the rain are not the same. Since, moreover, sometimes the vapour is more abundant in many parts, and sometimes the smoke, it happens that in some years the greatest force and quantity of rain falls, while in other years winds and droughts plague the land. Sometimes, however, in one region there is a greater force and quantity of dry exhalation, and in another a greater quantity of the moist kind; hence it happens that one region receives many showers, while another grows rough with drought, is agitated by winds, and is drenched with few showers or none. Winds also usually follow rain, when the earth, soaked by the rain itself and warmed from within and heated from above, gives off those exhalations in which the force of the winds lies; and in this way the winds are stirred up. When these have subsided, the vapour, cooled, is condensed and turned into rain water. Therefore, when showers occur they check and calm the winds, and once the winds are calmed, showers arise again for these reasons, cooling the dry exhalations. Moreover, winds do not usually blow from those places towards which the sun bends its course, but from those from which it turns away, that is, from the north and the south. Where the earth receives the greatest abundance of water, the exhalations rise most frequently, just as smoke rises from freshly cut green wood. Thus from such dry breaths very many winds, and indeed the chief ones, are usually born; of these, those that blow from the north are called north winds, and those from the south are called south winds. Although the smoke moves forward in a straight line, the motion of the winds is nonetheless bent and oblique, because the surrounding air follows the rotation of the heavenly spheres. Hence it is evident from this that the origin of the motion of the winds comes from a higher place, while the cause of the matter comes from a lower one. For this reason, before the winds begin to blow, the air is usually brightened, whether clouds or mist were previously in the air. And where the winds begin to blow, their force is weak, and the farther they advance, the more remarkable and greater they become. Therefore in the north winds hardly blow at their strongest, although, having been created there and blowing gently, they at last become most violent after advancing further. One may judge the same of the other winds, from the place where they begin to blow.

units.la: CAP. XVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVI.

units.la: Cur interdum venti cessent, interdum excitentur, & vnde, & quo tempore flare soleant.
units.tr: Why winds sometimes cease and sometimes are stirred up, whence they come, and at what times they are wont to blow.

units.la: OLventos & concitare, & reprimere dicitur. Suo enim calore exhalationes dissipat & resoluit, ac propterea terram antè exsiccat, quàm tota exhalatio eleuata sursum fit, perinde ac si exigua materies in magnam ignis vim incidens prius sæpe vsta videtur, quàm sufumum edat. Quas ob res Sol flatus reprimit, exoriríque prohibet: propterea tum cœlum tranquillum est: fit autem tale duabus de causis, vel frigore, quod exhalationis calorem extinguit, vel æstu, qui illam consumit. Propterea Hyeme & Æstate cœlù tranquillum est. Mediæ etiam anni partes interdum tranquillæ sunt, vel quòd nondum huiusmodi aridæ exhalationes excitatæ sint, vel quòd iam euanuerint, nec tum ullæ fiant. Nihilominus tamen Autumni initio, quando Orion oritur, varij excitatur venti, eo quòd tum variæ fiant aëris mutationes. Etesiæ post caniculæ ortum & solstitium æstiuum flare consueuerunt, non autem cum Sol proximè ad nos accedit, vel à nobis longissimè abscedit, propterea quòd cum proximus est, antè exhalationem consumit, quàm eleuata sit. Cum autem paulatim à nobis abscedit, tum calor in aëre moderatus est, & propterea terra quæ colliquatas niues recipit, tum à proprio calore, tum à Sole exsiccata respirat, & fumum emittit. Nostu flandi finem faciunt, & interdiu duntaxat spirant, quoniam ea quæ congelata erant, liquescere desinunt, propter noctium frigus. Quòd autem huiusmodi anniuersarij Aquilones post æstiuum solstitium flare soleant, Austri vero non post brumale spirent, non iniuria usuenit. Nam Aquilo ab iis locis flat, quæ ad Septentrio-nes spectant, & aqua niueque referta [?]fuit,
units.tr: The wind is said both to stir up and to restrain. By its heat it scatters and dissolves the exhalations, and so dries the earth before the whole exhalation is raised on high, just as a small quantity of material falling into a great fire is often seen to be scorched before it gives off smoke. For these reasons the sun restrains the blasts and prevents them from rising, and so the sky is then calm. This happens for one of two reasons: either from cold, which extinguishes the heat of the exhalation, or from heat, which consumes it. Therefore the sky is calm in winter and in summer. The middle parts of the year are also sometimes calm, either because such dry exhalations have not yet been stirred up, or because they have already vanished and none are then produced. Nevertheless, at the beginning of autumn, when Orion rises, various winds are stirred up, because then various changes take place in the air. The Etesian winds are wont to blow after the rising of the Dog Star and the summer solstice, but not when the sun is very near us or very far from us. For when it is nearest, it consumes the exhalation before it is raised; but when it gradually withdraws from us, the heat in the air is moderate, and the earth, which receives the melted snows, is dried both by its own heat and by the sun, and breathes out and sends forth smoke. The Etesians make an end of blowing at night and blow only by day, because the things that had been frozen cease to melt on account of the cold of the nights. That these annual north winds are wont to blow after the summer solstice, while the south winds do not blow after the winter solstice, happens not without reason. The north wind blows from those places that face the Septentriones, and which are full of water and snow...

units.la: [?] Last word cut off at the foot of the page; the reading "fuit," is doubtful. quibus à Sole liquefactis post æstiuum solsti tium potius quàm in eo Etesiæ stant. Etenim magnus oritur æstus non cum Sol proximè ad Septentriones accedit, sed cùm ad calefaciendum ei plus temporis datur, & adhuc propinquus est. Eodem modo venti, qui Ornithiæ dicuntur, post hybernum solstitium stare consueuerunt, qui Etesiis inbecilliores sunt, & minores, ac serius stant: propterea quòd Sol, qui procul à nobis abest, minus virium habet. Nec vero continenter spirant, sicut Etesiæ: quoniam materia, ex qua oriun tur, tenacius congelata est, & Solis calor colliquescens remissior. Tenacius enim congelata maiorem caloris vim requirunt, quàm ea, quæ leuiter conglaciata sunt. Aquilones autem venti quasi ἀπωγ[?] πνευμ[?] dicuntur, eo quòd à terra flent, & illic desinant. Quare in ea parte terræ, quæ ad Vrsam pertinet, finem flandi faciunt, nec longius progredi possunt. Auster verò, non à superiore vertice flat, sed ab æstiuo solstitio, & à loco, qui calore vritur, ut & ab hyberno Aquilo, quoniam venti sunt ex aduerso flantes. Veruntamen Auster, quòd Aquilonibus multo vastior sit, maiorque & vehementior faciliúsque huc ad nos peruenit, quàm Septentriones, ad eos, qui sunt supra nos & in superiore polo. Ille enim per regionem longè maiorem & apertiorem, quàm hi fertur. Hæc de Aquilonum & Austri causa & ori-
units.tr: [Editor's note: the last word is cut off at the foot of the page, and the reading "fuit" is doubtful.] ...which, once liquefied by the sun, the Etesians blow after the summer solstice rather than during it. For a great heat arises not when the sun comes very near the north, but when more time is given it for warming, while it is still close. In the same way the winds called Ornithiae are wont to blow after the winter solstice. They are weaker and smaller than the Etesians, and they blow later, because the sun, being far from us, has less strength. Nor do they blow continuously, as the Etesians do, because the material from which they arise is more firmly frozen, and the melting heat of the sun is weaker. For things frozen more firmly require a greater force of heat than those that are only lightly frozen. The north winds are called, as it were, "winds blowing from afar" [ἀπωγ... πνευμ...], because they blow from the earth and cease there. Therefore in that part of the earth which belongs to the Bear they make an end of blowing and cannot advance further. The south wind, however, does not blow from the highest pole but from the summer solstice, and from the region that is burned by heat, just as the north wind comes from the winter solstice, since they are winds blowing from opposite directions. Yet the south wind, because it is much vaster than the north winds, larger and more violent, reaches us here more easily than the north winds reach those who are above us and near the upper pole. For the former travels across a region far larger and more open than the latter. This is what I have to say on the cause of the north and south winds and their origin...

units.la: CAP. XVII.
units.tr: CAP. XVII.

units.la: Ventorum situs, oppositio, & numerus.
units.tr: The position, opposition, and number of the winds.

units.la: V N C autem de ventorum situ di- cendum est, quíque inter se contrarij sint, & qui vnà flare possint, aut non: praeterea qui & quot sint.
units.tr: Now we must speak of the position of the winds: which of them are opposed to one another, which can blow together and which cannot, and further, which and how many there are.

units.la: At contrarij sunt propter loca contraria, quae plurimum inter se distant, quemadmodum ea specie contraria sunt, quae plurimum specie differunt. Ea autem loca plurimum inter se distant, quae media linea, quam <bl>διάμετρον</bl> [?] nominant, inter se absunt. Huiusmodi sunt occasus aequinoctialis, & ortus aequinoctialis, polus arcticus, & polus antarcticus, ortus aestiuus, occasus aestiuus, ortus hybernus, occasus hybernus. Ea etiam opponuntur loca, quae per mediam lineam plurimum remota sunt. Ex quibus patet eos ventos inter se contrarios esse, qui diametro inter se distant. Quare Zephyrus, id est Fauonius, ab aequinoctiali occasu flans, Subsolano, qui ab aequinoctiali ortu flat, contrarius est. Praeterea Auster Aquiloni aduersatur, eo quòd hic ab Vrsa, ille à Meridie spiret. Caecias item ab aestiuo ortu spiras Affrico, qui ab occasu hyberno flat, contrarius est. Quinetian[?] Eurus,id est Vulturnus[?] ab ortu hyberno flas Coro,ceu Argefti, quem nonnulli Olympiā & Scironem nominat, ab æstiuo occasu spi-rans aduersatur. Sunt & alij venti,qui unâ fla re possunt ut Thrafias, qui inter Corû & A-quilonem interiectus est, & Meses,qui me-dium tenet locum inter Aquilonem & Cæ-ciam.hi enim duo venti non sibi mutuò ad-versantur. Cur autem ab Vrsa plures[?] flant, quàm à Meridie hæc causa est, quòd longè maior aquæ & niuis copia in Septen-trionalem regionem,quàm in Meridianam delabatur. Quare niuibus à Sole liquefactis necessario plures efferuntur exhalationes, quæ ad plura loca pertinent. Regio autem Meridiana Soli subiecta est, & eius orbi, ac conuersioni: quam ob rem tot exhalationi-bus non affluit. Ex iis autem commemoratis ventis tres ab Vrsa flant Aquilo,Thracias & Meses: Cæcias autem Subfolano & Boreæ communis est: sed à Meridie duo duntaxat spirant, Auster & Affricus: ab ortu æquino-ctiali Subfolanus & Vulturnus. Phœnicias autem utriusque particeps est.Zephyrus Co-rum continet: Fauonius Aquiloni attribui solet,atque frigidiufculus est,eo quòd ab oc-casu flet. Subfolani vero, quòd calidiores sint, & ab ortu spirent Austro adiunguntur. Calidiores enim ij sunt, qui ab ortu flant, quàm qui ab occasu, propterea quòd diutius sub sole positi sint. Adde quòd celerius Sol rerecedit[?] ab eo loco, in quo occidit,& tardius ad eundem accedit. Ex his constat ventos, qui sibi aduersantur simul non flare, quippe cum e regione siti linea media sint. Qui vero non ita dispositi sunt, ij simul flare possunt. Cæterum contrariis temporibus venti contrarij maxime flare debent: vt in æquinoctio verno Cæcias, in Autumnali Affricus, in æsti-uo Solstitio Fauonius, in brumali Vulturn*. Alios autem ventos reprimunt ac sedant Aquilones, Thracias, & Corus, propterea quod loca vnde excitatur maxime sint Vrsae propinqua, & proximo e loco flare incipiat. Tum enim vi sua cæteros compescunt, ac nubes abigunt, & serenitatem cœli afferunt, nisi quum frigidi sunt: tunc enim serenitatis causa non sunt. Nam si frigidiores sint quam vehementiores, nubes ante solent cogere, quam pellere. Cæterum venti vicissim mutantur, pro Solis mutatione. Nam ipsorum origo a Solis motu est, quorum humidi, vt Affricus & Cæcias humorem afferunt: aridi vero, vt Corus & Subsolanus, id est, Vulturnus siccitatem. Meses autem & Septentrio, qui Aquilo est, niues efficiunt, eo quòd frigidissimi sint. Grandinem etiam gignunt Aquilo, Thracias & Corus quia frigidi sunt, & celerem densandi cogendíque vim habet. Calorem Auster, Fauonius atque Vulturnus. Nubes cogit Cæcias & Affricus. Cæcias enim cum Aquilone, & Vulturno comunionem habet, quia frigidius est, & propterea nubes cogit. Etsi Septentrio Thracias & Corus serenitatis causa sunt, tamen fulgura generant, quia frigidi sunt, & è loco Vrsæ proximo flat. Ful-gur enim frigore gignitur, præsertim cum frigus cogitur, nubibus coactis. Nonnulli denique venti ecnephias, hoc est, procellas afferre solent, & maxime Autumno, deinde Vere, quoniam tum excitantur procel-læ: cùm nonnulli venti in alios flantes in-currunt. Hactenus de ventorum natura & origine, atque de cuiusque proprietatibus dictum est. units.tr: The winds are opposed because of contrary regions, which lie furthest apart from each other, just as those things are contrary which differ most in species. Now those regions lie furthest apart which are separated from each other by the middle line, which they call the diameter [?]. Such are the equinoctial setting and the equinoctial rising, the arctic pole and the antarctic pole, the summer rising, the summer setting, the winter rising, the winter setting. Those regions are also set in opposition which are most remote from each other across the middle line. From these things it is clear that those winds are contrary to one another which lie apart along the diameter. Hence the Zephyrus, that is the Favonius, blowing from the equinoctial setting, is contrary to the Subsolanus, which blows from the equinoctial rising. Further, the South wind opposes the North wind, because the one blows from the Bear and the other from the South. Likewise the Caecias, blowing from the summer rising, is opposed to the Africus, which blows from the winter setting. Moreover the Eurus, that is the Vulturnus, blowing from the winter rising, is opposed to the Corus, or Argestes, which some call Olympias and Sciron, blowing from the summer setting. There are also other winds which can blow together, such as the Thracias, which lies between the Corus and the North wind, and the Meses, which holds the middle place between the North wind and the Caecias; for these two winds are not opposed to each other. As to why more winds blow from the Bear than from the South, the cause is this: a far greater quantity of water and snow flows down into the northern region than into the southern. Hence, when the snows are melted by the sun, necessarily more exhalations are sent up, and these pertain to more places. The southern region, however, lies under the sun and its orb and course, and therefore it does not receive so many exhalations. Of the winds mentioned, three blow from the Bear: the North wind, the Thracias and the Meses; the Caecias is common to the Subsolanus and the Boreas; but from the South only two blow, the Auster and the Africus; from the equinoctial rising, the Subsolanus and the Vulturnus. The Phoenicias partakes of both. The Zephyrus is associated with the Corus; the Favonius is usually attributed to the North wind and is somewhat cold, because it blows from the setting. The Subsolani, indeed, because they are warmer and blow from the rising, are joined with the South wind. For those winds which blow from the rising are warmer than those from the setting, since the sun has been over them for longer. Add to this that the sun recedes more quickly from the place where it sets and approaches it more slowly. From these things it is established that winds which oppose each other do not blow at the same time, since they are placed directly across the middle line. But those which are not so disposed can blow together. Moreover, at contrary seasons contrary winds ought especially to blow: thus at the spring equinox the Caecias, at the autumn equinox the Africus, at the summer solstice the Favonius, and at the winter solstice the Vulturnus. The North winds, the Thracias and the Corus restrain and calm the other winds, because the places from which they arise are very near the Bear, and they begin to blow from the nearest place. For then by their force they check the rest and drive away the clouds, and bring clearness of sky, unless they are cold; for then they are not the cause of clear weather. For if they are colder than they are strong, they are accustomed to gather clouds before they drive them away. Moreover, the winds change in turn according to the change of the sun. For their origin depends on the motion of the sun: of these, the moist ones, such as the Africus and the Caecias, bring moisture, while the dry ones, such as the Corus and the Subsolanus, that is the Vulturnus, bring dryness. The Meses and the Septentrio, which is the North wind, produce snows, because they are very cold. The North wind, the Thracias and the Corus also generate hail, because they are cold and have the power of quickly condensing and congealing. The South wind, the Favonius and the Vulturnus produce heat. The Caecias and the Africus gather clouds. For the Caecias shares a kinship with the North wind and the Vulturnus, because it is rather cold, and therefore gathers clouds. Although the Septentrio, the Thracias and the Corus are the cause of clear weather, nevertheless they generate lightnings, because they are cold and blow from a place near the Bear. For lightning is produced by cold, especially when the cold is compressed by gathered clouds. Finally, some winds, the ecnephiae, that is, are accustomed to bring storms, and especially in autumn, then in spring, since storms are then stirred up, when some winds rush into others blowing against them. So far concerning the nature and origin of the winds, and the properties of each has been spoken of. units.la: CAP. XVIII.
units.tr: CAP. XVIII.

units.la: Terrae motionis causa
units.tr: The cause of earthquakes

units.la: TERRA gravitate sua, nisi summa vi, moveri non potest. Quare id, quo movetur, maximam vim habeat, necesse est. At nec aliud esse potest, nisi quod naturae vi longissimè progreditur, & maximo impetu erumpit, id quod nihil praeter ventum esse potest: quoniam vim movendi & expellendi maximam habet, qui aeque intra terram oritur, atque in aere. Etsi enim terra per se sicca est, tamen vi imbrium, magnam humoris copiam habet: Propterea cum incalescit, partim calore Solis, partim ignis, qui intus includitur, tum magna ventorum materies & foras erumpit, & in terrae visceribus cohibetur. Atque ex ea siccae exhalationis parte, quae foras erumpere nequit, terram moveri pelliqve oportet. Nec vero absurdum est, si aliquis terrae motus, flante vento, contingat, quippe cum interdum plures simul ventos flare cernamus, quorum si quis in terra vim impetumque facit, terrae motus futurus est. Plures tamen ac maiores terrae motiones noctu eveniunt, ut saepe interdiu circa Meridiem, propterea ꝙ[?] fere fit diei pars omniū tranquillissima, praesertim ꝙ[?] tum Sol terrae exhalationes dissipadi vi maxima habeat. noctes etiam dieb[?] tranquiliores sunt, propter Solis absentiam. Præterea si in interiores terræ partes principium ventorum spiritúsque intret, terræ motum maiorem diuturniorémque efficiat, necesse est. Atque in locis, in quibus mare fluctuat, maximi terræ motus fieri consueuerunt, ut in regionibus, quæ & rarae & cocauæ sunt, quohiam vehemens ventorum impetus, qui efflat ex terra, & vi naturæ erumpit, ob-iectu impetuque maris, quod illic magnam vim habet, in terram repellitur. Regiones quoque omnes (ut summatim dicamus) quæ rarae sunt & concauæ, quod magnam vim & copiam ventorum recipiant, crebrius quati solent, & maxime Autumno & Vere. Hæc enim tempora vi ventorum non parua agitari consueuerunt, sed maxime Autumnus, eo quod in siccitatibus aer flatuosus sit: quandoquidem tum plus aridæ expirationis quam humidæ effertur. Æstate vero propter æstum, & Hyeme propter gelu terra manet inconcussa. Per imbres etiam, quod maior halituum copia in interioribus terræ locis excitetur, & maxime in angustioribus, fit terræ motus. Cùm præterea terræ cavitates aquæ sunt refertæ, tum sicci halitus in angustiorem locum compelluntur, qui cum aqua superiores sunt, & magna eorum copia in paruum locum concluditur, tum ventus & eruptione & impetu suo terram impellit. Atque quemadmodum in nostris cor-poribus poribus flatus, vi nostri caloris ex pituita ex-citatus, tremoris pulsusque praeter naturam causa est: sic ventus in interioribus terrae inclusus exitum quaerens, ipsam quatit & mo-uet. Nam terrae motus quasi eius tremor & pulsus est. Quantam autem vim spiritus terrae & ventus habeat,non solum ex iis, quae in aere eueniunt,perspiciendum est: sed etiam ex animantium corporibus, in quibus nervorum rigores atque distentiones a flatibus excitantur. Propterea cum ingens terrae motus futurus est,non statim,nec semel sistitur: sed plerunque ad multos usque dies prorogatur. Diuturni autem motus terrae causa est, partim nimia aridae exhalationis copia, partim locorum per quae fertur angustia. Ubicunque enim ventus reprimitur, nec facile erumpit, ibi vehementer terram quatiat necesse est. Atque quemadmodum in corpore hominis arteriae non repente, sed paulatim cum febre declinante vehementer pulsare desinunt:sic materies, ex qua fit ille flatus, qui terram mouet,non statim consumitur. Tandiu enim ille terram quatit, quoad siccorum halituum reliquiae sint consumptae. Soni etiam,qui sub terra redduntur audiuntúrque, ab arido halitu proficisci videntur, etiam fi absque terrae motu fiat. Etenim quemadmodum aer, cum verberatur, tu multos variosque sonos efficit: sic cum verberat, & percutit. Quod enim pellit, id etiam pellatur,necesse est. Sonus porrò motum terrae antece-dit, quoniam fumus, qui ex tenuibus admo-dum partibus constat, & non multus est, ex-peditius omnia peruadit quàm ventus. Pro-pterea cum fumus ille minor est, quàm vt prę tenuitate terram moueri possit, tum eam non mouet, sed facile dissoluitur. Cùm ve-rò in cauas terrae partes diuersas habentes fi-guras incurrit, tum voces varias ita fundit, vt terra quasi mugire audiatur. Itaque ventus siue a summa terrae parte, siue ab ima ex-eat causa est, quae non solum in terra, & in ae-re, sed in aquis motum affert, id quod vndæ & fluctus perspicue demonstrant.
units.tr: The earth cannot be moved by its own weight unless some very great force is applied. Therefore that which moves it must have very great force. Nothing else can be this, except that which advances furthest by the power of nature and breaks out with the greatest impetus, and that is nothing but wind, since it has the greatest power of moving and driving out, and it arises inside the earth just as it does in the air. For although the earth is dry in itself, nevertheless, by the action of rains, it holds a large quantity of moisture. Therefore, when it grows warm, partly from the heat of the sun and partly from the fire that is enclosed within it, then a great store of winds both breaks out and is confined within the bowels of the earth. And it must be that the earth is moved and shaken by that part of the dry exhalation which cannot break out. Nor is it absurd that some earthquake should happen when a wind is blowing, since we see that sometimes several winds blow at once, and if any one of them exerts its force and impetus upon the earth, there will be an earthquake. Yet more and greater earthquakes occur at night, and often in the daytime around noon, because the middle part of the day is generally the calmest of all, especially since the sun then has the greatest power to disperse the exhalations of the earth. Nights are also calmer, on account of the absence of the sun. Moreover, if the beginning of the winds and the breath enters the inner parts of the earth, it must produce a greater and longer-lasting earthquake. And in places where the sea surges, the greatest earthquakes are wont to happen, as in regions which are both rare and hollow: because the violent impetus of the winds that blow out of the earth and break forth by the force of nature is driven back into the earth by the onrush and impetus of the sea, which there has great power. All regions also (to speak summarily) which are rare and hollow are wont to be shaken more often, because they receive a great quantity and force of winds, and especially in autumn and spring. For these seasons are customarily agitated by no small force of winds, but especially autumn, because in dry weather the air is windy, since then more of dry exhalation than moist is sent forth. In summer, however, the earth remains unshaken on account of the heat, and in winter on account of the frost. Earthquakes also occur during rains, because a greater quantity of vapours is stirred up in the inner places of the earth, and especially in the narrower ones. Moreover, when the cavities of the earth are filled with water, the dry vapours are driven into a narrower place, and since they are above the water and a great quantity of them is shut up in a small space, then the wind, by its eruption and impetus, strikes the earth. And just as in our bodies a breath, roused by the force of our heat out of phlegm, is the cause of a tremor and a pulse contrary to nature, so the wind enclosed in the inner parts of the earth, seeking an exit, shakes and moves the earth itself. For an earthquake is, as it were, its tremor and pulse. But how great a force the spirit and wind of the earth have must be perceived not only from those things which happen in the air, but also from the bodies of living creatures, in which the stiffenings and distensions of the nerves are excited by winds. Therefore, when a great earthquake is about to happen, it does not stop at once, nor after a single shock, but for the most part is prolonged for many days. The cause of a lasting motion of the earth is partly the excessive abundance of dry exhalation, and partly the narrowness of the places through which it passes. For wherever the wind is held back and does not easily break out, there the earth must be violently shaken. And just as in the human body the arteries do not cease to beat strongly all at once, but gradually, as the fever subsides, so the matter from which that blast arises which moves the earth is not used up at once. For it shakes the earth for as long as the remains of the dry vapours are consumed. Sounds also, which are produced and heard under the earth, seem to proceed from a dry vapour, even if it happens without an earthquake. For just as air, when it is struck, produces many and various sounds, so does wind when it strikes and beats. For what drives must also be driven. Moreover, sound precedes the motion of the earth, since smoke, which consists of very thin parts and is not abundant, pervades everything more readily than wind. Therefore, when that smoke is too small to move the earth by its thinness, it does not move it but is easily dissolved. But when it rushes into the hollow parts of the earth, which have diverse shapes, then it gives out various voices, so that the earth is heard as if bellowing. Thus the wind, whether it issues from the highest part of the earth or from the lowest, is the cause which brings motion not only to the earth and the air, but also to the waters, as waves and surges clearly show.

units.la: CAP. XIX. Fulguris, tonitrus, typhonis, & turbinis causa.
units.tr: CAP. XIX. The cause of lightning, thunder, typhon, and whirlwind.

units.la: OSTHAEC de fulgure, tonitru, vortice, qui typhon dicitur, & turbine accenso, quem præstera vocant, atque de fulminibus, dicendum est. Horum autem omnium eadem causa & origo existimatur. Cum enim vtriusque exhalationis concretio in nubem cogitur, tum necessario calor, qui in extrema illius parte inest, deficit: & propterea pars illa & frigidior & densior redditur. Quamobrem ex ea procellæ fulmina, aliaque huius generis deturbantur, quanquam, naturæ vi, quicquid caloris particeps est, in sublime ferri solet. Sed istius concretionis iactus in contrariam rei densæ partem non aliter fit, quàm in nucleis, qui ex digitis exiliunt. Hi enim quanuis graues sint, & ponderosi, tamen hoc pacto fur-sum uersus subsiliunt. Propterea fumus in superiorem aërem sublatus, & illic à nubis de-sitate[?], & frigore cocretus dispergitur, ac dis-sipatur. Quantum enim ipsius aridæ exhalationis in refrigerato aëre intercipitur, id totum cohæsione nubis densæ exprimitur, dis-ploditurque. Quod quidem cum vi fertur, & ad circumstantes nubes alliditur, tum ictum efficit, cuius sonus tonitru dicitur. Ille autem sonus non aliter fit, quàm cum in foco flamma crepitat. Vt enim multæ exhalationis copia ex accensis lignis erumpens, ac proximum aërem diuerberans talem sonum efficit: ita exhalatio sicca ac ventus, cum ex crassis nubibus eliditur, tonitru facit. Ac ex aëre varia audiuntur sonorum genera propter nubium inæqualitatem, qua ex parte continuatio densitatis ipsarum deficit. Hoc igitur tonitru est, & eam ob causam in nube fit. Exturbatus etiam siccus halitus & è nube expressus plerunque paruo imbecillóque ardore corripitur, ex eóque illud fit, quòd fulgur, aut fulgetrum, vel corruscatio dicitur. Hic enim halitus e nubibus elisus igneo colore suffusus cernitur. Fit autem fulgur post tonitru & ictu aridæ exhalationis, etiam si ante videatur, propterea quòd visus
units.tr: Next we must speak of lightning, thunder, the whirlwind called typhon, and the kindled whirl that they call prester, and of thunderbolts. The cause and origin of all of these is thought to be the same. When the exhalation of each kind is gathered together into a cloud, the heat that is within its outer part necessarily fails, and for that reason that part becomes both colder and denser. Hence the lightning flashes of a storm and other things of this kind are hurled down from it, although, by the force of nature, whatever shares in heat is usually carried upward. But the casting of this condensation into the opposite part of the dense matter happens in the same way as with the nuts that leap out from the fingers. For these, though they are heavy and weighty, nevertheless spring upward in this manner. Therefore the smoke, lifted into the higher air, is there checked by the density of the cloud and gathered together by the cold, and is scattered and dissipated. For as much of the dry exhalation as is caught in the cooled air, all of it is pressed out and burst apart by the cohesion of the dense cloud. And when this is driven with force and dashed against the surrounding clouds, it produces a blow, and the sound of this blow is called thunder. That sound is produced in no other way than when a flame crackles in a hearth. For just as a large quantity of exhalation bursting from kindled wood and beating against the nearby air makes such a sound, so a dry exhalation and wind, when it is struck out of thick clouds, makes thunder. And from the air various kinds of sounds are heard, on account of the unevenness of the clouds, where the continuity of their density is lacking. This, then, is thunder, and it happens in the cloud for that reason. The dry breath also, driven out and squeezed from the cloud, is for the most part seized by a small and weak heat, and from this comes what is called lightning, or a flash, or a glare. For this breath, squeezed out of the clouds and suffused with a fiery colour, is seen. Lightning, however, comes after the thunder and the blow of the dry exhalation, even if it appears before, because sight

units.tr: CHAPTER XX.

units.la: Ecnephia, id est procella, & Typhonis, ac omnium fulminum causa & origines.
units.tr: Ecnephia, that is, the storm, and the cause and origins of typhons and of all thunderbolts.

units.la: S[?]E reliquis autem meteoris, quæ ex sicca exhalatione in nube inclusa efficiuntur, etiam differere convenit. Cum enim flatus ille, qui ex crassis nubibus elicitur, & paulatim sparsim-que diffunditur, ac diflatur: si tenuior fit, to-nitrua, & fulgura facit: si densior & confertim deiicitur, procellam, quam Græci [illegible, ~6 letters] nominant, quæque vehemens ventus est & violentus. Quoniam autem in nube exha-latio utraque inest potestate, fit ut si alteru-tra ex ipsa nube excitetur, procella gignitur, aut imber, prout alter halitus alterum superat. Imber enim tum effunditur cum vapor, qui fumo & flatui contrarius est, expri-mi secernique incipit. Fit quoque typho, qui Latinis vortex dicitur, cum flatus ex una nube exturbatus, & ab altera in quam flat repulsus compellitur rotaturque in rapidæ vertiginis modum, quemadmodum fieri solet in ianuis, vel viis, cum ex amplo loco in angu-stum ventus cogitur. Deorsum enim hic halitus cietur, propter superioris nubis densita-tem, tem,quam perfringere non potest. Atque ab initio vsque ad finem in orbem voluitur, eo quod pars ea,quæ origni est proxima semper flatum consequitur, donec in vnum id cogatur,quod orbis formam refert. Ac huiusmodi vertigines sic in terra circunaguntur, vt in nubibus. Neque verò cum frigus est,aut nix, procella vortexque excitatur,eo quòd vtrûque flatus[?] fit,qui exhalatio est calida & sicca. Nam gelu frigusque semper omnis exhalationis originem offert: quod quidem nisi adesset nunquam nix foret,necAquiloniæ aquę rigerent: quippe cùm hæc ipsa, dominante frigore,gigni soleant: nec etiam imbres fierent neque venti, nisi vtraque exhalatio excitaretur. Vortex itaque tum fit, cum procella è nube erumpere non potest, id quod euenit propter vertiginem, quæ reflectitur, quotiescúque in terram demittitur: quæque cum distrahi non possit, tum nubem secum abripit. Quinetiam quatenus arcto motu vortex cietur, eatenus flatu suo quancunque rem arripuerit, mouet, & in orbem contorquet, ac eandem rem prostratam rursum in cœlum excitat. Cùm verò idem flatus diuulsus ardorem concipit, si tenuior euadat, tum præster,id est accensus turbo, fit, qui proximum aerem incedit,quem contingit. Quòd si ex eadem nube multus ac tenuis flatus erupat, id fulmen dicitur. Si verò præt enuis[?] ex ipsa nube exeat, & propter plurimam tenuitatem nihil eorum quæ contigerit incendat, fulminis genus fit, quod Argeta Poetæ vocant. Quòd si minus tenuis sit, nec incendat, excitatur aliud fulminis genus, quod à Poetis Psoloes dicitur. Illud quidem propter maximam tenuitatem flatus celeri lapsu ante præterit, quàm quicquam incendat, & nigrorem inducat. Hoc verò nigro colore inficit, eo quòd tardius moveatur: nec nihil incendit[?]dit, propterea quòd adustione ante perdat, quàm quicquam contingat. Ex quo fit, ut ea corpora, quæ huiusmodi fulmini resistunt, incorrupta maneant. Veruntamen eo ipso æs, vel ferrum, quo scutum tegitur, ligno integro & illæso liquatur: quippe cùm propter ligni raritatem flatus ante prætereat, quàm ipsum lignum afficere possit. Eodémque modo præteriens vestes non adurit, sed duntaxat lacerat. Itaque hæc omnia fulminis genera fumos esse inflammatos, ex his satis perspicuum est.
units.tr: Next, it is fitting to distinguish the other meteors, which arise from a dry exhalation enclosed in a cloud. For when that blast, drawn out of the thick clouds, is gradually scattered and dispersed, then if it is thinner it produces thunder and lightning; if it is denser and is driven down all at once, it produces a storm, which the Greeks call ecnephia [ἐκνεφίαν], and which is a strong and violent wind. Since both kinds of exhalation are present in the cloud, it follows that if either one is stirred up out of the cloud itself, a storm or a rain shower is produced, according as one exhalation prevails over the other. For rain is poured down when the vapour, which is opposed to smoke and wind, begins to be pressed out and separated. A typhon, which the Latins call a vortex, also arises when a blast, forced out of one cloud and driven back by another into which it blows, is whirled round in the manner of a swift eddy, as usually happens in doorways or streets, when wind is forced from a wide place into a narrow one. For this exhalation is driven downward on account of the density of the upper cloud, which it cannot break through. From beginning to end it rolls in a circle, because the part nearest the origin always follows the blast, until it is gathered into one mass that takes the form of a circle. Such whirlwinds spin on the earth just as they do in the clouds. Nor is a storm or vortex raised when it is cold or snowing, since the blast in that case is cold and dry. For frost and cold always supply the source of every exhalation; and if this were not present, there would never be snow, and the waters of the north would not freeze, since these are usually generated when cold prevails; nor would rains or winds come about unless both kinds of exhalation were stirred up. A vortex therefore arises when a storm cannot burst out of the cloud, which happens because of the whirling motion, which is turned back whenever it is driven down to the earth; and since it cannot be dispersed, it carries the cloud away with it. Moreover, insofar as the vortex is set in motion by a tight circling, to that extent it moves with its blast whatever thing it has seized, twists it round in a circle, and again lifts up to heaven the same thing once it has been thrown down. When the same blast, once loosed, takes fire, if it becomes thinner, then a fiery whirlwind, that is, a kindled eddy, is formed, which sweeps the air nearest to it. But if a great and thin blast breaks out of the same cloud, this is called lightning. If, however, a very thin blast comes out of the cloud itself and, because of its extreme thinness, sets fire to nothing that it touches, it becomes a kind of lightning which the poets call argetes. If it is less thin and does not set fire, another kind of lightning is stirred up, which the poets call psoloes. The former, because of its extreme thinness, passes by swiftly before it sets anything alight and brings on blackness; the latter, however, stains with a black colour because it moves more slowly, and it sets fire to nothing, since it loses its heat by burning before it touches anything. Hence it comes about that those bodies which resist this kind of lightning remain unharmed. Yet the bronze or iron with which a shield is covered is melted by it while the wood beneath stays whole and unhurt, since, because of the rarity of the wood, the blast passes by before it can affect the wood itself. In the same way, passing by, it does not burn clothes but only tears them. From these facts it is sufficiently clear that all these kinds of lightning are smoke set on fire.

units.la: CAP. XXI.
units.tr: CAP. XXI.

units.la: Halonis & ireos causæ, & ortus.
units.tr: The causes and origin of the halo and the rainbow.

units.la: Ehalone, hoc est corona, & arcu, quid utrùque sit, quámque ob causam oriatur, dicere expedit, ac etiam de Pareliis & virgis, atque denique de aliis huius generis. Hæc enim omnia ab iisdem causis proficiscuntur. Differunt dútaxat reflexionis modo, propterea quòd nó ab eisdem corporibus reflexio fiat. Itaque Halo circulus est circum Solem, Lunam, clará que sydera noctu interdiúque apparens, qui ex reflexione radiorum alicuius huiusmodi astrorum oritur. Iris verò semicirculus est, nec maior quàm dimidiatus orbis. Quotiescunque enim sensus oculorum inter Solem & nubem interiicitur, quædam imago ac species, quæ arcus est, à nube nigra reflectatur, necesse est. Propterea Iris reflexio est radiorum Solis à nigra nube in nostrum aspectum. Nec solùm ab aëre & aqua referuntur imagines, sed etiam à læuibus politisque corporibus, vt à speculis, in quibus imagines eorum, quæ obiiciuntur, repræsentari videntur. Ac quemadmodum in aqua simulachra rerum obiectarum, aut colores videntur, ita ab aëre reflexio fit, cùm cogitur & incrassescit, quamuis sæpe absque vlla concretione ipse aër ex se reflexionem imbecillis oculis effundat & reddat: quemadmodum ei euenit, cui hebes visus erat, cuius meminit Aristoteles, tertio Meteororum libro. Lusciosus enim ille incedens, semper ante se faciei suæ imaginem conspiciebat, ob visus eius imbecillitatem: Etenim facies eius ab aëre ad oculos referebatur. Vt autè aqua ad nostrum aspectum ea referat, quæ ei obiiciuntur, nulla cócretione indiget, quoniam per se crassa est. Ab illis etiam corporibus, quæ plana sunt ac lænia perpolitáque, reflexio fieri potest. Sed in nonnullis speculis nō solum colores nobis exprimuntur, sed etiam eorum simulacra, quæ obiiciuntur. In aliis verò duntaxat colores apparent, quoniam parua sunt, nec vllam ad sensum dīuisionem rerum admittunt. In his enim nulla effigies cerni potest, quandoquidem omnis effigies vsquequaque diuidua est. At verò quia omnino in eis aliquid appareat necesse est, profecto color tantummodo cernitur. Corona autem & arcus radiorum syderum ad nostrū aspectum reflexiones sunt: sed hic versus Solem aut Lunam duntaxat fit, propterea semper è regione vtriusque cernitur: illa vero circum hæc & alia errantia. Verùm vtraque reflexio, non solùm colorū varietate distinguitur, sed etiā aliis ex rebus. Arcus enim ex aqua fit nigra & eminus: corona verò ex aëre incrassato, qui suapte natura candidior aqua est, & cominus apparet. Propterea arcus, cùm fieri incipit, tum puniceus cernitur, quoniam splendidus color per atrum appa-rens punicei coloris speciem præbet. Nam quemadmodum in viridium lignorum igne flamma videtur rubra, propterea quòd magnæ fumi copiæ admixtus sit ignis, qui lucidus est, & præsulgens: sic Sol si per caliginē & fumum, aut nubem cernitur, phœniceus apparet. Medius autem color arcus cernitur viridis, propterea quòd tum debilior reflexio xio fit & à copioso lumine remotior. Tertius vero caeruleus est, quoniam eo in loco adeo debilis reflexio est, ut vix aspectus lumen reflexum recipiat. Propterea hoc coloris genus iam ad nigritiem vergit. Ac in arcu interdum flauus color apparet inter phæniceum & viridem interiectus, propterea quod ex vtroque constat. Nam phæniceus color iuxta nigrum positus albescit, ut etiam cum euanescere incipit [?]. Flauescit etiam arcus, propterea quod alba nubes, cum iuxta viridem colorem incurrit, tum flaua apparet. Caeterum huiusmodi vaporum concretio, nō diu aduersus Solem consistit, sed vel in pluuiam mutata destillat, vel ab ipsius Solis vi, attenuatur dissipatúrque. Corona vero tot coloribus non præedita est, quoniam vaporis concretio, ex qua constat, tenuior est. Nam si talis caligo densaretur, sicut ea, quæ aquæ est, aut alicuius rei atræ, profecto speciem colorati orbis præberet, quemadmodum is arcus est, qui circum lucernas conspicitur. Hyeme enim maxima ex parte huiusmodi arcus circum eas cernitur, ab iis potissimum, quibus oculi sunt humidi, & admodum lubrici. Tales nanque ob visus imbecillitatem facile huiusmodi reflexionem recipiunt, quæ ex fuligine flammæ fit ad videntis oculos. Quamobrem propter fuliginis humidæ nigritiem, atque lucernæ lumen non candidum, sed rubrum & rotundum hæc reflexio speciem arcus praefe fert. Arcus etiam ille, quem remi e naui sublati repraesentant, eodem modo, quo coelestis apparet: sed color eius ad eum qui in lucerna cernitur, propius accedit & phoeniceus est. Nec aliter huiusmodi arcus fit, quam fi quis tenuib9 admodum aspersionibus aquam ad locum Soli oppositum ita effundat, vt vna eius pars a radiis Solis illustretur, altera opacetur. Qui autem aquam affundit, manu pro remo vtitur[?]. Caeterum tum coeli arcus, tum etiam corona non minus noctu quam interdiu apparet. Sed arcus a Luna fit, ea vel plena, vel crescente, decre-scentéve. Plures autem coelestes arcus, simul esse quam duo non possunt, quoniam tertius obscurior appareret, nec reflexio ad Solem vsque peruenire posset. Ipsum etiam coeli arcum nec orbem fieri posse, nec dimidia parte circuli maiorem, ex eo intelligi potest, quod altera nubis pars,in qua arcus apparet, sub orizonte occultetur. Est praeterea femicirculus, propterea quòd omne corpus vi Naturae agens, semper id in quod agit, sibi simile efficere nititur. Atqui Sol, qui arcum efficit, rotundam habet figura: ac propterea arcum effingere rotundum conatur. Materies autem huius vtriusque meteori vapor est, qui fi non extenuatur nec dissipatur, sed concrescit densatúrque, certissimum praebet pluuiae futurae signum. Ob eamque causam ex cunctis vaporibus condensatis pluuia fit: alij vero qui dissipantur, ventorum tum causæ sunt, tum prænuncij. Postremo arcus cœli Mundum nequaquam vniuersali diluuio obrui nobis indicat. Cum enim nobis appareret, tum non vniuersus nubilus est, qualem ad vniuersum diluendum fuisse oportuit, sed maior eius pars à Sole illustratur.
units.tr: It is worth explaining what the halo (that is, the crown) and the rainbow are, why each arises, and likewise the parhelia and the rods, and finally other things of this kind. For all of these arise from the same causes. They differ only in the mode of reflection, because the reflection does not come from the same bodies. So the halo is a circle around the sun, the moon, and bright stars, appearing by night and by day, which arises from the reflection of the rays of such heavenly bodies. The rainbow, however, is a semicircle, and no larger than half an orb. For whenever the sight of the eyes is placed between the sun and a cloud, some image or appearance, which is the arch, must necessarily be reflected from the dark cloud. Therefore the rainbow is a reflection of the sun's rays from a dark cloud to our sight. Images are reflected not only from air and water but also from smooth, polished bodies, such as mirrors, in which the images of the things set before them seem to be presented. Just as in water the likenesses or colours of objects appear, so reflection occurs from air when it is gathered together and thickened, although often the air itself, without any condensation, sends out and returns a reflection to weak eyes. This happened to the man with feeble sight whom Aristotle mentions in the third book of the Meteorology. That one-eyed man, as he walked, always saw the image of his own face before him, because of the weakness of his sight; his face was being reflected from the air to his eyes. But for water to reflect to our sight the things set before it, it needs no condensation, since it is dense of itself. Reflection can also come from bodies that are flat, smooth and polished. In some mirrors, however, not only colours but also the images of the objects set before them are shown to us. In others only colours appear, since they are small and admit no division of things perceptible to the senses. In these no figure can be discerned, since every figure is divisible in every part. But since something must necessarily appear in them, only colour is seen. The crown and the arch of the stars' rays are reflections to our sight; but the crown occurs only opposite the sun or moon, and so is always seen in the region of each, whereas the arch appears around these and the other wandering bodies. Yet each reflection is distinguished not only by the variety of colours but also by other things. The rainbow is made from dark water and is seen from afar; the crown is made from thickened air, which by its nature is whiter than water, and it appears close at hand. Therefore the rainbow, when it begins to form, appears purple, since the bright colour showing through the dark presents the appearance of purple. For just as in the flame of green wood the fire looks red, because the bright and shining fire is mixed with a great quantity of smoke, so the sun, when seen through mist, smoke or cloud, appears crimson. The middle colour of the rainbow is seen as green, because the reflection there is weaker and further from the abundant light. The third colour is blue, since in that place the reflection is so weak that the eye scarcely receives the reflected light. Therefore this kind of colour already tends toward blackness. Sometimes a yellow colour also appears in the rainbow, placed between purple and green, because it consists of both. For purple placed beside black becomes whitish, as also when it begins to fade. The rainbow also turns yellow, because when a white cloud runs up against the green colour, it then appears yellow.
