Moreover, such a condensation of vapour does not stand long against the sun, but either melts into rain or is thinned and dissipated by the force of the sun itself. The crown, however, does not have so many colours, because the condensation of vapour of which it consists is thinner. For if such a mist were thickened, like that of water or of some black thing, it would certainly present the appearance of a coloured orb, just as the arch seen around lamps does. In winter such arches are seen around lamps for the most part, especially by those whose eyes are moist and very watery. Because of the weakness of their sight, such people easily receive this kind of reflection, which comes from the soot of the flame to the eyes of the beholder. Therefore, on account of the blackness of the moist soot and the lamp's light, which is not white but red and round, this reflection takes on the form of an arch. The arch that oars raised from a ship display also appears in the same way as the heavenly one, but its colour is closer to that seen in a lamp, and it is purple. Such an arch arises only if someone sprinkles water very finely toward a place opposite the sun, so that one part of it is lit by the sun's rays and the other part is shaded. The man who pours the water uses his hand in place of an oar. Moreover, both the heavenly arch and the crown appear by night no less than by day. But the arch is made by the moon, whether full, waxing or waning. More than two heavenly arches cannot be present at once, since a third would appear more obscure and its reflection could not reach the sun. It can also be understood from this that the heavenly arch cannot be a full orb, nor larger than half a circle, because the other part of the cloud, in which the arch appears, is hidden below the horizon. Furthermore, it is a semicircle because every body acting by the force of Nature always strives to make what it acts upon like itself. But the sun, which makes the arch, has a round figure, and so it tries to shape the arch as a circle. The matter of both these meteors is vapour, which, if it is not thinned or dissipated but condenses and thickens, gives a very certain sign of coming rain. For this reason rain comes from all the vapours that condense, while the others that are dissipated are both the causes and the forerunners of winds. Lastly, the arch of heaven shows us that the world is by no means to be overwhelmed by a universal flood. For when it appears, the cloud is not wholly overcast, as it would have had to be to drown the whole world, but the greater part of it is lit up by the sun.

units.la: CAP. XXII.
units.tr: CAP. XXII.

units.la: Pareliorum & virgarum causæ.
units.tr: The causes of parhelia and rods.

units.la: ASDEM etiam causas reddi exi- stimamus, cur imagines Solis & virgæ in aere nobis appareat, quas halonis & ireos esse demonstrauimus. Igitur imago Solis euenit, cum radij ipsius Solis in crassam nubem, quæ à latere Solis quiescit, refleƈuntur. Virgæ autem, quæ rectæ sunt lineæ, nobis in nubibus apparent, è quibus Solis radij referuntur. Earum color partim puniceus est, partim viridis, interdum flauus, prout incipiunt esse, aut desinunt. Ac quemadmodum cœli arcus in ea nube fit, quæ ex aduerso Solis posita est: ita huiusmodi virgæ iuxta Solem oriuntur in nube inæquali, & quæ iā dispergitur: ac propterea pluuiam portendere dicuntur. Parelius vero, hoc est, Solis imago tum apparet, cum æquabilis nubes & densa in latere ipsius Solis cohfistit. Fiunt autem duo, si in vtroque latere Solis singulæ nubes huiusmodi sint, At densa sit oportet ea nubes, quæ imagine Solis recipit, quoniam raram hæc imago facile transfiret, nec appareret. Sit etiam æqualis & stabilis expedit. Si enim mobilis esset, & inæqualis, profecto Solis imaginem non reciperet, sed potius confunderet: quemadmodum ex agitata aqua scire possumus, in qua nihil prorsus cerni licet. Ob eas etiam causas Parelius nobis albus apparet. Nam Solis reflexio in densa nube, quæ nondum in aquam mutata est, sed breui mutanda, facit ut color ipsius Solis in ea nube albus appareat: Quoniam autem Sol splendidus est, Parelius etiam albus sit, necesse est. Cæterum pluuiam prædicit Parelius, ob nubis densitatem & æquabilitatem, quæ aquæ gignendæ magnam vim habet. Videntur Parelij & virgæ Sole vel oriente, vel occidente, atque ex obliquo, nec admodum prope Solem, nec omnino procul ab eo. Nam si densa nubes proxima Soli esset, profecto ipse eam dissiparet: si remota, nihil etiam reflexionis foret. Atque hæc fere sunt ac talia effecta, quæ in sublimi ab illa exhalatione, quæ ex terra & à Sole oritur, concrescere consueuerunt.
units.tr: We think the same causes also explain why the images of the Sun and the rods appear to us in the air, which we have shown to be halos and iridescence. The image of the Sun occurs when the rays of the Sun itself are reflected from a thick cloud that lies at the side of the Sun. The rods, which are straight lines, appear to us in clouds from which the rays of the Sun are reflected. Their colour is partly purple, partly green, sometimes yellow, according as they begin or cease to be. And just as the rainbow forms in the cloud that is placed opposite the Sun, so such rods arise close to the Sun in a cloud that is uneven and already being dispersed; for this reason they are said to portend rain. The parhelion, that is, the image of the Sun, appears when an even and dense cloud settles at the side of the Sun. Two appear if there are such clouds on each side of the Sun. The cloud that receives the image of the Sun ought to be dense, since a thin one would easily let the image pass through and it would not appear. It is also advisable that it be even and steady. For if it were mobile and uneven, it would certainly not receive the image of the Sun but rather blur it, as we can tell from agitated water, in which nothing at all can be seen. For these same reasons the parhelion appears white to us. For the reflection of the Sun in a dense cloud, which has not yet been turned into water but is about to be, makes the colour of the Sun itself appear white in that cloud; and since the Sun is bright, the parhelion must also be white. Moreover, the parhelion foretells rain because of the density and evenness of the cloud, which has great power to generate water. Parhelia and rods are seen with the Sun either rising or setting, and obliquely, neither very near the Sun nor altogether far from it. For if a dense cloud were close to the Sun, the Sun itself would certainly disperse it; if it were distant, there would be no reflection at all. And these are more or less the effects of this kind, which are wont to condense on high from that exhalation which arises from the earth and from the Sun.

units.la: CAP. XXIII.
units.tr: CAP. XXIII.

units.la: Metallorum & omnium fossilium causæ & origines.
units.tr: The causes and origins of metals and of all fossils.

units.la: VAE denique intra terram, & in interioribus eius partibus, expiratio efficiat, explicare conuenit. Sed quoniam ipsa expiratio duplex est: una vapor, altera fumus, fit ut intra terram duo corporum genera sint, quorum alia fossilia dicuntur, alia metalla. Ea autem expiratio, quæ arida est ardorem concipiens fossilia efficit, cuiusmodi omnia sunt lapidum genera, quæ liquari non possunt, & præter hæc Sadaraca,occhra, minium, sulphur, & alia huius generis plurima. Exhalationis vero humidæ omnia sunt metalla, & quæ fusilia dicuntur, ac produci possunt, ut ferrum, aurum & æs: quæ quidem omnia ab humida expiratione intra lapides inclusa, efficiuntur. Nam per lapidum frigiditatem & siccitatem, expiratio huiusmodi in unum corpus cogitur ac concrescit, instar roris & pruinæ, quæ a calida & sicca exhalatione supra terram dissipatur. Sed metalla intra terræ saxa ante formentur, quam eorum materies dissoluatur oportet. Itaq; quædam ex parte aquea sunt, quoniam eorum materies aqua potestate erat: quædam vero non sunt: quandoquidem non oriuntur ex aqua, quæ quadam affectione & sapore prædita sit, sed unumquodque eorum ex exhalatione humida concrescit, antequam ex ea oriatur aqua. Ignescunt autem omnia, quod terram admistam habeant: Nam in ea exhalatione ex qua concrescunt, altera sicca inest. Unum tamen aurum minime aduri dicitur.
units.tr: It remains to explain what the exhalation produces within the earth and in its inner parts. Since the exhalation itself is of two kinds, one a vapour and the other a smoke, there are two classes of bodies within the earth: one is called fossils, the other metals. The dry exhalation, which takes on heat, produces fossils, such as all the kinds of stone that cannot be melted, and besides these sandarach, ochre, minium, sulphur, and many others of this sort. The moist exhalation produces all the metals, those called fusible and capable of being drawn out, such as iron, gold and bronze; all of these are formed when the moist exhalation is enclosed within stones. For through the cold and dryness of the stones, this kind of exhalation is gathered into one body and condenses, like dew and hoarfrost, which the hot and dry exhalation disperses above the earth. But metals are formed within the rocks of the earth before their matter must be dissolved. Accordingly some are partly watery, since their matter was in potency water; others are not, since they do not arise from water endowed with a certain quality and flavour, but each of them condenses from the moist exhalation before water is produced from it. All of them are, however, liable to burn, because they contain some earth mixed in; for within the exhalation from which they condense there is also a dry part. Gold alone, however, is said not to be burned at all.

units.la: CAP. XXIIII. Vires & effecta quatuor primarum qualitatum elementorum. Quid putredo sit, & eius causa.
units.tr: Chapter 24. The powers and effects of the four primary qualities of the elements. What putrefaction is, and its cause.

units.la: X primis quatuor qualitatibꝰ[?], qua-rum copulationes causae elemen-torum sunt, duae calor & frigus vim faciendi habet, reliquae duae humor & siccitas patiendi: Nam omnibus in rebus, quae natura constant, videntur calor & frigus determinare, formare, coagmentareque ac mutare: hoc est, indurare, emollire, tam ea quae eiusdem generis sunt, quam quae diuer-si. Siccitas vero & humor determinantur formantur mantúrque, & alias affectiones, quae exposi-tae sunt, excipere possunt, quoniam corporum, quae formantur & copulantur, materia praebent. Calida igitur & frigida ut efficientia statuuntur, quandoquidem id cogunt ac for-mant in quod agunt. Id enim quod quidpiā cogit, efficiens sit necesse est. Humidum ve-ro & siccum ea sunt, quae patiuntur, & in quae calor & frigus agunt, quorum prima actio est simplex generatio, & contraria eius corruptio naturalis. Utraque enim mutatio tum stirpibus, tum animantibus, eorumque om-nium partibus conuenit. Naturalis autem ac perfecta generatio mutatio est, quam hae qualitates tali vi praeditae afferunt, quando materiae, quae cuique naturae subiicitur, proportionem obtinent. Hæc autem materia, sunt siccum & humidum, quæ qualitates dicuntur patibiles. Quæ vero generant, calor & frigus sunt, cum eam vincunt materiam. Sed cum non superiora sunt, tum cruditas consequi solet, aut imperfecta concoctio, si aliquatenus eam mutauerint materiam.
units.tr: Of the first four qualities, whose combinations are the causes of the elements, two, heat and cold, have the power of acting, and the other two, moisture and dryness, the power of being acted upon. For in all things which consist by nature, heat and cold seem to determine, form, join together and change; that is, to harden and to soften, both those things which are of the same kind and those which are different. Dryness and moisture, however, are determined, formed and changed, and can receive the other affections which have been set out, since they supply the matter of bodies which are formed and joined together. Hot and cold are therefore established as active qualities, since they compel and shape that upon which they act. For whatever compels something must necessarily be an agent. Moist and dry, however, are those things which are acted upon, and upon which heat and cold work; of these, the first action is simple generation, and its natural contrary is corruption. For each change applies both to plants and to animals, and to all their parts. Natural and perfect generation, however, is a change which these qualities, endowed with such power, bring about, when they attain the proper proportion to the matter which is subject to each nature. This matter is the dry and the moist, which are called passive qualities. Those qualities which generate are heat and cold, when they overcome that matter. But when they are not superior, crudity usually follows, or imperfect concoction, if they have changed the matter to some extent.

units.la: Atque vt absolutæ concoctioni cruditas contraria est, ita simplici generationi corruptio. Putredo vero generationis, & concoctionis commune contrarium est, ad quam corruptio tendit, veluti senectus [?] & marcor: quandoquidem putredo eorum omnium, quæ natura constant, si corrumpantur, finis est, quemadmodum si os, caro, aut quiduis aliud comburatur. Cæterum quæ putrescunt omnia, primum humida sit, necesse est: deinde tandem arida reddantur: quoniam ex his duobus, ut ex materia rerum omnium, quæ natura constant, generatio est, in qua siccitas humore terminatur, regitur-que opera munereque aliarum qualitatum, quæ agendi facultate præditæ sunt. Huiusmodi autem corruptio vi eius euenit, quod circumfusum est, & extraneum, quod aëris calor est, qui ipsum humorem eorum, quæ in Natura sunt, dissipat & resoluit. Propter-ea putredo corruptio est proprij natural-is-que caloris cuiusuis humoris ab alieno ca-lore, & exteriore facta. Ex quo perspicuum est caetera corpora, quae in Natura rerum sunt, uno igne excepto putrescere posse. Nam terra & aqua, atque aer putrescere possunt, quòd igni ut materiei, substernantur, quae alicuius humoris particeps est.
units.tr: And just as crudity is the contrary of complete concoction, so corruption is the contrary of simple generation. Putrefaction, however, is the common contrary of generation and of concoction, and towards it corruption tends, as old age and withering do; for the putrefaction of all those things which consist by nature is their end, when they are corrupted, just as when a bone, flesh, or anything else is burnt. Moreover, all things which putrefy must necessarily first become moist, and then at last be made dry; since generation of all things which consist by nature arises from these two, as from their matter, in which dryness is limited by moisture, and is governed by the work and office of the other qualities, which are endowed with the faculty of acting. Such corruption, however, happens by the force of what is poured around and is foreign, namely the heat of the air, which dissipates and dissolves the very moisture of those things which are in nature. Therefore putrefaction is a corruption of the proper and natural heat of any moisture, brought about by an alien and external heat. From this it is clear that the other bodies which are in the nature of things can putrefy, with the single exception of fire. For earth, water and air can putrefy, because they lie beneath fire as its matter, and partake of some moisture.

units.la: Exarescunt autem omnia & in simplicem vertuntur terram, quaecunque putrescunt: quandoquidem eorum, quae hoc modo corrumpuntur, humor unà simul cum proprio insitóque calore exhalat, & exprimitur.
units.tr: Moreover, all things which putrefy are dried out and turned into simple earth; since the moisture of those things which are corrupted in this way is exhaled and expressed together with their own innate heat.

units.la: Caeterum frigidis tem-poribus minus quàm calidis res, quae natura constat, putrescere solent, propterea quòd tum aer circumfusus & aqua minus caloris habeant, quàm aliis tem-poribus. Quod nanque gelu concretum est, id non putredine affici, satis hactenus omnes norunt: tum enim calor aeris (cuius est putredinem mouere) adeò debilis est, ut alterum, qui in re gelida innatus est, superare nō possit. Similiter id quod fluit, & loco mouetur, minus putrescit, quod quiescit, & stat: quoniam calor aeris imbecilior est, quàm ut illam possit afferre mutationem rei, quae mouetur. Eadem denique causa est, cur id, cuius magna moles est, minus putrescat eo, cuius vis & essentia minor existit. In eo enim quod maius est, plus caloris insiti, aut frigoris in-est: ex quo fit, ut vires aeris ambientis melius superet. Itaque mare in partes distributum, breui corrumpitur & putrescit, id quod universo non euenit. Alia item aquarum genera, sunt huiusmodi. Bestiolæ autem in iis quæ putrida sunt, nasci solet, propterea quòd naturalis calor eorum quæ à re putri secreta sunt, vim habet ea cogendi & coagmentādi.
units.tr: Moreover, in cold seasons things which consist by nature usually putrefy less than in warm ones, because at that time the surrounding air and water have less heat than at other times. For that everyone already knows well enough that what is congealed by frost is not affected by putrefaction; for then the heat of the air (whose office it is to stir up putrefaction) is so weak that it cannot overcome the other heat which is innate in the frozen thing. Similarly, that which flows and is moved from place to place putrefies less than that which is at rest and stands still; since the heat of the air is too feeble to bring about that change in a thing which is moved. Lastly, the same cause explains why that whose mass is great putrefies less than that whose force and substance is smaller. For in what is greater there is more innate heat or cold, and so it better overcomes the strength of the surrounding air. Thus the sea, when divided into parts, is soon corrupted and putrefies, which does not happen to the whole. Other kinds of waters are of this sort too. Little beasts are wont to be born in those things which are putrid, because the natural heat of those things which have been separated from the putrid matter has the power of gathering and joining them together.

units.la: CAP. XXV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXV.

units.la: Quid concoctio sit, & quid cruditas?
units.tr: What is concoction, and what is crudity?

units.la: Q[?]UID fit generatio, & quid corru-ptio dictum est: sequitur, vt etiam concoctionem exponamus, & contrariam eius cruditatem. Est autem cococtio caloris opus, cruditas frigoris. Co-coctionis vt genera sunt tria, maturitas, eli-xatio, & assatio: ita etiam cruditatis, nimirū maturitatis priuatio, leuis elixatio, & imper-secta assatio. Concoctio quidem, perfectio est à naturali proprioque calore profecta, & ex qualitatibus patibilibus, quæ materia cu-iuscunque rei concoquendæ propria sunt. Etenim quæcunque concoquuntur, simulac concocta sunt, perfecta dicuntur: atque id quod potestate erat, plane essentia formamque adipiscitur. Verum tametsi perfectionis concoctionisque origo & præcipua causa nativo calori proprioque rei concoquendæ at-tribuitur, illa tamē externo calore, velut adiumento perficitur. Propterea cibi conco-ctio à balneis aliisque eiusdem generis adiuuatur, etsi origo & principium concoctionis eius est calor insitus rei, quæ alitur; finis verò natura & forma. In nonnullis rebus etiam concoctio, quandam acquirit formam, & ad aliquem finem perducit, dum videlicet humor vel affationis, vel elixationis, vel putredinis, calore coctus victúsque redditur utilis. Sic multum dicitur coctum, ut, & quæ in phymatibus colliguntur, cùm suppurata sunt. Huiusmodi autem concoctionis genus omnibus vsuuenit corporibus, postquàm naturalis calor materiam humoremque domuit, ac determinauit. Quamobrem concocta omnia esse crassa consueuerunt. Id quod perspicuè apparet in lotio, & aluì deiectionibus eorum, qui à morbo convalescunt, quæ postquam calor naturalis superauit, crassiora redduntur. Concoctioni crudi-tas aduersa est, cuius species est ἀπεψία[?], quæ est cococtionis imperfectio aut priuatio propter caloris natiui penuriam, qui nihil aliud est, quàm quod frigus. Huiusmodi autè cru-ditas & concoctionis imperfectio contrariorum patibilium est, quæ cuique concoctioni materia sunt.
units.tr: Having said what generation is and what corruption is, we now come to explain concoction and its opposite, crudity. Concoction is the work of heat; crudity is the work of cold. As there are three kinds of concoction, namely ripening, boiling and roasting, so there are three kinds of crudity: the lack of ripening, a weak boiling, and an imperfect roasting. Concoction is the perfecting that proceeds from the natural and proper heat of a thing, and from the passive qualities that belong to the matter of whatever thing is being concocted. For whatever things are concocted are called perfect as soon as they are concocted, and what was in potency then attains its full being and form. Yet although the origin and chief cause of perfection and concoction is ascribed to the innate heat and to the heat proper to the thing being concocted, it is still brought to completion with the help of external heat. Thus the concoction of food is aided by baths and other things of the same kind, although the origin and beginning of concoction is the innate heat of the thing that is nourished, and its end is nature and form. In some things concoction also takes on a certain shape and is brought to some end, namely when the moisture, whether roasted, boiled or putrefied, is cooked by heat and made useful for nourishment. Thus things are commonly said to be "cooked" when the matter gathered in boils has suppurated. This kind of concoction happens in all bodies once the natural heat has mastered and settled the matter and moisture. For this reason things that are concocted are usually thick. This is plainly seen in the urine and the excrements of the bowels of those who are recovering from illness, which become thicker once the natural heat has prevailed. Crudity is opposed to concoction; one of its forms is apepsia [ἀπεψία], which is an imperfection or lack of concoction caused by the scarcity of the innate heat, and which is nothing other than cold. This kind of crudity and imperfect concoction belongs to contrary passive qualities, and these are the matter of every concoction.

units.la: CAP. XXVI.
units.tr: CAP. XXVI.

units.la: Concoctionis tria esse genera.
units.tr: That there are three kinds of concoction.

units.la: ATURITAS concoctio est succi fructuum cuius vis arboris, quæ tum absoluta est, cùm femina in fructibus inclusa, talia sunt reddita, dita, vt ex his posthac arbores similis generis produci possint. Ea tamen translatione quadam matura dicuntur, vt phymata, pituita, aliíque humores, & morbi, cum à naturali calore victa sunt. Etenim fieri non potest, vt calor humorem terminet, increscetque, nisi eum vicerit. Itaque ea, quæ maturescunt, ex aëreis aquea, ex aqueis terrena redduntur, & ex tenuibus crassa, quoniam natura eorum quæ maturescunt, alia ad se allicit, & alia reiicit. Propterea [ἀπεψία], quæ maturitati adversa est, vel aërea, vel aquea existit, vel ex utraque constat. Est autem imperfectio quædam, quoniam maturitas perfectio est. Huiusmodi crudítas ex eo est, quòd naturalis calor vel exiguus vel immoderatus humorem non vincat. Quare immaturarum rerum succi admodum tenues sunt & frigidiores quàm calidiores, nec ad vescendum, aut bibendum apti. Nullum tamen humoris genus per se, & absque siccitate maturescit, quoniam nunquam crassesceret. Propterea ex omnibus humidis sola aqua calefacta non densatur, hæc crassescit; eo quòd siccitate omnino careat. Cæterum vt maturitas, sic etiam cruditas, multis modis dicitur. Propterea tum deiectiones, tum destillationes & humores contra naturam cruda dicuntur, eò quòd à calore non victa sint, nec concreta. Hæc de maturitatis immaturitatisque causis breui dicta sint; ad elixationem ejusque causam pergendum est. Elixatio omnino est rei crudæ concoctio ab humido calido facta. Est autem res elixanda humor æreus & spi-rabilis, vel aqueus, cuius concoctio abeo ca-lore fit, qui in eo humore innatus est. Pro-pterea quæ in sartagine coquuntur non eli-xantur, sed assantur, quippe cum ab igne & mutentur afficiantúrque. Igneus enim ille calor & exterior humorem in quem agit, ex-siccat & exhaurit. Sed in eo, quod elixatur contrà fit. Nam ex hoc humor, ab eo calore exprimitur, qui in altero humore externo in-est. Propterea assis elixa sunt siccio-ra, quoniam humore proprio & natiuo destituuntur. Ne-que enim quæ elixantur, ad se humorem eli-ciunt, propterea quod exterior calor inte-riorem & insitum superet. Si enim interior esset superior, profecto humorem ad se tra-heret. Ex his perspicuum est non quoduis corpus elixari posse, in quo humor inest. Pro-pterea lapis, aut aliud huius generis elixatio-ni ineptum est. Ea igitur elixantur, quibus humor inest ab externo calore patibilis, ut e-tiam, quæ craßiora ab igne reddi possunt, aut graviora: vel ea, quorum una pars attenua-tur & altera codensatur. Huiusmodi lac est, quod elixatione in butyrum, caseum & serū dividitur. Oleum autem per se non elixatur, propterea quod ei nihil horum advenire po-test. Cruditas autem ea, quæ elixationi ad-versa est, caloris penuria evenit, qui in circu-fuso fuso humore inest. Restat adfatio,quae a sicco calore est & externo. Haec autem duplex est, vna perfecta, imperfecta altera: posterior cruditatis genus est, quae tum fit, cum interius humidum non plane concoctum est caloris exterioris penuria. Ex omni coctionum genere vna naturalis est, quae maturitas dicitur,&alia quae alimenti confectio est:duo reliquae elixatio & affatio arte comparantur: quoniam ars naturam imitatur. Propterea cibi coctioni,quae in animato corpore perficitur similis elixatio est. Vtraque enim a calore in humido calido fit. Quamobrem nonnullae ciborum cruditates elixationi imperfectae similes sunt. Nec vero in ea cibi concoctione, quae in ventriculo fit vllus vermis gignitur, sed in ciborum excrementis putrescentibus. Putrescunt autem non in ventriculo,sed in aluo,vbi a natura reiiciuntur.
units.tr: Ripening is the concoction of the juice of fruits, whose strength is that of the tree, and which is complete when the seed enclosed in the fruit has been made such that trees of the same kind can afterwards be produced from it. By a certain transfer, however, things are also called ripe when phlegms, pituita, other humours and diseases have been overcome by the natural heat. For heat cannot end a humour and make it grow unless it has first overcome it. Thus the things that ripen are changed from airy to watery, from watery to earthy, and from thin to thick, since the nature of things that ripen draws some things to itself and rejects others. Therefore [ἀπεψία], which is opposed to ripeness, is either airy or watery, or consists of both. It is a kind of imperfection, since ripeness is perfection. This crudity arises because the natural heat, either too weak or too strong, does not overcome the humour. So the juices of unripe things are very thin and rather cold than warm, and are not fit for eating or drinking. Yet no kind of humour ripens by itself and without dryness, since it would never thicken. For this reason, of all moist things, water alone does not become dense when heated; it does thicken, but only because it entirely lacks dryness. Moreover, just as ripeness, so crudity is spoken of in many ways. Therefore both evacuations and discharges and humours are called raw contrary to nature, because they have not been overcome by heat, nor solidified. These things concerning the causes of ripeness and unripeness shall be said briefly; we must now proceed to boiling and its cause. Boiling is, in general, the concoction of a raw thing effected by moist heat. A thing to be boiled is an airy and breathable humour, or a watery one, whose concoction takes place by that heat which is innate in that humour. Therefore things cooked in a frying pan are not boiled but roasted, since they are changed and affected by the fire. For that fiery heat, external to the humour on which it acts, dries it up and drains it. But the opposite happens in what is boiled. For from this the humour is squeezed out by that heat which is present in another, external humour. Therefore boiled things are drier than roasted ones, since they are deprived of their own and native humour. Nor do the things that are boiled draw the humour to themselves, because the external heat overcomes the internal and inherent heat. For if the internal heat were stronger, it would certainly draw the humour to itself. From these things it is evident that not every body in which humour is present can be boiled. Therefore stone, or anything of this kind, is unfit for boiling. Those things are boiled, then, in which there is a humour that is susceptible to external heat, as also those things which can be made thicker or heavier by fire, or those of which one part is rarefied and another condensed. Milk is of this kind, which by boiling is divided into butter, cheese and whey. Oil, however, is not boiled by itself, because none of these changes can come upon it. The crudity which is opposed to boiling arises from a lack of heat, which is present in the humour that surrounds it. There remains roasting, which comes from dry and external heat. This is twofold: one is perfect, the other imperfect; the latter is a kind of crudity, which occurs when the moist inside is not fully cooked because of a lack of external heat. Of every kind of cooking, one is natural, which is called ripening, and another is the preparation of food; the other two, boiling and roasting, are produced by art, since art imitates nature. Therefore the boiling is similar to the cooking of food which is perfected in an animate body. For both are effected by heat in a moist and warm humour. Wherefore some crudities of food are similar to imperfectly boiled things. Nor indeed is any worm generated in that concoction of food which takes place in the stomach, but in the putrefying excrements of food. They putrefy, however, not in the stomach but in the belly, where they are rejected by nature.

units.la: CAP. XXVIII.
units.tr: CAP. XXVIII.

units.la: Affectiones, quae qualitates patibiles consequuntur.
units.tr: The affections that follow from the passible qualities.

units.la: NVNC superest vt ea affectionum ge-nera exponamus, quae a patibilibus qualitatibus proficiscuntur. Patibiles quidem qualitates principia sunt corporearum affectionum, quae terminationis corporum causas afferunt, quoniam quasi glutinis locum obtinent. Ob eamque causam utroque principio nempe humore & siccitate omne mistum corpus definitum est, quoniam ex quatuor elemetis terra maxime siccitatis est, aqua humoris. Propterea omne mistum corpus vel durū est, vel molle, quoniam quod ex utroque elemento conflatur, id tale fit, oportet, prout unum altero superius est. Itaque primæ affectiones misti corporis sunt durities & mollities. Durities autem duri corporis affectio est, ut mollities mollis. Propterea durū corpus id est, quod tactui non cedit. Molle contrà, quod cedit, si prematur. Sed quanuis aqua tactui cedat, nō mollis est, propterea quōd summa eius pars intrò pressa, non maneat integra, sed diuidatur. Hæc de duro & molli simpliciter sumpto dicta sint, non autem de altero, quod ad aliud confertur, quod indefinitum est. Propterea dura huiusmodi & mollia magis & minus talia esse dicuntur, quorum omnium iudex tactus est: quoniam sensilia sensu percipiuntur.
units.tr: Now remains for us to set out those kinds of affections which arise from the passible qualities. The passible qualities are indeed the principles of bodily affections, which supply the causes of the termination of bodies, since they hold the place of a kind of glue. For this reason every mixed body is defined by both principles, namely moisture and dryness: of the four elements, earth is chiefly dry, and water moist. Hence every mixed body must be either hard or soft, since whatever is compounded of both elements necessarily becomes such, according as one prevails over the other. Thus the first affections of a mixed body are hardness and softness. Hardness is the affection of a hard body, just as softness is that of a soft one. Accordingly a hard body is that which does not yield to touch, and a soft body, on the contrary, is that which yields when pressed. Yet although water yields to touch, it is not soft, because when its surface is pressed inward it does not remain whole but is divided. These things have been said of the hard and the soft taken simply, not of the relative sense, in which one thing is compared with another, and which is indefinite. Hence hard and soft things of this kind are said to be more or less such, and the judge of all of these is touch, since sensible things are perceived by the sense.

units.la: CAP. XXIX. Omne corpus definitum esse durum vel molle.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIX. That every body is defined as either hard or soft.

units.la: TAQUE[?] omne corpus suo termino definitum esse durum, vel molle, necesse est, propterea quod vel tactui cedit, vel resistit, si prematur. At concretione tale utrunque fit. Quare primum de cocretione differere expedit. Est autem cocretio quodamodo exsiccatio, & utraque agentis opus. Agens autem dicitur esse duplex calor & frigus, quorum frigus magis corrumpendi causa est, quàm generandi: quod interdum etiam calefacere dicitur & uerè, non caloris instar, sed quia ipsum calore cogit & coercet. At patibile in quod calor & frigus agit, uel humidum est, uel siccum, uel utriusque particeps. Si humidum est, id exsiccari & concrescere debet. Exsiccantur autem & conuerfcunt uniuersa uel calore uel frigore: calore (inquam) uel infito, uel externo. Externus is est, quo elixatio fit: insitus uero, quo elixorum humor absumitur. Quæ uero humectantur, duplici modo affici pos-sunt, uno cum uapor in aquam mutatur: altero, cum id quod frigore concretum est, calore liquescit, & in aquam uertitur. Sed quæ concrescunt, talia uel frigore fiunt, uel calore, uel utroque expirare: quanquà ægrè expi-rat, propter aeris lentore, qui aquæ expirationem prohibet. Multa etiam calore ignis craffef-cit, eo quo ex eo effluat aqua, & in uapore dif-soluatur. Terræ quidem tribuendum est, quod eorum, ex quibus uapor igne elicitur, aliquid superfit. Quæcunque igitur frigoris opera crassescunt ad aquam pertinent, quæ uero igne coguntur partim terræ & aquæ, partim aeris sunt, quorum mel maximè ad terram pertinere uidetur, oleum ad aquam & aerem. Lac uero & sanguis plus habent terræ, quàm aquæ, quemadmodum hi[?] humores, ex quibus constant sal & nitrum. Cur autem miltorum corporum quaedam omnino in aquam resolui possint, vt sal, & nitrum:alia non possunt, vt lateres: & praeterea quaedam mollescant, vt cornua:nonnulla indurescant, vt lateres, & nonnulli lapides, ea est causa,quod contrariorum causae sint contrariae.Propterea quae frigore & siccitate coacta sunt, ea calore & humore resoluuntur necesse est. Contra quae igne resoluuntur,ea concrescunt aqua. Sed quae vtroque concrescunt,neutro resolui possunt, vt ea quae ante calefacta & post refrigerata coguntur, vt lateres, & fictile genus omne. Ita enim fit, vt cum imprimis calor humorem materiei, ex qua sunt,in vaporem exprefiit[?], tum reliquias multae terrae participes adeo comprimit, vt posthac omnis via humori intercludatur. Quamobrem huiusmodi corpora igne dis-solui non possunt, nec aqua. Quae praeterea frigore indurescunt,ea calore liquantur. Ligna vero,etsi dura sunt, non liquescunt, neque molliuntur,sed quia aerea sunt, comburuntur, atque in summa aquae parte extant, praeter ebenum nigrum, quod ea de causa nō innatat,partim quia ex eo aerea pars euanuit, partim quod in eo plus terrae infit[?], quam caeterorum elementorum. Idem,de ligno fan-cto, & iunipero quae sic aquae fundum & imu petunt,iudicare licet.
units.tr: Since every body, bounded by its limit, must be either hard or soft, because it either yields to touch or resists when pressed, and both of these arise from concretion, it is useful to discuss concretion first. Concretion is in a way drying, and both are the work of an agent. The agents are said to be twofold, heat and cold, of which cold is more a cause of corruption than of generation; it is sometimes even said, and truly, to heat, not in the manner of heat, but because it constrains and confines heat itself. But the patient upon which heat and cold act is either moist, or dry, or partakes of both. If it is moist, it must be dried and concreted. All things are dried and hardened either by heat or by cold: by heat (I say) either innate or external. The external heat is that by which boiling is done; the innate is that by which the moisture of boiled things is consumed. Things that are moistened can be affected in a twofold way: in one, when vapour is changed into water; in the other, when that which has been concreted by cold is liquefied by heat and turned into water. But things that are concreted must either be made so by cold, or by heat, or by both, and they harden with difficulty, on account of the viscosity of the air, which prevents the evaporation of water. Many things also are thickened by the heat of fire, so that water flows out of them and is dissolved into vapour. Indeed it must be attributed to earth that something remains of those things from which vapour is drawn out by fire. Whatever things are thickened by the work of cold therefore pertain to water; but those things which are compelled by fire are partly of earth and water, partly of air; of these, honey seems chiefly to pertain to earth, oil to water and air. Milk and blood, however, have more earth than water, as do those humours from which salt and nitre consist. Now, why some bodies can altogether be resolved into water, as salt and nitre, while others cannot, as bricks; and moreover why some soften, as horns, and some harden, as bricks and certain stones, the cause is this: that the causes of contraries are contrary. Therefore those things which are compelled by cold and dryness must necessarily be dissolved by heat and moisture. On the contrary, those things which are dissolved by fire are concreted by water. But those things which are concreted by both cannot be dissolved by either, such as those things which, being heated beforehand and afterwards cooled, are compacted, like bricks and every kind of earthenware. For it comes about that, when heat first presses out the moisture of the matter of which they consist into vapour, then it so compresses the remaining earth, which partakes of many things, that afterwards every way for moisture is cut off. Wherefore bodies of this kind cannot be dissolved either by fire or by water. Moreover, those things which harden by cold are melted by heat. Woods, indeed, although they are hard, do not melt nor soften, but because they are airy they burn, and they remain on the surface of the water, except black ebony, which for this reason does not float, partly because its airy part has vanished, partly because there is more earth in it than of the other elements. The same may be judged of hallowed wood, and of juniper, which thus seek the bottom and depths of the water.

units.la: CAP. XXX.
units.tr: CHAP. XXX.

units.la: Affectiones corporum, quæ mista sunt.
units.tr: The affections of mixed bodies.

units.la: MISTA corpora calore concrescere, & frigore, ex superioribus satis perspicuum est. Huiusmodi enim qualitates incrassando & cogendo ipsa efficiunt corpora: id quod ex eo intelligi potest, quod in nonnullis ita compactis & definitis calor reperiatur, in aliis frigus, qua ex parte eis calor deficit. Quare si vtraque qualitas effectrix causa fit, & siccitas humorque patiendi vim habeat, mista corpora sint his quatuor qualitatibus praedita expediet: sed siccitas & humor, aliis duabus, vt mate-ries, substernuntur. Propterea animalia, stirpes, metalla, & quaecunque alia quae ex halitu partim humido, partim sicco in terrae interioribus inclusa cocrefcunt, his quatuor qualitatibus praedita sunt. Huiusmodi autem sunt omnia, quae vel liquari, vel concrescere, vel flecti, aut alio quouis modo affici possunt: quorum quae crassescunt a contrariis qualitatibus afficiuntur. Quaedam enim horum a calore, qui humorem exsiccat, afficiuntur: quaedam a frigore, quod calorem vincit pellitque. Quare quae ex aqua constant, cogun-tur caloris penuria: Quae vero terrena sunt humoris exsiccatione concrescunt, & humo-re liquantur, nisi ita coguntur, vt in eis nulli meatus, qui humorem excipiant, relinquantur, vt lateres: caetera quae meatus habent, humore liquescunt, vt sal,nitrum,& caeuum.
units.tr: That mixed bodies thicken and solidify through heat and cold is sufficiently clear from what was said above. For these qualities make bodies by thickening and compacting them, as can be understood from the fact that in some compact and defined bodies heat is found, and in others cold, to the extent that heat is lacking in them. Therefore, if each quality is an efficient cause, and dryness and moisture have the power of being acted upon, it will be right to say that mixed bodies are endowed with these four qualities; but dryness and moisture are placed beneath the other two, as matter. Hence animals, plants, metals, and whatever else solidifies inside the interior of the earth, enclosed from a vapour partly moist and partly dry, are endowed with these four qualities. Now all those things which can be liquefied, solidified, bent, or affected in any other way are of this kind; and those which thicken are affected by contrary qualities. For some of these are affected by heat, which dries up moisture, and some by cold, which overcomes heat and drives it out. Hence those things which consist of water are compelled by a lack of heat; but earthy things solidify by the drying out of moisture and are liquefied by moisture, unless they are so compressed that no passages remain in them to receive moisture, as with bricks; the others, which have passages, are liquefied by moisture, as salt, nitre, and copper.

units.la: Sed quae caloris priuatione coguntur, calore liquari solent, vt gelu, plumbum, & caetera metalla. Ex concretis autem ea mollescere possunt, quae terrena sunt, ex quibus non totus humor expressus est, quaeque producuntur, ii percutiantur, vt ferrum, vt aurum. Sed ex aqua concreta non molefcunt, vt gelu: nec ea ex quibus totus humor expressus est, vt sal & nitrum, lapides, lateres, omnéque fictilium genus. Ligna quoque molliri non possunt, rò quòd ex aere & terra constent, sed com-buruntur. Deinde quae frigore concrescunt, liquari possunt, vt gelu, & metalla. Ea etiam liquantur, quae aqua poris diruptis recipiunt, vt terra, quae humore perfunditur, & nitrum.
units.tr: But those things which are compelled by the privation of heat are usually liquefied by heat, as ice, lead, and the other metals. Among solidified things, those can be softened which are earthy, from which the whole moisture has not been squeezed out, and which are produced, and are struck, as iron and gold. But things solidified from water do not soften, as ice; nor do those from which the whole moisture has been squeezed out, as salt and nitre, stones, bricks, and every kind of earthenware. Wood also cannot be softened, because it consists of air and earth, but it is burned. Furthermore, those things which solidify through cold can be liquefied, as ice and metals. Those are also liquefied which receive water when their pores are broken open, as earth which is drenched with moisture, and nitre.

units.la: Nonnulla item humectari possunt, vt quae po-rosa sunt, & humorem recipere possunt, vt lana & terra, atque fructus & femina multa.
units.tr: Likewise some things can be moistened, namely those which are porous and can receive moisture, as wool and earth, and many fruits and seeds.

units.la: Praeterea corpora, quaedam flexilia sunt, quae rursus dirigi possunt, vt vimina, quorum lon-gitudo ex rotunda figura in rectam, & ex re-cta rursus in rotundam mutari potest. Nam flexio & in connexum, & concauum motio est. Adhaec quaedam rumpi simul & frangi possunt, vt lateres: Nonnulla rumpuntur, & non franguntur, vt ligna: quaedam contra frangi possunt & non rumpi, vt gelu, lapis, ossa. Hoc enim differunt fractura & ruptio, quod illa in magnas partes dividit, hic in quasibet, & plures duabus. Quæcunque igitur sic compacta sunt ut transfuersos habeant poros & fibras, fragilia sunt: quibus vero fibræ in longitudinem exporrectę sunt,rumpi dicun-tur. Alia autem, quæ poros fibrasque habent in longitudinem, & latitudinem exporrectas, & rumpi simul, & frangi possunt, ut lateres & fictilia. Alia etiam sunt, quibus quidpiam imprimi potest,ut æs, ut cera. Alia, in quibus nihil imprimi potest ob summam vel siccitatem,ut fictilia, vel humorem,ut aqua. Est enim impressio recessus summæ partis corporis in interiores pulsu, vel ictu, vel omnino tactu factus. Ac etiam in summę sic-cis,ut in lateribus nihil imprimi potest: quoniam extremæ eorum partes intrò non pel-luntur,nec cedunt. Alia ite facile premi pos-sunt,quorū copreffio statim euanescit, ut la-na,spogia. Omnia(ut paucis absolua) premi possunt, quæ capulsa inter se cohæret, ut etiá ea,quæ meatus corporis no inanes habet, sed aquæ plenos, qualis est madefacta spongia. Caro etiá & cerá prætmuntur, quoniam meatus plenos habent. Premi contrà non pos-sunt; quæ nullos habent poros, aut si quos habent,ij rebus duris pleni sunt, ut ferrum, la-pis. Humida quoq; omnia premi nō possunt, quoniam eorum partes intrò non pelluntur. Præterea quædam ductilia sunt,quorum extrema uno & eode ictu simul in latitudine & altitudinem omnibus ex partib. movetur. Quædam duci possunt, & premi ut lana, æs, & multa alia metallorum. Quinetiam quædam sunt fissilia, ut ligna, alia non fissilia, ut lateres. Fissilia autem ea sunt, quæ fecundum longitudinem diuidi possunt, ut feftilia, fe-cundum latitudinem. Ac ex duris corporibus ea sunt feftilia, quæ frangi possunt. Quædam etiam ex ipsis duris simul & frangi & rumpi possunt, ut fiftilia. Glacies, lapis, offa, franguntur, & non rumpuntur* quoniam ea quæ meatus fibrasque simul copulatas habent, fragilia dicuntur, ut offa: quibus vero longius patent, ea ruptilia sunt. Adhæc omnia, quæ glutinosa sunt & duci & dilatari possunt, ut & mollia, quorum ea sunt contraria, quæ friabilia dicuntur. Ea insuper subigi condensariqué possunt, quæ firmas compressiones ferunt. Alia etiam comburi possunt, ut lignum, lana, offa, & quæcunque poros habet & fibras, aut aëreu humorem, ut olea & pin-guedines. Alia non comburi possunt, ut lapides, gelu, ut & quæcunque humore caret, quem etsi habent ad urendum inepta sunt, nisi vehementiore igne, ut ligna admodu viridia. Nonnulla item exhalant, quæ, tametsi humore prædita sint, non tamen vaporem emittunt, nisi igni apponantur: quandoquidé vapor quædam humida expiratio est, in aëre facta à calore & ex humore. Alia vero ad suffitus apta sunt, quorum halitus aridus est, & humidi excretio communis est ab vrente calore excitata. Ac huiusmodi exhalatione, quae fumus est, emittunt ossa [?], crines, & infinita propemodum alia, dum vrutur, quorum fumi varia sortiuntur nomina. Propterea rei pinguis exhalatio fuligo est, & graueolens fumus. Eius vero quod oleosum est & glutinosum ac pingue, nidor nominatur, & arida exhalatio est, & non vapor. Aqua item vaporem & non fumum emittit: sed vinum, quod dulce est, fumum reddit, propterea a frigore non cogitur. Haec tadem omnia, quae exhalant, comburi possunt. Caeterum eorum quae ad comburendum idonea sunt, quaedam flammam emittunt, quaedam minime: ea autem flammam emittunt, quae aqueo humore carent, & siccam duntaxat exhalatione habent, vt pix, oleum, cera, ligna. Ea etiam, quae suffitui apta sunt, flammam emittunt, nec liquantur, maxime terrena sunt, & siccitatem cum igne communem habent. Ob eamque causam flamma spiritus est, aut fumus ardens: Alia vero, vtrunque praestare possunt, vt thus & mastiche, quod multo aere praedi-ta sint. Lignorum autem exhalatio fumus dicitur: cerae, thuris, picis, & aliorum huiusmodi fuligo.
units.tr: Moreover, some bodies are flexible and can be straightened again, as twigs, whose length can be changed from a round shape into a straight one, and from a straight one back into a round one; for bending is motion both into a curve and into a hollow. Besides, some things can be broken and shattered at the same time, as bricks; some are broken but not shattered, as wood; and some, on the contrary, can be shattered but not broken, as ice, stone, and bones. For fracture and rupture differ in this, that the former divides into large parts, the latter into any parts whatever, and more than two. Therefore whatever bodies are so compacted that they have transverse pores and fibres are brittle; but those whose fibres are stretched lengthwise are said to be ruptured. Others, which have pores and fibres stretched both lengthwise and crosswise, can be both ruptured and shattered at the same time, as bricks and earthenware. There are also things on which something can be impressed, as bronze and wax; others on which nothing can be impressed, either because of extreme dryness, as earthenware, or because of moisture, as water. For an impression is the withdrawal of the outer part of a body into its interior, made by a push, a blow, or indeed by mere touch. And among extremely dry things, as in bricks, nothing can be impressed, since their outer parts are not driven inward and do not give way. Other things can also be pressed easily, whose compression vanishes at once, as wool and sponges. In short, everything that holds together in a mass can be pressed, including even those which have bodily passages not empty but full of water, such as a soaked sponge. Flesh and wax are also pressed, since they have passages full of matter. On the contrary, those things cannot be pressed which have no pores, or if they have any, those pores are filled with hard matter, as iron and stone. Moist things also cannot be pressed, since their parts are not driven inward. Furthermore, some things are ductile, whose extremities are moved in all directions, in width and height, by one and the same blow at once. Some can be drawn out and pressed, as wool, bronze, and many other metals. Indeed some things are fissile, as wood, others not fissile, as bricks. Fissile things are those which can be divided lengthwise, as split wood can be divided crosswise. And among hard bodies, those are fissile which can be broken. Some things, too, of the hard kind can be both shattered and ruptured, as fissile things. Ice, stone, and bone are shattered and not ruptured, since those which have passages and fibres held together at the same time are called brittle, as bone; but those whose passages extend further are ruptile. Moreover, all things which are glutinous can be drawn out and expanded, as also soft things; those which are opposed to them are called friable. Besides, those things can be worked and condensed which bear firm compressions. Other things can also be burned, as wood, wool, bone, and whatever has pores and fibres, or an airy moisture, as oil and fats. Others cannot be burned, as stones and ice, and whatever lacks moisture; even those which have moisture are unfit for burning unless with a very vehement fire, as very green wood. Likewise some things give off vapours, which, although they are endowed with moisture, nonetheless do not emit vapour unless they are placed on the fire; for vapour is a kind of moist exhalation made in the air by heat and from moisture. Other things are fit for fumigation, whose breath is dry, and whose moist exhalation is common, excited by a burning heat. And by this kind of exhalation, which is smoke, bones, hair, and almost countless other things emit, while they are burned, whose smokes receive various names. Hence the exhalation of a fatty thing is soot, and a heavy-smelling smoke. But the exhalation of what is oily, glutinous, and fat is called stench, and is a dry exhalation, not a vapour. Water likewise emits vapour and not smoke; but sweet wine gives off smoke, and for that reason is not solidified by cold. Finally, all those things which give off exhalations can be burned. Yet of those things which are suited to burning, some emit flame and some not at all; those emit flame which lack watery moisture and have only a dry exhalation, as pitch, oil, wax, and wood. Those also which are fit for fumigation emit flame and do not melt; they are chiefly earthy, and share dryness with fire. And for this reason flame is a spirit, or burning smoke; but others can produce both, as frankincense and mastic, because they are endowed with much air. The exhalation of wood is called smoke; that of wax, frankincense, pitch, and other things of this kind is called soot.

units.la: CAP. XXXI.
units.tr: CAP. XXXI.

units.la: Similarium corporum origo.
units.tr: The origin of similar bodies.

units.la: CORPORA quæ similaria sunt in-ter se differunt, distinguuntur-que o-doribus,saporibus,coloribus,& iudicio tactus: quorum quædam e terra eruuntur, ut aurum,æs, argentum, stannum, ferrum,lapis, cæteraque eiusdem generis, quæ in illa ex utraque exhalatione procreantur.
units.tr: Similar bodies differ from one another, and are distinguished by their odours, flavours, colours, and the judgement of touch. Some of them are dug out of the earth, such as gold, copper, silver, tin, iron, stone, and the other things of this kind, which are produced in the earth from both exhalations.

units.la: Quædam etiam similarium corporum in a-nimantibus reperiuntur, quæ illorum primæ partes sunt, & simplices, ut caro, offa[?], neruus, cutis, viscera, fibræ, venæ: ex quibus membra, ut facies, manus, pes, & alia id genus constant.
units.tr: Some similar bodies are also found in animals; these are their first and simple parts, such as flesh, bone, sinew, skin, viscera, fibres, and veins. From these the members are made, such as the face, hand, foot, and others of this kind.

units.la: Eadem item similaria in stirpibus ha-bentur; ut cortex, lignum, folium, radix, & alia eiusdem generis, quorum materies hu-mor est, & siccitas: efficiens vero calor & frigus. Corporum quidem similarium, quæ ita formata sunt, alia liquida habentur, alia mollia, quædam dura. Liquidorum, quæ ex se vaporem emittunt, ea ad aquam pertinet: quædam ex terra & aqua constant, ut lac, sanguis: alia ex aqua & aëre, ut oleum. An ne vero ex liquidis vinum fit, iure quæri potest, quippe quod & exhalationem reddat siccam, & calore concrescat, quale novum est, quod quidem magis terrenum est, quàm vetus. Quare ex vinis liquida sunt vetera, & defecata. Ex concretis etiam & duris, quæ frigore coguntur ad aquam similiter pertinent, ut glacies, nix, gradō, pruina, metalla, & lapidū nonnulli, & quæcunque igne liquescunt. Quæ vero calore & frigore indurantur,ex terra & aqua constant,ut lateres,& fictilia vasa,quae tu coguntur,cum refrigerantur priuatione caloris & humoris,qui vna cum calore exprimitur. Succinum autem,myrrha & gummi, atque alia huius generis frigore concrescunt, & eo modo quo mel, cum decoquitur & in frigida aqua demittitur. Mollia item ad terram etiam pertinent,& ad aquam: quoniam ex eis non totus humor expressus est. In hoc genere sunt etiam cornu & ferru. Propterea quaecumque similaria corpora igne liquescunt ea ad aquam pertinent, ut metalla, & lapidum multi. Aquosa etiam sunt vina quaedam, urina, acetum, lixiuium, ferū,ichor, quoniam frigore concrescunt. Terrena autem sunt ferrum nondum defecatum, cornu, vnguis, os, neruus, ligna, pili,omnesque arborū lachrimae, atque nonnulli lapides, & fruges, ac legumina, atque frumentū,quorum quaedam magis, alia minus talia dicuntur. Sanguis vero & seme[?] genitale ad terram, aquam, & aera pertinent, quanquam sanguis ille,qui fibras habet,magis terrenus est alio. Propterea frigore cogitur, & humore liquescit. Qui vero fibris caret ad aquam pertinet, nec propterea crassescit. Semen genitale frigore cogitur, sed postquam humor vna cum calore effluxit.
units.tr: The same similar bodies are likewise found in plants, such as bark, wood, leaf, root, and others of this kind. Their matter is moisture and dryness, and their efficient cause is heat and cold. Of the similar bodies formed in this way, some are regarded as liquid, some as soft, and some as hard. Among liquids, those which give off vapour from themselves belong to water. Some consist of earth and water, such as milk and blood; others of water and air, such as oil. Whether wine is made from liquids may rightly be asked, since it gives off a dry exhalation and thickens with heat; such wine, being new, is more earthy than old wine. Hence old and clarified wines are liquid. Among solid and hard bodies, those which are compacted by cold likewise belong to water, such as ice, snow, hail, hoarfrost, metals, some stones, and whatever melts in fire. But those which are hardened by heat and cold consist of earth and water, such as bricks and earthenware vessels, which are baked, since when they cool they lose heat and moisture, which is squeezed out together with the heat. Amber, myrrh and gum, and other things of this kind, thicken by cold, and in the same way as honey, when it is boiled and let down into cold water. Soft bodies likewise belong to earth as well as to water, since not all their moisture has been pressed out of them. Horn and hoof are also in this class. Therefore whatever similar bodies melt in fire belong to water, such as metals and many stones. Some wines, urine, vinegar, lye, whey, and ichor are also watery, since they thicken by cold. Earthy bodies, however, are unrefined iron, horn, nail, bone, sinew, wood, hair, all the tears of trees, and some stones, and fruits, pulses, and grain, some of which are called such more, others less. Blood and the generative seed belong to earth, water, and air, although that blood which has fibres is more earthy than the other. For this reason it is compelled by cold and melts with moisture. But blood which lacks fibres belongs to water and does not on that account thicken. Generative seed is compelled by cold, but only after its moisture has flowed out together with the heat.

units.la: CAP. XXXII.
units.tr: CAP. XXXII.

units.la: Corporum similarium temperamentum.
units.tr: The temperament of similar bodies.

units.la: Iis, quæ dicta sunt facile cogno-sci possunt corpora, siue liquida, siue concreta quæ calida sunt, vel frigida. Ea quidè quæ ad aquam pertinent, magna ex parte frigida sunt, nisi adventitium calorem adepta sint, vt lixiuium, vrina. Terrena vero quæ calo[?]re formantur fere calida sunt omnia, vt calx, atque cinis.
units.tr: From what has been said, bodies can easily be recognised as hot or cold, whether they are liquid or solid. Those that belong to water are for the most part cold, unless they have acquired an adventitious heat, as lye and urine do. Earthy bodies, however, which are formed by heat, are nearly all hot, such as quicklime and ash.

units.la: Ea autem, quorum omnium materies terra est & aqua, quæ frigida sunt, & qualitates habent patibiles, potius frigida haberi debent, quàm calida, nisi ab externo calore afficiantur. Propterea ea aqua, quæ per cinerem colata est, feruida percipitur. Cinis enim calorem ignis retinuit. Etenim in omnibus, quæ ab igne affecta fuerunt, vis caloris maior, aut minor inest. Quæ tamen ex terra & aqua constant, ea fere sunt calore prædita: quoniam maxima illorum pars vi caloris, qui ea concoxit, concreta est. Quamobrem tantisperdum suam retinet naturam calida sunt.
units.tr: Those whose whole matter is earth and water, and which are cold and have passive qualities, ought rather to be regarded as cold than hot, unless they are affected by an external heat. Hence water strained through ash is perceived to be hot, for the ash has retained the heat of the fire. Indeed, in all things that have been affected by fire, the power of heat is either greater or less. Those things which consist of earth and water are nearly always endowed with heat, since the greater part of them has been solidified by the power of the heat that concocted them. Therefore, for as long as they keep their own nature, they are hot.

units.la: Huiusmodi sunt sanguis, semen, genitale, medulla, coagulum, & cætera huius generis, quæ cùm corrumpuntur & à sua discedunt natura, tum non sunt calida, sed frigida, quoniam eorum materies, quæ aqua est, & terra remanet. Ea vero, in quibus materies est aquæ plurimum, frigida sunt, & igni aduersantur: sed ea, in quibus plus est terræ vel aeris, quàm aquæ, calida sunt. Quæ denique igne coguntur, ea frigida sunt, si calore priuentur: sin non calore destituuntur ignita sunt, atque instar ardentis aquæ vrunt.
units.tr: Such are blood, semen, marrow, curd, and other things of this kind; when these are corrupted and depart from their own nature, they are then not hot but cold, since what remains is their matter, which is water and earth. Those in which the matter is mostly water are cold and opposed to fire; but those in which there is more earth or air than water are hot. Finally, those things which are solidified by fire are cold if they are deprived of heat; but if they are not deprived of heat, they are burning and burn like flaming water.

units.la: CAP. XXXIII. Formam diffimilarium partium facilius cognosci a nobis, quàm fi-milarium.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXIII. That the form of the dissimilar parts is more easily known by us than that of the similar parts.

units.la: OS THAEC quid sit caro, os, & a-liæ similares animalium partes, dicere licet. Ex his enim ita diffimi-lium corporum natura constat, vt ea ex quatuor elementis. Sunt enim hæc elementa communis materies mistorum corporum, quæ etiam ex materia constant & forma: forma autem, id est, quo quid quicque sit, declaratur, in membris, & diffimilaribus corporibus, quorum generatio postrema est, multò magis nobis conspicua est, quàm in similaribus, propterea quòd illa instrumenta sint, & ad quendam vsum à natura data. Quare formæ priuatio in posteriore generatione, quę instrumentorum est, multò clarius apparet, quàm in priore, quę similarium partium & ex elementis est. Perspicuum enim magis est mortuum hominem ὁμωνύμως[?] hominem dici, quàm carnem mortuā carnem. Itaque diffimilarium corporum forma nobis notior est, quàm similarium partium animalis. Quamobrem ægrius ea cognoscun-tur quæ materiei viciniora sunt, quàm quæ remotiora, propterea quòd materies per se nobis ignotior sit,quà id quod extra constat.
units.tr: We may say what flesh, bone, and the other similar parts of animals are. For the nature of such dissimilar bodies consists of these, just as it does of the four elements. For these elements are the common matter of mixed bodies, and these too consist of matter and form. Form, that is, that by which each thing is what it is, is made clear in the limbs and dissimilar bodies, whose generation comes last, and it is far more evident to us than in the similar parts, because those are instruments given by nature for a certain use. Hence the privation of form in the later generation, which belongs to instruments, appears much more clearly than in the earlier, which belongs to the similar parts and is made from the elements. For it is more obvious that a dead man is called a man only equivocally, than that dead flesh is flesh. Thus the form of dissimilar bodies is better known to us than the form of the similar parts of an animal. For this reason, things nearer to matter are known with more difficulty than things further away, since matter in itself is less known to us than what lies outside it.

units.la: Proinde mortuam manum facilius manum esse percipimus, quàm carnem mortuam carnem. Adde quod omnium[?] suo munere ac ossi-cio definita sunt. Propterea quæ corpora mu-nus suum exequi possunt,ea re vera sunt membra : veluti oculus verus est, st[?] cernat. Sed quod membrum suo munere fungi non po-teft, id eodem nomine, sed eo æquiuoco appellatur: vt hominis mortui oculus, vel lapideus nominatur oculus. Quemadmodum enim lapidea ferra, non ferra est; sed quædam ferræ imago: ita mortui hominis oculus, vel alius lapideus, nihil aliud est,nisi viuentis o-culi imago. Eodem etiam modo stirpiu[?] partes, & ea omnia quæ inanimata sunt, suis muneribus facultatibusque declarantur, cu-iufmodi sunt æs & argentum. Omnia nanq; corpora quæ natura constant,facultate qua-dam, vel efficiente, vel patiete prædita sunt, vt caro,& neruus. Verum tamen illæ faculta-tes, quibus ipsorum corporum effentia defini-tur,non exacte sunt compertæ. Ex quo fit a-liquado vt an illis insint,vel minimè, non facile sit perspicere : Neque paruo negotio hæc distinguntur, si omnino ea facultas, qua singulæ res naturales prædictæ sunt, euanue-rit, & solæ earum figuræ remaserint, quem-admoádmodum cadaueribus vetustis euenit, quæ in loculis asseruata de repente in cinerem rediguntur. Huiusmodi etiam sunt fructus diu reconditi, qui vetustate consimili solam habent figura, nec amplius sensum gustus mouere possunt, vt alij. Quæ præterea ex laéte concreta sunt, tandem viribus effœta reddunt̃, vt veterrimi cafei. Itaque similares animalium partes, vt & quæ corpora inanimata sunt, tũm calore, tum frigore concre-scunt, atque distinguntur dilatatione, contractione, duritie, mollitie, aliisque huius generis affectionibus, quæ caloris & frigoris munera sunt. Verũ tamen quę partes ex similarium genere conflatæ sunt, vt membra, à calore & frigore conformari, nemini videbuntur, tamen si ita res habeat. Quemadmodum enim caloris frigorisque motio, causa producendi æris, vel argenti est, aut etiam ferræ, & gladij: ita in dissimilaribus partibus eadem ratio valere videtur, in quarum conformatione natura calore vtitur & frigore, tanquam instrumentis.
units.tr: Accordingly we perceive a dead hand more easily as a hand than dead flesh as flesh. Add that all members are defined by their office and function. So those bodies which can carry out their own office are truly members: thus an eye is a true eye if it sees. But a member which cannot perform its function is called by the same name only equivocally: as the eye of a dead man, or a stone eye, is called an eye. For just as a stone statue of a wild beast is not a beast but a certain image of one, so the eye of a dead man, or another stone eye, is nothing but an image of a living eye. In the same way the parts of plants, and all those things which are inanimate, are described by their functions and powers, as are bronze and silver. For all bodies which subsist in nature are endowed with some faculty, either active or passive, as flesh and sinew are. Yet those faculties by which the essence of these bodies is defined have not been exactly ascertained. Hence it is sometimes not easy to see whether they are present at all or not. Nor is this distinction a small matter if that faculty by which each natural thing is endowed has altogether vanished and only their shapes remain, as happens with old corpses kept in coffins, which suddenly turn to ash. Such also are fruits long stored away, which, through similar age, keep only their shape and can no longer stimulate the sense of taste, as others do. Moreover, things that have been curdled from milk at last become exhausted in their strength, like very old cheese. Thus similar parts of animals, as well as inanimate bodies, are formed by heat and cold, and are distinguished by dilation, contraction, hardness, softness, and other affections of this kind, which are the works of heat and cold. Yet it will seem to no one that those parts which are made up of the kind of similar parts, such as the limbs, are shaped by heat and cold, even if the matter stands so. For just as the motion of heat and cold is the cause of producing bronze or silver, or even iron and a sword, so the same principle seems to hold for dissimilar parts, in whose formation nature uses heat and cold as instruments.

units.la: Finis meteorologiæ.
units.tr: End of meteorology.

units.la: INSTITVTIONVM PHYSICARVM TER-TIA PARS, QVAE ANIMA-TORVM CORPORVM NATURAM EXPLICAT, & DE ANIMA INSCRIBI SOLET. PRÆFATIO.
units.tr: THE THIRD PART OF THE PHYSICAL INSTITUTES, WHICH EXPLAINS THE NATURE OF ANIMATED BODIES AND IS USUALLY ENTITLED ON THE SOUL. PREFACE.

units.la: VANQVAM in honore & pretio habetur omnis scientia, tamen alia præstantior, quam alia ac maior digniorq; existimatur, vel quod certior fit, vel quia in rebus præstantioribus, & maiorem admirationem excitantibus versatur. Quare ea, quæ de anima instituitur o-ratio, recte in hoc genere collocatur, videturque eius cognitio ad omnem veritatem, tum vel maxime ad naturæ cognitionem magnum afferre adiumentum: quippe cum ani-mantium stirpiumque quasi fons quidam sit & principium anima. Propterea huius scien-tiæ subiectum ipsa anima corpori indita co-iunctaque vitæ & cæterarum vitalium facultatum causa habeatur. Sed animæ a corpore separatæ (cuiusmodi hominis mens esse potest) scientia & cognitio non ad Physicum, sed ad primum Philosophū, qui Theologus est, spectare videtur. Finis autem ac scopus physicæ scientiæ est animam cum suis asse-ctionibus, quæ variæ sunt, cognoscere: quarum quædam propriæ sunt, quædam communes ipsi animæ & corpori. Huiusmodi autem sunt, metus, audacia, gaudium, misericordia, amor, odium & huius generis similes: quibus aliquid patitur corpus & anima: Id quod certè perspici potest ex hominibus, quorum alii interdum a paruis quibusdam causis, isque obscuris ita concitantur, atque is, qui irascitur. Nonnulli etiam sunt, qui nulla re terribili obiecta, nec ullo imminente periculo perinde perturbantur ac ii, qui metu afficiū-tur. Hoc igitur cum ita sit, affectiones huiusmodi motiones esse animæ cum materia coiunctæ, consequens est. Ob eamque causam physici est, vel omnis animæ, vel alicuius, & talis cognitionem habere propositam. Attamen aliter Physicus & aliter Dialecticus una quanque harum affectionum definiet. Ut si quaeratur quid ira sit, hic libidinem ultionis, aut simile aliquid dicet: ille vero feruorem sanguinis, aut caloris eius, qui in corde inest. Atque sic alter materiam & genus reddit: alter rationem & formam, quæ necessaria est, si sit rei, quæ in huiusmodi materia consistit. Veruntamē is Physicus non est, qui in earum affectionum materia ita occupatus est, ut formam aut ignoret, aut relinquat: nec is etiam Dialecticus, qui solam reddit rationem, & formam earum declarat, sed qui utraque afsumit. Constat igitur neminem esse, qui circa materiæ corporisque affectiones versetur præter Physicum Philosophum. Is enim circa ea omnia, in quibus agendi patiendiquæ vis inest, versatur. In iis autem, quæ non huiusmodi sunt, non Physicus sed alius Philosophus occupatur, nempe Mathematicus & Metaphysicus Theologúsque : Quorum ille ea quæ separabilia à materia non sunt, mente abstrahit ac separat: hic vero essduntaxat contemplatur, quæ à materia separata sunt.
units.tr: Although every science is held in honour and esteem, one is nonetheless judged more excellent, greater and worthier than another, either because it is more certain or because it deals with more excellent things that arouse greater wonder. Hence the discourse on the soul is rightly placed in this kind of learning, and its knowledge seems to bring a great aid to every truth, and above all to the knowledge of nature, since the soul is, as it were, a certain fount and principle of living creatures and plants. For this reason the subject of this science is the soul itself, as it is infused into and joined with the body and is regarded as the cause of life and of the other vital faculties. But the knowledge and science of the soul when separated from the body (such as the mind of man may be) does not seem to belong to the natural philosopher, but to the first philosopher, who is the theologian. The end and aim of physical science, however, is to know the soul with its affections, which are various: some of them are proper to the soul, and some are common to the soul and the body. Such affections are fear, boldness, joy, pity, love, hatred and others of this kind, by which body and soul both suffer something. This can certainly be seen in men, some of whom are sometimes stirred up by small and obscure causes, and so are the angry ones. There are also some who, though nothing terrible is set before them and no danger threatens, are disturbed in the same way as those who are affected by fear. Since this is so, it follows that affections of this kind are movements of the soul joined with matter. For this reason it is the physicist's task to have as his aim the knowledge of the whole soul, or of some part of it, and of such affections. Yet the natural philosopher and the dialectician will define each of these affections in different ways. Thus if someone asks what anger is, the one will say it is a desire for revenge, or something similar, whereas the other will say it is the heat of the blood, or of the heat that is in the heart. So the one gives the matter and the genus, the other the reason and the form, which is necessary if the thing is to consist in such matter. However, he is not a physicist who is so occupied with the matter of these affections that he either ignores or leaves aside the form; nor is he a dialectician who gives only the reason and declares the form, but he who takes up both. It is clear, therefore, that no one concerns himself with the affections of matter and body except the natural philosopher. For he deals with all those things in which the power of acting and of being acted upon is present. But with things that are not of this kind, it is not the natural philosopher but another philosopher who is occupied, namely the mathematician and the metaphysician or theologian: the former abstracts and separates in the mind those things which are not separable from matter, whereas the latter contemplates only those things which are separated from matter.

units.la: CAP. I. Veterum Philosophorum sententiæ de animæ essentia.
units.tr: CHAPTER I. The opinions of the ancient philosophers concerning the essence of the soul.

units.la: VONIAM quod animam habet, id ab eo, quod inanimum est, motu distinguitur & sensu, nonnulli prifcerum Philosophorum id animam esse dixerunt, quod primū ac maximè mouet corpus. Sed quid istud esset non rectè intellexerunt. Quare Democritus animam esse ignem existimauit, eo quòd ex minutissimis partibus ille constet, & ex omnibus elementis maximè corpore vacet, moueátque primum cætera corpora, quæ natura constant. Idem Philosophus animam esse mentem dixit, putauitq; eā ex primis corporibus indiuiduis constare. In qua sententia Leucippus fuit. Propterea atomorū fluxū facillimè ad vniuersum peruadere, & cætera omnia mouere existimauit, eo ꝗ anima id esset, quod motum animantibus affert. Eodem pertinet id quod olim à Pythagoreis traditum fuit. Eorum enim nonnulli animam ea esse corpuscula dixerunt, quæ perpetuo motu in aëre cieri videntur. Fuerunt & alij, qui animam se mouere arbitrati sunt. Anaxagoras animam id etiam esse dixit, quod corpus mouet, sed eam à mente non distinxit, vt nec Democritus. Empedocles item vnum quodque elementorum animam esse tradidit. Eodem modo Plato in Timeo eam ex elementis esse fecit. Alij præterea animam numerum esse se-ipsum mouentem existimauerunt, propterea quod id anima sit quod & ad mouendum & cognoscendum vim habet. Anaxagoras autem eandem vim cognoscendi & mouendi meti attribuit, eamq; maxime rerum omnium principium esse posuit, eo cp[?] simplex sit, & ab omni corruptione libera. Thales etiam existimauit animam quiddā esse, quod mouendi vim habet. Ob eamq; causam in Herculeo lapide, quem Magnetem nominant, animam esse dixit, eo quod ad se ferrum attrahat. Diogenes quoque putauit animam esse aërem, propterea quod ipsum omnium corporum tenuissimum esse putauerit. Nam ea ex parte aërem esse principium dicebat, qua cognoscit cætera corpora: & qua ex parte tenuissimus est, ex ea vim mouendi obtinere. Heraclitus etiam animam principium esse censuit, & fluxilem exhalationem, ex qua constant omnia. Etenim omnia moveri & continenter fluere ille putauit, ut & plerique alij. Præterea Alcmæon idem de anima sensit, eámque immortalem esse dixit, propterea quòd rebus immortalibus, quæ semper moventur, similis sit, ut Soli, Lunæ, totíque cœlo, quod quidam diuinum esse existimauit. Quinetiam nonnulli animam aquam esse dixerunt, ut Hippon, qui in hanc sententia adductus fuit, eo quòd omnium rerum feme esset humidum. Quoniam item anima per scientiam cuncta comprehendit, eam ex omnibus elementis constare nonnulli existimauerunt. Alij vero eam esse unum ex eis, puta ignem vel aërem posuerunt. Quidam eandem constare ex contrariis asserebant: Alij calorem esse vel frigus: calorem (inquam) quòd vita quasi feruor esset: frigus vero, quoniam propter respirationem refrigerationemque anima Græcis ψυχὴ dicta est. Hæ sunt veterum philosophorum de anima sententiæ, quas Aristoteles hunc in modum ingeniose refellit, sumpto à motu exordio.
units.tr: Since that which has a soul is distinguished from that which is inanimate by motion and sensation, some of the older philosophers said that the soul is that which first and most of all moves the body. But they did not rightly understand what this was. Hence Democritus thought the soul to be fire, because it consists of the smallest particles and is most free of body among all the elements, and because it first moves the other bodies which consist of nature. The same philosopher said that the soul is mind, and he held that it consists of primary indivisible bodies. Leucippus was of this opinion. For this reason he thought that a flow of atoms penetrates easily into the whole and moves all other things, since the soul is that which brings motion to living things. To this belongs also what was once handed down by the Pythagoreans. For some of them said that the soul is those tiny bodies which are seen to be stirred perpetually in the air. There were also others who thought that the soul moves itself. Anaxagoras said that the soul is also that which moves the body, but he did not distinguish it from the mind, nor did Democritus. Empedocles likewise taught that each one of the elements is a soul. In the same way Plato in the Timaeus made the soul out of the elements. Besides these, others thought that the soul is a number moving itself, because the soul is that which has the power both of moving and of knowing. Anaxagoras, however, attributed the same power of knowing and moving to mind, and he laid it down that mind is the principle of all things most of all, because it is simple and free from all corruption. Thales also thought that the soul is something which has the power of moving. For this reason he said that in the Herculean stone, which they call the magnet, there is a soul, because it draws iron to itself. Diogenes too thought the soul to be air, because he judged it to be the most subtle of all bodies. For he said that air is the principle in that respect in which it knows other bodies, and that in so far as it is most subtle it obtains the power of moving. Heraclitus also judged that the soul is a principle, and a fluid exhalation from which all things consist. For he thought that all things are moved and flow continually, as did many others. Besides, Alcmaeon thought the same about the soul, and said that it is immortal, because it is like immortal things which are always in motion, such as the Sun, the Moon and the whole heaven, which some thought to be divine. Moreover, some said that the soul is water, as Hippon, who was led to this opinion because moisture is the seed of all things. Since the soul also comprehends all things by knowledge, some thought that it consists of all the elements. Others, however, held that it is one of them, namely fire or air.
