Some asserted that it consists of contraries; others that it is heat or cold: heat, I say, because life is as it were a glow; cold, however, because the soul was called by the Greeks psyche on account of breathing and cooling. These are the opinions of the ancient philosophers concerning the soul, which Aristotle refutes ingeniously in this manner, taking his beginning from motion.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAP. II.

units.la: Animam non moveri. Mentem hominis æternam esse.
units.tr: That the soul is not moved. That the mind of man is eternal.

units.la: VOBVS [?] modis id moveri potest, quod movetur: primo per se & sua vi: secundo per aliud & ex accidente. Posterior modus in priore est, & in eo quod per fe mouetur: vt Nauta in naui mouetur, sed nó eo modo super aquam quo ipsa nauis. Anima autem neutro modo moueri potest.Nā per se nó mouetur.Si enim per se mouetur,aut vno motuum genere,aut pluribus,aut omnibus moueatur,necesse est, Etenim motus genera quatuor sunt,mutatio ad locum, alteratio, accretio, & diminutio, quæ omnia in loco fiunt.Sed in anima nullus inest locus, in quo hæc motus genera fieri possint. Igitur anima per se non mouetur.
units.tr: A thing that is moved can be moved in two ways: first, through itself and by its own power; second, through another and by accident. The second way lies within the first, in that which is moved through itself. Thus a sailor is moved in a ship, but not in the same way over the water as the ship itself. The soul, however, cannot be moved in either way. It is not moved through itself. For if it were moved through itself, whether by one kind of motion, several, or all, it would have to be so moved, and there are four kinds of motion: change of place, alteration, increase, and diminution, all of which take place in a place. But there is no place in the soul in which these kinds of motion could occur. Therefore the soul is not moved through itself.

units.la: Quod si per se vique [?] sua non mouetur, profecto per aliud moueri non potest. At si perinde mouetur vt albor in corpore,& vt ea magnitudo, quæ trium cubitorum est: profecto motus eius non erit proprius & per se, sed alienus & externus. Mouentur enim hæres, sed ex accidente,& externo motu,propterea quod moueatur corpus, in quo insunt. Sed hoc modo anima moueri non potest,quoniá non in corpore est vt accidens. Quoniam etiam anima corpus mouet, cŏsentaneum est eam eodé motu cieri,(si mouetur)quo ipsum corpus. Sed animalis corpus loco mouetur.
units.tr: But if the soul is not moved through itself or by its own power, it certainly cannot be moved through another. And if it were moved in the way whiteness is moved in a body, or a magnitude that is three cubits long, then its motion would not be proper and through itself, but foreign and external. For such things are moved only accidentally and by an external motion, because the body in which they inhere is moved. But the soul cannot be moved in this way, since it is not in the body as an accident. Again, since the soul moves the body, it is consistent that, if it were moved, it would be moved by the same motion as the body itself. But the body of an animal is moved in place.

units.la: Quare anima loco mutabitur. Propterea si e corpore excedat, rursum in ipsum intrare poterit. Ex quo sequetur bruta animantia e morte excitari posse, & reuiuiscere. Quod proculdubio fieri non potest: quandoquidé eorum animæ non à corporibus separabiles sunt. Præterea si per se anima mouetur, violenter etiā & alieno motu moueri poterit. Nā quæ perse mouētur, ea etiā vi alienā, & motu externo cieri possunt, vt ex animantibus, quę violenter mouentur, scire licet. At anima alie-no motu cieri non potest, quoniam omnis motionis interius principium est. Cæterum quispiam forte obiecerit animam moueri dum ipsa dolet, timet, confidit, irascitur, sentit, & intelligit. Hæc enim omnia motus sunt. Sed huiusmodi motiones[?] affectionesq; non solius animæ sunt, quanuis ab ea prosi-cifcuntur sed hominis. Si enim anima ira-sceretur, etiam texere posset, & ædificare. At hoc præstare non potest. Igitur homo est, qui per animam miseretur, discit, cogitat, aliáque præstat negotia. Propterea nullus motus in anima est, sed ab ea proficiscitur o-mnis. Nec audiendus fuit Democritus qui globosas atomos secum vnà mouere omnia corpora existimauit, propterea quòd hæ nū-quam quiescant. Nam animal non sic ab ani-ma mouetur, vt nunquam quiescat: interdū ducitur, sed quodam sensus iudicio & appetitu, vel mente. Errauit etiam Plato in Ti-mæo, duas ob causas: Primùm quòd animam ex elementis constare, & harmoniæ partici-pem esse dixerit. Deinde quòd vniuersi ani-mam talem esse voluerit, qualis mens est, & non sentiens, aut appetens, quippe cùm harum motio non cõuersio sit. Nam vniuersitatis animam in orbem moueri censuit. Primum fi anima Mundi ex elementis constet, profecto magnitudo est. Et fi magnitudo est, illa non intelligit: Aut fi intelligat, nullus vnquam erit ei intelligendi cognoscendique modus & finis: quandoquidem punctorum, quae magnitudinis partes licet nominare, numerus est infinitus. Praeterea fi in orbem ver fatur vniuersi intellectus, profecto circulus est, cuius intellectio conuersio fit, oportet. Itaque vniuersi anima semper idem intelligit, quippe cum vniuersi conuersio perpetua fit, qua idem semper vertitur. Sed intellectionibus earum rerum, quae intelliguntur, certi sunt quidem fines propositi, quoniam alicu-ius causa sunt. Deinde quaecunque contemplamur, rationibus determinantur. Sed ratio num alia definitio est, alia ratiocinatio, alia demonstratio. At demonstrationes & a prin cipio fumutur, & finem sibi propositum habent nempe ratiocinationem, vel conclusionem. Quod fi intellectiones non terminan-tur, profecto ad principium non redeunt, sed medium & extremum semper aflumentes, re da in infinitum proficiscuntur. Definitiones etiam finitae sunt: Ergo quaecunque contemplamur, finita sunt. Ex quibus con-stat animam nec magnitudinem esse, nec per consequens ex elementis constare. Adde quod fi ex elementis ea constaret, corruptioni obnoxia effet. At homines mens non ex hominis femine oritur, sed extrinsecus corpori aduenit, ac quæda substantia est, quæ corrupi non potest. Si enim corruptioni obnoxia esset, profecto ab eo marcore, qui senectuti euenit, maximè corrumperetur. Idè enim tum ei contingeret, quod sensibus, qui tandem deficiunt, instrumentis eorum corruptis. Sed si senex homo talem haberet oculum qualis in iuuene est, haud dubiè non minus acriter, quàm iuuenis cerneret. Senectus igitur homini euenit, nō quòd anima quicquam patiatur, sed corpus, in quo ea inest. Ex quibus perspicuū est intelligendi vim & cogitandi nihil proprie pati, nec tandem corrumpi, quoniam mens quoddam diuinum est.
units.tr: Therefore the soul would change place. Hence, if it departed from the body, it could enter it again. From this it would follow that brute animals could be roused from death and come back to life, which undoubtedly cannot happen, since their souls are not separable from their bodies. Moreover, if the soul were moved through itself, it could also be moved violently and by a foreign motion. For things that are moved through themselves can also be set in motion by a foreign force and an external motion, as we know from animals that are moved violently. But the soul cannot be stirred by a foreign motion, since it is the inner principle of all motion. Yet someone might perhaps object that the soul is moved when it grieves, fears, trusts, is angry, perceives, and understands, for all these are motions. But such motions and affections belong not to the soul alone, although they proceed from it, but to the man. For if the soul were angry, it could also weave and build, and yet it cannot do these things. Therefore it is man who, through the soul, pities, learns, thinks, and performs other tasks. Hence no motion is in the soul, but all motion proceeds from it. Nor should Democritus have been heard, who thought that globular atoms, by moving together, set all bodies in motion, because they never rest. For an animal is not moved by the soul in such a way that it never rests; sometimes it is led, but by the judgement of the senses, by appetite, or by the mind. Plato also erred in the Timaeus, for two reasons. First, because he said the soul consists of the elements and is a participant in harmony. Second, because he wished the soul of the universe to be such as mind is, and not sentient or appetitive, since the motion of these is not a rotation. For he thought the soul of the universe is moved in a circle. First, if the soul of the world consists of the elements, it is certainly a magnitude. And if it is a magnitude, it does not understand; or if it understands, there will never be for it any mode or end of understanding and knowing, since the number of points, which may be named parts of a magnitude, is infinite. Moreover, if the intellect of the universe turns in a circle, it must certainly be a circle, whose understanding is its rotation. Thus the soul of the universe always understands the same thing, since the rotation of the universe is perpetual, by which the same thing is always turned. But for the acts of understanding of those things that are understood, there are certainly fixed ends of purpose, since they are for the sake of something. Further, whatever we contemplate is determined by reasons. But reason is one thing as definition, another as reasoning, and another as demonstration. Demonstrations are taken from a principle and have as their goal the reasoning or conclusion. If, then, acts of understanding did not have an end, they would certainly not return to the principle, but would proceed to infinity, always taking up a middle and an extreme. Definitions too are finite. Therefore whatever we contemplate is finite. From these things it is clear that the soul is neither a magnitude nor, consequently, made of the elements. Add to this that if it were made of the elements, it would be subject to corruption. But the mind of man does not arise from the seed of man, but comes to the body from outside, and is a certain substance which cannot be corrupted. For if it were subject to corruption, it would surely be most corrupted by that decay which comes with old age. For then it would suffer what happens to the senses, which at last fail when their organs are corrupted. But if an old man had an eye such as a young man has, undoubtedly he would see no less keenly than a young man. Old age therefore comes to man not because the soul suffers anything, but because the body, in which the soul is, does. From these things it is evident that the power of understanding and thinking properly suffers nothing, nor is it finally corrupted, since the mind is something divine.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CAP. III.

units.la: Animam nec harmoniam esse, nec numerum seipsum mouentem.
units.tr: That the soul is neither a harmony nor a self-moving number.

units.la: NON minus etiam ij[?] hallucinati sunt, qui animam esse harmoniam tradiderunt. Nam harmonia permistorum contrariorumque ratio est, aut compositio. Anima autem neutrum eorum esse potest. Non enim mistionis ratio est, quoniam eadem esset ratio mistionis elementorum in carne, osse, caeterisque corporis animalis partibus. At cuiusque partis diuersum esse temperamentum, satis perspicuum est. Quod si in singulis partibus corporis animalis eadem esset mistiomistionis ratio, profecto ipsum animal plu-rium animarum particeps esset: quandoquidem omnes eius partes ex permistis elementis conflantur. Itaque ab elementorum harmonia & temperatione[?] anima quid diuersum est. Omnium autem, quæ iam commemora-ta sunt, illud multo absurdissimum est, quod veterum nonnulli tradiderunt, nempe ani-mam numerum esse seipsam mouentem. Nam si anima seipsam moueret & mobilis esset, si-bi aduersaretur. Simul enim & mouens & motu esset. Deinde si ea numerus est, quan-titas erit, non autem animati corporis pars. At anima forma est & substantia[?] animati cor-poris. Præterea numerus ex vnitatibus constat, quæ vel corporis puncta sunt, vel ipsius animæ. Quod si animæ sunt, profecto animæ & corporis puncta simul in eodem loco e-runt: atque pun-ctum animæ corporis pun-ctum occupabit. Id quod esse non potest. Ac si duo puncta simul eodem in loco sunt, plura etiam ac infinita simul ibi esse possunt. Quorum enim locus indiuiduus est, & ea quæ in eo collocata sunt, indiuidua sint, necesse est. Ad hæc si punctorum numerus, qui in corpore inest, ipsa fit anima, quæritur cur non omnia corpora sint animata? Etenim in cunctis innumerabilia sunt puncta. At non omnia corpora esse animata, satis per-spicuum est. Metalla enim, lapides, & alia pro-pemodum infinita, non viuunt. Illa autem animata sunt, quæ partes habeht diffimilà-res, ut stirpes & animantia. Si denique anima numerus esset ex punctorum infinitate corporis constans, profecto nulla animata interirent. Nullo enim modo puncta à corpo-ribus seiunguntur, propterea quòd lineæ in puncta minimè diuidi possunt. Sed mortem esse animæ dissolutionem, separationemque a corpore, satis norunt omnes Naturæ interpretes. Quare anima non est numerus.
units.tr: Those who taught that the soul is a harmony have erred no less. For harmony is the proportion or composition of mixed and contrary things. But the soul can be neither of these. It is not the proportion of a mixture, since the proportion of the mixture of elements would be the same in flesh, bone and the other parts of the animal body. Yet it is quite plain that the temperament of each part is different. And if in the individual parts of the animal body the mixture were the same, the animal itself would surely partake of many souls, since all its parts are compounded of mixed elements. Therefore the soul is something different from the harmony and tempering of the elements. Of all the views already mentioned, however, the most absurd is that which some of the ancients taught, namely that the soul is a number moving itself. For if the soul moved itself and were movable, it would be at odds with itself: it would at once be both mover and moved. Again, if it is a number, it will be a quantity, and not a part of the animated body; but the soul is the form and substance of the animated body. Moreover, a number consists of units, which are either points of the body or points of the soul itself. If they are points of the soul, then the points of the soul and the points of the body will be together in the same place, and a point of the soul will occupy the place of a point of the body. This cannot be. And if two points are together in one place, many, indeed infinitely many, points could be there at the same time, for where the place is indivisible, the things placed in it must be indivisible too. Besides, if the number of points that are in the body is itself the soul, why is it not the case that all bodies are animated? For in all of them there are innumerable points. Yet that not all bodies are animated is quite plain: metals, stones and almost infinite other things do not live. Those things are animated which have dissimilar parts, such as plants and animals. Finally, if the soul were a number consisting of the infinity of points of the body, then surely nothing animated would ever perish. For points can in no way be separated from bodies, since lines cannot be divided into points at all. But that death is the dissolution of the soul, its separation from the body, all the interpreters of nature know well. Therefore the soul is not a number.

units.la: CAP. IIII. Animam ex elementis non constare:
units.tr: CHAPTER 4. That the soul is not composed of the elements:

units.la: LIM non etiam defuerunt, quibus animam ex elementis constare vi-sum fuit, eo quòd ea quæ sunt, sentiat & rerum unamquamque cognoscat. Nam dicebant simile à simili cognosci, atque propterea animam res ipsas esse, quæ sunt. Sed elementa non sola sunt in natura rerum: imò præterea infinitæ res aliæ, quæ ex his constant, propemodum in universo insunt. Propterea anima non res omnes cognoscet, sed ipsa duntaxat elementa, ex quibus constat. Præterea Deum, ho-minem, carnem, & os, quæ elementa nō sunt, anima non cognoscet: At verò hæc omnia apprehendit hominis anima. Deinde si ex elementis anima hominis constat, nullas certę categorias intelliget, præter eas, quæ ad substantiam pertinent. Atqui omnes categorias, & omnia quæ sunt, anima hominis per scientiam cognoscit. Eorum enim quæ sunt, quoddam genus ad substantiam spectat, quoddam ad quantitatem, aut qualitatem, aut ad quandam aliam categoriam. At dixerit nemo animam esse quantitatem, aut qualitatem, aut aliud categoriarum genus, præter substantiam. Quinetiam si ex elementis anima constat, cur non omnia quæ in inferiore Vniuerso insunt plane animam habent: cum nihil sit in natura rerum, quod non aut elementum sit, aut ex pluribus, aut denique ex omnibus constet? Sed in Mundo innumerabilia propemodum sunt inanimata corpora. Adhæc si anima ex elementis orta est, aliquid esse, quod eam contineat, necesse est: quandoquidem elementa rationem materiei obtinent, quæ non continet, sed continetur. Atqui quod continet, id principatum obtinet: Sed in animantium & stirpium genere nihil anima præstantius habetur, & maxime hominis mente, quæ omnium domina est. Itaque non anima continetur, sed corpus. Si denique quævis anima ex elementis constaret, illa profecto corpus esset. Atque sic duo corpora simul eodē in loco es-sent, quēadmodū si illa numerus esset, multa infinitaque puncta in uno loco consisterent: sed hæc absurda sunt. Quare ex his constat animam non eo ipso res cognoscere, quod ex elementis constet, nec verum esse eam quouis modo moueri. Cæterum quispiam quæret an tota anima intelligamus, sentiamus, cæteraque faciamus & patiamur? an vero quædam horum vnius partis animæ sint: quædam alius? Vtrum etiam vita in aliquo horum infit? an in pluribus? an etiam in omnibus? Nonnulli quidem animam esse diu duam posuerunt, cuius vna pars intelligit, alia sentit, & alia denique appetit. Sed si ex partibus constat, certè illa corpus est & continetur. At nihil est, quod animam continent. Imo vero corpus ab ea continetur. Nam é corpore separata ipsum corpus extinguitur & putrescit. Quæri etiam illud poterit de partibus animæ, quam tandem vim vna quæque in corpore habeat? Si enim totum corpus anima tota continet, conueniet etiam aliquid corporis ab vna quaque parte eius coti- neri. Id quod profecto fieri nó potest Nullâ enim corporis partem mens cotinet. Ex quo constat animam indiuiduam esse, atque nos per eam totam sentire, intelligere, moueri, cæteraque facere & pati. Quòd autem stirpes diuisæ viuant, & quædam animantia, quæ infecta dicuntur, etiam diuisa, eo fit quòd in vno quoque eorum anima insit, quæ non numero sed specie vna & eadem est. Quoniam igitur tota anima est indiuidua, fit vt omnes eius partes inter se eiusdem speciei sint, cuius tota est anima. Ex his perspicuum est, stirpes & animantia commune principium habere, nempe animam, sine quo nihil horū est, quod viuere possit.
units.tr: Once upon a time there were also those who thought the soul was composed of the elements, because it perceives the things that exist and knows each thing. For they said that like is known by like, and so the soul is the very things that exist. But the elements are not the only things in nature; indeed, countless other things, made up of these, are found almost everywhere in the universe. Therefore the soul would not know all things, but only the elements of which it is made. Moreover, the soul does not know God, man, flesh, and bone, which are not elements; yet the human soul grasps all of these. Again, if the soul of man were made of elements, it would understand no categories except those that pertain to substance. But the human soul knows by science all the categories and all that exists. For of the things that exist, one kind belongs to substance, another to quantity, or quality, or some other category. Yet no one would say that the soul is quantity, or quality, or any category other than substance. Furthermore, if the soul were composed of elements, why do not all the things in the lower universe have a soul altogether? For there is nothing in nature that is not either an element, or made of several, or finally made of all. Yet in the world there are almost countless inanimate bodies. Besides, if the soul arose from the elements, there must be something that contains it, since the elements hold the nature of matter, which does not contain but is contained. But what contains holds the first place; yet among living things of the animal and plant kinds nothing is considered more excellent than the soul, and above all the mind of man, which is mistress of all. Therefore it is not the soul that is contained, but the body. Finally, if any soul were composed of the elements, it would surely be a body. And so two bodies would be in the same place at once, just as if it were a number, many infinite points would stand in one place; but these things are absurd. Hence it is clear that the soul does not know things merely because it is composed of elements, nor is it true that it is moved in any way at all. Furthermore, someone will ask whether we understand, perceive, and do or suffer the other things with the whole soul, or whether some of these belong to one part of the soul and some to another. Also, does life inhere in one of these parts, or in several, or even in all? Some have indeed held that the soul is twofold, one part of which understands, another perceives, and another finally desires. But if it consists of parts, then surely it is a body and is contained. Yet nothing contains the soul; rather the body is contained by it. For when separated from the body, the body itself is extinguished and rots. The question can also be raised about the parts of the soul: what power does each one have in the body? For if the whole soul contains the whole body, it would follow that some part of the body is contained by each of its parts. This certainly cannot happen, for the mind contains no part of the body. From this it is established that the soul is indivisible, and that through it, as a whole, we perceive, understand, move, and do and suffer the other things. But that plants, when divided, live, and that some animals, which are called insects, also live when divided, happens because in each of them there is a soul which is not one in number but one and the same in species. Since, therefore, the whole soul is indivisible, it follows that all its parts are of the same species among themselves as the whole soul is. From these things it is plain that plants and animals have a common principle, namely the soul, without which nothing of these can live.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: Generalis definitio animæ.
units.tr: The general definition of the soul.

units.la: Osthæc quidnā anima sit, & eius communis ratio, explicandū nobis est. Itaque aut substantia est, aut accidens: quandoquidem eorum, quæ esse dicuntur plura non sunt genera. Sed anima accidens esse non potest, quoniā omnium animati corporis functionum facultatūmque illa fons est & principium: Anima igitur substantia est. Sed quod substatiæ genus sit, rursus quærendum est. Substantiarum enim alia materies est, & τοῦ[?] po-testate, quæ per se rei alicuius singularis naturam non habet: alia forma & species, quaquidem iā res singularis est, quoniā ipsius rei ratio existit, & perfectio. Tertium substantiæ genus ex materia constat & specie, ac naturale corpus est. Huiusmodi autem corporis duplex genus habetur, vnum quod eorum est, quæ viuunt: alterum aliorum, quæ inanimata sunt. At quæ viuunt ea nutriuntur, crescunt, & minuuntur: quoniam nutritio, augmentatio, & imminutio ab anima fiunt. Quare anima substantia sit, necesse est, perinde ac forma corporis naturalis, organici. quod viuere potest. Ex quo perspicuum est, huiusmodi substantiam perfectione esse naturalis corporis, quae vt scientia & habitus, vita vero, vt contemplatio. Ac quemadmodum scientia contemplatione prior est, ita anima vitam antecedit, & vitae causa est: quoniam anima est prima corporis physici organici entelechia: vita vero fecunda. Propterea anima non solum vitae animantis causa est, sed etiā somni & vigiliae atque aliarum affectionum quibus omne animal praeditum est. Vitae autem instrumenta, quibus anima vtitur, sunt partes corporis diffimilares, quarum vnaquaeque suum obit munus. Atq; ftirpiu[?] partes quamuis similares sint, instrumenta animae habentur, quarum fibrae & radices locum oris tenent: quoniam ad fe his partibus ipsae stirpes alimentum attrahunt. Prima igitur perfectio corporis naturalis organici anima est, fecunda vero vita. Propterea anima est natura & forma corporis physici & organici, atque motus & status eius principium. Id quod proculdubio ex cuius vis animalis partibus & membris intelligere quisque potest. Si enim oculus animal effet, profecto visus anima eius haberetur, propterea quod visus effentia oculi fit: ipse vero oculus illi[?] visus instrumentum. Quare sublata vi videndi, non oculus est, nisi nomine, qualis lapideus est & pictus. Id autem quod de parte disputatum est, ad totum corpus vitae particeps, referri expedit. Quare corpus, ex quo anima excesserit præterquam humanum non potestate viuised illud ipsum, quod anima præditum est. Cæterùm semen & fructus non actu animam habent, sed potestate, quoniam animalia, vt plantæ entelechian nondum obtinent. Anima igitur vt instrumenti perfectio est, & corporis naturalis forma: ipsum verò corpus instrumetum, quo illa functiones suas & munera exequi potest. Hoc igitur modo generatim quid anima sit, explicatum est.
units.tr: Now we must explain what the soul is and what its general nature is. It is either a substance or an accident, since the things said to exist do not form more than these kinds. But the soul cannot be an accident, since it is the source and principle of all the functions and faculties of an animate body. The soul is therefore a substance. But we must still ask what kind of substance it is. Of substances, one is matter, which, being only potential, does not by itself have the nature of any particular thing; another is form and species, which is already a particular thing, since the essence and perfection of the thing itself lies in it. The third kind of substance consists of matter and form together and is a natural body. Of such bodies there are two kinds: one of things that live, and the other of things that are inanimate. Living things are nourished, grow and diminish, since nutrition, growth and diminution come from the soul. The soul must therefore be a substance, just as the form of a natural, organic body that has the capacity to live is. From this it is clear that this kind of substance is the perfection of a natural body, in the way that knowledge and habit are perfections, while life is like contemplation. Just as knowledge comes before contemplation, so the soul comes before life and is its cause, since the soul is the first actuality (entelechy) of a physical, organic body, and life is the second. Therefore the soul is the cause not only of the life of an animal, but also of sleep and waking and the other affections with which every animal is endowed. The instruments of life that the soul uses are the dissimilar parts of the body, each of which performs its own office. And although the parts of plants are similar, they are regarded as instruments of the soul; their fibres and roots take the place of a mouth, since the plants draw nourishment to themselves through these parts. The soul, then, is the first perfection of a natural organic body, and life is the second. Therefore the soul is the nature and form of a physical and organic body, and the principle of its motion and rest. Anyone can surely understand this from the parts and members of any animal. For if the eye were an animal, its soul would certainly be sight, because sight is the essence of the eye, while the eye itself is the instrument of that sight. So when the power of seeing is taken away, it is an eye only in name, like a stone or painted eye. What has been said of a part should also be referred to the whole body, which shares in life. Hence a body from which the soul has departed, if it is not human, does not live even potentially, and so is no longer what it was, a body endowed with soul. Moreover, seed and fruit have a soul not in actuality but in potentiality, since, like plants, they have not yet attained their entelechy. The soul, then, is the perfection of the instrument and the form of the natural body; the body itself is the instrument by which the soul can carry out its functions and offices. In this way, then, what the soul is in general has been explained.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CAP. VI.

units.la: Specialis definitio animæ ex causis sumpta.
units.tr: A specific definition of the soul, taken from its causes.

units.la: E Q̄V E autem animæ definitio sol̄um rem esse, declarare debet, quemadmodum plurimæ defini-tiones explicant, quæ logicæ sunt, sed etiam causam exponat, necesse est. Proinde anima, id est, quo primum viuimus, sentimus, mouemur, & ratiocinamur. Vita autè, qua inanimū ab animato distinguimus multis modis dicitur, quoniā id viuit, in quo aliquid horum inest, nempe mens, sensus, motus ad locum, & statio in loco. Ac eo motu, qui in nutritione fit, & augmentatio dicitur, surpes viuere deprehenduntur.
units.tr: Now, the definition of the soul ought not only to declare the thing itself, as most definitions do that belong to logic, but it must also set out the cause. Accordingly, the soul is that by which we first live, sense, move, and reason. Life, by which we distinguish the inanimate from the animate, is said in many ways, since whatever has any one of these in it is said to live: mind, sense, motion from place to place, and standing in a place. And plants are found to live by that motion which takes place in nutrition and is called growth.

units.la: Neque enim solummodo sursum auge-scunt, & deorsum, sed etiā omni ex parte nu-triuntur, & eousque viuunt, quousque alimētum capere possint. Atque hæc quidem vis absque alis esse potest,id quod in ipsis stirpi-bus animaduerte licet, in quibus vis animæ nulla alia est.Cæteræ autem in animalibus ab hac separari non possunt. Itaque vita omni-bus,quæ nutriuntur,inest,nó sensus. Isenim est,per quem animal præcipue dicitur. Propterea quæ non loco per fe mouentur,fifen-tiunt,non solùm viuunt, sed etiam animalia sunt.At vero omnium sensuum[?] tactus inest primus cunctis animantibus. Ac quemadmo-dum vis nutriendi absque aliis animæ facul-tatibus esse potest,ita tactus absque aliis sen-fibus . Propterea quædam sunt animantia, quæ duntaxat vno sensu, tactuque prædita sunt.Cæterùm quæritur vtrum vnumquod-que horum,nimirum vis aliendi, sentiendi, ratiocinandi,atque mouendi,quæ in homine insunt,anima fit tota?an animæ pars seu fa-cultas? De vna quidem,quæ ratiocinandi vis est,facile respondetur, quoniam sola homi-nis forma est; reliquæ vero eius facultates sunt.Sed de vi sentiendi & nutriendi dubitā-dum est:quandoquidem nonnullę stirpes di-uisę viuere videntur,vt & ea animalcula,quę incifuras habent, quorum quælibet pars fe-&a sentit,& mouetur. Sed eorum omnium animam esse partibilem non cofequitur. Vi-uunt enim diuisæ stirpes, & huiusmodi ani-malium partes sentiunt. Propterea quodin vno quoque eorum yna actu infit anim:, & plures potentia. Ab hac autem sentiente animæ, ea quæ intelligit longè diuersa est: quoniâ intelligens à corpore separabilis est, sentiens verò à corpore non seiungi potest, sed simul cum moriente animali extinguitur aboletúrque, quoniam animati corporis pars est. Itaque ex his constat alicui animantium generi omnes inesse animæ facultates, vt hominum quibusdam nonnullæ, aliis vna duntaxat, quæ tactus est. Nam omnium sensuum propriorum primus est tactus, & maximè necessarius. Quare ipse solos animantia ab aliis distinguit, quæ inanimata sunt. Quoniam igitur anima, id est, quo primùm viuimus, sentimus, mouemur & intelligimus, ratio sit necesse est & forma, nō materies & subiectum. Nam materies potestate est ens, forma verò actus & perfectio animati corporis. Proinde anima non corpus est, sed eius ratio & perfectio, quod eam vim habet, vt animatum sit,
units.tr: For plants do not grow only upward and downward but are nourished on every side, and they live for as long as they can take in nourishment. This power can exist without the others, as can be seen in plants themselves, in which there is no other power of the soul. In animals, however, the other powers cannot be separated from this one. So life belongs to everything that is nourished, but not sensation; sensation is what chiefly makes an animal be called an animal. Therefore those things that do not move themselves from place to place, yet do sense, are not only alive but are also animals. Moreover, of all the senses, touch is the first that belongs to all living creatures. And just as the power of nourishment can exist without the other faculties of the soul, so touch can exist without the other senses. Hence there are some living creatures that are endowed with only one sense, touch. But the question is whether each of these powers, namely the power of nourishing, sensing, reasoning, and moving, which are in man, is the whole soul, or a part or faculty of the soul. About the power of reasoning, indeed, the answer is easy, since it alone is the form of man, while the rest are his faculties. But concerning the power of sensing and nourishing there is doubt, since some plants seem to live when divided, and likewise those tiny creatures that have segments, each part of which, when cut, senses and moves. Yet it does not follow from this that the soul of these creatures is divisible. For divided plants live, and the parts of such animals sense; this is because in each of them one soul is present in act and several in potency. But the sensitive soul is very different from the intellective soul: the intellective soul can be separated from the body, whereas the sensitive soul cannot be separated from the body, but is extinguished and perishes together with the dying animal, since it is a part of the animated body. Thus it is clear from these things that all the faculties of the soul are present in some kind of living creature, as some faculties are present in certain men, and in others only one, namely touch. For touch is the first and most necessary of the proper senses. Therefore touch alone distinguishes living creatures from those things that are inanimate. Since, then, the soul, that by which we first live, sense, move, and understand, must be a principle and a form, and not matter and a subject. For matter is being in potency, whereas form is the act and perfection of the animated body. Therefore the soul is not a body, but the principle and perfection of that body which has the power to be alive.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CAP. VII.

units.la: Quotnam sint animæ facultates.
units.tr: How many faculties the soul has.

units.la: TAQVE facultates animæ quin que sunt, nempe alendi, sentiendi, appetendi, loco mouendi & ratiocinandi: quarum ea quæ alendi est, sola in plantis reperitur: in animantibus brutis & hæc & illa quæ sentit, in hominibus omnes. Atque cui vis sentiendi est, ei etiam & appetendi. Appetitus nomine continetur cupiditas,ira & voluntas. Cui autem sensus est,ei etiá voluptas & dolor,perceptióq; rei jucundæ & molestæ. Nam quęcunque voluptatem capiunt & molestiam,ea cibum sentiunt ac pastum, quoniam tactu qui sibi sensus est,prædita sunt. Tactus autem siccorum, humidorum,calidorum,& frigidorum judex est,quibus omnia animalia vescuntur. Ea etiam quæ sapore prædita sunt,sub sensum tactus cadunt. Eis igitur quæ sintiunt[?] fames insit & sitis,necesse est,quoniam utraque affectio appetitio est. Nam fames rei calidæ & humidæ appetitus est:sitis vero frigidę & humidæ. Itaque ex his constat in animantibus, quæ tangendi vim habent appetitum incesse, & sine tactu eis nullu aliorum sensuum tribui,tametsi is absque aliis esse possit. Complura enim animantia sunt,quæ nullum habet visum, nec auditum, nec plane ullum odoris sensum. Eorum etiam quę sensum habent,in quibusdam vis mouendi e loco in locum inest,in aliis nulla:in paucissimis mes[?] & ratio. animantibus, quibus vis ratiocinandi tributa est,iis etiam caeterę facultates animę.
units.tr: There are five faculties of the soul, namely nourishing, sensing, desiring, moving from place to place, and reasoning. Of these, the nourishing faculty alone is found in plants; in brute animals both it and the faculty of sensing are present, and in humans all of them. And whoever has the power of sensing also has the power of desiring. The term appetite comprehends desire, anger, and will. Whoever has sensation also has pleasure and pain, the perception of what is agreeable and what is distressing. For whatever creatures take pleasure and displeasure, they perceive food and pasture, since they are endowed with the sense of touch. Touch is the judge of dry, moist, hot, and cold, by which all animals are sustained. Things endowed with flavour also fall under the sense of touch. Therefore hunger and thirst necessarily belong to those creatures that perceive, since both states are kinds of appetite: for hunger is the appetite for what is hot and moist, thirst for what is cold and moist. Thus it is established that in animals which possess the power of touch there is a desire for food, and that no other senses are granted to them without touch, although touch can exist without the others. For there are many animals which have no sight, nor hearing, nor indeed any sense of smell at all. Among those which have sensation, some possess the power of moving from place to place, others do not; and in very few there is also a faculty of reason. To those animals to which the power of reasoning is given, the other faculties of the soul also belong.

units.la: CAP. VIII. Quot sunt omnium animæ facultatum obiecta.
units.tr: Chapter VIII. How many objects does each faculty of the soul have?

units.la: QUONIAM autem obiecta facultates ipsas mouent, ea primum nos cognoscere & contemplari convenit. At eorum tria esse genera statuuntur, flatuuntur, quorum unum cibus, sive alimentum est: alterum sensile: tertium τὸ νοητόν, & intelligibile. De alimento primùm & de ge-neratione dicendum est, quoniam nutriendi vis & prima est, & ceteris animæ facultatibus convenit, ac communis causa est, qua cuncta viuentia vitam agunt. Huius autem nutricis facultatis officia duo sunt, nutrire & generare suum sibi simile. Etenim omnium officiorum ac munerum [?] eorum quæ viuunt (dom-modo omnibus suis partibus absoluta sint, & ex semine orta) nullum Naturæ aptius & accomodatius est, quàm sui simile procrea-re, ut animal aliud animal, stirps stirpem, ut æternitatem diuinitatemque quàm maximè possint, imitentur. Quoniam autem eà cun-cta animantia consequi nequeunt, propterea quòd nihil eorum, quæ interitura sunt, idem vnumque numero permanere potest, sit ut generatione speciei eorum conferventur, & permaneant. Propterea generatio & nutritio eiusdem facultatis animæ sunt. Cùm igitur alendi vis omnium animæ facultatum prima sit, de alimento differere convenit. Sed in primis quæri solet, utrum simile à simili, vel contrarium à contrario & ali, & augeri possit. Fuerunt enim nonnulli, qui simile à simili ali augerique negarunt, propterea quòd nihil à simili pati possit. Quicquid haud.dubiè mutatur semper in contrarium, aut in id quod interiectum est, mutetur, necesse est. Propterea cibus ab eo,quod alitur, quadam ex parte mutatur. Ad hoc autem respondendum est alimentum duplex esse, vnum quòd primùm ingeritur & crudum est, alterum, quod ad extremum nutrito corpori additur, & assimilatur, ac coctum est: atque vtroque animatum corpus nutritur. Quatenus crudus est cibus, ea ex parte contrarium a contrario alitur: sed quatenus coctus est, simile a simili. Quoniam autem nihil vitae expers alitur, profecto quod alitur id animatum fit, necesse est: atque alitur, quatenus animae est particeps. Itaque alimentum per se, nec ex accidente & fortuito ad animatum corpus refertur. Verum tamen alimenti diuersa ratio est. Quatenus enim quantum est eatenus vim habet id augedi quod alitur: sed quatenus quaedam substantia est, hac ex parte corpus nutrit. Valet autem ad generandum nō id quod alitur, sed quod simile est rei quae alitur. Nā quod alitur iam id in rerum natura est, & coferua-ri duntaxat postulat. Conferuatur autem per animam: ad quod munus obeundum alime-to ea vtitur. Itaque si ei, quod alitur, cibus de-trahatur, intereat necesse est. Caeterum ad nutritionem tria requiruntur: primum id quod nutritur: alterum quo nutritur: postremum quod nutrit. Hod autem anima est: id verò, quod nutritur, animatum corpus: aliud quo ipsum corpus nutritur, non solùm alimentū est, sed etiam calor: quoniam huiusmodi debet esse alimetum,ut concoqui possit. Con-coquitur autem a calore,qui concoquendi vim habet. Quare in animatis omnibus naturis calor infit necesse est. Sunt & aliae nutrientis animae vires, quibus quaelibet tum animantis,tum stirpis pars praedita est. Earum una est alimentum attrahendi:secunda ipsum retinendi:tertia concoquendi:postrema expellendi quod excrementum est. Quoniam autem a fine om[?]es res denominantur,finisque animae propositus est aliquid simile ei procreare,quod eam habet,haud dubie prima vis & principium generandi huiusmodi simile ipsa anima est.
units.tr: Since objects move the faculties themselves, it is fitting that we first know and consider them. It is held that there are three kinds of them: one is food, or nourishment; another is the sensible; the third is τὸ νοητόν [the intelligible], that is, the intelligible. We must first speak of nourishment and of generation, since the nutritive faculty is both the first and common to all the other faculties of the soul, and is the common cause by which all living things carry on their life. The offices of this nutritive faculty are two: to nourish and to generate what is like itself. For of all the functions and duties of living things (provided they are complete in all their parts and arise from seed), none is more suited and fitting to Nature than to produce what is like itself, so that animal may make animal and plant plant, and so imitate, as far as they can, eternity and divinity. But since not all living things can attain this, because nothing that is destined to perish can remain the same and one in number, it comes about that they are preserved and endure by the generation of their species. Therefore generation and nutrition belong to the same faculty of the soul. Since, then, the nutritive power is the first of all the faculties of the soul, it is fitting to discuss nourishment. But the first question usually asked is whether like can be nourished and increased by like, or contrary by contrary. For some have denied that like is nourished and increased by like, on the ground that nothing can be acted upon by its like. Whatever is undoubtedly changed must always be changed into its contrary, or into what lies between. Therefore food is in some respect changed by that which it nourishes. To this it must be replied that nourishment is twofold: one kind is that which is first taken in and is raw, the other that which is finally added to the nourished body, assimilated and cooked; and the animate body is nourished by both. In so far as food is raw, in that respect contrary is nourished by contrary; but in so far as it is cooked, like is nourished by like. Since, however, nothing devoid of life is nourished, it is necessary that what is nourished become animate, and it is nourished in so far as it partakes of soul. Thus nourishment is referred to the animate body per se, and not by accident and by chance. Yet the nature of nourishment is diverse. For in so far as it is a quantity, it has the power of increasing that which it nourishes; but in so far as it is a substance, in this respect it nourishes the body. Moreover, what is nourished does not serve for generating, but what is like the thing that is nourished. For what is nourished already exists in the nature of things and requires only to be preserved. It is preserved through the soul, and in discharging this office the soul uses nourishment. Therefore, if food is withdrawn from that which is nourished, it must perish. Furthermore, three things are required for nutrition: first, that which is nourished; second, that by which it is nourished; last, that which nourishes. The last is the soul; that which is nourished is the animate body; and the other, by which the body itself is nourished, is not only food but also heat, since food of this kind must be such that it can be digested. Now it is digested by heat, which has the power of digesting. Hence heat must necessarily be present in all animate natures. There are also other powers of the nutritive soul, with which every part of an animal or of a plant is endowed. One of these is the attracting of food; the second, retaining it; the third, digesting it; the last, expelling what is excrement. Since, moreover, all things are named from their end, and the proposed end of the soul is to produce something like that which possesses it, undoubtedly the first power and principle of generating such a like thing is the soul itself.

units.la: CAP. IX. De vi sentiendi.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX. On the power of sensing.

units.la: RIMUM autem de omni sensu comuniter, deinde speciatim de vnoquoque disputandum est. Sensus quidem tum fit, cum corpus aliquod afficitur,quoniam quaedam alteratio est. Quemadmodum autem duobus modis aliquid sentire dicitur,actu nimirum, & potentia:ita duobus modis sensus dicitur. unus enim sentiendi vis est:alter ipse actus & sentiendi operatio. Eodemque modo sentire actu dicitur,quo contemplari & intelligere actu. Sed hoc interest,quod ea, quae sensum mouent,extra sensum sunt,propterea quod rerum singularium & externarum sensus sit:sed quae intelligutur in ipso intellectu sunt:ut universalia,quorum scientia est. Itaque intelligere,cum volumus, nobis non licet, sed sentire nihil possumus nisi aliquod sensile adsit,quod sensum moueat. Id quod etiam euenit in artibus, & iis scientiis, quæ in sensilibꝰ rebus versantur, propterea quod sensilia sint singularia & exteriora. Itaque nō medicina erit absque copiam corpore animalis in quo fiat.
units.tr: First, we must discuss sense in general, and then each sense in particular. Sensation does occur when some body is affected, since it is a kind of alteration. Just as something is said to be sensed in two ways, namely actually and potentially, so sense is also said in two ways: one is the power of sensing, the other is the act itself and the operation of sensing. In the same way, to sense actually is spoken of in the same sense as to contemplate and to understand actually. But there is this difference: the things that move the senses lie outside the sense, since sense concerns particular and external things, whereas the things understood are in the intellect itself, like universals, of which there is science. Hence we cannot understand whenever we wish, but we can sense nothing unless some sensible object is present to move the sense. This also happens in the arts and in those sciences that deal with sensible things, because sensible things are particular and external. Hence there would be no medicine without a supply of an animal body in which it might be practised.

units.la: CAP. X. * Sensilium tria esse genera.
units.tr: Chapter 10. That there are three kinds of sensibles.

units.la: OSTHAEC de iis,quæ sensus mouent,ordine dicendum est:atque ita primum distinguere convenit. Itaque sensilium tria sunt genera,quorum duo per se sentiuntur,tertiu vero per aliud & ex accidente. Duorum autē illorū,quæ per se sentiuntur unum est uniuf-cuiusque sensus proprium:alterum commune omnium. Proprium sensile dicitur,quod suo sensu & non alio percipi potest: ut color obiici nō potest,nisi visui,nec sonus nisi auditui neque sapor, nisi gustatui. Tactus autē plures habet rei sensilis differentias, de quibus æque iudicat atque reliquorum sensuum vnusquisque de suo sensili,nec fallitur. Propterea visus cum obiectum suum colorem esse indicat,tum non errat, nec auditus cum sonum percipit. Verum enimuero quid sit coloratum,aut quid sonet,neuter sensus pro prie percipit,quoniam nullo sensu percipiūtur substantiæ.Communia vero sensilia sunt motus,quies,numer°[?],figura,magnitudo,quę nullius proprij sensus obiecta sunt propria. sunt & alia sensilia, quæ ex accidente cognoscuntur:cuiusmodi est corpus eo quod coloratum fit,propterea visu percipitur.Sic filius Petri videtur, quoniam albus est, vel niger, aut alio colore præditus.
units.tr: Next, I must speak in order about those things which move the senses, and it is fitting first to make this distinction. There are therefore three kinds of sensibles: two of them are perceived in themselves, and the third through something else and by accident. Of those two which are perceived in themselves, one is proper to each single sense, and the other is common to all. A proper sensible is that which can be perceived by its own sense and by no other: thus colour cannot be presented to any sense but sight, nor sound to any but hearing, nor flavour to any but taste. Touch, however, has several differences of the sensible thing, and it judges of these just as each of the other senses judges of its own sensible, and it is not deceived. Hence sight, when it declares that its object is colour, does not err, nor does hearing when it perceives sound. Yet neither sense perceives properly what is coloured or what sounds, since substances are perceived by no sense. The common sensibles, however, are motion, rest, number, figure, and magnitude, which are not the proper objects of any one sense. There are also other sensibles which are known by accident: of this kind is the body, insofar as it is coloured, and so it is perceived by sight. Thus the son of Peter is seen because he is white, or black, or endowed with some other colour.

units.la: CAP. XI. De visu & eius obiectis.
units.tr: CHAP. XI. Of sight and its objects.

units.la: Isvs[?] rei aspectabilis sensus est, cuius aspectabile color est, & aliud, quod nomine vacat. At color omnis eam vim habet id mouendi, quod actu & reipsa pellucidum est, vt lumen. Itaque singuli colores, vt cernantur, lumen requirunt. Quare primum de lumine differendum est,& quid sit explicandum. Est autem lumen perspicuum quiddam. Sed perspicuum duplex est: vnum quidem aspectabile non vi sua,& per se, sed per lumen: in quo genere aer est,& aqua, ac corporum multa ex his,quæ rara sunt & solida. Alterum autem perspicui genus lumen est, quod quidem alterius perfectio est & forma, ac velut color. Oritur lumen, aut ab igne, aut à cœlesti corpore,& simili splendido. Cætera autem aspectabilia, quæ nomine vacare dicuntur, nullo lumine, vt cernantur, indiget, sed in tenebris aspici possunt. Huiusmodi fut[?] ignita omnia, ac splendida:in quo genere fungus est & vitrum,atque piscium capita, & oculi, squam-mæ,lampyrides, ligna putria,& infinita pro pemodum alia,quibus nullus est proprius color. Sed ignis tum in tenebris,tum in cœlesti lumine cerni potest,propterea quòd lumen illius actu perspicuum est,alia autem quæ rara sunt,non nisi in tenebris lucent. Quoniā autem calor in primis ipsum aerem illustratum mouet,deinde aer oculo fit vt inter corpus movens & visum motum aliquod medium interponatur,quod perspicuum sit. Eadem est soni & odoris ratio,quæ de colore dicta fuit. Si quis enim instrumento sentiendi id,quod resonat,aut odorem efflat,app ofuerit, nullum certe sensum actu efficiet. Idem etiam tactui & gustatui contingit, tametsi non appareat.
units.tr: Sight is the sense of the visible thing, and its object is colour and something else that has no name. Every colour has the power of moving what is actually and in fact transparent, as light does. So individual colours need light in order to be seen. Hence we must first discuss light and explain what it is. Light is a kind of transparency. Transparency is twofold. One kind is visible not by its own power and in itself, but through light: air belongs to this kind, and water, and many bodies made of these, which are rare and solid. The other kind of transparency is light itself, which is the perfection and form of something else, like colour. Light arises either from fire or from a heavenly body or a similar luminous thing. Other visible things, which are said to have no name, do not need light in order to be seen, but can be seen in darkness. Of this kind are all things that are glowing and shining: in this class are fungus and glass, the heads of fish and eyes, scales, glow-worms, rotten wood, and almost countless other things that have no proper colour of their own. Fire, however, can be seen both in darkness and in heavenly light, because its light is actually transparent, whereas the other things, which are rare, shine only in darkness. Since heat first moves the air itself when it is illuminated, and then, in the case of the eye, some transparent medium comes to be interposed between the moving body and sight, the same reasoning holds for sound and odour as was said of colour. For if anyone brings near to the organ of sense the thing that resounds or emits an odour, he will certainly produce no sensation in act. The same thing happens with touch and taste, although it does not appear to be so.

units.la: CAP. XII. De auditu & sono.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII. On hearing and sound.

units.la: VPEREST vt de auditu & sono differamus. Est autem auditus vnus actu, alter potestate. Actu autem fit semper cum ictus alicuius corporis ex alio atque in alio fit. Ictus autem conflictus est, in aere qui sonum facit. Propterea sonus aeris impulsio est. Ex quo perspicuum est ab vno corpore sonum fieri non posse: quippe cum aliud fit oportet quod percutiat, & aliud quod percutiatur. Nec etiam quo,-
units.tr: Next we must discuss hearing and sound. Hearing is of two kinds, one actual and the other potential. It is always actual when the impact of one body comes from another and falls upon a third. An impact is a collision, and the sound is made in the air, so sound is an impulse of the air. From this it is clear that sound cannot arise from a single body, since there must be one thing that strikes and another that is struck. Nor is every impact of any bodies whatever a sound,

units.la: quorumcunque corporum pulsus sonus est, (non enim lana, aut spongia sonum efficit quantumuis percussa, sed eorum quæ solida sunt, lœuia, aut concaua. Aes quidem, quia lœue corpus est, sonum edit. Concaua vero reflexione sonant: quandoquidem post primū iđum alij complures posthac fiunt, quorum aer motus illinc exire non potest absque sono: & quemadmodū in aere illuminato colo res cernuntur, ita fonin aere & aqua audiuntur, propterea quod hæc duo corpora sunt elementorum media. Vt autem sonus in aere fiat solida corpora inter fe & cum ipso aere confligere oportet: id quod tum fit denique cum motus aer nec diffunditur neque dissipatur. Itaque fi aer derepente & vehementer, percutiatur, sonat. Hæc de sono generatim dicta sunt: de echo restat differere, quoniam sonus est, qui ex alio sono velut resilit, cum aer, qui ob cocauum locum, vbi terminatur, atque dissolui prohibetur, factus vnus quasi pila repellitur. Sonus enim semper reflectitur, & in eo perinde fit, atq; in lumine, quod semper refertur, alioqui non vbique luceret, sed extra eum locum, quo radij Solis perueniunt, tenebræ effunderentur. Audiendi autem instrumento inest etiam quidem aer natura insitus, qui simul impellitur, ac cum externus percussus in eum fertur. Itaque nō ex omni parte animal audit, neque omnem in partem externus aer agitatus fe insinuat, sed in eam,quæ animatum aerem habet, qui mo ueri possit.Huiusmodi autem auris est,aut aliud eius rationem habens.Atque ad audiendum externus aer expers soni esse debet,quo niam eius motio sonus est.Is etiam qui intus reconditus in auribus est. soni expers sit, ne cesse est, vt acriter omnes soni differentias sentiat.Ac non solum in aere audit animal, sed etiam in aqua, eo quod in ipsum interiorem aerem ea non intro[?]gat, nec intra aures,quoniamtortuosum sinnosumque iter habent.Quod si aqua in aures intret,non audimus,quemadmodum non etiam videmus dum membrana,quæ pupilla obducit,impedita est & ægrotat.Cum pręterea aer in auribus insitus agitatur,tum sonus fit,sed alienus:quoniam sonus est agitatio eius corporis,quod eo motu cietur,quo ea quæ resiliut a lævibus corporibus quæ percutiuntur.Sonorum autem differentiæ duæ sunt, vnus acutus,alter grauis.Acutus sensum breui tempore multum afficit: grauis parum & longo tempore auditum mouet.Hæc autem soni generatim dicuntur ex iis,quæ sub ca-stum cadunt.Atque de sono hæc generatim dicta sunt:de voce etiam differere conuenit.
units.tr: for wool or a sponge makes no sound however hard it is struck, but only bodies that are solid, smooth or hollow do. Bronze makes a sound because it is a smooth body. Hollow bodies sound by reflection, since after the first impact several others follow, and the air set in motion cannot escape from them without sound. Just as coloured things are seen in illuminated air, so sounds are heard in air and water, because these two bodies are the intermediaries of the elements. For a sound to be made in the air, solid bodies must collide with one another and with the air itself; this happens when the moved air is neither spread out nor dissipated. So if the air is struck suddenly and violently, it sounds. These things have been said about sound in general. It remains to discuss the echo, which is a sound that rebounds, as it were, from another sound, when the air, which is confined by a hollow place where it ends and is prevented from dissolving, is driven back as one mass, like a ball. For sound is always reflected, and it behaves just as light does, which is always reflected; otherwise it would not shine everywhere, but darkness would spread beyond the place reached by the rays of the sun. Now the instrument of hearing contains air implanted by nature, which is moved at the same time as the external air is struck and carried into it. So an animal does not hear from every direction, nor does the external air agitated in every direction insinuate itself, but only into that which contains animated air capable of motion. Such is the ear, or something having the same function. For hearing, the external air must be free of sound, since its motion is sound. The air shut up inside the ears must likewise be free of sound, so that it may perceive keenly all the differences of sound. And an animal hears not only in air but also in water, because the water does not penetrate the inner air or enter the ears, since they have a twisting and winding passage. If water enters the ears, we do not hear, just as we do not see when the membrane that covers the pupil is blocked and diseased. Moreover, when the air implanted in the ears is agitated, sound is produced, but it is an alien sound; for sound is the agitation of that body which is stirred by the motion by which the things that rebound from the smooth bodies that are struck are driven. There are two kinds of sound: one is high, the other low. A high sound strongly affects the sense in a short time; a low sound affects the hearing weakly and over a long time. These things are said of sounds in general, with regard to those that fall under the sense. Thus far on sound in general; it is fitting now to discuss the voice.

units.la: Est igitur vox animalis sonus:nihil enim inanimum vocale est.Veruntamen quædam similitudine quadam vocem fundere dicitur, vt lyra,& tibia,cæteraque inanima, quorum soni similes voces audiuntur. Multis autem animantibus non est data vox:quo in genere
units.tr: Voice, then, is the sound of an animal, for nothing inanimate is vocal. Nevertheless, by a certain resemblance, things such as the lyre, the pipe and other inanimate objects are said to pour out a voice, since sounds similar to voices are heard from them. Among many animals, however, voice has not been given, and in this class

units.la: ea maximè sunt, quæ sanguine carent, vt pi-sces, qui nullam vnquam emittunt vocem. At que in Achetro fluuio vocem fundere dicuntur, suis branchiis, aut aliquo eiusdem generis duntaxat resonant. Ea igitur animantia vocem emittunt, quæ aerem intus attrahunt: quoniâ tum sonus fit, cùm aliquid percutit, & aliud percutitur, atque in aliquo, quod quidem aer est, aut aqua. Ac vt linguæ vsus est duplex, vnus gustandi causa, alter sermonis, quorum gustatus necessarius est: sermo verò boni alicuius causa comparatus: ita aer, qui spirando attrahitur ad duo pertinet, & ad internum calorem, qui necessitatis est, & ad vocem, in quo bonum aliquod potius quàm necessitatem natura respexit. Quoniâ autem vox pulsus est aeris respiratione attra cti, guttur instrumentum eius sit, necesse est, quoniam pulmonis causa à natura datur. Respiratione enim eget ille locus, in quo cor cotinetur. Aerem enim cor intrare, cùm inspiratur, expedit. Cæterùm non omnis sonus animantium vox est. Lingua enim talem sonum efficere potest, qualis est tussis, quæ nō alicuius boni natura fit. Deinde vox semper cum imaginatione est: sed tussis sine imaginatione fit. Propterea vox sonus quidam est alicuius rei interpres. Neq; verò respirationis pulsus eodem modo vox est, quo tussis, in qua fit aeris cofliclus cum arteria, id quod ex eo intelligi potest, quia is vocem emittere nō potest, qui spiritū ducit, sed is qui ipsum retinet. Ex quo etiam pespicuum est cur vox piscibus non data sit. Neque enim guttur habet, propterea quòd spiritum non ducunt, nec respirant.
units.tr: are chiefly those that lack blood, such as fishes, which never emit any voice. And in the river Achelous they are said to pour out a voice; they only resound with their gills or something of the same kind. Those animals therefore emit a voice which draw air inward, since sound is made when one thing strikes and another is struck, and this happens in something that is air or water. And just as the tongue has a double use, one for tasting and the other for speech, of which tasting is necessary, while speech is provided for some good, so the air drawn in by breathing serves two purposes: the internal heat, which is a necessity, and the voice, in which nature has regarded some good rather than necessity. Since voice is an impulse of air drawn in by respiration, the throat must be its instrument, and it is given by nature for the sake of the lungs. For that place in which the heart is contained needs respiration; it is useful for the heart to take in air when it is breathed in. But not every sound of animals is a voice. The tongue can produce a sound such as a cough, which is not made by nature for any good. Moreover, voice always involves imagination, but a cough is made without imagination. Therefore voice is a certain sound that expresses something. Nor is the impulse of breathing a voice in the same way as a cough, in which air collides with the windpipe; this can be understood from the fact that one who draws in breath cannot emit a voice, but one who holds it can. From this it is also clear why voice was not given to fishes: they have no throat, because they do not draw in breath and do not respire.

units.la: CAP. XIII. De olfactu & odore.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIII. Of smell and odour.

units.la: DE odore & odoratu nobis etiam disputandum est: sed non perin-de perspicuum est quid sit odor, vt quid sonus, quid lumen, quidve color. quoniam odoratus nō in nobis acer est. Remissè enim homo olfacit, nec quicquā eorum quæ odorem spirat sine molestia, aut voluptate percipit, quòd in eo non sit subti-lis hic sensus. Acquemadmodum animantes, quibus oculi sunt duri, vt cancri, sine his duabus affectionibus cernere non possunt, eo quòd imbecillum habeant visum: sic etiā in-becilliter odores genus humanū distinguit. Videtur autem odoratus quādam habere co-gnationem cum gustatu, propterea quòd o-dorum nomina ex saporum nominibus de-sumpta sint. Vt enim sapor alius est dulcis, alius amarus, sic odorum alij suaues, alij tetri & ingrati, sed gustatus in nobis acrior est quàm olfactus, propterea quòd ille tactus[?] quidem fit, qui in homine est acerrimus. Cùm enim cæteris sensibus à brutis longè multùm-que superemur, tamen iudicium tactus in nobis acrior est quàm in plerisque eorū. Itaque belluis homo prudentia antecellit: hinc homines ex sensu tactus excellelleti [?] ingenio atque tardo praediti sunt, nec ex vllo alio. Propterea quibus praedura caro est, ij tardo sunt ingenio, quibus contrà mollis, ingeniosi. Iam vero quemadmodum auditus est rei quae audiri, & non audiri potest, & visus aspectabilis & non aspectabilis, & quisque similiter sensuum, ita odoratus est rei odoriferae, & inodorae. Inodorum autem partim eo dicitur, quod omnino odore caret, partim quia illum habet exiguum. Fit etiam odoratus per medium aerem, aut aquam ut visus, & auditus. Propterea odorem sentiunt aquatiles bestiae, tu aliae sanguine praeditae sunt; tu exangues, sicut & quae in aere versantur, quarum nonnullae procul ad pastum odore illectae commeant. Caeterum non eodem modo animantes odorem percipiunt, sed aliae respirando, ut quae pulmonem habent, & sanguine sunt praeditae: aliae non respirando, ut quae in aqua versantur, quaeque pulmone carent, & exangues sunt: quarum quaedam pereunt ab iis rebus quae tetri acrisque odoris sunt, cuius generis est bitumen, sulphur, aliaque similia. Nec quoque vllum animal olfaciet, si odor vel procul remotus sit, vel si res odorifera naribus superponatur: quandoquidem nullus fit sensus actu, si res sentienda instrumento superponatur, praeter tactum, cuius medium una cum suo instrumento coiungitur. Instrumentum autem odoratus in animantibus eodem modo differre videtur,quo molles oculi à duris.Molles enim palpebris,quasi inuolucris sepiuntur,quæ nisi aperiantur, cernere non possunt:sed eis animatibus,quæ duros habent oculos,nullę à natura datę sunt palpebræ. Eodem modo odorandi instrumentum in animantibus, quæ spiritum non ducunt,nullo velamine tectum est: iis autem quæ respirant,quoddam operculu[?]natura largita est,quod,cum ea respirant,aperitur,venis meatibusque distentis. Idcirco in aqua animantia, quæ spiritum ducunt, olfacere non possunt,quoniam respirando odorem percipiunt. Differt autem odor à sapore, quòd illę rei aridæ obiectum sit, hic vero rei humidæ.
units.tr: We must also discuss odour and the sense of smell. Yet it is not as plain what odour is as what sound, light or colour is, since our sense of smell is not keen. Man smells rather weakly, and he perceives nothing that gives off an odour without discomfort or pleasure, because this sense is not refined in him. Just as animals whose eyes are hard, such as crabs, cannot see without these two affections, because their sight is weak, so the human race also distinguishes odours feebly. Smell appears to have some kinship with taste, since the names of odours are taken from the names of flavours. For just as one flavour is sweet and another bitter, so some odours are pleasant and others foul and unpleasant. But taste is keener in us than smell, because the sense that is most acute in man is touch. For although we are far surpassed by the brutes in the other senses, our power of touch is keener than in most of them. Hence man excels the beasts in prudence, and men endowed with a sense of touch that is delicate have a sharp wit, while those with a coarse sense are dull. Those whose flesh is very hard are dull of wit, and those whose flesh is soft are clever. Now, just as hearing is of a thing that can and cannot be heard, and sight of a thing that can and cannot be seen, and likewise each of the senses, so smell is of a thing that has an odour and of one that is odourless. Something is called odourless either because it has no odour at all or because it has only a faint one. Smell also operates through the air or water, as sight and hearing do. For this reason aquatic creatures perceive odour, as do other creatures that have blood, and also the bloodless ones, such as those that live in the air, some of which come from afar, drawn to their food by smell. However, animals do not all perceive odour in the same way: some do so by breathing, as those that have lungs and blood; others do not breathe, as those that live in water and lack lungs and are bloodless. Of the latter, some are destroyed by things of a foul and sharp odour, of which kind are pitch, sulphur and other such things. Nor will any animal smell if the odour comes from far away, or if the odorous thing is placed right over the nostrils, since no sensation occurs in act when the object to be perceived is placed upon the organ, except in touch, whose medium is joined to its organ. Now the organ of smell in animals seems to differ in the same way as soft eyes differ from hard ones. For soft eyes are enclosed by eyelids, as by coverings, and cannot see unless these are opened; but those creatures that have hard eyes were given no eyelids by nature. In the same way, the organ of smell in creatures that do not draw breath is uncovered by any veil; but those that breathe have been given by nature a kind of lid, which is opened when they breathe, the veins and passages being distended. Hence creatures in water that draw breath cannot smell, since they perceive odour by breathing. Odour differs from flavour in that the former is the object of a dry thing, the latter of a moist thing.

units.la: CAP. XIIII. De gustatu & sapore.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIIII. Of taste and flavour.

units.la: VOD[?] gustari potest,id quiddam tractabile est.eoque fit ut non sentiatur per externū medium. Nullo enim huiusmodi interiecto medio tactus percipit.Id autem corpus, in quo tanquam in materia est sapor, qui gustatur, humidum existit,propterea tactus quoddam obiectum est. Nihil igitur siccum mouet saporis sensum. Omne autem falsum corpus, etsi actu siccum est, potestate humidum exi-stit,eo quod facilę liquari possit vimque ha-bet beat ad liquorem gignendum in lingua.Pro-pterea gustatum mouet. Atque quemadmo-dum visus rei aspectabilis, & non aspectabi-lis est (tenebrae enim non aspectabiles sunt, etsi earum iudicio in visu consistit, nec praeterea res splendida cerni potest, tametsi in vi-sum cadat): sic auditus iudicium sonoru est & silentij, quorum illi audiuntur, hoc non au-ditur, nec vehementissimi soni, qui sic audi-tum labefaciunt[?], ut res splendida visum: gu-status etiā rei est, quæ gustari potest, & alius, quæ gustatum mouere nequit, quale id est, quod vel nullum habet saporem, vel malum & tetrum, ac quod hunc sensum labefactat. Cùm igitur quod gustari potest, sit humidu, certe gustatus instrumetum nec actu, nec po-testate humidum esse oportet. Ab eo enim quod gustatur quodammodo afficitur. Instrumentum autem gustatus non humidum esse intelligi potest ex lingua, quæ si admodum humida sit aut valde arida, saporem non sentiet, propterea quibus per ardetes febres lingua redditur sicca, iis omnia videntur amara, propterea quod in his biliosus humor abū-dat. Demum saporum genera ita se habent, ut colorum.Nam dulce & amarum simplicia sunt contraria, etsi dulci inhæret pingue, a-maro salsum, quibus interiecta sunt media, nempe acre, austerum. acerbum, & acidu. Hę[?] ferè sunt omnes saporum differentię, & omnia quæ gustatum mouent, & afficiunt.
units.tr: What can be tasted is something tangible, and so it is not perceived through an external medium, since touch perceives it without any such medium in between. The body in which the flavour that is tasted resides, as in its matter, is moist, and for that reason it is an object of touch. Nothing dry, therefore, moves the sense of taste. Every salty body, though it is actually dry, is moist in potency, because it can easily be dissolved and has the power to produce liquid in the tongue; therefore it moves the taste. And just as the object of sight is both visible and not visible (darkness is not visible, though judgement of it rests with sight; nor can a bright thing be seen, though it falls upon the sight), so the judgement of hearing concerns sound and silence, of which the former is heard and the latter is not; nor are the most violent sounds, which so damage hearing, its object, any more than a bright thing is the object of sight. So too taste has as its object what can be tasted, and there is something else which cannot move the taste, such as what has either no flavour at all or a bad and foul one, which weakens this sense. Since, then, what can be tasted is moist, the organ of taste must be neither actually nor potentially moist, for it is affected in some way by what is tasted. That the organ of taste is not moist can be seen from the tongue: if it is very moist or very dry, it does not perceive flavour. That is why, in those whose tongue is made dry by burning fevers, everything seems bitter, because bilious humour abounds in them. Finally, the kinds of flavour relate to one another as colours do. For sweet and bitter are simple contraries, although fatty is joined to sweet and salty to bitter, and between them lie the intermediates, namely sharp, astringent, tart and sour. These are nearly all the differences of flavour, and all the things that move and affect the taste.

units.la: CAP. XV. De vi tangendi.
units.tr: CAP. XV. On the power of touch.

units.la: Raedictorum sensuum sin-guli unius repugnantię esse videtur, ut visus rei albæ & nigræ, auditus soni acuti & grauis, gustatus saporis dulcis & amaritsed[?] tactus multa-rum repugnantiarum est, quarum alia calida & frigida, alia sicca & humida, dura, & mollis, & si qua sunt huius generis. Quare cum complura sint, quæ tactum mouent, sequitur ipsum tangendi sensum non unum esse, sed multiplicem. Sed hæc facile diluetur dubitatio, si in aliis sensibus etiam plures repugnantias esse, quis animaduertat. Nam in voce nō solūm sonus est acutus & grauis, sed etiā magnus & paruus, lenis & asper. Coloris etiam plures sunt differentiæ. Non enim solūm al-bor est, & nigror, sed rubor, & cæteri inter-iecti colores, & mixti, sed quidnam sit tactui unum generale subiectum, ut sonus auditui, perspicuum nobis non est. Medium autem quo sua apprehendit obiecta sensus tangendi unà cū suo instrumento copulatum est, quod quidā animantibus sanguine præditis caro est, in a-liis autem, quæ imperfecta sunt, aliquid car-nis rationem obtinens. Atque quemadmodū aer & aqua ad visum, auditum, & odoratum se habent, ita caro & lingua ad tactum & gu-statum. Sed hoc interest quòd illi tres sensus non afficiantur fi eorum instrumenta & sensilia fe cotingant,veluti visus nihil percipiet fi extremis oculorum aliquod album,aut nigrum superponatur. Sed hi nimirum tactus & gustatus id sentiunt quod eorum instrumentis superponitur: quoniam illa pars corporis in qua vis inest tagendi interior est, & cum medio iunda[?].Itaque caro medium eius est,quod tactum mouere potest.Ea autem quæ tactum mouet corporum naturalium, differentiæ sunt,nempe calidum,frigidum, ficcu, & humidum. Instrumentum vero quo huiuf modi qualitates percipiuntur, & in quo sensus tactus est situs, tale potestate esse debet, qualia actu sunt ea,quæ ipsum mouent tactu: quoniam omne agens in id agit quod potentia tale,est quale id quod actu agit. Propterea quemadmodum id quod nigrorem,vel alborem sensu percepturu est, nec album actu aut nigrum esse oportet, sed duntaxat tale potentia: ita etiam tactus organum,nec calidu actu,nec frigidum esse debet. Eadem est ratio aliorum & sensuum & fenforiorû. Quin etiam ut visus est rei aspectabilis & non aspectabilis,cæterique sensus contrariorum obiectoru, sic tactus rerum est tractabilium, & non tractabilium.Id autem non tractabile est, quod exiguam admodum differentiam qualitatum tractabilium habet, quale aer est.Verum tamen tractabilium qualitatum exuperantiæ tactum lædunt: in quo genere sunt affectiones quae vim corrumpedi corpora habent, nempe calor, frigus, humor, ariditas, & caeteras tractabiles, quando modum excedunt.
units.tr: Each of the other senses seems to have a single contrariety: sight, of white and black; hearing, of high and low pitch; taste, of sweet and bitter. Touch, however, has many contrarieties: some are hot and cold, others dry and moist, hard and soft, and any others of this kind. Therefore, since several things move the sense of touch, it follows that the sense of touching is not one but many. But this doubt is easily resolved if one considers that in the other senses too there are many contrarieties. For in sound there is not only high and low, but also loud and soft, smooth and harsh. Colours too have many differences: there is not only white and black, but red and the other intermediate and mixed colours. Yet what the one common subject of touch is, as sound is of hearing, is not clear to us. The medium by which the sense of touch apprehends its objects is joined together with its instrument; in some animals endowed with blood this is flesh, while in others, which are imperfect, it is something having the nature of flesh. And just as air and water stand in relation to sight, hearing and smell, so flesh and the tongue stand in relation to touch and taste. But there is this difference: the first three senses are not affected if their instruments are touched by sensible objects; for example, sight perceives nothing if something white or black is placed on the outer surface of the eyes. Touch and taste, however, sense exactly what is placed upon their instruments, since that part of the body in which the power of touching resides is interior and is united with the medium. Thus flesh is the medium of that which can move touch. The qualities of natural bodies that move touch are differences such as hot, cold, dry and moist. The instrument, however, by which qualities of this kind are perceived, and in which the sense of touch is situated, must be in potency such as those things are in act which move it by touch; for every agent acts upon that which is potentially such as the thing acting is in act. Therefore, just as that which is to perceive black or white by sight must be neither actually white nor actually black, but only potentially such, so the organ of touch must be neither actually hot nor actually cold. The same reasoning applies to the other senses and their organs. Moreover, just as sight is of visible and invisible things, and the other senses of contrary objects, so touch is of tangible and intangible things. That is intangible which has only a very slight difference of tangible qualities, as air is. Yet excesses of tangible qualities injure touch; in this class are the affections which have the power of corrupting bodies, namely heat, cold, moisture, dryness and the other tangible qualities when they exceed their measure.

units.la: CAP. XVI.
units.tr: CAP. XVI.

units.la: Cur sensus non sentiunt?
units.tr: Why do the senses not sense themselves?

units.la: MNE genus sensuum id esse dicitur quod vim habet suscipiendi rerum sensilium formas & species absque eorum materia, perinde atque cera aurei annuli signum absque auro capit. Eodemque modo vnusquisque sensus ab obiecto afficitur, quod aut colore, aut sapore, aut sono, aut odore, aut aliqua tractabilium qualitatum praeditum est. Id quod sane non fit quatenus vnumquodque horum omnium est haec vel illa substantia, sed quia qualitatem habet & ratione vnumquenque sensum afficiendi. Sentiendi autem instrumentum, id est, in quo talis haec vis reperitur. Atque quod sentit, id quaedam magnitudo est, non ratio facultatis sensitricis: nam sensus non magnitudo est, sed illius vis & ratio atque forma. Ex quibus perspicua est causa, cur sensilium exuperatiae sensuum instrumenta labefactant.
