Nam si in sensus fede instrumentoque vehementior facta fit motio ab obiecto, haud dubie instrumenti ratio ac forma in qua constitit sentiendi vis, dissoluitur. Illud hinc etiam perspicuum est quamobrem stirpes
units.tr: Is that said to be a kind of sense which has the power of receiving the forms and species of sensible things without their matter, just as wax takes the impression of a gold ring's seal without the gold? Each sense is affected by its object, which is either coloured, or flavoured, or sounding, or odorous, or endowed with some tangible quality. Certainly this does not happen insofar as each of these things is this or that substance, but because it has a quality and a manner by which it affects each sense. The instrument of sensing, however, is that in which such a power is found. What senses is a certain magnitude, not the reasoned principle of the sensitive faculty, for the sense is not a magnitude but its power, reason and form. From these points the cause is clear why excessive sensibles break down the instruments of the senses. For if a more violent motion is produced by the object in the seat and instrument of the sense, the structure and form in which the power of sensing resides undoubtedly dissolves. This too is plain from this: why plants

units.la: C.11. l. 2. de anima.
units.tr: Ch. 11, bk. 2, On the Soul.

units.la: CAP. XVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVII.

units.la: An praeter quinque iam expositos sensus, sitne alius quispiam?
units.tr: Whether, beyond the five senses already set out, there is any other sense.

units.la: NON autem plures esse sensus pro priós quinque, visu (inquam) auditu, odoratu, gustatu, & tactu, ex his intelligi potest. Primum omnibus sensibus praeditae sunt perfectae animantes, quae duntaxat quinque habent. Quibus si sensus aliquis deesset, eis quoque instrumentum aliquod deesse oporteret, quoniam id sentiendi principium est. Atqui perfectae animantes omnibus sentiendi instrumentis praeditae sunt. Propterea nullo sensu caret. Hinc ne talpa quidem excipitur, quamuis non videat, quoniam videndi instrumentis nō orbatus est. Oculos enim sub cute ipsum habere satis cōstat. Praeterea omnis sensus per interiectum corpus medium sentit. At vero nos utrunque habemus, & ipsum (inquam) quod cum instrumento sentiendi copulatum est, per quod quidem tangentes qualitates, quae tactum movet, nos percipimus: & etiā aliud externum, quo procul quaedam sentimus. Hoc autem posterius duplex est, unum aer, alterum aqua, per quae plura sensilia, ut color, sonus, & odor percipi possunt, quoniam utrunque medium pellucidum est. Ex his nanque duobus elementis[?] sensuum huiusmodi obiecto-rum instrumenta constant: propterea pupilla naturam aquę imitatur: auditus instrumentum, & odoratus aereum est. Ignis autē nullius instrumenti sensuum est, sed omniū communis. Quadoquidem nihil sine calore vim sentiedi habet. Terra item aut nullius sensorij est, aut certē in eo consistit, quod tangendi vim habet. Itaque constat ex his non plures proprios sensus esse, quàm quinq; expositos, quorum cuique suum est instrumentum. Nec vero fieri potest ut ullum sit organum com-munium sensilium, nempe motus, quietis, figurae, magnitudinis & numeri, quoniā uno-que sensu( sed ex accidente ) ea percipimus. Etenim ea omnia motu cognoscimus, & motum visu. Motu autem magnitudo cognoscitur, ut etiam figura: quippe cum figura sit, in magnitudine quadam. Quod etiam quiescit, id priuatione motus percipitur: numerus ite naturę continuatę cohærentisque priuatio-ne. Huc accedit quòd si cuius vis sensilium communium ullus esset proprius sensus & organum, fieret ut rerum essentias perciperet. Atqui nullus est sensus, cui ea vis sit illas sentiendi, sed ex accidente percipiuntur. Propterea pterea nō alia ratione Cleonis filium cernimus, nisi quia ipsi album esse, aut nigrum, aut alio colore praeditum accidit. Sed hoc loco quaeri poterit, quid ita plures sensus, non vnus tantum nobis datus sit ad percipiendum ea quae communia sensilia sunt. Haud dubie hoc factum oportuit vt a propriis sensilibus recte ea distinguerentur. Nam si magnitudine perinde atque colorem solo visu percipere-mus, certe nulla re ipsam magnitudine a colore discrepare cognosceremus.
units.tr: That there are not more senses than the five proper ones, sight (I mean), hearing, smell, taste and touch, can be understood from the following. First, perfect animals are endowed with all the senses, and they have only these five. If any sense were lacking to them, they would also have to lack some organ for it, since the organ is the principle of sensing. But perfect animals are equipped with all the organs of sense. Therefore they lack no sense. Hence not even the mole is an exception, though it does not see, since it is not deprived of the organs of sight. For it is quite certain that it has its eyes beneath the skin. Moreover, every sense perceives through an intervening body. Now we have both: the organ itself, which is joined to the instrument of sensing, through which we perceive the qualities that touch moves; and also something external, by which we sense certain things from a distance. This latter is twofold, one being air and the other water, through which many sensible things, such as colour, sound and odour, can be perceived, since both are transparent media. For the instruments of senses of this kind of object are made of these two elements: thus the pupil imitates the nature of water, while the organ of hearing and of smell is of air. Fire, however, belongs to no sense-organ but is common to all, since nothing has the power of sensing without heat. Earth likewise either belongs to no sense or certainly consists in that which has the power of touch. Thus it is clear from these that there are not more proper senses than the five set out, each of which has its own organ. Nor indeed can it be that there is any organ of the common sensibles, namely motion, rest, shape, magnitude and number, since we perceive these by no single sense but incidentally. For we know all these things by motion, and motion by sight. Magnitude is known through motion, and likewise shape, since shape is a certain kind of magnitude. What is at rest is perceived by the privation of motion; and number, by the privation of continuous and cohering nature. Moreover, if the power of the common sensibles had some proper sense and organ, it would follow that it perceived the essences of things. But there is no sense to which this power of sensing them belongs; they are perceived incidentally. Therefore we perceive the son of Cleon in no other way than because it happens to him to be white, or black, or endowed with some other colour. But here it may be asked why there are several senses, and not just one given to us for perceiving those things which are common sensibles. Doubtless this was necessary, so that they might rightly be distinguished from the proper sensibles. For if we perceived magnitude by sight alone, just as we perceive colour, we would surely not know that magnitude differs from colour in any respect.

units.la: CAP. XVIII. An sit sensus communis.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVIII. Whether there is a common sense.

units.la: Q[?]VONIAM autem nos & videre & audire percipimus, id profecto aliquo sensu fieri videtur. Sed visus nō est, neque auditus. Visus enim se videre nō percipit, nec auditus se audire. Eadem est ratio caeterorum sensuum. Quare alius sit oportet, qui & ipsum percipiat visus, & ipsius visus obiecti, qui color est. Eiusdem enim subiecti coloris duo non sunt sensus. Igitur visus nullo sensu alio proprio se videre percipit. Nam si alius sit sensus, qui ipsum percipiat visum, profecto sentiendi progressus infinitus erit. Semper enim alius sensus alium percipiet. Itaque alia est facultas, quae obiecta a suis sensibus apprehendi percipit, & per quam nos non sentientes obiectum diiudicamus ipsum & priuatione eius.Propterea cùm nihil cernimus, tum te-nebras à lumine discernimus,sed non eodem modo. Sentiendi igitur duplex est facultas propria vna,vt visus, cuius proprium videre est,auditus audire,gustatus gustare,odoratus olfacere,tactus tangere:altera communis, quæ prædictarum causa est.& cuius opera animal eius quod cernit vel audit sensu efficitur.Nec etiâ dulcia ab albis discernere possumus nisi hac sentiendi facultate.Est itēq; [?]causa,cur animal id visu percipiat,quod cernit,& dulcis ab amaris distinguit. Hæc enim cuncta fiunt quadam communi parte, quæ vniuersa fouet sensoriarum genera.Sensuum enim omnium vnus est præcipuus, vt & vnum sensorium. Cæterum dubitauerit quispiam & quæsiuerit qui fiat vt communis ille sensus diuersa simul sensilia discernat,& in indiuiduo tempore, cùm fieri nequeat idem, quod indiuiduum est,in distincto tepore contrariis motionibus cieri. Sed hoc nihil mirari oportet, cùm visus simul & eodem tempore albu m & nigrum distinguat & diiudicet, quamuis diuersa sint.Propterea sensus communis fi mul nigrum & amarum, quæ nō aduersa sunt,discernere potest.
units.tr: Since we perceive both seeing and hearing, this certainly seems to happen through some sense. But it is not sight, nor is it hearing. For sight does not perceive that it sees, nor does hearing perceive that it hears. The same reasoning applies to the other senses. Therefore there must be another faculty, which perceives sight itself and the object of sight, which is colour. For two senses do not belong to one and the same subject of colour. Sight, then, does not perceive itself to see through any other proper sense. For if there were another sense which perceived sight itself, the progress of sensing would be infinite, since each sense would always need another to perceive it. So there is another faculty, which perceives the objects apprehended by their own senses, and through which we judge, without sensing it, the object itself and its privation. Hence when we perceive nothing, we still distinguish darkness from light, though not in the same way. There is therefore a twofold faculty of sensing: one proper, like sight, whose proper act is seeing, hearing's hearing, taste's tasting, smell's smelling, and touch's touching; and the other common, which is the cause of those just named, and by whose work the animal is made aware, through sense, of what it sees or hears. Nor could we distinguish sweet things from white ones except by this faculty of sensing. This is also the reason why an animal perceives by sight what it sees, and distinguishes the sweet from the bitter. For all these things happen through a certain common part, which unifies the kinds of sense organs. For of all the senses there is one chief, just as there is one sensory organ. But someone may doubt and ask how that common sense distinguishes different objects at the same time, and, in an indivisible moment, is moved by contrary motions, which cannot happen to what is indivisible in a distinct time. But we ought not to wonder at this, since sight at the same time and in the same moment distinguishes and judges white and black, although they are different. Therefore the common sense can discern at once black and bitter, which are not opposites.

units.la: CAP. XIX.
units.tr: CAP. XIX.

units.la: Qua sensilia sensus ipsos & instrumenta laedat.
units.tr: What sensible things injure the senses and their instruments.

units.la: ÆTERVM sensilia nec sensus, nec orgona labefactant, nisi mo-dum excedant. Quare grauis so-nus & acutus auditum laedit, vt & visum colores splendidissimi & obscurissimi, odoratum grauissimi & teterrimi odores, quoniam sensus velut quaedam commoderatio est. Quamobrem sensilium ea, quae commoderata sunt sensus delectant. Contraria vero eos labefactant. Proinde tactui simplex calidum, aut frigidum, aut aliud tale non iucundum est & amicum, sed quod ad rationem temperationemque redactum est.
units.tr: Sensible objects never weaken the senses or the organs, unless they exceed the due measure. Thus a deep sound and a sharp one injure hearing, and likewise the most brilliant and the darkest colours injure sight, and the heaviest and most foul odours injure smell, because sense is, as it were, a certain moderation. Hence those sensible things which are moderate delight the senses, while contrary ones weaken them. Accordingly, to touch, a simple warmth or cold, or anything else of that kind, is not pleasant and agreeable, but only that which has been brought into due proportion and temperature.

units.la: Sensus enim velut ratio est: propterea sensilium ea quae exuperant, aut ipsi molestiam afferunt, aut tandem eum corrumpunt: quoniam mouentis actio est, sensus vero & instrumenti perpessio. Caeterum rei sensilis actioni, & sensus instrumetique passioni nomen vnum impositum est, vt auditui actu, & sono actu auditio, visui actu & coloris, visio, gustatui gustatio, & tactui tractatio, olfactui olfactio.
units.tr: For sense is, as it were, a kind of reason: therefore those sensible things which exceed the measure either cause it discomfort or finally destroy it, since the action belongs to the thing that moves, while the sense and its instrument undergo the passion. Yet one name has been given both to the action of the sensible thing and to the passion of the sense and its instrument: thus hearing in act and sound in act are called "auditio," sight in act and colour "visio," tasting "gustatio," touching "tractatio," and smelling "olfactio."

units.la: CAP. XX.
units.tr: CAP. XX.

units.la: Discrimen phantasiae, sensus opinionis, & mentis.
units.tr: The difference between imagination, sense, opinion, and mind.

units.la: Uniâ[?] sensu & intellectu res om-nes nostra anima iudicat & cognoscit, veteres philosophi, praeter Aristotelem, sentire & intelligere idem esse putarunt. Sed hoc falsum esse, hinc perspici potest, quod omnes animantes sint sensus participes, & in paucis, ut in hominum genere, mes[?] reperiatur. Praeterea sensus pro-priorum obiectorum semper verus est. Sed sæpenumero evenit, ut quis falsò ratiocine-tur, nec ulli ratiocinatio conveniat, nisi cui ratio est. Itaque sensus & intellectus variæ sunt animæ facultates. Differt etiam phanta-sia à sensu (tametsi absque eo illæ esse non pos-sit) quoniam sensus semper est eorum quæ sunt: sed in phantasia nonnunquam nobis a-liqua apparent quæ non sunt: in quo genere ea sunt, quæ in somniis videntur. Deinde animali semper sensus est, non autem phantasia. Hac enim omnino caret apes, formicæ, ver-mes & similia. Præterea omnis sensus verus est, si animal valet: sed plerunque imagina-tiones falsæ sunt. Differt etiam phantasia ab opinione existimationeque, quod phantasia in nostra potestate sit: licet enim nobis sin-gere, & aliquid ob oculos ponere, cùm li-bet, perinde atque ij faciunt, qui memoriæ causa quædam simulachra, & imagines ef-fingunt. Opinari autem in nobis non situm est dum volumus.quippe cùm opinantem, vel verum, vel falsum dicere, necesse sit. Præterea si id sit phantasia, in quo sit phantasma, ipsa non una est earum facultatum, quibus vel recte vel falsò diiudicamus & percipimus: cuiusmodi sunt sensus, opinio, intellectus & scientia, quæ habitus & non facultas est. Deinde fides opinionem sequitur: quoniam fides omnia approbat, quæ opinamur. Bestiarum autem nulli fides data est, tametsi plerisque imaginandi facultas insit. Quinetiam perfuasio, quæ à ratione oritur, fidem sequi consueuit. Atqui nullis bestiis ratio inest. Igitur imaginatio non est opinio cum sensu, nec per sensum hausta, nec opinionis & sensus coniunctio. Si enim imaginatio esset opinionis sensusque coniunctio, profecto opinio non cuiusuis rei esset, sed eius duntaxat, cuius sensus est. Præterea imaginatio nullo modo esse potest coniunctio cum illa opinione, qua aliquid esse bonum dicitur. Est igitur imaginatio motio quædam cum sensu: quoniam nisi sentientibus inest. Huiusmodi autem motio vel vera est, vel falsa. Vera quidem cum non sensus fallitur. At proprij obiecti semper verus est. A communi sensili duntaxat decipi potest, eo quod ex accidente ipsum percipit, & proprium per se. Propterea vitus fallitur, qui pedalem esse Solem iudicat. Itaque imaginatio vera est, præsente sensu actu, & sensili proprio: sed falsitur cum à sensu omnino sensile abest. Maxime autem phantasia visio dicitur: eo quòd non sine lumine visus fiat. Quoniam tandem huiusmodi imaginationes à sensu profectæ in anima impressæ manent, fit, vt sæpenumero per illas multa animantes conentur & faciant:aliæ, quòd mentis expertes sint vt be-stiæ,aliæ, vt homines, quibus mens interdū, vel perturbatione,vel morbo,vel somno im-pedita obscuratáque est.
units.tr: Our soul judges and knows all things by sense and intellect alone. The ancient philosophers, except Aristotle, thought that to sense and to understand are the same. That this is false can be seen from the following: all living things share in sense, but mind is found in few, such as the human race. Moreover, sense is always true with regard to its proper objects. But it often happens that someone reasons falsely, and reasoning belongs only to one who has reason. So sense and intellect are different faculties of the soul. Imagination also differs from sense, although it cannot exist without it, since sense is always of things that are, but in imagination some things sometimes appear to us that are not; of this kind are the things seen in dreams. Again, an animal always has sense, but not always imagination: bees, ants, worms and similar creatures lack it altogether. Furthermore, every sense is true if the animal is healthy, but imaginations are often false. Imagination also differs from opinion and judgment, in that imagination is in our power: for we can form images and set something before our eyes whenever we like, just as those do who make certain likenesses and pictures for the sake of memory. But to hold an opinion is not in our power when we wish it, since one who holds an opinion must necessarily say either what is true or what is false. Moreover, if imagination is that in which the image is present, it is not itself one of those faculties by which we judge and perceive rightly or wrongly, such as sense, opinion, intellect, and knowledge, which is a habit and not a faculty. Again, belief follows opinion, since belief approves all that we hold as opinion. Yet belief is given to no beast, although most beasts have the faculty of imagining. Indeed, persuasion, which arises from reason, usually follows belief; but no beast has reason. Therefore imagination is not opinion joined with sense, nor is it something drawn in through the senses, nor the conjunction of opinion and sense. For if imagination were the conjunction of opinion and sense, opinion would surely belong not to every thing but only to that of which there is sense. Moreover, imagination can in no way be a conjunction with that opinion by which something is said to be good. Imagination is therefore a certain motion accompanying sense, since it is present only in those that sense. Such a motion is either true or false: true when the sense is not deceived; and the proper object of sense is always true. It can be deceived only by a common sensible, because it perceives that incidentally and not through itself as its proper object. Hence the man with jaundice is deceived when he judges the sun to be a foot wide. Thus imagination is true when the sense is actually present and the proper sensible is present, but it is false when the sensible is wholly absent from the sense. Imagination is also called especially vision, because it does not occur without light. Finally, since such imaginations, arising from sense, remain impressed on the soul, it comes about that living things often attempt and do many things through them: some, because they lack mind, like beasts; others, like men, in whom the mind is sometimes hindered and darkened by agitation, by disease, or by sleep.

units.la: CAP. XXI.
units.tr: CAP. XXI.

units.la: De intellectu potestate, qui ab intelligibilibus afficitur, & propria forma caret.
units.tr: On the power of the intellect, which is acted upon by intelligibles and has no form of its own.

units.la: ARS autem animæ,quæ cognoscit & intelligit, explicanda est. Propterea si intelligere est, vt sentire & aliquid accipere & pa-ti,vt nonnulli existimarùt, profectò id ab eo erit,quod intelligi potest. At nihil à suo si-mili affici certum est. Itaque impatibilis sit mens necesse est, sed iam vim duntaxat ha-beat,vt & species rerū accipere possit, & eis talis esse,non autem,vt sit res ipsæ,quæ intel-liguntur.Cæterùm quam rationem sensus ad sensilia habet,eandem ipsa mes ad ipsa intel-ligibilia. Æque enim rerum intelligendarum species mens recipit,atque sensus simulachra sensilium. Propterea rectè senserùt, qui ani-mā esse formarū locum dixerunt, nō omnē, sed eam duntaxat, quæ rationis & intelligen-tiæ particeps est. Cùm igitur mes omnia in-telligat,& eorum imagines recipiat, simplex sit,necesse est. Si enim materiata esset,prose-ctò à calore & frigore afficeretur, & aliquo vteretur instrumento, sicut alia animæ pars, qua animal sentit. At nullū ei est. Et tametsi eàdem habeat ratione ad intelligibilia quàm fenfus ad fenfilia, attamen fenfus [illegible, ~7 letters] & mentis non effe fimilem ex fenfuum inftrumetis,& ipfo fenfu perfpici poteft, fenfus enim fuo munere fungi non poteft, percepto excellenti aliquo fenfili: fed mens cum intel lexit aliquid, quod vix intelligi poteft, tum acrius & melius intelligit. Ad hæc fenfus cū corpore mixtus eft: mens vero ab eo fepa rabilis: quæ cūm omnia in fe recipere pof fit obiecta eius varia fint,neceffe eft: quan doquidem eorum quæ funt, quædam fenfilia funt & materiata:nonnulla omni materia ca rent, cuiusmodi funt fimplices effentiæ,quę actu intelligibilia dicuntur. Itaque materia ta, poteftate intelligibilia funt, nec ante in telligi poffunt, quàm ab efficiente intelle-ctu in actum redacta funt, & eorum abftra-ctæ fpecies. Atque ut aliud eft res, & rei ef fentia, veluti aliud caro eft,& aliud carnis ra tio & forma, aliud magnitudo, ac aliud ma gnitudinis effe: fic aliud eft intelligibile po teftate,quod prius in fenfum cadit quàm in telligatur, & aliud intelligibile actu, quod fimplex eft, & omni materia vacat. Huiuf modi autem eft intellectus, propterea actu feipfum intelligit. Alia vero vt actu intelli gantur , abftrahi ab efficiente intelle-ctu,ne ceffe eft. Abftrahit autem non vt Mathema ticus, fed vt primus philofophus, qui rerum ideas omnino ab omni materia feparat ac di uidit.Sed fi intellectus fimplex eft & impatibilis, quæritur qui intelligat, cùm intelligere fit ab aliquo affici & pati. Ad hoc respondendum est intellectum, dum intelligit, formasque rerum accipit, non pati: quandoquidem à materiatis rebus omnis perpessio est, quæ quiddā commune habent, quo pati & affici ab agente possint. Intellectus etiam instar tabulæ est, in qua nihil scriptum apparet. Itaque omnium formarum, quas ipse intelligere potest, expers est. Rursum quæritur cur nō semper nostor [?] intellectus intelligit, cùm omni materia careat? In causa esse videntur intelligibilia potestate, cuiusmodi materia sunt, quæ minimè intelligi possunt, nisi ab agente intellectu eorum formæ abstrahantur, atque actu intelligibilia reddantur. Quare quùm hæc nonsemper talia fiant, fit, ut intellectus nō perpetuò intelligat. Alia autem intelligibilia, quæ materiæ expertia sunt, actu intelliguntur, cuiusmodi ipse intellectus est, qui se intelligit: quam ob causam dixit Aristoteles idem esse intelligens, & quod intelligitur, quemadmodum idem est contemplativa scientia, & id quod scitur ac in ea cadit.
units.tr: The faculty of the soul that knows and understands must now be explained. If to understand is, as some have thought, the same as to sense, to receive something and to undergo something, then clearly it comes from that which can be understood. But it is certain that nothing is acted upon by its like. So the mind must be impassible, but it has only the power to receive the species of things and to become such as they are, not to be the things themselves that are understood. Moreover, the relation that sense bears to sensible things, the mind bears to intelligible things in the same way. For the mind receives the species of things to be understood just as sense receives the likenesses of sensible things. So those were right who called the soul the place of forms, not the whole soul but only that part which shares in reason and understanding. Since the mind understands all things and receives their images, it must be simple. For if it were material, it would certainly be affected by heat and cold, and would use some organ, as the other part of the soul does, by which the animal senses. But it has no such organ. And although the mind stands to intelligibles in the same relation as sense stands to sensibles, nevertheless that the sense and the mind are not alike can be seen from the instruments of the senses and from sense itself. For sense cannot perform its function once it has perceived some excellent sensible object, whereas the mind, once it has understood something that can scarcely be understood, then understands more keenly and better. Besides, sense is mixed with the body, while the mind is separable from it. Since the mind is able to receive all things into itself, and their objects are various, it must be so. For of the things that exist, some are sensible and material, while some lack all matter, such as simple essences, which are said to be intelligible in act. Thus material things are intelligible in potency, and cannot be understood before they are brought into act by the agent intellect and their abstract species are taken out. Just as the thing is one thing and the essence of the thing another, as flesh is one thing and the reason and form of flesh another, magnitude one thing and the being of magnitude another, so the intelligible in potency, which falls under sense before it is understood, is one thing, and the intelligible in act, which is simple and free of all matter, is another. Of this kind is the intellect, and therefore it understands itself in act. But other things, in order to be understood in act, must necessarily be abstracted by the agent intellect. It abstracts them not as the mathematician does, but as the first philosopher does, who entirely separates and distinguishes the ideas of things from all matter. But if the intellect is simple and impassible, the question arises, what is it that understands, since to understand is to be affected and to undergo? To this it must be replied that the intellect, while it understands and receives the forms of things, does not undergo anything; for all undergoing belongs to material things, which have something in common by which they can be acted upon and affected by an agent. The intellect is also like a tablet on which nothing is written; therefore it lacks all the forms that it is able to understand. Again it is asked why our intellect does not always understand, since it lacks all matter. The cause seems to be that intelligibles exist in potency, being of a material kind, which can scarcely be understood unless their forms are abstracted by the agent intellect and made intelligible in act. Therefore, since these do not always become such, it follows that the intellect does not understand continually. Other intelligibles, however, which are free of matter, are understood in act, such as the intellect itself, which understands itself. For this reason Aristotle said that the one who understands and what is understood are the same, just as the contemplative science and what is known and falls within it are the same.

units.la: CAP. XXII. Utrunque intellectum ad intelligendum esse necessarium.
units.tr: Chapter 22. That both kinds of intellect are necessary for understanding.

units.la: VEMADMODUM in omni natura quædam sunt, quorum unum unicuique generi materies est, quod quidam potest omnia esse: alterum verò vero efficiens causa est, quod ad agendum talem habet rationem, qualem ars ad materiam: ita in anima hominis huiusmodi differentiae insunt. In ea enim intellectus unus est talis vt omnia fiat & recipiat: alter vero, qui omnia efficit, & vt habitus est quidem & perinde ac lumen. Nam vt lumen colores, qui potestate aspectabiles erant, facit vt actu cernantur: ita intellectus agens intelligibilia, quae potestate erant, actu vt sint, efficit. Est autem separabilis, & simplex omnisque affectionis expers, quoniam ἐντελέχεια[?] est & substantia hominis. Separatus igitur immortalis est & perpetuus est. Alterum autem, quia patibilis est, & potestas, vna cum corpore extingui censet Aristoteles, & sine agente nihil intelligere: addit quoque nos vita defunctos nihil recordari, eo quod ipse agens intellectus perpessionis expers sit.
units.tr: Just as in every nature there are certain things, of which one is the matter of each kind, which in a way can become all things, while the other is the efficient cause, which stands towards acting as art stands towards its material; so in the soul of man there are differences of this kind. For in it one intellect is such that it becomes and receives all things, while the other is what makes all things, and it is like a state or habit, and just as light is. For just as light makes colours, which were visible only potentially, actually seen, so the agent intellect makes intelligible things, which were only potentially intelligible, actually to be. It is, moreover, separable, simple and free from all affection, since it is the actuality [entelecheia] and substance of man. Being separate, therefore, it is immortal and everlasting. The other, however, because it is passible and a potentiality, Aristotle thinks is extinguished together with the body, and understands nothing without an agent; he adds also that we who have departed this life remember nothing, because the agent intellect itself is free from passion.

units.la: CAP. XXIII.
units.tr: CAP. XXIII.

units.la: Primam intellectus actionem theoricam in simplicibus versari: secundam in iis in quibus verum sit, ac falsum.
units.tr: The first action of the intellect is theoretical and concerns simple things; the second concerns those things in which there is truth or falsity.

units.la: IMPLICIVM indiuiduorumque intellectio in iis versatur, in quibus falsitas non est. At in iis, in quibus est falsum & verum, iam notionum quaedam compositio coiunctioque animadvertitur, perinde ac si vnum quiddam consisterent, veluti Empedocles dicebat. Quod fi illa compositio in illis versetur : quæ fiunt, aut fuerunt, aut futura sunt, mens simul tem pus concipit. Nam nō solùm hoc falsum est, aut verum, Cleon est albus, sed erit, aut fuit. Itaque falsitas semper in notionum coniunctione perspicitur : verbi gratia, si quis albū existimet nō album esse. Id autem quod simplicia coniungit & copulat mens est. Quoniam autem simplex & indiuiduum, quod ipsa mens concipit duobus modis dicitur, aut actu aut potestate fit, vt mens id concipiat vt indiuiduum, quod potestate, diuidua est. Verbi gratia longitudo potestate diuidua est, quæ cum mente apprehenditur, tum reipsa indiuidua est. Eodem modo tempus diuiduum dicitur, & indiuiduum. Proinde cum longi-tudinem intelligimus, non licet diuisim & seorsim apprehendere quid sit in vtraque parte istius: quoniam vna, & simplicem longitudinem mens apprehendit. Quod attinet ad illud indiuiduum & simplex, quod non quantitate, sed forma diuidi non potest, in indiuiduo tempore, & indiuidua mentis notione intellectioneque percipitur. Quod ve-rò intelligit, & tempus in quo intelligit, non indiuidua dicuntur ex accidente quà quæ in-telliguntur diuidua sint, sed indiuidua. Punctum etiam, & id quod similiter actu & potestate indiuiduum est, vt vnum, perinde atque priuatio intelligitur. Eodem modo malum & nigrum mens cognoscit. Ex contratio enim quodam modo intelligit. Quod au-tem hoc modo cognoscit aliud esse potest, quàm est, & unum contrariorum in eo esse debet. Propterea existimauit Aristoteles patibilem mentem unà cum corpore extingui, & eam, quae agens est, separabilem esse & aeternam. Quamobrem his addit ipsam causam se cognoscere, & separabilem esse, cui omnino nullum est contrarium. Sed utraque mens (meo iudicio) forma non distinguitur, sed duntaxat opere & facultate. Postremò non omnis intellectio vera est & falsa, sed ea duntaxat, quae aliquid de aliquo dicit, & enunciatio dicitur. Affirmatio huiusmodi est, & omnis vera esse, aut falsa perhibetur. Sed nō omnis intellectio huiusmodi est. Ea enim duntaxat vera est, qua quid sit res mete concipitur, & cuius forma intelligitur. Ac quem-admodum proprij subiecti semper visus actu verus est, ita intellectio eorum omnium, quae materia carent semper vera. Postrema autē metis intellectio syllogismus est, quo aliquid verum esse, aut falsum demonstramus.
units.tr: The understanding of things that are simple and indivisible is concerned with those things in which there is no falsity. But in those things in which there is falsity and truth, a certain composition and combination of notions is noticed, as if they formed one thing, as Empedocles used to say. If that composition concerns things that are done, or have been done, or are going to be done, the mind grasps time at the same moment. For this is not only true or false, "Cleon is white," but "he will be" or "he was." Thus falsity is always seen in the combination of notions: for example, if someone thinks that what is white is not white. Now the mind is what joins and couples simple things. Since what the mind grasps as simple and indivisible is said to be so in two ways, either in act or in potency, the mind grasps it as indivisible when it is divisible in potency. For example, length is divisible in potency; when it is apprehended by the mind, it is in reality indivisible. In the same way time is called divisible and indivisible. Therefore, when we understand length, we cannot separately and distinctly apprehend what is in each part of it, since the mind apprehends one and simple length. As for that indivisible and simple thing which cannot be divided in quantity but only in form, it is perceived in the indivisible time and by the indivisible notion and understanding of the mind. But what understands, and the time in which it understands, are not called indivisible because of an accident, as if the things understood were divisible, but are indivisible in themselves. A point too, and whatever is likewise indivisible in act and in potency, such as the one, is understood in the same way as a privation. In the same way the mind knows evil and black; for it understands in a certain way by contraries. But what knows in this way can be other than it is, and one of the contraries must be in it. For this reason Aristotle thought that the passive mind perishes together with the body, while the active mind, which acts, is separable and eternal. For this reason he adds that it knows its own cause and is separable, to which there is absolutely no contrary. But in my judgment neither mind is distinguished in form; they differ only in function and faculty. Finally, not every understanding is true or false, but only that which says something about something, and is called a statement. Such an affirmation is of this kind, and every affirmation is said to be either true or false. But not every understanding is of this kind. For that understanding is true only by which the nature of a thing is conceived by the mind and whose form is understood. And just as the sight of its proper object is always true in act, so the understanding of all those things which lack matter is always true. But the last act of the mind's understanding is a syllogism, by which we demonstrate that something is true or false.

units.la: CAP. XXIIII. Id in mente bonum & malum esse, quod in sensu dolor & voluptas. Quae-nam sit mentis actio practica?
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIV. That in the mind the good and the bad are what pleasure and pain are in sense. What is the practical action of the mind?

units.la: Vi sentit,aut intelligit, non prō-prie patitur & alteratur, sed alio motus genere excitatur, eo videlicet, qui rei perfectæ est. (Motus enim rei imperfectę, imperfecta actio etiam est.) At sensus & intellectus actio perfecta est. Qui enim sentit, aut intelligit horæ momento non minus sentit,aut intelligit,quàm si totam horam: quoniam huiusmodi actiones momento temporis fiunt. Quare sensus & intellectus affectiones improprie dicuntur, & inter se quodammodo conueniunt. Sensus enim cum dolorem, aut voluptatem adesse indicat, tum facta velut affirmatione, aut negatione alterutrum appetit, vel fugit. Appetit (inquam) quod velut bonum esse ei videtur, & ab eo quod malum est declinat. Mens simili modo cum phantasmata, quæ ei obiiciuntur esse bona, aut mala intelligit, tum ea sequitur & optat, aut fugit. Nā absque phantasmatis non intelligit. Propterea cūm in eis species rerum cognoscit, & aliquid appetendum esse, aut declinandum proponit, tum interdum absque vllius sensus opera mouetur: veluti ei vsuenit, qui sensu communi percipies procul signum face datum ignem esse, ac ipsum moueri, hostem adesse sibi persuadet, ac propterea mete [?] perturbatur. Nonnunquam vero ipsa mens propter ipsa phantasmata ratiocinatur deliberatque, ac res futuras cum præsentibus coiungit, atque cūm hic vel illic aliquid iucundum esse, aut molestum ait, aut negat, tum illinc fugit, aut hoc sequitur, atque omnino aliquid agit, cuius actio intellectio practica dicitur, quæ quidem solo fine à theorica differt: quandoquidem verum & falsum, sine vlla actione sunt, bonum & malum, in actione versantur.
units.tr: Whether it perceives or understands by its power, it does not properly suffer or get altered, but is stirred by a different kind of motion, namely that which belongs to a finished thing. (For the motion of an unfinished thing is also an unfinished action.) But the action of sense and of understanding is a finished action. For one who perceives or understands does not perceive or understand any less in a moment of an hour than if he did so for a whole hour, since actions of this kind happen in an instant of time. Hence sense and understanding are improperly called affections, and in a way they agree with each other. For sense, when it indicates that pain or pleasure is present, then, as if by an affirmation or a negation, seeks or shuns one of the two. It seeks (I say) what seems to it to be good, and turns away from what is bad. In the same way the mind, when it understands the appearances put before it to be good or bad, then follows and desires them, or flees from them. For without appearances it does not understand. Therefore, when it recognises in them the forms of things and proposes that something is to be sought or avoided, it is sometimes moved even without the work of any sense: as happens to a man who, perceiving by the common sense from a distance that a sign given by a torch is a fire and that it is moving, persuades himself that an enemy is at hand, and is therefore [?] disturbed in mind. Yet sometimes the mind itself, on account of those very appearances, reasons and deliberates, and joins future things with present ones; and when it says or denies that something here or there is pleasant or troublesome, then it flees from that place, or follows this, and in short does something; this action is called practical understanding, which differs from theoretical understanding in its end alone: since true and false are without any action, while good and bad lie in action.

units.la: CAP. XXV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXV.

units.la: Animam quodam modo omnia esse.
units.tr: That the soul is in a certain way all things.

units.la: VNc autem quæ de anima dicta sunt, paucis repetentes dicimus cū Philosopho animam quodam mo- do,non autem omnino, & (vt loquuntur) formaliter vniuersa esse quæ aut intelligibilia sunt, aut sensilia, sed vt subiectum: quoniam eorum omnium formas & species recipit, quibus similis est. Sic etiam scientia quodam modo est res ipsæ, quæ sciuntur & mente concipiuntur: & sensus ea ipsa quæ sensu percipiuntur, eo etiam quod eorū species recipiat. Ex quibus satis constat res ipsas, quæ vel intelliguntur, vel sentiuntur non esse in anima nec in sensu. Profecto ipse lapis, qui vel intelligitur, vel sensu percipitur, non in anima est, sed eius species & imago. Atque anima vt manus est. Quemadmodum enim manus instrumentum instrumentorum est, ita intellectus forma formarum, & sensus itidem sensilium species. Quoniam autem in ipsis rerum sensilium formis sunt a-liae formae, quae intelligibiles dicuntur tum earum rerum, quae abstractae vocantur, tum eorum etiam sensilium, fit vt is qui non sentit, nihil discere vel intelligere possit: & qui contemplatur vna cum phantasmate intelligat. Ipsa namque phantasmata, veluti sensilia sunt, quanuis non materiata sint. Sunt enim phantasmata mentis obiecta, vt sensilia sensus, etsi nec quid verum vel falsum affirmant, aut negant: quoniam affirmatio & negatio veri falsive est & complexio primorum conceptuum notionumque intellectus. At phantasmata primae sunt mentis notiones, non autem secundae absque phantasmatis esse non possunt. Caeterum quae abstracta dicuntur mens absque vlla materia intelligit, vt concauum, cui nullum est certum definitumque subiectum. Non enim vt simum est, quod quidem absque sub-iecto naso[?] intelligi non potest. Ex quo constat mathematica esse abstracta tanqua con-cauum, si conferantur cum physicis, quae sunt velut simum. Si vero cum metaphysicis com-parentur, certę illa tanquam simum, hæc ve-rò velut concauum sunt. Quæ cùm ita sint, perspicuum est exquisitissimē mentem resi-psas, quatenus sunt, Metaphysici more, & nō Mathematici abstrahere: quadoquidem minus Mathematicus quàm Metaphysicus res ipsas mente abstrahit.
units.tr: Now, to repeat briefly what has been said about the soul, we say with the Philosopher that the soul is, in a certain way and not absolutely, and (as they put it) formally, all the things that are either intelligible or sensible, but as a subject, since it receives the forms and species of all of them, to which it is similar. So too knowledge is in a certain way the things themselves that are known and conceived by the mind, and sense is the very things perceived by sense, also because it receives their species. From this it is quite clear that the things themselves that are understood or perceived are not in the soul or in the sense. Surely the stone itself, which is understood or perceived by sense, is not in the soul, but its species and image is. And the soul is like the hand. For as the hand is the instrument of instruments, so the intellect is the form of forms, and the sense likewise the species of sensibles. Since, however, among the forms of sensible things themselves there are other forms, which are called intelligible, both those of things called abstract and those of sensible things too, it follows that one who does not sense can learn or understand nothing, and one who contemplates understands along with the phantasm. For phantasms are, as it were, sensibles, although they are not material. Phantasms are the objects of the mind, as sensibles are of the sense, although they do not affirm or deny anything as true or false, since affirmation and negation belong to truth and falsity and are a combination of the first concepts and notions of the intellect. Phantasms are the first notions of the mind, while the second notions cannot exist without a phantasm. Moreover, what are called abstract things the mind understands without any matter, as the concave, which has no fixed and definite subject. For it is not like the snub, which cannot be understood without a subject, a nose. From this it is established that mathematical things are abstract like the concave, if they are compared with physical things, which are like the snub. But if they are compared with metaphysical things, then the former are certainly like the snub, and these latter like the concave. Since these things are so, it is clear that the mind abstracts things as they are, most exactly, in the manner of the Metaphysician and not of the Mathematician, since the Mathematician abstracts things in the mind less than the Metaphysician does.

units.la: CAP. XXVI. Quanam sit illa vis animæ, qua loco moueantur animantes.
units.tr: CHAPTER 26. What is that power of the soul by which living beings are moved from place to place.

units.la: O S T Q_V A M de ea animæ vi, qua a-nimantes cognoscunt & iudicant disseruimus, ad aliam, quæ loco mo-uendi est, progredi licet. Hanc autem non ef-se nutriendi vim, hinc perspici licet, quod stirpes moueri possent, & instrumenta[?] ad motum idonea haberent. Nec vero facultas sentiens esse videtur: quippe cum pleraque animantes sint, quæ semper stant, vt ostrea.
units.tr: Having discussed that power of the soul by which living beings perceive and judge, we may now proceed to the other power, which is that of moving from place to place. That this is not the power of nourishing can be seen from this: plants could then be moved, and would have organs suited to motion. Nor does it seem to be the faculty of sensing, since there are many living beings which always remain fixed, such as oysters.

units.la: Nec quoque omnis vis ratiocinandi huius motionis causa est. Theorica enim mens nec quicquam fugiendū persequendumque ait. Sed huiusmodi motio semper est animalis aliquid vel fugientis vel appetentis. Verum tamen mens practica, cum quid agendum sit deliberat, ac meditatur, tum id fugiendum esse, aut sequendum præscribit. Interdum vero iubet aliquid fingiendum esse, cui homo, eo quod impotens sit non obtemperat, sed agendum cupiditate ducitur instar belluæ. Nec tamen ipse appetitus cunctis hominibus hunc motum excitat. Continentes enim cupiditatibus incitati inflammatique no ea faciunt, quorum cupiditate ducuntur, sed rationi mentiqúe obtemperant, & ij maxime, qui spiritu Dei reguntur.
units.tr: Nor is every power of reasoning the cause of this motion either. For the theoretical mind does not pursue or shun anything. Rather, such motion is always that of an animal either fleeing or seeking something. Yet the practical mind, when it deliberates and reflects on what is to be done, then prescribes that this is to be shunned or that is to be followed. Sometimes, however, it orders that something be left undone, which a man, because he is powerless, does not obey, but is driven to act like a beast by desire. Nor does appetite itself stir this motion in all men. For those who are continent, though incited and inflamed by desires, do not do the things they are driven to desire, but obey reason and the mind, and especially those who are governed by the Spirit of God.

units.la: CAP. XXVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER 27.

units.la: Animantia loco moueri mente practica, & appetitione.
units.tr: That animals are moved from place to place by practical mind and by appetite.

units.la: AE e igitur duo mens & appetitus causæ sunt, cur animantes loco moueantur. Sed mentem eam intelligimus, quæ ratiocinatur alicuius causa, & agendi principium est. Propterea propositum finem habet, quoniam alicuius causa est omnis actio. Altera autem totum opus suum in contemplando ponit. Appetitus etiam omnis finem sibi propositū habet. Quare recte hæc duo mens & appetitus progressionis animalium principia sunt:
units.tr: There are therefore two causes why living creatures are moved from place to place: mind and appetite. We understand by mind that which reasons for the sake of something and is the principle of action. Hence the mind has a purpose as its end, since every action is done for the sake of something. The other faculty, by contrast, places its whole work in contemplating. Appetite too always has an end set before it. Rightly, then, these two, mind and appetite, are the principles of the movement of animals.

units.la: Quoniam autem mens absque aliquo appetitu, nihil agit, hæc hominem mouere potest, propterea voluntas est appetitus mentis, & motus eius voluntarius. Sed mens practica ceu ratio, & ea cupiditas, quæ a sensitiua imaginatione proficiscitur, inter se discrepant. Mens enim propter futurum tempus voluptati obsistendum esse iubet homini: contrà cupiditas præsentem voluptatem confecta- tur, & appetit, ut in bestiis, & stolidis hominibus fieri solet. Præsens enim voluptas, quam appetunt, non plane bonum est, sed boni species, propterea quòd futuri temporis rationem minimè habeat.
units.tr: Since, however, the mind without some appetite does nothing, the mind can move a man; therefore the will is the appetite of the mind, and its voluntary motion. But practical mind, as reason, and that desire which arises from the sensitive imagination, differ from one another. For the mind bids a man resist pleasure on account of future time; desire, on the contrary, pursues present pleasure and craves it, as is customary in beasts and foolish men. For the present pleasure which they crave is not truly good, but the appearance of good, because it takes no account of future time.

units.la: Quod igitur animantes mouet, duplex est, nimirum ratio & cupiditas, quorum obiectum est ipsum verè bonum agendum, aut boni species,fi me-ti,aut phantasiæ offeratur. Cæterum in pro-greffione motúque animalium tria sunt con-fideranda, primum id quod mouet, alterum id quo motus est,tertium quod mouetur. At-que id quod mouet duplex est, vnum immo-bile, vt bonum quod agendum est, alterum mouet & mouetur, vt appetédi principium. Id enim mouetur quod appetit, qua ex parte appetit,& appetitio quædam est motio. Ac id quod mouetur & appetit animal est. Id vero, quo motus est,corpori vt instrumento attribuitur. Omnino igitur eoipfo animal fe mouet, quod appetat. Sed appetitus absque phantasia non est : Ac omnis phantasia, aut rationis, aut sensus particeps est, sed huius bruta participantia sunt, illius verò genus humanum.
units.tr: What moves animals is therefore twofold, namely reason and desire, whose object is either the truly good to be done, or the appearance of good, which is offered either to the mind or to the imagination. Moreover, in the progression and motion of animals three things are to be considered: first that which moves, second that by which there is motion, and third that which is moved. And that which moves is twofold: one thing is immovable, such as the good that is to be done; the other moves and is moved, as the principle of appetite. For that which desires is moved, in so far as it desires, and appetition is a kind of motion. And that which is moved and desires is the animal. Now that by which there is motion is attributed to the body as an instrument. Altogether, therefore, the animal moves itself by that very fact that it desires. But appetite is not without imagination, and every imagination partakes of either reason or sense; yet brutes partake only of the latter, while the human race partakes of both.

units.la: CAP. XXVIII.
units.tr: CAP. XXVIII.

units.la: Causa motionis animantium, quæ imperfectæ dicuntur.
units.tr: The cause of the motion of animals, which are called imperfect.

units.la: OSTHAEC de imperfectis be-ftiis, in quibus duntaxat tangendi sensus inest, videndum est quid id fit,quod eas inpellat, vtrum fit imaginatio, cupiditásve nécne? At cum in eis dolorem & veluptatem inesse constet, eisdem profecto cupiditas etiam infit, necesse est, qua loco mouentur. Sed quia earum cupiditas incerto quodammodo eis inest,propterea indefinitè etiam mouentur, quòd imaginatione careant. Imaginatio enim sensus particeps non omnibus inest animantibus, quæ rationis expertes sunt. Altera verò, quæ deliberatiua est, soli homines præditi sunt. Hæc autē ex pluribus phantasmatis opinionem efficit. Ex quo fit, vt multæ animantes non opinantur, eo quòd eam non habeant imaginatione, quæ rationis est particeps, sed eam dutaxat, quæ sensu & cupiditate est prædita. Quoniam autem in cupiditate nullus consilio locus est, propterea ea interdum voluntatem vincit, & ad id agendum impellit, quod non bonum est: nonnunquam verò alia cupiditas aliam repellit, mouetque ho-minem, & eum maximè, qui impotens est. Ea autem mens, quæ scientijs prædita est, nihil hominem ad quicquam agedum mouet, sed stat immota, quoniam theorica est, & in sola meditatione versatur. Itaque animantiū quædam ad agendum voluntate impelluntur, vt homines: quædam cupiditate, quorum quæ imperfecta sunt, incerto motu aguntur.
units.tr: Next, concerning the imperfect beasts, in which the sense of touch alone is present, we must consider what it is that drives them on: is it imagination or desire, or not? Yet since it is agreed that pain and pleasure are present in them, desire certainly is also present in them, and it is necessary that by it they are moved from place to place. But because their desire is in some way indefinite, they also move in an indefinite way, since they lack imagination. For imagination, which shares in sense, is not present in all animals that lack reason. The other kind, which is deliberative, is possessed by men alone. Now this produces opinion from many appearances. From this it follows that many animals do not form opinions, because they do not have that imagination which shares in reason, but only that which is endowed with sense and desire. Since, however, there is no place for counsel in desire, desire sometimes overcomes the will and drives it to do what is not good; but sometimes another desire repels one desire and moves a man, and especially one who is without self-control. But that mind which is endowed with knowledge does not move a man to do anything; it stands unmoved, since it is contemplative and is occupied with pure meditation alone. Thus some animals are impelled to act by the will, as men are; others by desire, and of these the imperfect ones are driven by an unclear motion.

units.la: CAP. XIX. Quisensus animantibus necessarij sunt?
units.tr: CAP. XIX. Which senses are necessary for animals?

units.la: VIC QVID viuit ea anima, in qua vis alendi posita est, præditum sit, necesse est: quandoquidem crescit, vigorem ætatis habet, & senescit: quæ omnia absque nutritione esse nullo modo possunt. Nec vero quæcunque viuunt, sen-tire expedit, & quæ maximè ibi suum habet cibum, vbi orta sunt, vt stirpes omnes, quæ nullo indigent sensu, quo alibi suum quæri-tant alimentum. Sola igitur viuentium sensu indigent animatia & maximè tactu, fine quo, ne vllum quidem animal esse potest. Nisi e-nim sentiret animal, qui(quæso)nutriretur? Nec, nisi tangendi vim haberet, suum non perciperet alimentum, quod tractabile est: quoniam omne corpus naturale tangi po-teft. Propterea gustatus, qui quasi tactus est, alimenti sensus proprius censetur. Cæteris autem sensibus alimentum nō obiicitur, sed vel sonus, vel color, aut odor, quæ quidem nō nutriunt. Quare tactus & gustatus ad nutri-tionem animalium necessarij sunt. At cæteri sensus alicuius boni gratia gradienti anima-li conueniunt: Nam fi animal conseruari de-beat, non solùm tangendo, sed etiam procul, quod [?] sibi necessarium est, sentiat, oportet.
units.tr: Whatever lives, in which the power of nourishing is placed, must of necessity possess that soul, since it grows, has the vigour of its age, and grows old; none of these things can happen without nutrition. Yet it is not expedient that all living things should have sense, and those which have their food close at hand, where they are born, as all plants do, need no sense by which to seek their nourishment elsewhere. Therefore only animals among living things need sense, and above all touch, without which no animal at all can exist. For if the animal did not perceive, how (I ask) would it be nourished? And unless it had the power of touch, it would not perceive its food, which is tangible, since every natural body can be touched. For this reason taste, which is a kind of touch, is considered the proper sense of food. But food is not presented to the other senses; rather sound, colour or smell, which indeed do not nourish. Hence touch and taste are necessary for the nutrition of animals. The other senses, however, serve a living creature that moves for the sake of some good: for if an animal is to be preserved, it must perceive not only by touching but also from afar what is necessary for it.

units.la: CAP. XXX.
units.tr: CAP. XXX.

units.la: Nullum animal ex vno elemento posse constare.
units.tr: That no animal can consist of one element.

units.la: VLLVM corpus simplex tactu præ-ditum esse potest: quandoquidé ta-ctus est omnium tractabilium quali-tatum iudex, & quædam mediocritas. Neque enim instrumentum tangendi solùm terræ qualitatum, quæ tractabiles sunt, sed etiam aliorum elementorum particeps est. At omne corpus cuiusuis animalis tactum habet, & tangendo sentit. Ergo nullum corpus animalis simplex est, sed ex quatuor elementis compositum. Si enim terra duntaxat costaret, profecto non sentiret. Quam ob causam ossa & pili, atque aliæ huiusmodi partes non sentiunt, propterea quod terrenæ sint. Præterea nullus alius sensus absque tactu haberi potest, propterea quod sine eo instrumenta aliorum sensuum nihil omnino sentire pos-sent. Sentiut enim duntaxat per aliquod medium. At tactus per se, atque hoc ipso nomine nuncupatur. Itaque cum absque tactu nullus alius possit esse sensus, & necessario omne animal tactum habeat, consequitur cuncta interire animantia, & mori, si hoc sensu desti-tuantur. Neque fieri potest ut sensum nō habeat animal. Neque (si animal est) alium sensum præter tactum habere, necesse est.
units.tr: No simple body can be endowed with touch, since touch is the judge of all tangible qualities, and a kind of mean between them. For the organ of touch is a sharer not only in the tangible qualities of earth but also in those of the other elements. Now every body of any animal has touch and perceives by touching. Therefore no animal body is simple, but is composed of the four elements. For if it were made of earth alone, it would certainly not feel. This is why bones, hair, and other such parts do not feel, because they are earthy. Moreover, no other sense can exist without touch, since without touch the organs of the other senses could perceive nothing at all. For they perceive only through some medium, whereas touch is immediate, and is named for this very reason. Thus, since no other sense can exist without touch, and every animal necessarily has touch, it follows that all living creatures would perish and die if they were deprived of this sense. Nor can an animal lack sensation. Nor, if it is an animal, is it necessary that it have any sense besides touch.

units.la: Quod autè attinet ad ea, quæ sensilia sunt, quædam suis exuperationibus per se animal non corrumpunt: color (inquam) sonus & odor, sed per accidens, eo quod instrumenta labefactent: veluti si vnà cum sono aliqua vehemens impulsio fiat, lædetur auris; oculus etiam à luminoso aspe&abili, vt odoratus à re supra modum fœtida & teterrima offenditur. Sapor etiam, eo ipso gustandi orgahum corrumpit,quòd tractabilis fit. Propterea qualitatum tractabilium exuperantię, vt caloris ignei, frigoris summi & aliorum huiusmodi per se animal interficiunt. Nam omnium sensilium excedens vis instrumentum sensus labefactat. Quare excellens tractabile per se ipsum corrumpit tactum, quo sensu definitum est omne animal. Quamobrem excessus tractabilium, non solùm instrumentum huius sensus: verùm etiam ipsum animal corrumpunt; & interimunt, quoniam tactum animal habeat, necesse est. Cæteros autem sensus animal habet, non vt sit, sed vt melius & perfectius, veluti visum vt cernat, quia & in aëre, & in aquâ; omninoque in re perspicua degit: Gustatum vt in cibo aut voluptatem, aut dolorem percipiat: Visum ite vt cibum expetat, atque ad ipsum peruenit: deinde auditum vt aliquid ei significetur.
units.tr: As for sensible things, some do not destroy an animal by their excess in themselves: colour, I mean, sound and smell; they do so only accidentally, because they damage the organs. For example, if a violent blow accompanies a sound, the ear is injured; the eye too is harmed by an excessively bright visible object, and the sense of smell by something extremely foul and stinking. Taste also corrupts the organ of tasting in itself, because it is tangible. Therefore excesses of tangible qualities, such as extreme heat of fire, extreme cold, and others of this kind, kill an animal in themselves. For the excessive force of any sensible thing weakens the organ of sense; hence an excessive tangible thing corrupts touch itself, by which sense every animal is defined. Accordingly, excesses of tangible things corrupt not only the organ of this sense but the animal itself, and destroy it, since an animal must have touch. The other senses an animal has not so that it may exist, but so that it may live better and more perfectly: sight, so that it may see, since it lives both in air and in water, and altogether in transparent matter; taste, so that it may perceive in food either pleasure or pain; and sight again, so that it may seek food and reach it; then hearing, so that something may be signified to it.

units.la: Finis tertia partis Institutionum physica-rum, quæ de anima est.
units.tr: End of the third part of the Physical Institutions, which concerns the soul.

units.la: INSTITVTIONVM PHYSICARVM POSTREMA PARS, QVA AFFECTIONES ANIMAE & CORPORIS COMMUNES, QVAE VVLGO PARVA DICVNTVR PHYSICA, PERSPICVE DEMONSTRANTUR.
units.tr: THE LAST PART OF THE PHYSICAL INSTITUTES, IN WHICH THE AFFECTIONS COMMON TO SOUL AND BODY, WHICH ARE COMMONLY CALLED THE SMALL PHYSICAL WORKS, ARE CLEARLY DEMONSTRATED.

units.la: De sensu, sensili, & sentiendi organo.
units.tr: On sense, the sensible, and the organ of sensing.

units.la: OMMVNIVM animæ & corporis affectionum sensus primum occurrit, eo quòd anima absque illius opera, sensilia cognoscere nô possit, nec vllum sit animal, nisi eo authore. Sed ex sensuum genere tactus & gustatus omnibus animantibus necessarij sunt, quorum tactus qualitates tractabiles dijudicat, gustatus cibum & alimentum. Hic enim sensus salutarem cibū à noxio ita secernit, vt insuauem auersetur, & gratum appetat. Alij autem animantibus, quibus gradiendi vis est, salutis & conseruationis causa à Natura dati sunt, vt & præsentiendo salubrem pastum animantia quærant, & exitiosum declinent. Sed iis animantibus, quæ prudentia sunt prædita melioris notæ causa tribuuntur: quandoquidem varias rerum dissimilitudines percipiunt, ex quibus, rerum tum intelligendarum scientia comparatur, tur, vt & agendarum prudentia. Horum autem sensuum visus per se ad vitæ commoditates præstantissimus est: Auditus verò ad intelligendum. Cæterum videndi facultas multiplicia rerum discrimina percipit, propterea quòd mista omnia sint colorata. Præterea hoc ipso sensu sensilia, quæ communia sunt, nempe figura, magnitudo, motus, status, & numerus percipiuntur, sed ex accidente. Auditus vero sonorum & vocis iudex est, ac paucas rerum dissimilitudines diiudicat, sed ad discendum maximum adfert adiumentum. Sermo enim & oratio, eo quòd audiatur, doctrinæ causa est, non perse, sed ex accidente, quippe quæ ex nominibus, quæ rerum notæ sunt, constat. Itaque qui alterutro horum sensuum à primo ortu priuati sunt, ad discendum cæci aptiores videntur, quàm muti & surdi: Posthæc de sensuum sedibus & organis simili brevitate differendum est. Olim non defuerunt præclari philosophi, vt Empedocles Timæus, qui visus sedem igneam esse perhibuerunt, eo quòd (vt inquiebant) visus exeunte quasi ex lucerna lumine, oriretur: Sed si visus emissione lucis euenireteur etiam in tenebris oculi non cernerent? Nec etiam probabile est, visum actu esse cuiusdam rei lucidæ emissione ex oculo: vel lumen, quod ex oculo emittitur, cum exteriore lumine coniungi atque confundi. Lumen enim cum lumine coniungi non potest nec confundi. Nam quiduis cum quouis non coni-iungitur, neque quod intus in oculo est cum eo, quod foris continetur, eo quòd membrana pupillam obuolues interponatur. Verun-tamen visum rei nullius fieri posse absque lumine iam demonstratum est, siue id sit, quod medium statuitur inter aspectabile & visum, siue illustratus aer. Et quemadmodum extrin-secus sine lumine nihil cerni potest, ita quod in oculo consistit pellucidum esse oportet, vt visus sedes sit: id quòd sanè ipsa aqua est. Quamobrem intimam oculi partem pellu-cida esse & lucis capacem expedit. Ex quo patet quodvis sensorium ita suo tribuendum esse elemento, vt videndi facultas aquæ tri-buatur, audiendi aeri, & odoradi igni. Odor enim est quædam fumida exhalatio, quæ ex igne est. Ob eamque causam odoratus senso-rium eo in loco est, qui cerebro vicinus exi-stit: quandoquidem rei frigidæ materies potestate calida est. Cerebrum autem omnium corporis partium humidissimum esse & fri-dissimū satis constat. Organum tactus terræ est & gustatus, qui ipsius tactus genus esse statuitur.
units.tr: Of all the affections common to soul and body, sense comes first, since the soul cannot know sensible things without its operation, and there is no animal without it. Of the senses, touch and taste are necessary to all living things. Touch judges tangible qualities, and taste judges food and nourishment. For this sense separates wholesome food from harmful, so that it shrinks from what is unpleasant and seeks what is agreeable. Other living things, which have the power of movement, were given by Nature for the sake of their health and preservation, so that by sensing beforehand they may seek wholesome pasture and avoid what is deadly. Those living things endowed with prudence are given a higher rank, since they perceive the various differences between things, from which the knowledge of things to be understood, and the prudence of things to be done, is acquired. Of these senses, sight is in itself the most excellent for the conveniences of life, while hearing is for understanding. Moreover, the faculty of sight perceives many differences between things, because all mixed bodies are coloured. Besides, by this same sense the common sensibles, namely shape, size, motion, rest and number, are perceived, but incidentally. Hearing is the judge of sounds and of the voice, and it distinguishes few differences between things, but it contributes greatly to learning. For speech and discourse, because they are heard, are a cause of teaching, not in themselves but incidentally, since they consist of names, which are the signs of things. Thus those who from their first origin have been deprived of either of these senses seem more apt for learning if they are blind than if they are mute or deaf. Next, the seats and organs of the senses must be discussed with similar brevity. Formerly there were no lack of distinguished philosophers, such as Empedocles and Timaeus, who maintained that the seat of sight is fiery, because (as they said) sight arises from a light flowing out as it were from a lamp. But if sight came about by the emission of light, would not the eyes see even in darkness? Nor is it probable that sight is actually the emission of some luminous thing from the eye, or that the light which is emitted from the eye is joined and mingled with external light. For light cannot be joined or mingled with light. For nothing is joined with just anything, nor is what is inside the eye joined with what is contained outside, since the membrane covering the pupil is interposed. Yet it has already been demonstrated that sight of any thing cannot occur without light, whether that be what is set between the visible object and the sight, or illuminated air. And just as nothing can be seen from outside without light, so what lies within the eye must be transparent, if it is to be the seat of sight; and this is certainly water itself. Therefore it is right to hold that the innermost part of the eye is transparent and capable of light. From this it is clear that each sense organ must be assigned to its element in such a way that the faculty of sight is attributed to water, hearing to air, and smell to fire. For odour is a certain smoky exhalation which comes from fire. For this reason the organ of smell is in the place which lies near the brain, since the matter of a cold thing is hot in power. Moreover, it is well established that the brain is the moistest and coldest of all the parts of the body. The organ of touch is earth, and so is taste, which is considered a kind of touch itself.

units.la: De memoria & recordatione.
units.tr: On memory and recollection.

units.la: OSTHAE c[?] de memoria & recordatione differendum est. Sed prin-cipio considerandum est, quænam memoriæ subiiciatur, quorū ignoratio sæpenumero nos in errorem impellit. At res futuræ ea non sunt, quoniam non nisi speci,opinionisque sunt.Nec quoque præsentes,quæ solo sensu percipiuntur. Quocirca præteritorum memoria est. Posthæc cuius facultatis animæ sit inquirendum. At ei animæ parti assignetur necesse est, cui phantasma redditur, nempe communi sensui. Etenim imagines speciesque eorum,quæ memoriæ quasi credita fuerunt ,in eo finguntur. Quoniam autem absque phantasmate nihil eorum quæ sentiuntur,intelligere possumus, ideo rerum intelligendarum est etiam memoria,sed ex accidente,sentiendarum verò per se. Cæterum quæsierit forte quispiã quì fiat ut absentium præteritorumque memoria sit,cum phantasma(cuius habitus memoria est) non absens sit, sed sensui communi præsens insit. Ad hoc sanè respondendum est memoriam non phantasmatis esse,sed ipsius rei,cuius ipsum phantasma nota est. Quemadmodum enim Cæsaris imago picta in tabula nostra memoriam Cæsaris absentis mo net:ita rei absentis simulachrum in sensu co-muni impressum memoriä ipsius rei excitat. Perspicuum est igitur memoriam affectione esse sensus cōmunis, & ibi consistere vbi ille est. Posthæc qui memoria valent, & qui minus, explicandū est. Primùm autè ij qui va-riis imaginationibus agitantur vel propter animæ perturbationes & morbos,atque longam ætatem memoria non valet: quàdoqui-dem iis perinde accidit, vt si in aqua profluente signum fiat. Nam ea imaginatio motióve, quæ per sensum in ipsa anima fit, quoddam phantasma ac simulachrü consignat, quem-admodum ij faciunt qui anulis aliquid obsi-gnant. Veruntamen senes aliam ob causam obliuiosi sunt & immemores, nempe ob frigentem naturam qua prædíti sunt, & ob duritiem ad recipiendas imagines inepta. Pueri quoque memoria non valent, eo quòd crescant & molles sint, ac propterea nihil aut parum quidem in sensu communi imprimi potest, & si quid impressum est, mox effluit. Qui etiam nimis acuto sunt ingenio, & hebetes non sunt memores, quoniam hi duriore craf-fioréque natura sunt: illi vero tenuiore. Ex quo fit, vt in acutioribus ingeniis imagines rerum asseruatæ breui pereant & dissoluan-tur: in aliis sensui communi non adhærent. Quapropter in pueris species rerum & imagines non remanent, in senibus non imprimuntur. Memoriam autem conseruant me-ditationes recolendo, quod nihil aliud est, nisi crebrò res quasuis anima ipsa intueri, quas non per se, sed per imagines & simulachra cernit. Propterea memoria non est aliud nisi habitus phantasmatis, tanquam imaginis eius rei, è qua ipsum phantasma sensui communi redditur. Hæc breui de memoria dicta sint. Reliquum est,ut etiam similibre-uitate de recordatione differamus. Sed in primis quantum à memoria distet, dicendū est. Nā recordatio in solo homine inest, memoria vero in cōpluribus animantibus. Propterea, recordatio quasi quaedam ratiocinatio est, qua quidem é prioribus & notioribus ad posteriora minusquàm nobis nota progredimur, eorumdémque cognitionem inuestigamus. Qui enim reminiscitur[?], is se antè id quod oblitum est,aut vidisse,aut audiuisse,aut aliud tale sensu percepisse secū reputat, ita ut recordatio quasi quaedam rerum inquisitio fit. Praeterea vis reminiscendi solis animantibus à Natura tribuitur quibus cōsultandi facultas data est. Consultatio autem quaedam ratiocinatio est. Quare recordatio mentis opus est. Verum reminiscendi facultas eis ablata est, qui sunt solliciti & multis obruti negotiis. Talibus enim remorata cogitatio est. Huiusmodi etiam sunt melancholici, quos plurima phantasmata mouent. Omnium vero maximè solliciti sunt ac perturbati, quibus magna humoris abundantia in eam animæ partem inciderit, in qua communis sensus est. Propterea animæ perturbationes hominem recordari prohibent: ut ira, pauor, & similes, quæ ægerrimè sedantur: imo verò magis magisque inualescunt ob ipsam humoris copiam. Qui de-nique superiores corporis partes habent humidiores & vastiores, quíque pomiliones sunt, ij sane recordatione non valent, propterea quod ea pars, quæ communis sensus sedes est, magno pondere oppressa sit.
units.tr: Next, memory and recollection must be discussed. But first it must be considered what things are subject to memory, since ignorance of this often drives us into error. Future things are not such, since they are only objects of hope and opinion. Nor are present things, which are perceived by sense alone. Therefore memory is of past things. Next, we must inquire which faculty of the soul it belongs to. It must be assigned to that part of the soul to which the phantasm is rendered, namely the common sense. For images and species of those things which have been, as it were, entrusted to memory, are formed in it. And since we can understand nothing of what is sensed without a phantasm, memory of things to be understood is also present, but incidentally, while memory of things sensed is so in itself. But someone may perhaps ask how it happens that the memory of absent and past things exists, since the phantasm (whose habit is memory) is not absent but is present in the common sense. To this one must certainly reply that memory belongs not to the phantasm but to the thing itself, of which the phantasm is the sign. For just as a painted image of Caesar on our tablet reminds us of the absent Caesar, so the likeness of an absent thing impressed on the common sense awakens the memory of the thing itself. It is clear, therefore, that memory is an affection of the common sense, and resides where it does. Next, it must be explained why some people have good memories and others poor. First, those who are troubled by various images, whether because of disturbances and diseases of the soul, or through long life, do not have a good memory; for it happens to them just as if a mark were made in flowing water. For that imagination or motion which takes place in the soul itself through the senses leaves a certain phantasm and likeness, just as those who seal something with rings do. Yet the old are forgetful and unmindful for another reason, namely because of the cold nature they have and the hardness unfit for receiving images. Children also have poor memories, because they are growing and soft, and therefore little or nothing can be impressed on the common sense, and if anything is impressed, it soon flows away. Those also who are of too keen a wit, and those who are dull, are not mindful, since the former have a harder and thicker nature, the latter a finer one. From this it comes that in the keener wits the images of things retained quickly perish and dissolve; in others they do not cling to the common sense. For this reason the forms of things and images do not remain in children, and are not impressed on the old. Meditation, by repeated recall, preserves memory, which is nothing else than the soul frequently regarding things, which it perceives not through themselves but through images and likenesses. Therefore memory is nothing other than the habit of a phantasm, as of an image of that thing from which the phantasm is rendered to the common sense. These things may be said briefly about memory. It remains that we discuss recollection with similar brevity. But first we must say how far it differs from memory. For recollection is found in man alone, while memory is found in many living things. Therefore recollection is a kind of reasoning, by which we proceed from earlier and better known things to later things less known to us, and investigate knowledge of them. For he who recollects reflects within himself that before what has been forgotten he either saw, or heard, or perceived something of that kind by the senses, so that recollection is, as it were, a kind of inquiry into things. Moreover, the power of recollecting is given by Nature to living things alone, to which the faculty of deliberation is given. Deliberation, however, is a kind of reasoning. Therefore recollection is the work of the mind. But the faculty of recollecting is taken away from those who are anxious and overwhelmed with many affairs, for thought is hindered in them. Melancholics are of this sort too, whom very many phantasms disturb. Yet those are most anxious and disturbed in whom a great abundance of humour has fallen into that part of the soul where the common sense is. Therefore the disturbances of the soul prevent man from recollecting, such as anger, fear, and the like, which are calmed with the greatest difficulty; indeed they grow stronger and stronger on account of the very abundance of humour. Finally, those who have the upper parts of the body moister and larger, and who are pot-bellied, certainly do not have the power of recollection, because that part which is the seat of the common sense is weighed down by a great burden.

units.la: Quid somnus, quid vigilia, & quanam sit utriusque causa.
units.tr: What sleep and waking are, and what the cause of each is.

units.la: I animal, id est, quod sensum habet, fieri quidem non potest quin vicissim dormire & vigilare possit: quadoquidé somnus & vigilia affectiones sunt sensus communis, qui prima sentiendi facultas est, sine qua nevllus quidem alius sentire potest. Quoniam autem somnus & vigilia contrariæ affectiones sunt, fit vt idem animal simul & dormire & vigilare non possit. Itaque aut dormit, aut vigilat. Dormit autem cum sensus nullo munere fungitur. Vigilat contra cum actu réque ipsa sentit. Quum i-girur sentire nec solius animæ proprium munus sit, nec corporis, patet sensum, qui actu est, motum esse animæ opera, & per corpus factum. Propterea sensus nec solius animæ est, nec vllum inanimum sentire potest. Itaque stirpes, tametsi animata sint corpora, nō sentiunt, nec consequenter dormiunt, neque vigilant. Ac quemadmodum nullum animal est, quod aut semper vigilando aut semper dormiendo vitam agat: ita vtraque affectio-ne priuari non potest: quadoquidem vnumquodque animal primæ sentiendi facultatis, quae sensus communis est, particeps esse dicitur. Quod si somnus quaedam affectio fit, & imbecillitas ob vigilandi exuperantiam, omne quod vigilat, id etiam dormiat, necesse est: quippe cum fieri non possit, ut quic quam sempiternū laborem ferat. Eodémque modo nihil perpetuo somno teneri potest. Nam cum somnus quaedam sit affectio facultatis sentientis, & quasi quoddam sensuum vinculum, ac immobilitas, fit ut omne quod dormit id etiam sentire possit. Ex his perspicuum est omni animantium generi, ut natâ-tium, ut volucrium, ut pedestrium, & reptilium communem sensum esse. Propterea piscium genera adeóque ea, quae molli cute tecta sunt, dormire visa fuerunt, ut & quae duros habent oculos, veluti gammari & cancri. Perspicuum est etiam animalia, quae insecta dicuntur, dormire, quanquam breui somno contenta sunt. Testacea vero an dormiat, non satis compertum est, tametsi ea dormire credibile sit, propterea quod sentiant. Animalia enim cuncta sensu definiuntur. Nunc vero cuius sensus, aut quorum opera animantes vigilent & dormiant, videndum est. Profecto nonnullae sunt quae sensus omnes habent: aliae certis carent, ut visu, & auditu: omnes tamen gustum & tactum habent, praeterea quae inchoata imperfectaque sunt. Atque etiam vis sentiendi duplex est una propria, ut visus, ut auditus, gustatus, odoratus, & tactus: altera communis, cuius vi singuli proprii sensus se sentire percipiunt, & quae in vnoquoque eorum versatur, maximeque coniungitur cum tactu, qui solus in toto animali fusus est.
