Ex quo fit, vt in ipso sensu communi somnus & vigilia consistant. Itaque omnibus animantibus haec vtraque asse-ctio inest, quoniam tactus in omnibus reperitur. Propterea si ipsius sensus communis instrumentum, ad quod referuntur reliqua sensoria, & quod omnium praecipuum est, aliqua re afficitur, caeteris quoque idem euenire necesse est. Quum igitur somnus & vigilia primae sentiendi facultatis affectiones sint, vnde oriatur haec vis, inuestigare non intempestiuum erit. At ibi ea fit, expedit, vnde motus ad locum proficiscitur: quandoquidem nihil per se ad locum mouetur, nisi sentiat. Sed sanguine praeditis sentiendi principium in corde inesse Aristoteli videtur: quoniam caloris insiti, & spiritus origo hoc viscus est. Spiritus autem atque naturalis calor primum ac praecipuum est animae instrumentum, quo animal sentit & mouetur, secundum omnium philosophorum sententiam. Exanguibus autem & in-sectis, ac omnibus generatim, quae non respirant ipsum motus & sensus principium in illa parte esse videtur, quae cordis locum habet, & in qua spiritus insitus dilatari & con-trahi conspicitur: Id quod sane in vespis apibus atque muscis aliisque huius generis animaduertere licet. Itaq; quo in loco vtraque sensus affectio,nimirum somnus & vigilia fiat, fatis perfpicuu est, sed qua ex causa, restat exponere. Videtur fomn̄[?], qui imbecillitas est illius partis, quæ sentiendi principiu dicitur, ex eo halitu fieri, qui à cibo exhalat. Alimentum enim dum coquitur, sursum halitum in cerebrum omnium corporis partium frigidissimum emittit, qui ibi condensatur, & spiritum[?] obruit, atque hoc modo somnum allicit. Sed in his animantibus, quæ cerebro carent, aliquid inest, quod locum eius & rationem obtinet, in quo alimenti vapor incrassatur somni causa. Propterea vt vapor, Solis calore sublatus in sublime propter frigus, quod ea in parte est maximum, refrigeratur cogiturque in aquam, quæ deinde deorsum suo pondere fertur: sic in nostro corpore halitus redundans vi caloris ad cerebrum elatus in pituitam vertitur. Refrigeratur autem cerebrum tenuitate & angustia venarum, quæ in eo sunt: Ex quo fit, vt ne facile vaporem ex fe discutiat. Qua-obrem catarrhi ex nostro capite oriuntur. Cum autem cibus coctus est, & fyncerus sanguis secretus, tum animal expergiscitur. Tantisper enim somnus perseuerat, dum secernatur sanguis, qui à cibo impurior gignitur. Quod cū factū est,tum denique animatia [?] a pondere,quod cibus afferebat,libera a somno excitantur.Itaque somnus vires per vigiliam imminutas reparat & reficit. Etenim animal per motum &sensus non paruam facit spiritus iacturam. Quare somni & vigiliæ vicissitudinem recte Natura cunctis animantibus instituisse videtur.
units.tr: Every animal, that is, every creature that has sensation, can certainly alternate between sleeping and waking, since sleep and waking are affections of the common sense, which is the first faculty of perception, and without which no other sense can perceive anything. Because sleep and waking are contrary affections, the same animal cannot sleep and wake at the same time, so it must do one or the other. It sleeps when its senses perform no function, and it wakes when it actually perceives and exercises its senses. Since perception belongs neither to the soul alone nor to the body alone, it is clear that the sensation which is actual is a motion brought about by the soul's work and carried out through the body. For this reason sensation belongs to no lifeless thing, and nothing inanimate can perceive. Accordingly plants, although they are living bodies, do not perceive, and so they neither sleep nor wake. Just as no animal lives always waking or always sleeping, so no animal can be deprived of both affections, since every animal is said to share in the first faculty of perception, which is the common sense. If sleep is a certain affection, and a weakness caused by the excess of waking, then everything that wakes must also sleep, since nothing can bear unending labour. In the same way, nothing can be held in perpetual sleep. For since sleep is a certain affection of the faculty of sensation, and a kind of binding of the senses and immobility, it follows that whatever sleeps can still perceive. From these points it is plain that the common sense belongs to every genus of animals, whether swimming, flying, walking, or creeping. For this reason the kinds of fish, and especially those covered with soft skin, were seen to sleep, as were those with hard eyes, such as shrimps and crabs. It is also plain that the animals called insects sleep, although they are content with brief sleep. Whether shellfish sleep is not sufficiently established, although it is credible that they do, because they perceive; for all animals are defined by sensation. Now we must consider which sense, or which organs, cause animals to wake and sleep. Certainly some animals have all the senses, others lack certain ones, such as sight and hearing, but all have taste and touch, and so do those which are imperfect and unformed. Moreover, the power of sensation is twofold: one is proper, as sight, hearing, taste, smell and touch; the other is common, by whose power the individual senses perceive that they are sensing, which resides in each of them and is most closely joined with touch, the only sense spread through the whole animal. Hence sleep and waking both lie in the common sense itself. So both affections are present in all animals, since touch is found in all of them. Therefore if the instrument of the common sense itself, to which the other sense organs are referred, and which is the chief of all, is affected by anything, it must necessarily happen to the others too. Since sleep and waking are affections of the first faculty of perception, it will not be out of place to inquire whence this power arises. It is useful to ask where motion sets out towards its place, since nothing moves of itself to a place unless it perceives. Yet in animals endowed with blood, Aristotle thought the principle of sensation lies in the heart, since this organ is the origin of innate heat and of spirit. And according to the opinion of all philosophers, the spirit and natural heat are the first and chief instrument of the soul, by which the animal perceives and moves. In bloodless animals, however, and in insects, and in all creatures generally that do not breathe, the principle of motion and sensation seems to lie in that part which holds the place of the heart, where the innate spirit is seen to expand and contract. This can certainly be observed in wasps, bees and flies and other creatures of this kind. So, it is quite clear in what place both affections of sense, namely sleep and waking, arise, but the cause still has to be explained. Sleep seems to arise from the weakening of that part which is called the principle of sensation, from the vapour that rises from food. For while food is being digested, it sends up a vapour to the brain, the coldest of all the parts of the body, and this vapour condenses there and overwhelms the spirit, and in this way induces sleep. But in those animals which lack a brain, there is something which takes its place and function, in which the vapour of food thickens to cause sleep. Thus, just as vapour lifted up by the heat of the sun is cooled on high by the cold, which is greatest in that region, and is compelled to turn into water, which then falls downward by its own weight, so in our body the surplus vapour, raised by the force of heat to the brain, turns into phlegm. The brain is cooled by the thinness and narrowness of the veins within it, and for this reason it cannot easily disperse the vapour from itself. Hence catarrhs arise from our head. When the food has been digested and the pure blood has been separated out, then the animal wakes. For sleep continues only as long as the blood, which is produced more impure from the food, is being separated. When this is done, then at last the animal, freed from the weight that the food brought, is roused from sleep. Thus sleep restores and refreshes the strength diminished by waking. For an animal, through motion and sensation, suffers no small loss of spirit. Therefore Nature seems rightly to have appointed the alternation of sleep and waking for all animals.

units.la: De somniis.
units.tr: On dreams.

units.la: OSTHAEC de somniis quærendum est, & primum cuius facultatis animæ sint. Cogitationis autem opinio-nisque opera non esse possunt, quoniā quod cogitare solemus non solum homo est, aut e-quus, aut aliud, sed etiam quid album, aut nigrum, de quibus nihil opinio sine sensu vere, aut falsò statuit, iudicatque. Eodem pacto inter dormiendum anima non solum hominis essentiam cernit, sed etiam eius accidentia, quæ non nisi in sensum cadunt. Huc accedit quod in somno interdum id videre solemus quod nos vigilantes sensu percepimꝰ. Neque tamen somnia sunt ea omnia, quæ in somno videntur: ut quæ vigilantes sensu percepimus: quandoquidem vera sunt: Sed somnium error est & affectio ei similis per quam nos febre ardente correpti vigilantes erramus, & aliquid captare putamus, quod nihil est. Veruntamen sive eadem sive alia fit animæ facultas, quæ phantasmata & sensa percipit,somniumque effecit, non sine alicuius rei verae aspectu, aut a[?]ofensu hallucinatio in somnis haud erit. Ex quo perspicuum est hac animae affectionem non esse facultatis opinantis,ratiocinantisque,sentientis: quoniam non alicui alij animę h[?]rti, somnus, alij somnium, sed eidem convenit. Idem enim est ea animę pars, cui phantasma obiiciuntur, quod ea quae sentiendi vim habet[?]. Adde quòd sine imaginatione non fit omniū[?]. Sed imaginatio motio[?] est a sensu orta. Propterea somnium appellatur phantasma, quod in somno offertur. Quare eius partis anima quae sensus est particeps & phantasmata recipit, somniare proprium est. Est igitur somnium primae sentiendi facultatis affectio. Sed quomodo id fiat ex iis, quae somno eveniunt, facillime intelligemus: quandoquidem somnium & somnus eiusdem animae partis affectiones sunt. Quae igitur in somno eveniunt, explicare convenit. Jam vero demonstratum est exteriora sensilia unumquodque sensorium afficere, atque eam affectionem, quam effecerunt, non solum tum esse, cùm ipsa sensoria afficiuntur, sed etiam cum sensus non amplius suo munere funguntur. Nam in huiusmodi sensoriorum affectione idem evenit, quod in iactu lapidis, qui quidem in aere movetur, manu remota, quae ipsum proiecit. Hoc idé, & simile in alteratione fit. Ut enim quod à calore calefactum est, id primum proximam quámq; parte calefacit deinde remotam, cuius calor adeoufq; perue[?]rat dum vis eius in remoto subiecto constat: Sic sensoriorum affectio à sensilibus facta tandem ad sensum communem peruenit. Quòd autem, sublato sensili, hæc affectio in sensorio remaneat perspicuè etiam[?]si fit in Solem intuentibus, qui cum ab eo ad[?]iuuendam opacum locum conuertunt visu, tum nihil cernunt, propter affectionem à lumine excitatam: aut si videant, id [?]tum, quod eis apparet flauum est. Si quis etiam diu colorem viridem, aut rubrum intueatur, ea res ad quam suos oculos converterit, simili colore apparebit. Verùntamen visus non solùm passio est, sed etiam [?]actio: Ut nitidis speculis, & splendidis, intelligere licet, quorum aliquod, si mulieres, quibus menstrua fluunt, intueantur, in eo nebula quædam cruenta apparebit. Sed ad affectionem sensus communis reuertendum est. Simili errore facilè decipimur sensus exterioris iudicio, dum animæ perturbationibus impellimur. Febricitantibus quoque non-nullis euenit, ut bestiolas in parietibus interdum captare putent. Idem etiam aliis valentibus, quibus Sol pedalis videtur, contingere solet. Itaque non solùm nobis vigilantibus ē sensibus motiones excitatur, quibus decipimur, verùm etiam dormientibus hæ euidentiùs apparent. Nam interdiu, quādo vis sentiendi & cogitandi operatur, huiusmodi sen-suum suum affectiones magna ex parte euanescut, sed noctu, quia exteriores sensus otiosi sunt, phantasmata apparent, quæ ipsa sunt som-nia. Cæterum nobis dormientibus somnia euenire non consueuerunt, nisi ciborum co-coctione peracta. Ex eis enim eleuantur vapores, qui somnia fieri prohibent. Propterea tum somnia excitantur, cùm à vaporibus ciborum expurgatum est sentiend. principiū.
units.tr: Next we must inquire about dreams, and first which faculty of the soul they belong to. They cannot be the work of thought or opinion. What we usually think about is not only a man, or a horse, or some other thing, but also what is white or black. About these, opinion pronounces truly or falsely only through sense. In the same way, while sleeping, the soul perceives not only the essence of a man but also his accidents, which fall only under the senses. To this must be added that in sleep we often see what we have perceived with our senses when awake. Yet not everything seen in sleep is a dream, as what we perceive by sense when awake is true, whereas a dream is an error, an affection like that by which we, seized by a burning fever, err while awake and think we grasp something that is nothing. Nevertheless, whether the same or a different faculty of the soul perceives images and sensations and produces the dream, there will be no hallucination in sleep without some sight or sense of a real thing. From this it is clear that this affection of the soul does not belong to the faculty that opines, reasons, or senses, since it does not belong to one part of the soul in sleep and to another in dreaming, but to the same part. For the part of the soul to which the images are presented is the same part that has the power of sensing. Add that nothing of this happens without imagination. But imagination is a motion arising from sense. Therefore the image offered in sleep is called a dream, and it is proper to that part of the soul which shares in sense and receives images to dream. A dream is therefore an affection of the first faculty of sensing. But we shall most easily understand how this comes about from the things that occur in sleep, since dream and sleep are affections of the same part of the soul. It is fitting, then, to explain what happens in sleep. It has now been shown that external sensible objects affect each sense organ, and that the affection they produce persists not only while the sense organs are being affected but also when the senses no longer perform their function. For in such an affection of the sense organs the same thing happens as in the throw of a stone, which continues to move through the air after the hand that threw it has been withdrawn. The same, or something similar, happens in alteration. For as what has been heated by heat first warms the nearest part and then the remote part, whose heat carries on as long as its force persists in the remote subject, so the affection of the sense organs produced by sensibles at last reaches the common sense. That this affection remains in the organ after the sensible object is removed is clear also from those who gaze at the sun: when they turn their sight to a dark place they see nothing, because of the affection excited by the light, or if they see something, it appears yellow. If anyone gazes for a long time at a green or red colour, the thing to which he turns his eyes will appear in a similar colour. Yet sight is not only passion but also action, as one can understand from polished and shining mirrors, in which, if women whose menses are flowing look, some bloody mist will appear. But we must return to the affection of the common sense. We are easily deceived by a similar error in the judgment of the outer sense while we are driven by disturbances of the soul. It also happens to some feverish people that they think they catch little beasts on the walls. The same is wont to happen to some who are in good health, to whom the sun seems a foot wide. Thus motions are excited from the senses not only in us while awake, by which we are deceived, but these appear more plainly in sleepers as well. For by day, when the power of sensing and thinking is at work, such affections of the senses for the most part fade away; but at night, since the outer senses are idle, images appear, and these are the dreams themselves. Moreover, dreams do not usually come to us while we sleep unless the digestion of food has been completed. For vapours rise from the food, and these prevent dreams from arising. Therefore dreams are stirred up when the principle of sensation has been cleansed of the vapours of food.

units.la: Nec pueris etiam & infantibus somnia incidunt, quòd sæpius & alantur, & cibum capiant. Sic enim eis vt nuper pransis ait cœnatis contingit: perinde, ac siquis aquam ba-culo vehementer commoueat: interdum in ea nullum videbit simulachrum, aut si vidit, illud deforme est ac confusum: sed sedata aqua & tranquilla, tum purum apparet. Sic etiam in somno phantasmata, quæ extrinsecus ex sensibilibus per sensus exhausta sunt, nonnunquam à quodam maiore motu obruuntur: interdum vero turbulenta apparent & prodigiosa in somno, veluti ea sunt, quibus affliguntur furentes, ardenteque febre correpti & ebrij. Cùm autem tranquillus est sanguis & defecatus, tum phantasmatum ac sensilium cuiusque sensus motiones conseruatæ sunt incolumes, fiuntque quieta & sedata somnia. Sed quæ semidormientibus apparent, ea nò verè somnia sunt, sed phantasmata ab intellectu orta, quæ nos nò fallunt. Itaque somnii phantasma quoddam est, sed fallax, ex
units.tr: Nor do dreams befall boys and infants, because they are fed more often and take food. For with them, as with those who have just dined or supped, it happens as if someone were to stir water vigorously with a stick: sometimes no image is seen in it, or if one is seen, it is misshapen and confused; but when the water is calm and still, the image appears pure. So also in sleep, images drawn from external sensibles through the senses are sometimes overwhelmed by a stronger motion; at other times they appear turbulent and monstrous in sleep, like those which afflict the mad, those burning with fever, and the drunk. But when the blood is calm and clarified, the motions of the images and of the sensibles of each sense are preserved unharmed, and dreams become quiet and tranquil. But what appears to those half asleep is not truly a dream, but an image arising from the intellect, which does not deceive us. Thus a dream-image is indeed something, but a deceptive one, produced from the remaining affections of the senses,

units.la: relitis sensuum affectionibus productum, quod quidem tum apparet, cum animal dormit.
units.tr: which appears whenever the animal sleeps.

units.la: De diuinatione[?], quæ ex somnijs fieri potest.
units.tr: On divination that can be made from dreams.

units.la: TAM diu clarissimi fuerunt medici, ꝗi somnia diligenter esse obseruanda, scriptum nobis reliquerunt[?]. Eorum autem alia notæ sunt, alia causæ, alia denique casus. Quæ notæ sunt ea nobis significant, quæ in corpore insunt, nimium humorum plenitudinem, aut vacuitatem & penuriam. Ut si flaua bilis redū-det, in somno, iurgia apparent & pugnæ, atque incendia. Si vero atra fit, omnia, quæ somniantur terrifica sunt, & tenebricosa, ac etiā dæmonia videri videntur. Sed sanguine præditis iucunda eveniunt somnia, ac sæpius cibi & potionis, reliquæque venereæ. Qui vero pituita abundant, imbres & aquas somniant, in quibus se natare putant. Nam ab huiusmodi humoribus in corpore humano redundantibus motiones phantasmataque in sensu communi facta potius per somnum, quam per vigiliam excitari solent, ob calorem, qui ad interiora revocatur. At cum omnium rerum principia sint exigua, perspicuum est morborum aliarumque corporis affectionū initia parua esse, quæ vigilantes latent, & per somnum se produnt. Quinetiam somniorū nonnonnulla esse nostrarum actionum causas, nihil absurdum est. Ut enim interdum de iis somniamus, quæ vigilates egimus, propterea quod rerum externarum imagines a sen-sibus susceptæ quasi viam ad internas asse-ctiones præparant, ita illæ motiones phan-tasmataque, quæ in somno eueniunt, sæpe-numero nostrarum actionum variarum causæ esse possunt, eo quod earum meditatio præ-cesserit. Atque hoc quidem modo quædam somnia nunc signa nunc causæ, sunt. Alia denique casu eueniunt quæ somniauimus, & hæc fortuita dicuntur eo quod interdum, sed ex accidente eorum euentus fiat:ut cum is ea su euenit, cuius antea somnium fuerit. Huius-modi autem somnia nec causæ sunt, nec signa eius rei quæ euenit, sed per accidens eis adiunguntur. Cæterum somnia a Deo immitti Ariftoteles negat, eo quod non solum homines, sed & quædam bruta somniant. Dein-de quia non soli viri optimi & prudentissimi somniant, sed & quiuis, quantumuis sto-lidus & incipiens. Sed Philosopho, oracula vaticiniaque per somnia piorum prophetarumque a Deo immissa ignoranti libenter condonandum est: quippe qui de iis dunta-xat, quæ natura animantibus eueniunt, verba eo in loco faciat. Verum tamen somnia a dæmoniis hominibus immitti ipse ait, & multos obscuro loco natos futura longe ante prospicere, & ariolari, ut etiam iis omnibus, quibus data est velut loquax & garrula natura, phantasmata varia offerri. Quoniam autem variis visis & simulachris agitantur, fœlicitèr rerum futurarum euenta conijciunt, & assequuntur, quales nonnulli sunt, qui partiendo paria accipiunt.
units.tr: The most distinguished physicians have long held that dreams must be carefully observed, and they have left us this written record. Some dreams are signs, others causes, and others come about by chance. The signs indicate what is in the body: an excess or a deficiency of humours. If yellow bile increases, quarrels, fights and fires appear in sleep. If it turns black, everything dreamed of is frightening and gloomy, and even demons seem to appear. But for those abounding in blood, dreams are pleasant, most often of food and drink and other sexual pleasures. Those who abound in phlegm dream of rain and water, in which they think they are swimming. For when humours of this kind overflow in the human body, movements and images are stirred up in the common sense, usually during sleep rather than waking, because the heat is drawn back to the interior. But since the beginnings of all things are small, it is clear that the beginnings of diseases and other affections of the body are small too, lying hidden while we are awake and revealing themselves in sleep. Nor is it absurd that some dreams are causes of our actions. Just as we sometimes dream of what we did while awake, because images of external things received by the senses prepare, as it were, a path to the inner affections, so the movements and images that occur in sleep can often be causes of various actions of ours, since their consideration has gone before. In this way some dreams are now signs, now causes. Finally, others come about by chance: we dream something, and it sometimes happens, but only by accident, as when the one who dreamed of it comes to that event. Dreams of this kind are neither causes nor signs of what happens; they are joined to it only by accident. Aristotle denies that dreams are sent by God, because not only men but some brute animals dream too, and not only the best and wisest men, but anyone at all, however dull and untrained. Yet we should willingly pardon the Philosopher for ignoring that oracles and prophecies are sent by God through the dreams of the pious and the prophets, since he speaks in that place only of what happens to animals by nature. Still, he himself says that dreams are sent to men by demons, and that many born in an obscure place foresee and foretell future things long beforehand, and that varied images are offered even to all those to whom a talkative and garrulous nature has been given. Since they are stirred by various visions and images, they conjecture and happily attain the outcomes of future things, as some do who receive equal shares by dividing.

units.la: Quanam sit communis causa motionis animalium? Quid cœlum mouet?
units.tr: What is the common cause of the motion of animals? What moves the heaven?

units.la: H[?]ACTENUS de sensibus, & iis quæ eos consequuntur disputatum est: nunc autem quæ communis causa sit perquam animantia quocunque motionis genere cieantur, explicanda est. Alia quidem eorum volant, alia natant, quædam gradiuntur, nonnulla aliis modis movetur. At motionis eorum causæ sunt variæ, quarum quæ præcipua est & prima ab omni motu libera est, ut anima. Aliæ verò quæ secundariæ dicuntur, non solum movent, sed etiam moventur, propterea quod instrumentariæ sint. Tametsi ab anima sua quodque animans ad locum moveatur, nullum moveri potest, nisi extrinsecus stet aliquid, ubi firmetur. Id quod maximè ex partibus animalis intelligere licet, quarum si una movetur, alia stat, qua, quæ movetur, niti & firmari possit: ut (exempli causa) cum humerus movetur, tum stat cubitus. Ob eamque causam articuli & flexuræ animantibus tributæ sunt, quibus loco cardinis vtuntur, dum mouentur. Itaque quicquid mouetur habeat extra se quidpiā necesse est, quod stet, & in quo firmetur, ac etiam vnde motus eius, quod mouetur, proficiscatur. Si enim (exempli causa) id quo pedes innituntur, semper cederet, nulla sane animalis progressio fieret. Itaque siue natet animal, siue volet, siue gradiatur, aut serpat, aliquid extrinsecus subesse oportet, quod ipsius animalis motioni resistat. Idcirco eorum quæ seipsa mouet, vna pars moueri debet, & altera stare, qua quæ mouetur, inniti-tur firmaturque. Quod autem cœlum mouet, id etiam immotū esse multis olim visum fuit. Propterea nonnulli aliquid esse existimarunt, quod eam haberet rationem ad cœlum, quam terra ad animantia: ideo Poetæ Atlantem quendam finxerunt pedes in ter-ra fixos habentem, quia[?] si linea dimetiens esset. Quod sane ratione consentaneum fuit, eo quòd terra perpetuo imobilis sit. Sed vis eius quod mouet, & eius quod mouetur non par est. Vis enim eius quod cœlum voluit infinita esse debet, eo quòd interminatus sit cœlestis motus. At quiescendi vis, quæ in terra inest, non infinita esse potest: quippe cùm ne terra quidem infinitæ magnitudinis sit: nec gravitas eius à qua quiescendi vis proficiscitur, non interminata est. Itaque à terra cœlum non mouetur: Propterea, si cœlum, vt moueatur, nullum requirat mouens, quod stet, perspicuum est motum eius non animatum esse, sed causam habere diuinam, qua perpetuo moueatur. Haec autem primus motor est, qui ita mobile antecedit, utpote ram opifex. Cęterūm inanima, quae cieri ad locum possunt nullo indigent immoto ut moueatur, siue id interius sit siue exterius, propterea quod exteriore motu agitentur. Quod autem exterius seu foris mouet, vel aliquod animal est, vel coeli conuersio. Quare inanima ab utroque mouentur. Hactenus de animatorum & inanimatorum motu disputatum est: superest, ut cau-fas, quibus omne animatium genus moueatur inquiramus. Haec autem sunt mens, phantasia, sensus, voluntas, electio & cupiditas, quae ad mentem & appetitum referuntur. Mens enim sensus & phantasia vim indicandi habent. Voluntas autem ira & cupiditas sunt appetitiones. Electio menti & appetitui co-munis est: quoniam quod sub electionem cadit id ad utrumque pertinet. Veruntamen non omne rationale eligi potest, sed id demum quod rerum agendarum finis est. Id autem quod nos ad agendum impellit bonum est, aut veri boni locum obtinet, nedum honestum. Sed quod veri boni speciem habet, ut quod iucundum est, ementitum bonum dicitur. At vere bonum perpetuum est & pulchrum, quod quidem diuinum habetur & infinitum, cuiusmodi primum mobile est Philosopho & primus motor.
units.tr: So far we have discussed the senses and what follows from them. Now we must explain what the common cause is by which animals are moved, whatever kind of motion they have. Some of them fly, some swim, some walk, and some move in other ways. The causes of their motion are various, and the principal and first of them, which is free from all motion, is the soul. The secondary causes, however, not only move but are also moved, because they are instruments. Although each animal is moved to a place by its own soul, nothing can be moved unless something outside it stands firm, on which it may be fixed. This is best understood from the parts of an animal: if one part moves, another stands, on which the moving part can lean and be supported. For example, when the upper arm moves, the forearm stands. For this reason joints and bendings have been given to animals, which serve them as hinges while they move. Therefore whatever moves must have outside itself something that stands and in which it is fixed, and from which the motion of what is moved proceeds. For if, for example, the ground on which the feet rest always gave way, no progression of the animal would take place at all. So whether an animal swims, flies, walks or creeps, something must lie beneath it from outside, which resists the motion of the animal itself. Hence in that which moves itself, one part must be moved and another stand, on which the moving part leans and is fixed. Moreover, many in the past have thought that the heaven, which moves, is itself unmoved. For this reason some have supposed that there is something which bears the same relation to the heaven that the earth bears to animals. So the poets feigned a certain Atlas with feet fixed in the earth, as if there were a line running through the diameter. This was indeed reasonable, since the earth is always immovable. But the power of that which moves and of that which is moved is not equal. For the power of that which moves the heaven must be infinite, since the heavenly motion has no end. The power of rest that is in the earth, however, cannot be infinite: the earth itself is not of infinite size, and its gravity, from which its power of resting proceeds, is not unbounded. Therefore the heaven is not moved by the earth. Hence, if the heaven requires no standing mover in order to be moved, it is clear that its motion is not animate but has a divine cause by which it is moved perpetually. This is the first mover, which precedes the mobile as its craftsman. Inanimate things, which can be moved to a place, need no immovable thing for their motion, whether it be inside or outside them, since they are driven by an external motion. What moves from outside, however, is either some animal or the revolution of the heaven, so inanimate things are moved by both. So far we have discussed the motion of animate and inanimate things. It remains to inquire into the causes by which every kind of animal is moved. These are mind, imagination, sense, will, choice and desire, which are referred to the mind and to the appetite. For mind, sense and imagination have the power of knowing. Will, anger and desire are appetites. Choice is common to mind and appetite, since what falls under choice belongs to both. Yet not everything rational can be chosen, but only that which is the end of things to be done. And what impels us to act is good, or holds the place of true good, not to say the honourable. But what has the appearance of true good, such as what is pleasant, is called a counterfeit good. True good is perpetual and beautiful; it is held to be divine and infinite, such as the first mobile is for the Philosopher and the first mover.

units.la: Bonum autem quod bona animalia appetūt finitum est: propterea illa quiescunt postquā ipsum consequuta sunt, Itaque omne animal motu cietur vel mente & opinione, vel appetitu, vt consequatur bonum, aut boni speciē.
units.tr: The good that good animals seek, however, is finite; therefore they come to rest once they have attained it. So every animal is moved, either by mind and opinion or by appetite, to attain good or the appearance of good.

units.la: Nullum tamen mouetur, nisi ante à sensibus alterentur membra eius. Ea enim iucundis obiectis calefacta ampliatur, sed tristibus refrigerata contrahi solent. Quemadmodum enim αὐτόματα rotulis quibusdam mouentur, quoniam semper aliud ab alio agitatur, sic animantis offa tanquam ligna sunt, & ferrum sponte se mouentium: nerui autem tanquam eorundem rotulæ: quibus ampliatis, remissioque & contractis mouetur animalis corpus.
units.tr: Yet nothing is moved unless its members are first altered by the senses. For they are warmed and expanded by pleasant objects, but chilled and usually contracted by sad ones. For just as automata [αὐτόματα] are moved by certain wheels, one being always driven by another, so the bones of an animal are like the wood and iron of self-moving machines, and the sinews are like the wheels of the same. By their expansion, relaxation and contraction, the body of the animal is moved.

units.la: Sed hoc inter se discrepant, quod sponte se mouentibus nulla alteratio euenit, sicut animalis partibus, quæ ob calorem dilatantur, & frigus comprimuntur. Dilatantur enim & comprimuntur, quod eis sensus qui alterationes sunt,Confestim inducantur. Quare quoties in corde quantulacunque fit mutatio, toties in animalis corpore & roboris, & palloris, horrorisque ac tremoris, harumque huiusmodi affectionum dissimilitudo adest.
units.tr: But these differ in this: that in things which move themselves no alteration occurs, as happens to the parts of animals, which are dilated by heat and compressed by cold. For they are dilated and compressed because the senses, which are alterations, are immediately induced in them. Hence whenever even the slightest change occurs in the heart, there follows in the body of the animal a corresponding difference in strength, pallor, horror and trembling, and other affections of this kind.

units.la: Quod autem animantium appetitum mouet aut mentem, id est, quod in rebus agendis persequendum est, aut fugiendū, nempe bonum & malum. Malum enim & quod dolorem affert, declinandum est: quod vero voluptatem expetendum. At quæ do-
units.tr: What moves the appetite or mind of animals is what is to be pursued or avoided in acting, namely good and evil. For evil, and what brings pain, is to be avoided; what brings pleasure is to be sought.

units.la: lorem & voluptatem pariunt, ea fere cū frigore, aut calore coniunguntur. Id quod sane ex animi perturbationibus perspici licet.Etenim audacia, metus, caeteriq; motus in animantibus suborientes,siue tristes sint,siue iucundi,absque calore, aut frigore non esse videntur.Ex quibus constat huiusmodi alterationes instrumentarias animalium partes ad motum praeparare,& animalium multos motores esse,quorum vnum nempe animā mouere,nec moueri alios vt instrumenta,& mouere simul & moueri. Animam autem in cor deinesse existimauit Ariftoteles,quoniā ab hoc viscere spiritu vitalis oritur, qui ita à Natura institutus esse videtur vt & mouedi vim habeat,& vires conferendi cuius duę motiones sunt pulsus & tractus. Quo fit vt cor & dilatari,& contrahi possit, quoniam spiritus origo est. Itaque cum anima primus sit animalis motor, & in corde resideat, quaeritur qui fiat vt caeteras corporis partes moueat? Ad hoc autem respondendum est animali ita institutum esse,vt reipu. quae bonis legibus gubernatur.Nam vt in ea repub. cum semel ordo constitutus est, tum nihil eorum desideratur,quae adesse oportet, in quocunque eorum quę geruntur absente principe,sed suū quisque munus exequitur vt praescriptum est, omniaque suo ordine gerūtur. Sic in animantibus hoc ipsum, Natura duce, efficitur,vt singula,quae ita comparantur, ad sua munia obeunda probè affecta sint. Itaque animam in quoque membro sitam esse non expedit, sed in quodam corporis membro, ex quo oriantur præcipuè vires, quibus aliquipar tes viuant, & suis muneribus fungantur. Verumtamen etsi voluntariis motionibus cien tur animantia, non desunt tamen quædam partes, quæ inuitis motionibus excitatur, vt cor & veretrum, quæ sæpenumero ex eo quod visui apparuerit, mouentur, quanquam mens nihil interea præscribit ac iubet. Non voluntariæ etiam sunt somnus, vigilia, respiratio, & aliæ, quarum nulli vel phantasia, vel appetitus plane imperat. Vt autem loco moueatur animatia, mutatione quadam naturali ab obiectis alterentur, necesse est, vt mutatæ illorum partes ad motionem extendi, contrahique possint. Id quod maximè in corde & veretro fieri videtur, eo quòd vtrumque membrum velut separatum animal sit. Cuius rei causa est vitalis spiritus, qui in vtroque continetur. Ille autem in corde conspicuus est. Ob id fons sensuum & principium habetur Aristotelis. At vero veretrum ad procreandum à Natura destinatum esse, hinc intelligi potest, quòd ab eo vis feminis quasi animal quoddam depromatur. Itaque optima ratione motiones à partibus in principium, à principio in partes contendunt, atque ita sese mutuò expetunt.
units.tr: Those things which produce pain and pleasure are generally joined with cold or heat. This can indeed be perceived from the perturbations of the mind. For boldness, fear and the other movements arising in animals, whether they are sad or pleasant, do not seem to occur without heat or cold. From this it is clear that such alterations prepare the instrumental parts of animals for motion, and that there are many movers of animals: one of them, namely the soul, moves without being moved, while the others, as instruments, are moved and move at the same time. Aristotle thought the soul resides in the heart, since the vital spirit arises from this viscus, and nature seems to have so constituted it that it has the power of moving and of conferring strength; its two motions are pulse and drawing. Hence the heart can both dilate and contract, since it is the source of the spirit. Therefore, since the soul is the first mover of the animal and resides in the heart, the question arises how it comes about that it moves the other parts of the body. To this it must be answered that the animal is so constituted as a commonwealth governed by good laws. For in such a commonwealth, once order is established, nothing is lacking of what ought to be present, even when the prince is absent from any of the affairs being carried out; each performs his duty as prescribed, and all things are done in their proper order. So in animals, with Nature as leader, this same thing is brought about: the individual parts, so arranged, are well disposed to discharge their functions. Therefore it is not expedient for the soul to be situated in every member, but in a certain part of the body, from which chiefly arise the powers by which some parts live and perform their offices. Nevertheless, although animals are moved by voluntary motions, there are still certain parts which are excited by involuntary motions, such as the heart and the penis, which often move from what has appeared to sight, although the mind meanwhile prescribes and commands nothing. Sleep, waking, respiration and others are likewise non-voluntary, and over none of them does imagination or appetite plainly have command. But for an animal to move from place to place, its parts must be altered by objects through a certain natural change, so that the changed parts can be extended for motion and contracted. This seems to happen most of all in the heart and the penis, because each of these members is, as it were, a separate animal. The cause of this is the vital spirit, which is contained in each; and that in the heart is conspicuous. For this reason it is held, according to Aristotle, to be the fount of the senses and the principle. But that the penis was destined by nature for procreation can be understood from this, that by it the power of the seed is drawn out as if it were some animal. Therefore, for the best reason, motions tend from the parts to the principle and from the principle to the parts, and thus mutually seek one another.

units.la: De diuturnitate & breuitate v t.
units.tr: On the length and shortness of life

units.la: [?]OSTHAEC cur animantium & plantarum aliæ aliis diuturniores vitę sin',[?] & aliæ breuioris, etiā videndum est. Sed priusquam hæc intelligi possint causas corruptionis eorum, quæ natura constat, explicare par est. Hęc autem contraria sunt. Propterea ignis, aqua, & quæ his cognata sunt corpora, quòd vim contrariam habeant, mutuas sibi ipsis causas generationis & corruptionis afferunt. Itaque vnumquodque aliorum corporū, quæ ex his constant eandem corruptionis rationem habere conuenit. Sed accidentia, quoniā varia sint, non eodem modo corrumpuntur. Nam illa, quæ contraria sunt, bifariam corrum-pūtur. Primum dum sese vicifim expellūt. Hoc enim pacto calidum a frigido corrumpitur, & frigidum a calido: ac siccum ab humido, & humidum a sicco. Deinde cum eorum subie-ctum labefactatur. Nā sublato animali, scien-tia, & valetudo, qua per vitam fruebatur, abo-lentur & exolscunt. Cætera vero accidetia, quæ non contraria sunt, similimodo corrum-puntur, suis subiectis (inquam) sublatis: vt di-mensiones nullæ restant, nec figuræ, corporibus corruptis. Nullum etiam corpus quā-tumuis corruptioni obnoxium, ibi corrum-pi potest vbi nihil est contrarium, quoniam nihil ibi labefactandi vim habet. Proinde i-gnis in locis superis, vbi nullum est contrarium, rium nō corrumpitur. Res enim cunctæ dū-taxat à cōtrariis in exitium perducuntur, eo quòd se mutuò contraria corrumpant. Ita-que cū substantia substantię non cōtraria sit[?], nulla per se corrumpitur. Sed fieri nō potest, vt ei, quod ex materia constat, non sit quodā modo cōtrarium, quoniam vsquequaque vel calor inest, vel aliud contrarium. Quare sia-gendi & patiendi principia simul versentur, & vnum agat, alterū patiatur, necessario mu-tatio consequatur, quæ semper è contrario in contrarium est. Præterea excrementum, quod substantia est, natura, quæ nutritur, corrūpit: quoniam contrariam habet naturam. Ex qui-bus perspicuū est contraria, quibus s & animaliū, & aliorū mistorū corpora sunt prædita, causam corruptionis æque atq; generationis præbere. Ea enim sūt materia mistorū corporū nempe calidum, frigidū, siccum & humi-dum. Verūm tamen in calido & humido vi-uentium natura consistit. Propterea omne viuum animal humidum est & calidum, mor-tuum verò siccum & frigidum, quoniam si-ca mors est, & frigida. Ea de causa senc[?]stus frigida & sicca est: atque quæ senescūt omnia necessario exsiccantur, quaquam humida ae-rea non facilè arescunt. Quam ob causam pin-guia ægrè putrescunt: cuius rei causa est aer, qui ad aquam & terram périnde se habet, at-que ignis, qui putredinis est expers, ad om-nia elementa. Propterea ad vitam conserua-
units.tr: Next it must also be considered why the lives of some animals and plants are longer than those of others, and some shorter. But before these things can be understood, it is necessary to explain the causes of corruption of those things which consist in nature. These are contrary things. Therefore fire, water and the bodies akin to them, because they have contrary powers, bring mutual causes of generation and corruption to one another. Hence each of the other bodies made up of these ought to have the same reason for corruption. But accidents, since they are various, are not corrupted in the same way. For those which are contrary are corrupted in two ways. First, while they expel each other in turn: thus the hot is corrupted by the cold, and the cold by the hot; the dry by the moist, and the moist by the dry. Second, when their subject is weakened. For when the animal is removed, the knowledge and health which it enjoyed through life are destroyed and perish. The other accidents, which are not contrary, are corrupted in a similar way when their subjects are removed; so that when bodies are corrupted, no dimensions remain, nor figures. Nor can any body, however liable to corruption, be corrupted where there is nothing contrary, since there is nothing there with the power of weakening it. Therefore fire, in the upper regions where there is no contrary, is not corrupted. For all things are led to destruction only by contraries, since contraries corrupt each other. Therefore, since substance is not contrary to substance, nothing is corrupted through itself. But it cannot be that that which consists of matter is not in some way contrary, since everywhere either heat is present or some other contrary. Hence, if the principles of acting and suffering are present together, and one acts while the other suffers, change necessarily follows, which is always from contrary to contrary. Besides, excrement, which is a substance, corrupts the nature that it nourishes, since it has a contrary nature. From these things it is clear that the contrary qualities with which the bodies of animals and of other mixed things are endowed provide the cause of corruption just as much as of generation. For these are the matter of mixed bodies, namely the hot, cold, dry and moist. Nevertheless, the nature of living things consists in the hot and moist. Therefore every living animal is moist and hot, but the dead is dry and cold, since death is dry and cold. For this reason the old man is cold and dry, and whatever grows old is necessarily dried out, although moist airy things do not easily wither. For this reason fat things putrefy with difficulty; the cause of this is air, which stands to water and earth as fire, which is free of putrefaction, stands to all the elements. Therefore, for the preservation of life, a not small supply of moisture is needed, since it would easily be drained and dried out by heat.

units.la: [?] Printed line reads "senc&us"; the word is unclear. dam non parua humoris copia opus est, quoniâ facile à calido exhauriretur, exiccaretúrque. Quamobrem & plantis & animantibus quæ quidem magnitudine præstanti sunt, fere longior vita data est. quippe cùm hoc cófentaneum sit vteis maiorem humoris copiâ natura dederit. Ut enim vita in multos annos producatur, duo requiruntur qualitas, & quantitas, nimirum ut illud humidum calidũ & multum sit quantitate, & temperatũ qualitate, ne facile exiccari absumiquě possit. Huiusmodi náque humidum aereum est, & pingue. Ob eámque causam hominis vita logior est quàm multorum animantium, quæ eum magnitudine superant. Sed ut diu animal vi-uat, nec facile intereat, excrementis abúdare non debet, quoniam ea naturæ animalis contraria sunt. Ex quibus conflat animantia, quæ ad concubitum procliuia sunt, cito senesce-re, propterea quod fœmæ excrementū quoddam sit naturæ benignum: quod cùm largius emissum est, tū animal marcescit. Quare mu-li quàm equi, & asini, à quibus gignitur, vita largior est, ut & fœminarū, quàm marium, si maresad venerem procliuiores sint. Quo fit etiam ut passeres masculi breuiorem agit vitam, quàm fœminæ. Præterea mares omnes, qui ad opus faciendum attentiores sunt, labore citius ad senectutem perducuntur. Labor enim exiccat, & ipsa senectus sicca est. Maribus tamen natura vitam diuturniorem rem largita est, quàm fœminis: quoniam in animalium genere, illis maior caloris copia inest, quàm his. Eadem item animantia quæ in calidis regionibus sunt, diutius viuût, quàm ea quæ in frigidis. Ob eam ipsam causam in illis insignis est multitudo eorum animantium, quę exanguia sunt & naturafrigida. Itaque illic & angues & lacertæ, atque bestiæ, quæ fquammis obduçę [?] sunt inu-fitatæ magnitudinis nafcûtur. Humor enim calidus & incremeti & vitæ diuturnioris causa est. In aliis autem regionibus, quæ nimio frigore obrigefcût humor indigenis animan-tibus aquosior est, ac propterea facile exarescit, & exiccatur. Animantia etiam quæ parû, aut nihil sanguinis habent, fiue in terra gradiantur, fiue aquatilia sunt: & quæ in locis ad Septemtrionem spectantibus nascuntur, minora sunt, & breuiorem agunt vitam. Eorum enim humor frigore concretus accretionem intercipit: Adhæc plantæ & animantia, vbicunque sint, nisi alimentum capiant, necefla-rió intereunt, nam id quod nullo sustenta-tur alimento, seipsum colliquat & consumit. Vt enim flamma non parua multum consumit pabulum, ita magnus naturalis calor & infi-tus, cui primum coquendi alimenti munus da-tum est, materiam in qua inest, absumit. Aquatilibus etiam breuior vita, quàm terrenis animantibus data est, non quòd illa omnino humida sint, sed potius quòd aquosa: quę qui dem[?] humoris natura facilè corrumpitur & exhauritur,eo quòd frigida fit. Ob eámque causam exaguibus breuis vita est, nisi magni tudine diu fe conferuent. Nam pingui olec-fóque humore,qui dulcis est.carent. Quare apes diutius viuunt,quàm alia exanguia iis maiora quòd hoc humore abundent. In ftir-pibus etiam longissima notatur vita,atque diuturnior,quàm in animantibus, plures ob causas,Primum enim minus aqúosè generan tür:ob eámque causam nō facilè frigore ob-rigescunt. Deinde pingue quiddam & len-tum habent:ac quanquam siccæ sunt & terre næ,tamen humor,quem habent, non facilè exarescit,eo quòd aeris particeps fit.Præter-ea semper repululant,florent,& quasi iuuen-tute reuirescunt.Ob eámque causam ad mul tos vsque annos perducuntur.Adde quòd c-tiam diuisæ in partes viuant,& ex vna duæ,& multæ fiant stirpes. Bestiolæ autem, quæ in-cifuras habent,etiamsi diuisę viuant, nō pro-pterea diu viuere possunt, propterea quòd instrumenta non habeant ad diuturnitatem vitæ accommodata quemadmodum stirpes, quæ omnino & radicem & truncum habent, quibus earum vita continuatur. Postremò stirpium earū longior vita est, quibus capita firmiora sunt tradita. Quo in genere nō sunt eæ,quę duntaxat annū viuunt,sed quæ in ar-borum genere censentur:quarum omniū ra-dices rationem capitum obtinent.
units.tr: Wherefore both plants and animals which are of outstanding size are usually given a longer life, since it is consonant that nature has given them a greater supply of moisture. For in order that life be prolonged for many years, two things are required, quality and quantity: namely that the moisture be hot and abundant in quantity, and tempered in quality, so that it cannot easily be dried up and consumed. For such moisture is airy and fat. For this reason the life of man is longer than that of many animals which exceed him in size. But in order that an animal live long and not easily perish, it ought not to abound in excrements, since these are contrary to the nature of the animal. From these things it is evident that animals which are prone to coition age quickly, because the female's seed is something benign to nature; when it is emitted more abundantly, the animal withers. Hence mules live longer than the horses and asses from which they are born, and so do females compared with males, if males are more prone to Venus. It also follows that male sparrows live a shorter life than females. Besides, all males who are more intent on the work of procreation are brought to old age more quickly through labour, for labour dries up, and old age itself is dry. Yet nature has granted males a longer life than females, since in the animal kind greater heat is present in them than in females. Likewise, animals which are in hot regions live longer than those in cold regions. For the same reason there is a remarkable multitude of those animals which are bloodless and cold by nature. Hence there are born there both snakes and lizards, and beasts covered with scales, of unusual size. For hot moisture is the cause both of growth and of a longer life. But in other regions, which are stiffened by excessive cold, the moisture of the native animals is watery, and therefore easily dries up and withers. Animals which have little or no blood, whether they walk on land or are aquatic, and those born in regions facing the north, are smaller and live a shorter life; for their moisture, congealed by cold, prevents growth. Besides, plants and animals, wherever they are, unless they take nourishment, necessarily perish, for that which is sustained by no food melts and consumes itself. For as a not small flame consumes much fuel, so the great natural heat implanted in us, to which the first office of cooking food has been given, consumes the matter in which it resides. Aquatic animals also are given a shorter life than land animals, not because they are wholly moist, but because they are watery; for the nature of watery moisture is easily corrupted and drained, since it becomes cold. For this reason bloodless creatures have a short life, unless by their size they preserve themselves for long; for they lack the fatty and oily moisture, which is sweet. Hence bees live longer than other bloodless creatures larger than they, because they abound in this moisture. Among plants also the longest life is noted, and longer than in animals, for several reasons. First, because they are generated less watery; for this reason they do not easily stiffen with cold. Then they have something fat and slow; and although they are dry and earthy, the moisture they have does not easily dry up, since it partakes of air. Besides, they are always putting forth shoots, flourishing and, as if in youth, growing green again; for this reason they are carried on to many years. Add that they also live when divided into parts, and from one stalk two or many plants are made. But small creatures which have incisions, even if they live when divided, cannot on that account live long, because they do not have instruments suited to length of life as plants do, which have both root and trunk, by which their life is continued. Lastly, the life of those plants is longer to which firmer heads have been given. In this kind are not those which live only a year, but those which are counted in the class of trees, the roots of all of which take the place of heads.

units.la: De iuuentute & senectute.
units.tr: On youth and old age.

units.la: IVVENTVS & senectus maximè eorum omnium quæ viuunt, ætā-tes sunt. At viuentium duo dun-taxat summa esse genera, nimirum animantia & stirpes, ab omnibus traduntur.
units.tr: Youth and old age are the most important of all the ages of things that live. It is commonly taught that living things comprise only two highest kinds, namely animals and plants.

units.la: Animatia, quatenus sunt catenus viuunt, sed non contrà, & qua ex parte viuunt, ea sunt, animantia quippe cum stirpes viuant, tametsi sensus expertes sint. Propterea neque idem est animal esse, & viuere.
units.tr: Animals live insofar as they are animals, but not conversely. The part in which they live is the part in which they are animals, for animals live just as plants do, even though they lack sensation. For this reason, being an animal and living are not the same thing.

units.la: Atque viuentium corpus in superiora diuiditur, & inferiora: in quorum medio principium alendi collocatum esse compertum est. Animantium autem superior pars ea est, qua alimentum cibúsque ingreditur, & attrahitur: inferior verò, qua primæ cibi reliquiæ depelluntur. Sed stirpes, quoniam loco moueri non possunt, cibum e terra, in qua sunt, attrahunt, propterea necessariò hanc partem, qua alimentum capiut, depreccam habent nempe radicem, quæ in ipsis stirpibus habet ratione, quam os in animantibus.
units.tr: The body of a living thing is divided into upper and lower parts, and the principle of nourishment is known to be located between them. In animals, the upper part is the one through which food and drink enter and are taken in, and the lower part is the one through which the first remains of food are expelled. Plants, however, cannot move from place to place, so they draw their food from the earth in which they stand. Therefore they necessarily have this part, by which they take in nourishment, placed low down, namely the root, which in plants serves the same purpose as the mouth in animals.

units.la: Perfectorum autem animantium corpora tres in partes distribuuntur, quarum vna est, qua cibum capiut, altera qua reliquias cibi depellunt, tertia his interiecta est, quæ in maximis animalibus pectus dicitur, in aliis aliquid quod locum eius obtinet. Principium autem facultatis nutricis in eiusmodi medio sita esse, & sensu & ratione demonstratur.
units.tr: The bodies of fully developed animals are divided into three parts: one by which they take in food, another by which they expel the leftover food, and a third lying between these, which in the largest animals is called the chest and in others is something that takes its place. That the principle of the nutritive faculty lies in such a middle position is demonstrated both by sense and by reason.

units.la: Multa enim animalia, quibus detractum & præcisum caput est, vivunt relicta ea parte media, in qua cor viget, aut id quod cordis locum cum habet, id quod aperte declarant infecta, ut vespes, apes, atque alia huius generis. Ani-ma enim, qua vivunt, actu una est, & potentia plures, quippe cum eo se modo habent, quo stirpes. Nam arbores auulsae per se vivunt, & ex uno principio multae nascuntur. Itaque tu infecta, tum arbores altrice anima præditæ sunt, quæ actu una est, & potentia plures. Eadem est ratio sentientis animæ: id quod sane infecta animalia testantur, quæ itidem diuisa sentiunt. Sed animantia, quæ perfectissima corporis coformatione præditæ sunt, si dissecentur[?], vivere non possunt, propterea quod eorum natura & forma una sit, & simplex. Itaque non sentiunt eorum partes dissectæ, quoniam tum sentiente anima carent. Præ-terea altricis facultatis originem cordi attribui, eo quod in medio corporis animalis situm sit, tum ex stirpibus, tum ex animalibus intelligere possumus. Stirpes nanque omnes, quæ ex femine oriuntur, ab eo sane quod ipsius feminis medium est, originem ducunt. Nam omnia stirpium femina duas partes intus habent, quasi geminas vuluas, & medium, quo coniunguntur, & ex quo truncus & radix nascuntur. In animantibus autem sangui-ne præditis cor primum omnium instrume-torum animæ gignitur: in exanguibus vero aliquid, quod cordis locum tenet. Propterea inter corporis animalis partes cor principa-tum obtinere debet, quoniam naturalis ca-loris fons est & principium. At sine eo infito calore nullum est animal, quod cibum coco-quat. Itaque reliquis partibus refrigeratis, vi-ta in corde remanet, quæ plane tollitur, eò extincto calore, qui in ipso corde inest. Ca-lor igitur & vita simul coseruantur, & ipsius caloris corruptio animati corporis mors est & dissolutio animæ ab ipso corpore. Corru-pitur autem calor marcore, & extinctione. Marcor autem senectus est, quem ipse calor sibi consciscit, cùm tabescit: Tabescit autem si immoderatus sit & nō refrigeretur, perin-de ac si non nutriatur. At extinguitur côtra-rio, nempe immoderato frigore: quæ caloris corruptio violeta est, & omnia animata cor-rumpit. Ipsum etiam contrarium interpelle-do cococtionem, facit quominus ipsum ani-matum corpus alatur: quam ob causam ipse calor similiter marcescit. Perspicuum est igi-tur, si calorem integrum ad vitam conservari[?] oporteat, ut quædâ ei adsit refrigeratio, quæ transpiratione fiat. Cuius quidem rei exem-plum fumi licet ex accensis prunis, quæ si in furno semper operiantur eas extingui vide-mus. Si vero ipsi furno operculum crebro tū affigatur, tum detrahatur, diu accensæ asser-uantur, sed ignis cinere obtectus non suffoca-tur, propterea quòd cineris raritate expirare possit. Itaque quemadmodum animantium calor & alimento & refrigeratione confer-uatur, sic & ille, qui stirpium est, benefi-cio attracti succi, & circumfusi aeris. Succus enim attractus sic stirpes nutrit reficitque, vt ingestum alimentum animantes, quae sumpto cibo refrigerantur. Profecto inedia & calorem & sitim affert, quoniam ventris aer & spiritus non agitatus semper calescit: sed sumpto cibo vsque adeo & mouetur & refrigeratur, quo ad cibus fit concoctus. Stirpes etiam exarescere solent cum circumfusus aer propter hyemen frigore saeuit: vt & ob vehementem æ[illegible, ~8 letters]. Ex quo fit, vt tum arbores hoc vnij genus sibi contrahant, qui sphacelismus, hoc est, syderatio nominatur. Quibusdam autem animalium ex aqua, aliis ex aere hoc refrigeradi beneficium suppetit. Qua ob causam alia in aqua, & alia in aere vitam agunt.
units.tr: Many animals, from which the head has been removed and cut off, continue to live with the middle part left intact, in which the heart is vigorous, or with whatever has the place of the heart. Insects clearly show this, such as wasps, bees and others of this kind. For the soul by which they live is one in act and many in potency, since they are related to it in the same way as plants. Indeed, uprooted trees live on their own, and many new plants arise from one principle. Therefore both insects and trees are endowed with a nourishing soul, which is one in act and many in potency. The same reasoning applies to the sentient soul: insects, which are likewise divided, clearly show this by continuing to sense. But animals whose bodies are formed with the most perfect organisation cannot survive if they are cut apart, because their nature and form are one and simple. Hence their divided parts do not sense, since they then lack the sentient soul. Moreover, we can understand from both plants and animals that the origin of the nutritive faculty is attributed to the heart, because it is situated in the middle of the animal's body. All plants that arise from seed certainly derive their origin from that which is the middle of the seed itself. For the seeds of all plants have two parts within, like twin wombs, and a middle where they are joined, and from which the stem and root arise. In animals endowed with blood, the heart is the first of all the instruments of the soul to be formed; in bloodless animals, something occupies the place of the heart. Therefore the heart ought to hold the chief place among the parts of the animal body, since it is the source and principle of natural heat. Without this innate heat there is no animal that can concoct its food. Thus when the other parts have grown cold, life remains in the heart, and it is wholly extinguished when the heat that dwells in the heart itself is put out. Heat and life are therefore preserved together, and the corruption of this heat is the death of the animated body and the separation of the soul from the body itself. Heat is corrupted by withering and by extinction. Withering is old age, which the heat itself brings upon itself when it wastes away; it wastes away if it is immoderate and is not cooled, just as if it were not nourished. It is extinguished, on the contrary, by immoderate cold; this corruption of heat is violent and corrupts all living things. Indeed, the opposite of concoction, namely the hindrance of digestion, prevents the living body from being nourished, and for this reason the heat itself likewise withers. It is therefore clear that if the heat is to be kept whole for life, some cooling must be present, which comes about through transpiration. An example of this may be seen in the smoke of burning coals: if they are always covered in the oven, we see them go out. But if the lid of the oven is repeatedly fixed on and then removed, the fire is kept alive for a long time, and the fire covered with ash is not suffocated, because it can breathe through the lightness of the ash. Just as the heat of animals is preserved by both food and cooling, so too is that of plants, by the benefit of the drawn-in sap and the surrounding air. For sap drawn in nourishes and restores plants just as ingested food nourishes animals, which are cooled when they have taken food. Indeed, fasting brings both heat and thirst, since the air and breath of the belly, not being stirred, always grows warm; but once food is taken, it is both stirred and cooled until the food is concocted. Plants also tend to wither when the surrounding air rages with cold because of winter, and also because of its vehement... From this it happens that trees then draw together this one kind of affliction, which is called sphacelism, that is, blasting. For some animals this benefit of cooling is supplied by water, for others by air. For this reason some live their life in water and others in air.

units.la: De respiratione.
units.tr: On Breathing.

units.la: Erespiratione dicere, & cur quibusdam animantibus data à Natura sit, inuestigare etiam nobis licet. Nam non omnia animantia respirant, sed ea duntaxat, quae non solum cor, sed etiam pulmonem habent, propterea quod maiore caloris copia sint prędita. Verū quibuscunq; exanguis fungosusque pulmo-nem est, ea minoris refrigerationis vsum requirūt.Quamobrem diu absque ulla respiratione salubria vivere possunt. Huiusmodi sunt ranarum genus, testudines, quae omnia diu in aquis versari possunt, eoq; od eorum pul-mo, qui propemodum exanguis est, exiguo calore praeditus sit. Verumtamen si quis huiusmodi animalia diu in aqua morari cogat, suffocentur, necesse est. Quae autem pulmonem multo sanguine refertū habent, ea, propter caloris copiam, respirationis indigent. Sed eorum, quae pulmone carent nullum respirat. Propterea nec pisces, nec ostrea, nec scolopendrae, neque infecta, quibus pulmo-nem Natura denegauit, respirare possunt. Etsi autem pisces aquam ore sumptam effundunt, non propterea aerem attrahunt, quoniam huiusmodi motio non respiratio est. Nam respiratio ex duabus constat partibus, quarum una expiratio est, altera inspiratio. Quare si pisces respirarent, propfecto qua parte inspirarent, eadem rursus expirarent. Sed fistula carent, qua circumfusus aer & attrahitur, & expellitur: & consequenter pul-mone. Id quod etiam ex eo constat, quod eorum nullus sit, qui ullam edat vocem. Praeterea si aerem attraherent pisces, certe hoc munus aerem attrahendi eorum ventri, qui arcta coniunctione ori cohaeret, tribuen-dum esset. Quod si ita esset, facile in aere re-spirarent: immo vero in eo suffocantur. Si quoque pisces ex circumfusa aqua spiritum in os suum attraherent, quid obstaret, quo-minus homines, & caetera animatia, quae pul-monem habent in eadem idem facere pos-sent. Sed id praestare non possunt in aqua, quod pisces. Si denique pisces respirant, cur in aere suffocantur? Hoc certe eis alimenti penuria non euenit: nec dicendum est eos in aere mori, quod eu largiorem [?] attrahat, & in aqua modicum: quandoquidem idem terrenis animatibus eueniret. Sed nullam eorum est, quod ob vehementem respirationem in aere intereat. Praeterea si omnia animantia respirarent, vt quibusdam philosophis olim placuit, profecto infecta respirarent. Sed eorum nulla in plures partes diuisa respirare videntur. Quod autem huiusmodi animantia non respirarent in muscis & apibus animaduerti potest, quae in summa aqua ad multum tempus viua natant, nisi ea praeter modum aut frigida sit, aut calida. At tandem suf-focantur, cum eorum venter aqua oppletur, ac is spiritus, qui in septo transuerso insitus inest, consumitur. Verum tamen si diu in cinere foueantur, reuiuiscunt. Non igitur omnia animantia respirat, sed ea duntaxat, quibus pulmo datus est. Haec autem sunt quae & foetum iam conceptu in lucem proferunt, & oua pariunt. Horum autem alia sunt penni-gera, vt aues quaedam squamis obducta, vt te-stitudines, vt lacertae, vt angues. Ac illa quidem pulmonem sanguine praeditum habent, haec fungosum: ac proinde rariusaliisrefpirant, Etiam respirant ac viuut in aquis hydri, mures fluuiatiles, ranæ, crocodilli, testudinésque marinæ & terrenæ, atque vituli marini, quæ omnia in loco sicco pariunt, & in aqua dormiunt extante rostro, respirandi causa.Quibus autē branchiæ datæ sunt, ea omnia aquæ haustu refrigerantur. Porrò branchiæ piscibus & aliis, quæ cartilagenea dicūtur, & quæ pedibus carent, datæ sunt. Ex iis sanè, quibus pedes à natura dati sunt vnus cordulus branchias habet: ac nullus adhuc visus fuit, qui pulmoné simul & branchias haberet. Id quod factū esse videretur, propterea quòd pulmo causa refrigerationis, quæ flatu affertur, comparatus est: propterea πνεύμονες[?] ἀπὸ πνευμονῆς[?], id est ex receptaculo spiritus nomen habuisse fertur. Ob eandem etiam refrigeratio nerh[?] branchiæ datæ sunt. Quibus autem pulmo datus est, ea bracheam habent arteriam, qua ipse pulmo aerem tum ad fe attrahit, tū à fe expellit caloris refrigerandi causa. Quæ vero branchiis prædita sunt, per earum opus aquam emittunt, & escam capiunt. Neque vllam habent arteriam: quò fit vt ex lapsu aquę in cordis locum nullo efficiantur detrimento. Cæterum cetæ, balenæ, & delphini respirant, propterea quòd & fistulam habent arteriā & pulmone, etsi in mari versantur: nec fo lum nutriendi causa aquā hauriunt, sed etiā pulmones refrigerandi: omniāque in maris summa aqua propter refrigeratione fluitant. Atque rostro extra aquam extante delphini dormiunt & stertunt.Quæcunque etiā moli testa obducta sunt,veluti locustæ & cancri exiguā defiderat refrigeraotinē,eo quòd exi-guus eorū calor sit, & sanguine careant. Propterea satis est eis,ut a circunfusa aqua refrigerentur.Itaq; omnium animantiū natura re frigerationis indiget propter calore, qui in corde est. Hanc autem refrigeratione ope be neficioq; respirationis nansiscūtur ea animā-tia,quibus non solùm cor,sed etiam pulmo-nem Natura dedit.Sed ea quibus pulmo san-guinis particeps datus est,celeriter refrigerari postulant,propterea quòd paruo mométo illorum calor qui intensus est, corrumpitur. Aer autem attractus citò refrigerat:quando-quidem natura sua tenuis est,ac derepete per omnes partes diffunditur. Aqua verò quòd crassa sit tardiùs refrigerat.Cæterū quo quidque eorum, quibus pulmo cum sanguine datusest,maiore calore præstat,eò plus refrigerationis requirit.Alioqui celeriter ipse calor labefactaretur. Corrumpitur autem aut cùm à contrariis extinguitur,aut cùm cōsumitur, sicut iam demonstratum est.
units.tr: It is also permitted to us to speak about respiration and to inquire why Nature has given it to some animals. Not all animals breathe, but only those that have not only a heart but also a lung, because they are endowed with a greater abundance of heat. Those whose lung is bloodless and spongy, however, need a smaller degree of cooling. For this reason they can live healthily for a long time without any respiration. Of this kind are the race of frogs and tortoises, all of which can remain a long time in water, because their lung, which is almost bloodless, has only a small amount of heat. Yet if someone forces such animals to stay a long time in water, they must necessarily be suffocated. Those that have a lung full of blood, on the other hand, need respiration because of the abundance of their heat. But none of the animals that lack a lung breathes. Therefore neither fish, nor oysters, nor centipedes, nor insects, to which Nature has denied a lung, can breathe. Although fish expel water taken in by the mouth, they do not for that reason draw in air, since this movement is not respiration. For respiration consists of two parts, one of which is expiration and the other inspiration. So if fish breathed, they would certainly breathe out again by the same part by which they breathed in. But they lack the windpipe through which the surrounding air is both drawn in and expelled, and consequently they lack a lung. This is also evident from the fact that none of them utters any sound. Moreover, if fish drew in air, this function of drawing in air would certainly have to be assigned to their stomach, which is attached to the mouth by a close connection. If that were so, they could easily breathe in air; indeed, they are suffocated in it. If fish also drew spirit into their mouths from the surrounding water, what would prevent men and the other animals that have a lung from doing the same in water? But they cannot do in water what fish do. Finally, if fish breathe, why are they suffocated in air? This certainly does not happen to them through lack of food. Nor should it be said that they die in air because they draw in too much of it and too little in water, since the same would then happen to land animals. But there is none of them that perishes from excessive respiration in air. Moreover, if all animals breathed, as once pleased certain philosophers, then surely insects would breathe too. But none of them that are divided into many parts seems to breathe. That insects do not breathe can be noticed in flies and bees, which swim alive for a long time on the surface of the water, unless the water is either unusually cold or unusually hot. In the end, however, they are suffocated when their stomach is filled with water and the spirit that is implanted in the transverse septum is used up. Yet if they are warmed for a long time in ashes, they revive. Therefore not all animals breathe, but only those to which a lung has been given. These are the animals that bring forth their young already formed and also lay eggs. Of these some are feathered, like birds; some are covered with scales, like tortoises, lizards and snakes. The former have a lung full of blood, the latter a spongy one, and therefore breathe less frequently than the others. Also breathing and living in water are the water snakes, water rats, frogs, crocodiles, sea and land tortoises, and seals, all of which give birth on dry land and sleep in water with their snout protruding, for the sake of breathing. Those to which gills have been given are all cooled by drawing in water. Gills are given to fish and to the others that are called cartilaginous, and that lack feet. Among those to which Nature has given feet, one kind, the cordyle, has gills; and so far no animal has been seen that has both a lung and gills. This would seem to have happened because the lung is designed for the cooling that is brought about by breath; for this reason the lungs [πνεύμονες] are said to have been named [from ἀπὸ πνευμονῆς], that is, from the receptacle of spirit. For the same reason gills were also given for cooling. Those to which a lung has been given have a windpipe-artery by which the lung itself draws air to itself and expels it from itself for the sake of cooling the heat. Those endowed with gills expel water through the working of these organs and take in food. They have no windpipe-artery; as a result, when water slips into the place of the heart, they are not harmed at all. Furthermore, whales, whales' kin and dolphins breathe, because although they live in the sea they have both a windpipe and a lung; they draw in water not only for feeding but also for cooling their lungs, and all of them float on the surface of the sea for the sake of cooling. Dolphins sleep and snore with their snout protruding from the water. Whatever animals are also covered with a hard shell, such as locusts and crabs, need only a small amount of cooling, because their heat is slight and they lack blood. Therefore it is enough for them to be cooled by the surrounding water. Thus the nature of all animals needs cooling on account of the heat that is in the heart. Those animals to which Nature has given not only a heart but also a lung obtain this cooling by the aid and benefit of respiration. But those in which the lung has a share of blood need to be cooled quickly, because in a very short time the heat in them, which is intense, is destroyed. Air that is drawn in cools quickly, since by its nature it is thin and suddenly spreads through all parts; water, because it is thick, cools more slowly. Moreover, the more any of those animals that have a lung with blood excels in heat, the more cooling it requires; otherwise its heat would quickly be weakened. Heat, however, is destroyed either when it is extinguished by contraries or when it is consumed, as has already been shown.

units.la: De morte & vita.
units.tr: On death and life.

units.la: MNIVM porrò animantiū generatio communis est & mors.Sed generatio viuentis est animæ altricis cū calore prima communio, cuius permanfio vita est. Mors vero non est distinctionis expers: quandoquidem alia vero lenta est, alia naturalis. Violeta[?] quidem caloris naturalis extinctio est: Naturalis vero ab ipsius caloris langore marcoreque est, quae temporis progressus affert. His enim duabus causis quaecunque viuunt interire possunt. At ex natiui caloris intentione & remissione quid iuuentus sit, & quid senectus, & ea aetas, quae harum est media, facile intelligi potest. Propterea iuuetus aetas est, in qua calor ille insitus vsque ad vigorem intenditur: quam ob causam dicitur esse Aristoteli, primae partis corporis animati accretio, quae magnam refrigerandi vim requirit quandoquidem crescit & imminuitur naturalis calor, prout magis vel minus refrigeratur. Qui autem in animantibus sanguine praeditis est, pulmone refrigeratur: in piscibus branchiis. Atque vt iuuentus caloris accretio est, ita senectus eiusdem diminutio, quae inter vtranque aetatem interiecta est, vigor dicitur & confirmata aetas. Caeterum in stirpibus siccitas hoc ipsum est, quod in animantibus senectus, & mors. Mors autem ea quae caloris insiti corruptio est, omnibus & animantibus & stirpibus ex aequo proponitur, etiam inchoatis. Inchoata dicuntur, vt ova, vt femina & animalium, & stirpium, quibus omnibus corruptio euenit propter caloris inopiam. At perfectis ea in parte contingit, in qua essentiæ fons est ac principium. Hoc porrò in stirpibus in medio germinis, & radicis collocatum est: Sed in iis animatibus quæ sanguinem habent in corde: in exangui-bus in aliqua eorum parte, quæ cordis ratio-nem obtinet. Horum autem quædam multa ha-bet potestate principia vitæ, & unû actu ut in secta, quæ in partes divisa viuut[?], alia dutaxat unû. Hæc autem origo vitæ omnibus animantibus tollitur, cum vitalis calor non refrigera-tur, quoniam à se ipso consumitur: atque is tu tabescit cum animalium aliis pulmo exares-cit, aliis branchiæ, quoniam huiusmodi par-tes nec se ipsæ dilatare possunt, neque cotra-here. Quod si his partibus hic morbus inua-lescat, ac calor natiuus consumatur morian-tur ea animalia, necesse est, quibus evenit, mors emisso spiritu. Moriuntur enim sine vl-lo magno cordis impulsu, nec propemodum animæ dissolutionem discessumque à corpo-re sentiunt. Cæterum in corde tres sunt motiones, quæ non eandem habent naturam, pal-pitatio, pulsatio, & respiratio. Palpitatio quidem est caloris insiti spiritúsque impulsio, quæ in corde talis est, qualis morbus ille existit, qui τρομὸς[?], id est tremor dicitur, & ut metu deprehenditur. Etenim, qui metu percel-luntur extremæ partes refrigerantur: quam ob rem calor intro in cor fugiens contrahi-tur, ubi ita, compulsus tantum facit motum, ut interdum ipsum animal enecet. Pulsus autem cordis,qui nunquam inter mittitur,pul-sationi pani [?]similis est, qui cum dolore pul-sat. Agitatur autem panus [?], propterea quòd sanguis in eo feruet & suppurescit:At vero cor-dis pulsus continuus est ob spiritum & hu-moremqui continue ex alimento ipsi cordi euenit. Hoc autem alimentum sanguis est. Ob eámque caussam in iuuenibus maiore pulsu,quàm in senibus cor agitatur, eo quòd illi maiore sanguinis copia quàm hi abun-dent.Adde quòd maior spiritus vis iuueni-bus infit:ob id in eis omnes arteriæ simul coagitatur,propterea quòd cor multum fer-ueat.Quoniam autem spiritus ex alimento genitus perpetuo pulsu cor agitat, illæ quo-que venæ continenter moueantur, necesse est.Respiratio verò tum est, cum cordis ca-lor augetur. At augescit alimento. Propte-rea si aliæ corporis partes alimentum requi-runt,multò magis quàm reliquæ calor ille suum:præsertim quòd eis alimenti caussa sit. Itaque cum ille augetur,tum effert pulmo-nem, qui respira tionis instrumentum est, quod quidem fabrorum folli simile videtur. Nam cum à calore inclusò pulmo effertur, tum aer exterior attrahitur,qui vi sua refri-gerandi immoderatum ignis calorem tem-perat.Ac quemadmodum augescente calore hoc viscus attollitur,ita eodem decrescente necessario deprimitur : cuius depressione qui attractus fuit,denuò exit.Is autem influes frigidus est, effluens vero calidus, propter calorem visceris a quo prouenit. Aeris autem introit inspiratio est, exitus vero expiratio. Idque perpetuatur continua quadam vicissitudine quandiu animatia vitam agunt, & pulmone agitantur. Ob eamque causam in inspiratione & expiratione vita consistit. Eodem quemodo pisces viuunt, cum per branchias motus eis excitatur. Tum enim attollunter cum piscium calor & spiritus effertur: Tum enim aqua illabitur, & ad cor usque peruenit, quod refrigerat. Mox eqedem branchiae se deprimunt, quarum depressione, aqua emittitur.
