Atque cum cordis calor semper efferatur, fit, ut semper refrigeretur. Hactenus de vita & morte.
units.tr: Generation is common to all living things, and so is death. Generation, however, is for a living thing the first participation in the nourishing soul together with heat, and its persistence is life. Death, on the other hand, is not without distinction, since one kind is slow and another natural. The violent kind is indeed the extinction of natural heat; the natural kind arises from the languor and decay of that heat, which the progress of time brings on. For it is by these two causes that whatever lives can perish. From the intensifying and slackening of innate heat, what youth is, what old age is, and that age which lies between them, can easily be understood. Youth, therefore, is the age in which that innate heat is intensified up to its vigour; for this reason youth is called, in Aristotle's words, the accretion of the first part of the animate body, which requires a great power of cooling, since natural heat grows and diminishes according as it is cooled more or less. Animals that have blood are cooled by the lungs, fishes by the gills. And just as youth is an increase of heat, so old age is its diminution; the period interposed between the two is called vigour, or the established age. In plants, dryness is the very thing that old age and death are in animals. Death, which is the corruption of innate heat, is set before all animals and plants alike, even those that are unformed. Unformed things are said to be such as eggs, seeds of animals and plants, all of which suffer corruption through lack of heat. But in perfect things it occurs in that part in which the source and principle of the essence lies. In plants this is placed in the middle of the shoot and the root; in animals that have blood it is in the heart, and in bloodless animals in some part that takes the place of the heart. Some of these have many principles of life in power, and only one in act, as in the sections which, divided into parts, go on living; others have only one. This origin of life is removed from all animals when the vital heat is not cooled, since it is consumed by itself; and in some animals, as the lung dries up, in others the gills, this wasting takes place, because such parts can neither dilate of themselves nor contract. If this disease gains strength in these parts, and the native heat is consumed, those animals to which it happens must die, with the breath expelled. For they die without any great beating of the heart, and scarcely feel the dissolution of the soul and its departure from the body. Moreover, in the heart there are three motions, which do not have the same nature: palpitation, pulsation, and respiration. Palpitation is indeed an impulse of innate heat and spirit, and in the heart it is such as that malady which is called tromos, that is, tremor, and which is caught from fear. For those who are struck by fear have their extremities cooled; therefore the heat, fleeing inward into the heart, is contracted, and when so compelled it makes only such a motion that it sometimes kills the animal itself. The pulse of the heart, which is never interrupted, is like the pulsing of a boil, which throbs with pain. A boil, however, is agitated because the blood in it seethes and festers; but the pulse of the heart is continuous on account of the spirit and moisture which continually arise in the heart from nourishment. And this nourishment is blood. For this reason the heart is agitated with a greater pulse in young men than in old, because they abound in a greater quantity of blood than these do. Add that a greater force of spirit is present in the young, so that all the arteries are shaken together in them, because the heart glows greatly. Since the spirit generated from nourishment moves the heart by perpetual pulse, the veins too must necessarily be continually moved. Respiration takes place when the heat of the heart is increased; and it is increased by nourishment. Therefore, if other parts of the body require nourishment, much more does that heat require its own, especially since it is the cause of nourishment for them. Thus when that heat is increased, the lung, which is the instrument of breathing, is raised up; and this seems like the bellows of smiths. For when the lung is raised by the enclosed heat, the external air is drawn in, which by its power of cooling tempers the immoderate heat of the fire. And just as this organ is lifted as the heat increases, so, when the heat decreases, it is necessarily pressed down; and by this depression the air that was drawn in is breathed out again. This inflowing air is cold, but the outflowing air is warm, on account of the heat of the organ from which it comes. The entry of air is inspiration, its exit expiration. This goes on by a continual alternation as long as animals live and are moved by the lung. For this reason life consists in inspiration and expiration. In the same way fishes live, when movement is stirred up in them through the gills. For they are raised when the heat and spirit of the fish are sent outward; then water flows in and reaches even to the heart, which it cools. Soon the gills sink down, and by their depression the water is expelled. And since the heat of the heart is always being sent outward, it is cooled always. So far concerning life and death.

units.la: De valetudine autem ac morbo non solum Medici est, verum etiam Physici aliquo modo causas explicare. Quid vero inter eos intersit, & quatenus in diuersis rebus versentur, intelligendum est: quandoquidem vtriusque præceptiones quodam modo finitimæ sunt. Nam & Medici omnes clari, & illustres aut valde diligentes de iis, quæ ad Naturam pertinent, dissererunt, illingue principia Medicinæ assumunt. atque etiam quæ res Naturæ interprætantur, fere in Medicinæ principiis finem suæ scientiæ statuunt.
units.tr: Yet to explain the causes of health and disease is not the task of the physician alone, but in some measure of the natural philosopher as well. What lies between them, and how far they are concerned with different matters, must be understood, since the precepts of each are in a sense neighbouring. For all the famous and distinguished physicians, and those who are very diligent, discourse about the things that pertain to Nature, and they assume the principles of Natural philosophy as the foundations of medicine; and those who interpret the workings of Nature mostly set the end of their science within the principles of medicine.
